stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted to hospital following a myocardial infarction. Four days after admission he develops a further episode of central crushing chest pain. Which is the best cardiac marker to investigate his chest pain?
explanation: Troponin stays raised 7–14 days, so for reinfarction at day 4 CK-MB (normal by 2–3 days) is more useful; a new hs-troponin rise > 20% is also used.

orig.stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted to hospital following a myocardial infarction. Four days after admission he develops a further episode of central crushing chest pain. Which is the best cardiac marker to investigate his chest pain?
orig.explanation: CK-MB CK-MB returns to baseline by day 3–4; troponin remains elevated up to ~10 days; CK-MB useful to detect reinfarction in days 4–10.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of progressive effort intolerance and an episode of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea three weeks ago. Her past medical history is negative for hypertension or diabetes. On examination, her jugular venous pressure is elevated up to her earlobes, she has a soft, tender hepatomegaly, bilateral pitting oedema up to the knees, bibasal crepitations, and an audible S3 on cardiac auscultation. A chest X-ray reveals cardiomegaly with interstitial infiltrates, and echocardiography shows global left ventricular hypokinesia with an ejection fraction of 25–30%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Dilated cardiomyopathy leading to congestive heart failure
explanation: Biventricular failure with cardiomegaly and global hypokinesia (EF 25–30%) in a young woman is dilated cardiomyopathy. Restrictive disease keeps systolic function.

orig.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of progressive effort intolerance and an episode of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea three weeks ago. Her past medical history is negative for hypertension or diabetes. On examination, her jugular venous pressure is elevated up to her earlobes, she has a soft, tender hepatomegaly, bilateral pitting edema up to the knees, bibasal crepitations, and an audible S3 on cardiac auscultation. A chest X-ray reveals cardiomegaly with interstitial infiltrates, and echocardiography shows global left ventricular hypokinesia with an ejection fraction of 25–30%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Dilated cardiomyopathy leading to congestive heart failure
orig.explanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy leading to congestive heart failure. The clinical findings are classic for dilated cardiomyopathy with systolic heart failure.

topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
stem: A 30-year-old woman has dilated cardiomyopathy with biventricular failure and an ejection fraction of 25–30%. Which of the following is a cornerstone of the medical treatment of her systolic heart failure?
explanation: ACE inhibitors (or ARB/ARNI) reduce HFrEF mortality and remodelling and are a cornerstone with beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2i. Non-DHP CCBs worsen HFrEF.

orig.stem: Which of the following is considered a cornerstone in the medical treatment of systolic heart failure in this patient?
orig.explanation: ACE inhibitors. ACE inhibitors improve survival by reducing afterload and remodeling.

topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
stem: In the same woman with dilated cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 25–30%, which of the following is another key medication?
explanation: Evidence-based beta-blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) cut HFrEF mortality by ~a third; start low when euvolaemic and titrate slowly.

orig.stem: Which of the following is another key medication in the management of systolic heart failure?
orig.explanation: Beta-blockers. Beta-blockers help reduce heart rate and improve left ventricular function.

stem: In the same woman with dilated cardiomyopathy, oedema and pulmonary crackles, which of the following is also an important part of her medical therapy?
explanation: Loop diuretics relieve congestion and symptoms but do not improve survival; use the lowest dose that keeps the patient euvolaemic.

orig.stem: Which of the following is also an important component of medical therapy in the management of this patient’s condition?
orig.explanation: Diuretics. Diuretics help manage fluid overload.

stem: Which complication is commonly associated with dilated cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction?
explanation: DCM predisposes to AF and ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden death is common; consider an ICD if EF stays ≤ 35% despite optimal therapy.

orig.stem: Which of the following complications is commonly associated with dilated cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction?
orig.explanation: Arrhythmias. Patients with dilated cardiomyopathy are prone to arrhythmias due to electrical instability.

stem: Which of the following is another potential complication of dilated cardiomyopathy?
explanation: Stasis in a dilated, poorly contracting ventricle (and atria in AF) causes mural thrombus and embolism; anticoagulate for AF or documented LV thrombus.

orig.stem: Which of the following is another potential complication of the condition described in this patient?
orig.explanation: Thromboembolism. Stasis of blood in a dilated ventricle predisposes to thrombus formation and embolism.

stem: In a patient with dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure, an audible third heart sound most likely indicates:
options: Volume overload of the left ventricle
explanation: S3 reflects rapid filling of a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle with high filling pressure (gallop rhythm). Opening snap = MS; pericardial knock = constriction.

orig.stem: The presence of an audible S3 heart sound in the above patient most likely indicates:
options: Volume overload of the left ventricle
orig.explanation: Volume overload of the left ventricle. An S3 gallop indicates increased volume load and reduced left ventricular function.

stem: Which one of the following is least likely to cause dilated cardiomyopathy?
explanation: DCM causes: alcohol, haemochromatosis, myocarditis, genetic, peripartum, anthracyclines, tachycardia. Hypertension causes concentric LVH and HFpEF, so is least likely.

orig.stem: Which one of the following is least likely to cause dilated cardiomyopathy?
orig.explanation: Hypertension Hypertension can cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy not dilated cardiomyopathy.

stem: The following are Causes of dilated cardiomyopathy EXCEPT:
explanation: Beta-myosin heavy chain (MYH7) mutations classically cause HCM. Alcohol, pregnancy and persistent tachycardia cause DCM (the last two may reverse).

orig.stem: The following are Causes of dilated cardiomyopathy EXCEPT:
orig.explanation: Beta-myosin heavy chain mutations Beta-myosin heavy chain mutations are associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

stem: A 67-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and ischaemic heart disease is taken to the Emergency Department with dyspnoea. On examination his respiratory rate is 24/min JVP is not elevated and crackles are heard in both lung bases. Which other finding would most strongly indicate that his dyspnoea is secondary to isolated left ventricular failure?
explanation: With COPD and IHD together, a gallop rhythm (S3) is the most specific sign that breathlessness is from LV failure with high filling pressure.

orig.stem: A 67-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and ischemic heart disease is taken to the Emergency Department with dyspnoea. On examination his respiratory rate is 24/min JVP is not elevated and crackles are heard in both lung bases. Which other finding would most strongly indicate that his dyspnoea is secondary to isolated left ventricular failure?
orig.explanation: Gallop rhythm Gallop rhythm is indicative of left ventricular failure.

stem: All of the fallowing drugs improve prognosis in heart failure Except:

orig.stem: All of the fallowing drugs improve prognosis in heart failure Except:
orig.explanation: Digoxin Digoxin does not improve prognosis in heart failure.

stem: A 65-year-old smoker, who has exertional angina, presents with shortness of breath, gallop rhythm and production of pink frothy spu tum.

orig.stem: A 65-year-old smoker, who has exertional angina, presents with shortness of breath, gallop rhythm and production of pink frothy spu tum.
orig.explanation: Pulmonary oedema Pink frothy sputum and gallop rhythm suggest pulmonary oedema due to heart failure.

topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
stem: A 65-year-old man with known heart failure is evaluated and found to have a reduced ejection fraction. How is his heart failure best classified?
options: HFpEF (heart failure with preserved ejection fraction)
HFrEF (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction)
explanation: By LVEF: HFrEF ≤ 40%, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥ 50% with raised filling pressures. High-output failure is a separate category.

orig.stem: A 65-year-old man with known heart failure is evaluated and found to have a reduced ejection fraction. How is his heart failure best classified?
options: HFpEF (heart failure with preserved ejection fraction)
HFrEF (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction)
orig.explanation: HFrEF (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction) A reduced ejection fraction defines heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).

stem: In a patient with HFrEF who experiences symptoms on exertion and has evidence of structural heart disease, which stage of heart failure is most likely?
explanation: ACC/AHA stages: A at risk, B structural disease without symptoms, C structural disease with symptoms, D refractory. NYHA classes grade symptoms separately.

orig.stem: In a patient with HFrEF who experiences symptoms on exertion and has evidence of structural heart disease, which stage of heart failure is most likely?
orig.explanation: Stage C Stage C heart failure includes patients with structural heart disease who have current or prior symptoms.

stem: Which medication is considered the mainstay of therapy in HFrEF?

orig.stem: Which medication is considered the mainstay of therapy in HFrEF?
orig.explanation: ACE inhibitors ACE inhibitors are a cornerstone of treatment in HFrEF as they improve survival and reduce remodeling.

stem: Which investigation is most useful to assess cardiac function in a patient with suspected heart failure?

orig.stem: Which investigation is most useful to assess cardiac function in a patient with suspected heart failure?
orig.explanation: Echocardiography Echocardiography is essential for assessing left ventricular ejection fraction and structural abnormalities.

stem: In a heart failure patient with left bundle branch block (LBBB), which intervention may improve left ventricular function?
explanation: CRT (biventricular pacing) for HFrEF with EF ≤ 35%, LBBB and QRS ≥ 150 ms despite optimal therapy restores synchrony and improves EF and survival.

orig.stem: In a heart failure patient with left bundle branch block (LBBB), which intervention may improve left ventricular function?
orig.explanation: Cardiac resynchronization therapy Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) can improve ventricular synchrony and function in patients with LBBB and HFrEF.

stem: One of the key advantages of ACE inhibitors in the management of heart failure is:
options: Reduction in mortality by antagonizing the renin-angiotensin system

orig.stem: One of the key advantages of ACE inhibitors in the management of heart failure is:
options: Reduction in mortality by antagonizing the renin-angiotensin system
orig.explanation: Reduction in mortality by antagonizing the renin-angiotensin system ACE inhibitors reduce mortality in heart failure by inhibiting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and reducing remodeling.

stem: A 56-year-old man with long-standing heart failure and hypertension is expected to show which electrocardiographic abnormality?
explanation: Long-standing hypertension causes LVH: tall voltages (S V1 + R V5/6 > 35 mm) with lateral ST–T 'strain'. RVH suggests pulmonary hypertension.

orig.stem: A 56-year-old man with long-standing heart failure and hypertension is expected to show which electrocardiographic abnormality?
orig.explanation: Left ventricular hypertrophy Chronic pressure overload in heart failure due to hypertension often results in left ventricular hypertrophy on the ECG.

stem: Which investigation is most important for further evaluating his cardiac function?

orig.stem: Which investigation is most important for further evaluating his cardiac function?
orig.explanation: Echocardiography Echocardiography is key to assess ejection fraction and structural abnormalities in heart failure.

stem: A 16-year-old boy presents with early fatigue during sports, two syncopal episodes, and a family history of sudden cardiac death. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Exertional fatigue and syncope with familial sudden death in a teenager is HCM, the commonest cause of sudden death in young athletes; ECG and echo first.

orig.stem: A 16-year-old boy presents with early fatigue during sports, two syncopal episodes, and a family history of sudden cardiac death. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy The history of exertional syncope and family sudden death in a young patient is most suggestive of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

stem: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, what is the primary cause of the systolic murmur heard on examination?
options: Mitral regurgitation due to valve prolapse
Fixed obstruction at the aortic valve
Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction
explanation: The HCM murmur comes from dynamic LVOT obstruction (septal hypertrophy plus systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve); it does not radiate to the carotids.

orig.stem: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, what is the primary cause of the systolic murmur heard on examination?
options: Mitral regurgitation due to valve prolapse
Fixed obstruction at the aortic valve
Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction
orig.explanation: Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction The systolic murmur in HCM is due to dynamic obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract.

stem: During the Valsalva manoeuvre in a patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, what happens to the intensity of the murmur?
explanation: Valsalva (like standing) reduces preload, the LV cavity shrinks and outflow obstruction worsens, so the HCM murmur gets louder; squatting and handgrip soften it.

orig.stem: During the Valsalva maneuver in a patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, what is the expected change in the murmur’s intensity?
orig.explanation: Increase in intensity Valsalva reduces preload, which increases the outflow tract obstruction and thus intensifies the murmur in HCM.

stem: What is the best next diagnostic test to confirm the suspected diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
explanation: Echo confirms HCM: unexplained wall thickness ≥ 15 mm (often septal), SAM and an outflow gradient. MRI and Holter refine risk.

orig.stem: What is the best next diagnostic test to confirm the suspected diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
orig.explanation: Echocardiography Echocardiography is the diagnostic test of choice to visualize myocardial hypertrophy and outflow tract obstruction.

stem: The syncope experienced by patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is most commonly due to:
options: Ventricular arrhythmias and dynamic outflow obstruction
explanation: Syncope in HCM is usually from ventricular arrhythmia or a surge in outflow obstruction; unexplained syncope is a major sudden-death risk factor favouring an ICD.

orig.stem: The syncope experienced by patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is most commonly due to:
options: Ventricular arrhythmias and dynamic outflow obstruction
orig.explanation: Ventricular arrhythmias and dynamic outflow obstruction Syncope in HCM is usually due to arrhythmias or severe dynamic obstruction reducing cardiac output.

stem: The term ‘orthopnoea’ refers to breathlessness (dyspnoea) in a particular situation. Which answer below describes that situation?
explanation: Orthopnoea is breathlessness soon after lying flat (venous redistribution), relieved by sitting up. PND wakes the patient after hours of sleep.

orig.stem: The term ‘orthopnoea’ refers to breathlessness (dyspnoea) in a particular situation. Which answer below describes that situation?
orig.explanation: Immediately on lying flat Orthopnoea occurs immediately on lying flat due to gravity-dependent changes in pulmonary capillary pressure causing alveolar oedema.

stem: Which of the following physical signs is associated with left ventricular failure?
options: A gallop rhythm with a fourth heart sound
A gallop rhythm with a third heart sound
Fixed splitting of the second heart sound

orig.stem: Which of the following physical signs is associated with left ventricular failure?
options: A gallop rhythm with a fourth heart sound
A gallop rhythm with a third heart sound
Fixed splitting of the second heart sound
orig.explanation: A gallop rhythm with a third heart sound A third heart sound is indicative of abrupt ventricular filling due to high left atrial pressures seen in left ventricular failure.

stem: A 65 year old female presents with chest pain, and the 12-lead ECG shows evidence of acute inferior myocardial infarction complicated by hypotension. An echocardiogram is performed and shows markedly reduced movement of the right ventricular walls, indicating that right ventricular infarction has occurred. Left ventricular function is only mildly impaired. Which of the following physical signs would be expected in this situation?
options: Tachycardia, a late systolic murmur and ascites
Tachycardia, and absent jugular venous pulse because of inability to develop right heart pressure
Tachycardia, acute development of peripheral oedema and acute ascites
Tachycardia, basal crepitations and a third heart sound
Tachycardia, elevated jugular venous pulse due to failure of right ventricular pump function, and hepatomegaly
explanation: RV infarction with inferior MI: hypotension, raised JVP, hepatomegaly and clear lungs. Give IV fluids and avoid nitrates and diuretics.

orig.stem: A 65 year old female presents with chest pain, and the 12-lead ECG shows evidence of acute inferior myocardial infarction complicated by hypotension. An echocardiogram is performed and shows markedly reduced movement of the right ventricular walls, indicating that right ventricular infarction has occurred. Left ventricular function is only mildly impaired. Which of the following physical signs would be expected in this situation?
options: Tachycardia, a late systolic murmur and ascites
Tachycardia, and absent jugular venous pulse because of inability to develop right heart pressure
Tachycardia, acute development of peripheral oedema and acute ascites
Tachycardia, basal crepitations and a third heart sound
Tachycardia, elevated jugular venous pulse due to failure of right ventricular pump function, and hepatomegaly
orig.explanation: Tachycardia, elevated jugular venous pulse due to failure of right ventricular pump function, and hepatomegaly Right ventricular infarction results in ineffective right ventricular ejection, leading to elevated JVP and hepatic congestion.

stem: What relationship does Starling’s Law of the heart describe?
options: Between blood pressure and cardiac output
Between cardiac filling and blood pressure
Between cardiac filling and cardiac output
Between heart rate and blood pressure
Between heart rate and cardiac output
explanation: Frank–Starling: stroke volume and output rise with ventricular filling (preload) up to a plateau; in heart failure the curve is flat, so extra filling causes congestion.

orig.stem: What relationship does Starling’s Law of the heart describe?
options: Between blood pressure and cardiac output
Between cardiac filling and blood pressure
Between cardiac filling and cardiac output
Between heart rate and blood pressure
Between heart rate and cardiac output
orig.explanation: Between cardiac filling and cardiac output Starling’s Law relates the degree of ventricular filling (preload) to the force of contraction and thus cardiac output.

stem: What underlying pathophysiological changes is chronic cardiac failure associated with?
options: Activation of the renin–angiotensin aldosterone system (RAAS)
Inhibition of the sympathetic nervous system
Reduced production of brain natriuretic peptide (BNP)
explanation: Low output activates RAAS and the sympathetic system: salt/water retention, vasoconstriction and remodelling — the targets of ACEi/ARNI, MRAs and beta-blockers.

orig.stem: What underlying pathophysiological changes is chronic cardiac failure associated with?
options: Activation of the renin–angiotensin aldosterone system (RAAS)
Inhibition of the sympathetic nervous system
Reduced production of brain natriuretic peptide (BNP)
orig.explanation: Activation of the renin–angiotensin aldosterone system (RAAS) Chronic heart failure leads to neurohormonal activation, including RAAS.

stem: Which of the following best describes dilated cardiomyopathy?
options: A disease of the myocardium characterised by chamber enlargement and thinning of the left and right ventricular walls
A disease of the myocardium characterised by disproportionate thickening of the interventricular septum
A disease of the myocardium characterised by infiltration of myocardial tissue resulting in restricted contraction and relaxation
Isolated dilatation of the atria, causing atrial fibrillation
Isolated dilatation of the right ventricle, causing ventricular tachycardia
explanation: DCM is dilatation (often biventricular) with thin walls and systolic dysfunction not explained by loading or coronary disease. Septal thickening = HCM.

orig.stem: Which of the following best describes dilated cardiomyopathy?
options: A disease of the myocardium characterised by chamber enlargement and thinning of the left and right ventricular walls
A disease of the myocardium characterised by disproportionate thickening of the interventricular septum
A disease of the myocardium characterised by infiltration of myocardial tissue resulting in restricted contraction and relaxation
Isolated dilatation of the atria, causing atrial fibrillation
Isolated dilatation of the right ventricle, causing ventricular tachycardia
orig.explanation: A disease of the myocardium characterised by chamber enlargement and thinning of the left and right ventricular walls Dilated cardiomyopathy is defined by dilation and thinning of the ventricular walls.

stem: Which of the following is a cause of dilated cardiomyopathy?
options: Mutation in cardiac sodium channel gene
explanation: Heavy alcohol (> 80 g/day for years) is a common, reversible cause of DCM. SCN5A mutations cause Brugada and long QT3.

orig.stem: Which of the following is a cause of dilated cardiomyopathy?
options: Mutation in cardiac sodium channel gene
orig.explanation: Heavy alcohol consumption Heavy alcohol intake is a known cause of dilated cardiomyopathy.

stem: By which of the following features is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy usually characterised?
options: Asymmetric left ventricular hypertrophy with marked thickening of the interventricular septum
Asymmetric left ventricular hypertrophy with marked thickening of the anterior left ventricular wall
Hypertrophy of both atria and both ventricles
Hypertrophy of the left ventricle and atrophy of the right ventricle
explanation: HCM: asymmetric LVH with disproportionate septal thickening (septum/posterior wall > 1.3), myocyte disarray and dynamic outflow obstruction in ~two-thirds.

orig.stem: By which of the following features is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy usually characterised?
options: Asymmetric left ventricular hypertrophy with marked thickening of the interventricular septum
Asymmetric left ventricular hypertrophy with marked thickening of the anterior left ventricular wall
Hypertrophy of both atria and both ventricles
Hypertrophy of the left ventricle and atrophy of the right ventricle
orig.explanation: Asymmetric left ventricular hypertrophy with marked thickening of the interventricular septum Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is classically characterized by asymmetric septal hypertrophy.

stem: Cardiac transplantation is considered in which group of patients with cardiomyopathy?
options: Frail elderly patients with end-stage heart failure
Patients who do not wish to take life-long medication
Patients who have poor quality of life despite optimal drug therapy
Patients who have symptoms but good quality of life on optimal drug therapy
explanation: Transplantation is for stage D heart failure with poor quality of life despite optimal drug and device therapy and no contraindications; LVAD is an alternative.

orig.stem: Cardiac transplantation is considered in which group of patients with cardiomyopathy?
options: Frail elderly patients with end-stage heart failure
Patients who do not wish to take life-long medication
Patients who have poor quality of life despite optimal drug therapy
Patients who have symptoms but good quality of life on optimal drug therapy
orig.explanation: Patients who have poor quality of life despite optimal drug therapy Transplantation is reserved for those with refractory symptoms despite optimal treatment.

stem: A 48 year old woman with no significant previous medical history collapses while running a marathon. Despite attempts at resuscitation, she does not survive. Postmortem examination reveals asymmetric left ventricular hypertrophy with disproportionate thickening of the interventricular septum. A postmortem diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is made. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s sudden collapse?
explanation: Sudden death in HCM is from VT/VF arising in fibrotic myocardium, often on exertion; risk is scored (ESC HCM Risk-SCD) and high-risk patients get an ICD.

orig.stem: A 48 year old woman with no significant previous medical history collapses while running a marathon. Despite attempts at resuscitation, she does not survive. Postmortem examination reveals asymmetric left ventricular hypertrophy with disproportionate thickening of the interventricular septum. A postmortem diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is made. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s sudden collapse?
orig.explanation: Ventricular arrhythmia Sudden death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is most commonly due to ventricular arrhythmias.

stem: A 30 year old woman has recently been diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy. Her diagnosis was made with echocardiography, which showed moderate left ventricular dilatation and impairment. She has noticed herself becoming increasingly fatigued on moderate exertion. Her younger sister died suddenly the previous year and she is very worried about the risk of sudden death. Which of the following treatments is known to reduce her risk of sudden death?
explanation: Beta-blockers reduce total and sudden death in HFrEF (as do MRAs and ARNI); consider an ICD if EF stays ≤ 35%. Verapamil is harmful; screen the family.

orig.stem: A 30 year old woman has recently been diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy. Her diagnosis was made with echocardiography, which showed moderate left ventricular dilatation and impairment. She has noticed herself becoming increasingly fatigued on moderate exertion. Her younger sister died suddenly the previous year and she is very worried about the risk of sudden death. Which of the following treatments is known to reduce her risk of sudden death?
orig.explanation: B-blocker (e.g. metoprolol) B-blockers have been shown to reduce the risk of sudden death in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy.

stem: A 55 year old woman presents with a history of acute, severe, constricting central chest pain associated with anterior ST segment elevation on the 12-lead ECG. She immediately undergoes coronary angiography, which shows no evidence of coronary artery disease and no coronary occlusion. An echocardiogram shows left ventricular apical dilatation, with normal left ventricular basal contraction. Which of the following factors is most likely to have precipitated this illness?
explanation: ST elevation, normal coronaries and apical ballooning in a postmenopausal woman after emotional stress is takotsubo cardiomyopathy; LV function usually recovers.

orig.stem: A 55 year old woman presents with a history of acute, severe, constricting central chest pain associated with anterior ST segment elevation on the 12-lead ECG. She immediately undergoes coronary angiography, which shows no evidence of coronary artery disease and no coronary occlusion. An echocardiogram shows left ventricular apical dilatation, with normal left ventricular basal contraction. Which of the following factors is most likely to have precipitated this illness?
orig.explanation: Acute emotional stress Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy is precipitated by acute emotional stress.

stem: The following medical treatments are all associated with improved symptoms in patients with heart failure due to left ventricular systolic dysfunction. However, which of the treatments has NOT been shown to also improve survival?
explanation: Loop diuretics relieve symptoms but do not improve survival. Bisoprolol, enalapril, sacubitril/valsartan, spironolactone and SGLT2i reduce mortality.

orig.stem: The following medical treatments are all associated with improved symptoms in patients with heart failure due to left ventricular systolic dysfunction. However, which of the treatments has NOT been shown to also improve survival?
orig.explanation: Furosemide Furosemide improves symptoms but has not been shown to improve survival.

topics: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
stem: An 80 year old woman presents with shortness of breath and swollen ankles. Her ECG showed some poor R-wave progression. She was referred for an echocardiogram and was found to have a high ejection fraction. Which of these conditions is the most likely cause of her presentation?
explanation: Heart failure with high EF and a pseudo-infarct ECG (low voltages) in an elderly woman suggests restrictive (amyloid) cardiomyopathy.

orig.stem: An 80 year old woman presents with shortness of breath and swollen ankles. Her ECG showed some poor R-wave progression. She was referred for an echocardiogram and was found to have a high ejection fraction. Which of these conditions is the most likely cause of her presentation?
orig.explanation: Restrictive cardiomyopathy A high ejection fraction with symptoms suggests restrictive cardiomyopathy.

stem: Neuroendocrine system activation is a feature of heart failure. Abnormalities of which hormone can cause heart failure rather than result from heart failure?
explanation: Thyroid disease causes heart failure: thyrotoxicosis gives high-output failure and AF; hypothyroidism a dilated heart. Check TFTs in all new heart failure.

orig.stem: Neuroendocrine system activation is a feature of heart failure. Abnormalities of which hormone can cause heart failure rather than result from heart failure?
orig.explanation: Thyroxine Thyrotoxicosis can cause heart failure rather than result from it.

stem: An army recruit is referred for assessment because there is a family history of sudden cardiac death and an uncle was diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. In what manner is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy commonly inherited?
explanation: HCM is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance (MYH7, MYBPC3); screen first-degree relatives with ECG and echo ± genetic testing.

orig.stem: An army recruit is referred for assessment because there is a family history of sudden cardiac death and an uncle was diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. In what manner is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy commonly inherited?
orig.explanation: Autosomal dominant Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is most commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion.

stem: An 83 year old woman presents with acute pulmonary oedema, BP of 180/100 mmHg and a SaO2 of 85%. Which treatment is UNLIKELY to be helpful in this setting?
explanation: Hypertensive pulmonary oedema: oxygen/CPAP, IV nitrates and IV furosemide. Dobutamine is for cardiogenic shock and only raises oxygen demand here.

orig.stem: An 83 year old woman presents with acute pulmonary oedema, BP of 180/100 mmHg and a SaO2 of 85%. Which treatment is UNLIKELY to be helpful in this setting?
orig.explanation: Intravenous dobutamine Dobutamine increases cardiac work and is not beneficial in hypertensive pulmonary oedema.

stem: A 43 year old woman with a past history of breast cancer is referred with a gradual onset of breathlessness. An echocardiogram demonstrates a dilated poorly contracting left ventricle. You wish to investigate potential causes of her dilated cardiomyopathy. Which of the following would be an irreversible cause of her dilated cardiomyopathy?
explanation: Anthracycline (doxorubicin) cardiotoxicity is cumulative, dose-dependent and largely irreversible. Alcohol, haemochromatosis and thyroid DCM can improve.

orig.stem: A 43 year old woman with a past history of breast cancer is referred with a gradual onset of breathlessness. An echocardiogram demonstrates a dilated poorly contracting left ventricle. You wish to investigate potential causes of her dilated cardiomyopathy. Which of the following would be an irreversible cause of her dilated cardiomyopathy?
orig.explanation: Anthracycline chemotherapy Anthracycline chemotherapy can cause irreversible dilated cardiomyopathy.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents to your emergency department appearing quite ill. His family says he has not had his normal energy for the last 6 months, and they noted he was confused and lethargic for the last day or two. As you take a history from the family, you palpate the patient’s radial pulse and notice a regular beat-to-beat variability of pulse amplitude, although his rhythm is regular. Indeed, as you later take his blood pressure, you note that only every other phase I (systolic) Korotkoff sound is audible as the cuff pressure is slowly lowered and that this is independent of the respiratory cycle. Based on this, you suspect this patient has which of the following?
explanation: Pulsus alternans (alternating strong and weak beats in regular rhythm, independent of respiration) indicates severe LV systolic dysfunction.

orig.stem: A 75-year-old man presents to your emergency department appearing quite ill. His family says he has not had his normal energy for the last 6 months, and they noted he was confused and lethargic for the last day or two. As you take a history from the family, you palpate the patient’s radial pulse and notice a regular beat-to- beat variability of pulse amplitude, although his rhythm is regular. Indeed, as you later take his blood pressure, you note that only every other phase I (systolic) Korotkoff sound is audible as the cuff pressure is slowly lowered and that this is independent of the respiratory cycle. Based on this, you suspect this patient has which of the following?
orig.explanation: Severe left ventricular dysfunction The presence of pulsus alternans (alternating pulse amplitude) is most commonly seen in severe LV dysfunction.

stem: A 78-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit with decompensated heart failure. He has longstanding ischaemic cardiomyopathy. ECG shows atrial fibrillation and left bundle branch block. Chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly and bilateral alveolar infiltrates with Kerley B lines. Which of the following is least likely to be present on physical examination?
options: Reversed splitting of the second heart sound
explanation: S4 needs atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, so it cannot occur in AF. S3, reversed splitting (LBBB) and Kussmaul's sign all fit.

orig.stem: A 78-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit with decompensated heart failure. He has longstanding ischemic cardiomyopathy. ECG shows atrial fibrillation and left bundle branch block. Chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly and bilateral alveolar infiltrates with Kerley B lines. Which of the following is least likely to be present on physical examination?
options: Reversed splitting of the second heart sound
orig.explanation: Fourth heart sound A fourth heart sound is not typically found in atrial fibrillation, making it the least likely finding.

stem: A 24-year-old man collapses while playing basketball. He has exertional chest pain, his father died suddenly at 44 with an enlarged heart, and he has a grade III/VI mid-systolic crescendo–decrescendo murmur and LVH on ECG. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is suspected. Which manoeuvre(s) would make the murmur louder?
options: Both standing and the Valsalva manoeuvre
explanation: The HCM murmur gets louder when LV volume falls, because a smaller cavity narrows the outflow tract further. Standing from squatting and the strain phase of the Valsalva manoeuvre both reduce venous return and increase the murmur. Squatting and passive leg raising increase preload, and handgrip increases afterload, so these make it softer (the opposite of aortic stenosis).

orig.stem: A 24-year-old man is referred to a cardiologist after an episode of syncope while playing basketball. He has no recollection of the event, but he was told that he collapsed while running. He awakened lying on the ground and suffered multiple contusions as a result of the fall. He has always been an active individual but recently has developed some chest pain with exertion that has caused him to restrict his activity. His father died at age 44 while rock climbing. He believes his father’s cause of death was sudden cardiac death and recalls being told his father had an enlarged heart. On examination, the patient has a III/VI mid-systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur. His ECG shows evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy. You suspect hypertrophic cardiomyopathy as the cause of the patient’s heart disease. Which of the following maneuvers would be expected to cause an increase in the loudness of the murmur?
orig.explanation: Standing and Valsalva maneuver Decreasing venous return (by standing or performing Valsalva) increases the outflow gradient in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, intensifying the murmur.

stem: A 66-year-old smoker who has recently travelled in South America has progressive exertional breathlessness and fatigue. Pulse 104/min irregularly irregular, BP 96/76 mmHg, with a raised JVP and marked leg oedema. Echocardiography shows an LVEF of 55%; images are shown. To establish the cause of his heart failure, which test is most appropriate next?
options: Positron emission tomography cardiac stress test
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis and light chain assay
explanation: Thick 'sparkling' myocardium with biatrial enlargement and preserved EF suggests amyloidosis: first exclude AL with serum/urine electrophoresis and free light chains.

orig.stem: A 66-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for progressive dyspnea on exertion and fatigue. He has a past medical history of tobacco abuse and is widely traveled, recently returning from a multicountry trip through South America. On presentation, his heart rate is 104 bpm and irregularly irregular. Blood pressure is 96/76 mmHg. You note an elevated jugular venous pulsation and marked lower extremity edema. Echocardiogram reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55%, and still images from his echocardiogram are shown in Figure V-20. To elucidate the etiology of his heart failure, which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test to perform next?
options: Positron emission tomography cardiac stress test
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis and light chain assay
orig.explanation: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis and light chain assay The echocardiographic findings are suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis; evaluation for a light chain paraproteinemia is the appropriate next step.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 38% has been hospitalized for the past week with acute decompensated heart failure. After diuresis and medication optimization, she is feeling immensely better. She is on the maximally tolerated doses of an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, B-blocker, and appropriate diuretic dose. You are planning for discharge today. On rounds, the nurse notes that the patient had several short (5-10 beats) runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT) and multiple premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) overnight, although she remained asymptomatic. A medical student on the team asks if the NSVT carries any prognostic significance and if any intervention is needed. What is the most appropriate response?
options: “NSVT is common in patients with cardiomyopathy and carries no significance.”
“NSVT is concerning in this patient. We should suppress the PVCs and NSVT with amiodarone.”
“NSVT is associated with an increased mortal ity in patients with heart failure. We will refer her for an automated implantable defibrillator.”
“NSVT is associated with an increased mortality in patients with heart failure. We should suppress the NSVT with flecainide.”
“NSVT is associated with an increased mortality in patients with heart failure. However, suppression of PVCs and NSVT with antiarrhythmic drugs does not change this prognosis.”
explanation: NSVT in heart failure predicts higher mortality, but antiarrhythmic suppression does not help (class I harmful, CAST); optimise HF therapy and electrolytes.

stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of myocardial infarction and congestive heart failure is comfortable at rest. However, when walking to his car, he develops dyspnoea, fatigue, and sometimes palpitations. He must rest for several minutes before these symptoms resolve. Which of the following is his New York Heart Association classification?
explanation: Comfortable at rest but symptoms on less than ordinary activity (e.g. a short walk) is NYHA class III.

orig.explanation: Class III Symptoms with exertion that resolve on rest indicate NYHA Class III.

stem: A 47-year-old postmenopausal woman is seen for onset of severe dyspnoea over the last few weeks. She reports no preceding chest pain, cough, sputum, or fever, although she does report leg swelling. Physical examination is notable for a blood pressure of 145/78 mmHg and heart rate of 123 bpm. Exophthalmos is present, as well as bilateral inspiratory crackles occupying approximately one-third of the lower chest with neck vein distention. She has a third heart sound with no murmur. Bilateral lower extremity oedema is also present, with warm extremities and a fine hand tremor. Which of the following is the most likely pathophysiologic explanation for her heart failure?
options: Chronic systemic hypertension with resultant left ventricular hypertrophy and nonsystolic heart failure
Myocardial infarction with depressed left ventricular systolic function
explanation: Heart failure with warm peripheries, tachycardia, exophthalmos and tremor is thyrotoxic high-output failure: beta-blocker, diuretic and treat the thyroid.

orig.explanation: Thyrotoxicosis with high-output state The presence of exophthalmos and tremor in conjunction with heart failure symptoms is most consistent with thyrotoxicosis.

stem: From a pathophysiologic perspective, all of the following are upregulated in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction EXCEPT:
options: Calcium uptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
explanation: In HFrEF angiotensin II, noradrenaline, natriuretic peptides and TNF rise, but SR calcium uptake falls (SERCA2a down-regulated), impairing relaxation.

orig.stem: From a pathophysiologic perspective, all of the following are upregulated in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction EXCEPT:
options: Calcium uptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
orig.explanation: Calcium uptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum In heart failure, calcium reuptake is impaired rather than upregulated.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath. He is found to have an elevated serum BNP. In addition to heart failure, all of the following may also cause an elevation in BNP EXCEPT:
options: Pulmonary embolism with right heart strain
explanation: BNP rises with age, female sex, CKD, AF, PE, sepsis and ACS. Obesity lowers BNP, so a 'normal' value does not exclude heart failure in obese patients.

orig.stem: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath. He is found to have an elevated serum BNP. In addition to heart failure, all of the following may also cause an elevation in BNP EXCEPT:
options: Pulmonary embolism with right heart strain
orig.explanation: Obesity Obesity is known to cause falsely low BNP levels.

stem: A ventilated patient with cor pulmonale has a tidal volume of 500 mL, FiO2 0.4, PEEP 20 cmH2O and a rate of 20/min; pH 7.40, PCO2 40 mmHg and SaO2 86%. All of the following would increase his right ventricular afterload EXCEPT:
options: Increasing FiO2 to raise SaO2 to 95%
explanation: Correcting hypoxaemia relieves hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and lowers RV afterload. High PEEP, large tidal volumes and hypercapnia raise it.

orig.stem: You are taking care of a patient with cor pulmonale in the medical intensive care unit. Unfortunately, he suffered a respiratory arrest at home and requires intubation and mechanical ventilation. Currently, with a tidal volume of 500 mL, FiO2 of 0.4, positive end-expiratory pressure of 20 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 20, his pH is 7.40, PCO2 is 40 mmHg, and oxygen saturation is 86%. You are concerned about the afterload experienced by his right ventricle. All of the following are likely to increase his right ventricular afterload EXCEPT:
options: Increasing FiO2 to increase arterial oxygen saturation to 95%
orig.explanation: Increasing FiO2 to increase arterial oxygen saturation to 95% Improving oxygenation reduces pulmonary vasoconstriction and RV afterload.

topics: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
stem: Mr. George is a 52-year-old man with long standing hypertension and poorly controlled diabetes. He presents complaining of several months of breathlessness with exertion, acute episodes of shortness of breath when recumbent, and lower extremity oedema. On examination, he has an elevated jugular venous pulse and an S4 on auscultation. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55% with a large left atrium. You suspect this patient has the syndrome of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Drugs targeting which of the following have convincingly demonstrated mortality reduction for patients with HFpEF?
explanation: No drug has convincingly reduced mortality in HFpEF; SGLT2i reduce the combined endpoint mainly via fewer admissions. Treat congestion and comorbidities.

orig.stem: Mr. George is a 52-year-old man with long standing hypertension and poorly controlled diabetes. He presents complaining of several months of breathlessness with exertion, acute episodes of shortness of breath when recumbent, and lower extremity edema. Drugs targeting which of the following have convincingly demonstrated mortality reduction for patients with HFpEF?
orig.explanation: None of the above No pharmacologic therapies have yet shown a mortality benefit in HFpEF.

stem: You are evaluating a 64-year-old woman with a history of nonischaemic cardiomyopathy. She presents to the emergency department for shortness of breath. You note that she has gained 11 kg since her last cardiology appointment 2 months ago. Physical examination confirms findings associated with acute decompensated heart failure, including pulmonary rales, elevated jugular venous pulse, abdominal ascites, lower extremity oedema, and a square wave blood pressure Valsalva response. Her extremities are warm, and blood pressure is 110/78 mmHg with a heart rate of 75 bpm. Her laboratory studies return with a sodium of 128 mEq/L and creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL (which is increased from her prior level of 1.2 mg/dL). Chest x-ray shows a diffuse alveolar filling pattern consistent with pulmonary oedema. What is the next most appropriate step?
options: Pulmonary artery catheter for haemodynamic monitoring
Dobutamine 5 micrograms/kg/min titrated to urine output
explanation: 'Warm and wet': start an IV loop diuretic (at least the oral dose). Inotropes are for 'cold' low-output states; ultrafiltration for diuretic resistance.

orig.stem: You are evaluating a 64-year-old woman with a history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy. She presents to the emergency department for shortness of breath. You note that she has gained 11 kg since her last cardiology appointment 2 months ago. Physical examination confirms findings associated with acute decompensated heart failure, including pulmonary rales, elevated jugular venous pulse, abdominal ascites, lower extremity edema, and a square wave blood pressure Valsalva response. Her extremities are warm, and blood pressure is 110/78 mmHg with a heart rate of 75 bpm. Her laboratory studies return with a sodium of 128 mEq/L and creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL (which is increased from her prior level of 1.2 mg/dL). Chest x-ray shows a diffuse alveolar filling pattern consistent with pulmonary edema. What is the next most appropriate step?
options: Insert a large-bore central IV line and prepare for ultrafiltration
Insertion of a pulmonary artery catheter for hemodynamic monitoring
Start dobutamine at 5 pg/kg/min and titrate to a urine output of 1 mL/kg/hr
orig.explanation: Administer furosemide 40 mg IV Initial management should be diuresis to relieve congestion.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding nesiritide is true in patients with acute decompensated heart failure requiring invasive haemodynamic monitoring?
options: Nesiritide has no significant effect on blood pressure
Nesiritide improves renal perfusion in states of acute decompensated heart failure
Nesiritide is associated with a decreased rate of rehospitalization, but not death, from acute decompensated heart failure
Nesiritide reduces pulmonary capillary wedge more rapidly than IV nitrates
None of the statements are true
explanation: Nesiritide (recombinant BNP) lowers wedge pressure faster than nitrates but causes hypotension and did not improve outcomes (ASCEND-HF).

orig.stem: Which of the following statements regarding nesiritide is true in patients with acute decompensated heart failure requiring invasive hemodynamic monitoring?
options: Nesiritide has no significant effect on blood pressure.
Nesiritide improves renal perfusion in states of acute decompensated heart failure.
Nesiritide is associated with a decreased rate of rehospitalization, but not death, from acute decompensated heart failure.
Nesiritide reduces pulmonary capillary wedge more rapidly than IV nitrates.
None of the statements are true.
orig.explanation: Nesiritide reduces pulmonary capillary wedge more rapidly than IV nitrates. While nesiritide lowers filling pressures, its overall clinical benefits are limited.

stem: A 21-year-old man is lethargic and breathless a week after a viral upper respiratory infection. BP 88/72 mmHg, HR 115, SpO2 90%, with crackles, a raised JVP, an S3 and cool extremities; creatinine 2.3 mg/dL, raised BNP and lactate. Echo shows an LVEF of 15% with global hypokinesis. Before dobutamine takes effect, which haemodynamic parameter is most likely increased?
explanation: In cardiogenic shock output falls and sympathetic vasoconstriction raises systemic vascular resistance (cool peripheries); mixed venous saturation falls.

orig.stem: Mr. Jones is a 21-year-old man who presents to the emergency department with several days of worsening shortness of breath and lethargy 1 week after a viral upper respiratory tract infection. His family brought him in after he lacked the energy to rise from the couch unassisted. His blood pressure is 88/72 mmHg, heart rate is 115 bpm, and room air oxygen saturation is 90%. Physical examination reveals pulmonary crackles, elevated jugular venous pressure, an audible S3 gallop, and cool extremities. He is lethargic and slow to respond to questions. Laboratory analysis reveals a creatinine of 2.3 mg/dL, elevated BNP level, and mildly elevated lactate. Bedside echocardiography reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction of 15% with global hypokinesis. You start dobutamine at 5 µg/kg/ min and prepare to insert a pulmonary artery catheter for hemodynamic monitoring. Which of the following hemodynamic parameters is most likely increased?
orig.explanation: Systemic vascular resistance In severe decompensated heart failure, low output leads to compensatory increase in SVR.

topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
stem: Which of the following statements regarding the initiation of B-blockers versus ACE inhibitors in HFrEF is most correct?
options: ACE inhibitors should always be started before B-blockers
B-blockers should always be started before ACE inhibitors
It does not matter which is initiated first; both are essential and should be optimally titrated
ACE inhibitors are more important than B-blockers in reducing mortality
B-blockers have a stronger dose effect on survival than ACE inhibitors
explanation: Beta-blocker or ACEi first gives similar outcomes (CIBIS III); start all four pillars early in low doses and titrate to target.

orig.stem: Which of the following statements regarding the initiation of B-blockers versus ACE inhibitors in HFrEF is most correct?
options: ACE inhibitors should always be started before B-blockers.
B-blockers should always be started before ACE inhibitors.
It does not matter which is initiated first; both are essential and should be optimally titrated.
ACE inhibitors are more important than B-blockers in reducing mortality.
B-blockers have a stronger dose effect on survival than ACE inhibitors.
orig.explanation: It does not matter which is initiated first; both are essential and should be optimally titrated. Studies show similar outcomes regardless of which drug is started first, as long as both are titrated to optimal doses.

stem: A 22-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus is on optimal doses of the three medications forming the foundation of neurohormonal therapy for HFrEF. Which additional therapy is most appropriate at this time?
options: None – she is already on optimal therapy
explanation: Adding an ARB or aliskiren to ACEi + MRA raises hyperkalaemia and renal risk without benefit; SGLT2i need caution in type 1 diabetes (ketoacidosis), so no change.

stem: A 21-year-old man has HFrEF. Which statement about prophylactic therapy to prevent sudden cardiac death is most appropriate?
options: An ICD is indicated if the LVEF remains 35% or less despite at least 3 months of optimal medical therapy
An ICD is indicated only in NYHA class IV
An ICD is not recommended in ischaemic cardiomyopathy
An ICD should be delayed until after 5 years of optimal therapy
No device therapy is ever indicated
explanation: Primary-prevention ICD: LVEF ≤ 35% despite ≥ 3 months of optimal therapy, NYHA II–III and reasonable survival. Recheck EF after myocarditis or peripartum disease.

orig.stem: Mr. Jones is a 21-year-old man with HFrEF. Which of the following is most appropriate regarding prophylactic therapy to prevent sudden cardiac death?
options: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) placement is indicated in patients with an LVEF <35%.
ICD is indicated only in patients with NYHA class IV symptoms.
ICD placement is not recommended in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy.
ICD placement should be delayed until after 5 years of optimal therapy.
orig.explanation: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) placement is indicated in patients with an LVEF <35%. ICD therapy is recommended for primary prevention in patients with reduced EF despite optimal medical therapy.

stem: A 19-year-old university rower presents for the pre-Oxford–Cambridge boat race medical evaluation. He is healthy and has no significant medical history. However, his brother died suddenly during football practice at age 15. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the brother’s death?

orig.stem: A 19-year-old university rower presents for the pre-Oxford–Cambridge boat race medical evaluation. He is healthy and has no significant medical history. However, his brother died suddenly during football practice at age 15. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the brother’s death?
orig.explanation: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes in the UK. It is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents to the heart failure outpatient clinic with increased shortness of breath and swollen ankles. On examination his pulse was 100 beats/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg and jugular venous pressure (JVP) +10 cm water. The patient currently takes furosemide 40 mg BD, spironolactone 12.5 mg, bisoprolol 2.5 mg OD and ramipril 2.5 mg BD. Which of the following is true?
options: Diuretics reduce the degree of neurohormonal activation in heart failure
Diuretics alone rarely provide rapid symptomatic relief
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are unlikely to induce hypotension if an adequate diuresis has been achieved with diuretics
explanation: Spironolactone cut HFrEF mortality by ~30% (RALES), eplerenone in milder HF (EMPHASIS-HF). Diuretics relieve congestion but activate RAAS.

options: Diuretics reduce the degree of neurohormonal activation in heart failure
Diuretics alone rarely provide rapid symptomatic relief
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are unlikely to induce hypotension if an adequate diuresis has been achieved with diuretics
orig.explanation: Treatment with spironolactone reduces mortality Treatment with spironolactone reduces mortality along with beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors in heart failure.

stem: A 65-year-old man has NYHA class III chronic heart failure. Despite conventional therapy with appropriate dosages of a diuretic, an ACE inhibitor and a beta-adrenergic blocker, his left ventricular ejection fraction hovers around 35%, and he continues to have shortness of breath on exertion. His latest urea and electrolytes test results were normal and you consider adding digoxin to his treatment regimen. Which one of the following is true regarding digoxin therapy in this situation?
options: A reasonable dosage is 0.50 mg/day orally
Serial drug levels are generally not necessary
A loading dose will be necessary
It is not likely to improve the ejection fractions
It is the treatment of choice if the patient’s ECG shows AV block
explanation: In chronic HF digoxin is given 62.5–250 µg daily without loading; levels only if toxicity, renal impairment or interactions. It reduces admissions, not mortality.

Serial drug levels are generally not necessary
A loading dose will be necessary
It is not likely to improve the ejection fractions
It is the treatment of choice if the patient’s ECG shows AV block
orig.explanation: Serial drug levels are generally not necessary Serial digoxin levels are not generally necessary; dosing is usually in the range of 125–250 mcg daily.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and fatigue. On examination you note pitting oedema in both his lower limbs. You suspect heart failure. Which investigation is most likely to demonstrate the aetiology?

orig.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and fatigue. On examination you note pitting oedema in both his lower limbs. You suspect heart failure. Which investigation is most likely to demonstrate the aetiology?
orig.explanation: Echocardiogram An echocardiogram is the most useful investigation to determine the cause of heart failure.

stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath. She comments that she feels particularly breathless when lying down and uses five pillows to sleep at night. On examination her pulse rate is regular at 122 beats/ min and her blood pressure is stable at 122/65 mmHg. You note bibasal crackles when listening to her chest. You suspect heart failure and order a CXR and echocardiogram. The following may all be features on her CXR EXCEPT?
options: Fluid in the left horizontal interlobar fissure
explanation: Heart-failure CXR: cardiomegaly, upper-lobe diversion, bat-wing oedema, Kerley B lines, effusions, fissure fluid. The left lung has no horizontal fissure.

orig.stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath. She comments that she feels particularly breathless when lying down and uses five pillows to sleep at night. On examination her pulse rate is regular at 122 beats/ min and her blood pressure is stable at 122/65 mmHg. You note bibasal crackles when listening to her chest. You suspect heart failure and order a CXR and echocardiogram. The following may all be features on her CXR EXCEPT?
options: Fluid in the left horizontal interlobar fissure
orig.explanation: Fluid in the left horizontal interlobar fissure Fluid in the left horizontal fissure is not a typical CXR feature of heart failure.

stem: A 66-year-old man with heart failure secondary to previous MIs is on regular digoxin and furosemide without much effect. A recent echocardiogram shows global dysfunction. His renal function is normal. Which medication should be added to his management?

orig.stem: A 66-year-old man with heart failure secondary to previous MIs is on regular digoxin and furosemide without much effect. A recent echocardiogram shows global dysfunction. His renal function is normal. Which medication should be added to his management?
orig.explanation: ACE inhibitors ACE inhibitors are first-line in managing heart failure and can improve outcomes when added to existing therapy.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with shortness of breath at rest. Physical examination reveals evidence of pitting oedema over the sacrum and leg oedema to the midthigh. An echocardiogram is requested which demonstrates an ejection fraction of 0.4. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
explanation: Breathless at rest with gross oedema: relieve congestion first with a loop diuretic; start/titrate ACEi and beta-blocker once less congested.

orig.stem: A 65-year-old man presents with shortness of breath at rest. Physical examination reveals evidence of pitting oedema over the sacrum and leg oedema to the midthigh. An echocardiogram is requested which demonstrates an ejection fraction of 0.4. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
orig.explanation: Diuretic In a fluid overloaded patient with heart failure, diuretics are the first-line treatment.

stem: A 72-year-old man with known cardiac failure comes to see his GP. He is currently on a diuretic. His GP decides to commence an ACE inhibitor. The following are all side effects of ACE inhibitors EXCEPT?
explanation: ACE inhibitors cause hyperkalaemia (less aldosterone), not hypokalaemia; also cough, angioedema, first-dose hypotension and AKI. Check U&E before and after dose changes.

orig.stem: A 72-year-old man with known cardiac failure comes to see his GP. He is currently on a diuretic. His GP decides to commence an ACE inhibitor. The following are all side effects of ACE inhibitors EXCEPT?
orig.explanation: Hypokalaemia ACE inhibitors are more commonly associated with hyperkalaemia rather than hypokalaemia.

stem: A 64-year-old man with known cardiac failure presents with acute shortness of breath and a cough productive of frothy pink sputum. He comments that he feels nauseous. On examination you note wheezes and crackles throughout his chest. What is the next most appropriate step in management?

orig.stem: A 64-year-old man with known cardiac failure presents with acute shortness of breath and a cough productive of frothy pink sputum. He comments that he feels nauseous. On examination you note wheezes and crackles throughout his chest. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
orig.explanation: Furosemide Furosemide is indicated to relieve pulmonary oedema in acute heart failure.

stem: A 21-year-old fit university student with no past medical history has sudden loss of consciousness 1 hour into a gym session. CPR is administered by bystanders. On arrival of the paramedics, he has regained consciousness. What is the most effective means of preventing sudden death in high-risk patients with asymptomatic HCM?
explanation: An ICD is the only proven way to prevent sudden death in HCM: after aborted arrest (as here) or when the ESC 5-year risk is ≥ 6%.

orig.stem: A 21-year-old fit university student with no past medical history has sudden loss of consciousness 1 hour into a gym session. CPR is administered by bystanders. On arrival of the paramedics, he has regained consciousness. What is the most effective means of preventing sudden death in high-risk patients with asymptomatic HCM?
orig.explanation: An implantable cardioverter–defibrillator (ICD) An ICD is the most effective modality for preventing sudden death in high-risk asymptomatic HCM patients.

stem: An elderly woman complains of abdominal distension, due to ascites, upper abdominal pain from an enlarged tender liver and flatulence. She is mildly jaundiced and has marked pitting of the legs. Her arterial pulse is rapid and irregular, and she is sitting propped up in bed where it is evident that her face is cyanosed, and her jugular veins are engorged and pulsating in systole. She is passing little urine and the urine contains 2+ of protein. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Ascites, tender liver, jaundice, AF, oedema, orthopnoea and systolic JVP waves (TR) mean congestive (biventricular) failure. Cirrhosis does not raise the JVP.

orig.stem: An elderly woman complains of abdominal distension, due to ascites, upper abdominal pain from an enlarged tender liver and flatulence. She is mildly jaundiced and has marked pitting of the legs. Her arterial pulse is rapid and irregular, and she is sitting propped up in bed where it is evident that her face is cyanosed, and her jugular veins are engorged and pulsating in systole. She is passing little urine and the urine contains 2+ of protein. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Congestive heart failure The clinical picture is consistent with congestive heart failure leading to hepatic congestion and ascites.

stem: A 31-year-old man presents with several months of shortness of breath and chest discomfort. An ECG shows evidence of T-wave flattening. You request an echocardiogram which demonstrates dilated ventricles with global hypokinesis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 31-year-old man presents with several months of shortness of breath and chest discomfort. An ECG shows evidence of T-wave flattening. You request an echocardiogram which demonstrates dilated ventricles with global hypokinesis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy The echocardiogram findings are classic for dilated cardiomyopathy.

stem: A 27-year-old footballer presents with laboured breathing and chest pain. An ECG shows evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 27-year-old footballer presents with laboured breathing and chest pain. An ECG shows evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can present with LVH on ECG and symptoms in athletes.

stem: A 78-year-old woman is admitted with heart failure secondary to aortic stenosis. Which sign is most likely to be present?
explanation: Decompensated aortic stenosis first raises LA and pulmonary venous pressure, giving bibasal crackles; raised JVP and oedema follow only with right failure.

orig.stem: A 78-year-old woman is admitted with heart failure secondary to aortic stenosis. Which sign is most likely to be present?

stem: A 55-year-old patient presents to you after a 3-day hospital stay for gradually increasing shortness of breath and leg swelling while away on a business trip. He was told that he had congestive heart failure, but is asymptomatic now, with normal vital signs and physical examination. An echocardiogram shows an estimated ejection fraction of 38%. The patient likes to keep medications to a minimum. He is currently on aspirin and simvastatin. Which would be the most appropriate additional treatment?
options: Begin an ACE inhibitor and then add a beta-blocker on a scheduled basis
Begin digoxin plus furosemide on a scheduled basis
Begin spironolactone on a scheduled basis
Given his preferences, no other medication is needed unless shortness of breath and swelling recur
explanation: EF 38% after heart failure (stage C) needs prognostic therapy: ACEi (or ARB/ARNI) plus beta-blocker, then MRA and SGLT2i, even if now asymptomatic.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is referred by an OB- GYN colleague for the onset of fatigue and dyspnoea on exertion 1 month after her second vaginal delivery. Physical examination reveals a laterally displaced PMI, elevated jugular venous pressure and 2+ pitting lower extremity oedema. Echocardiogram shows systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 30%. Which statement most accurately describes her condition?
options: This disease may occur unexpectedly years after pregnancy and delivery
About half of similar patients will recover completely
The condition is idiosyncratic; the risk of recurrence with a future pregnancy is no greater than average
This condition will require a different therapeutic approach than the typical dilated cardiomyopathy
This condition will require endomyocardial biopsy for diagnosis
explanation: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (EF < 45% late pregnancy to 5 months postpartum): about half recover fully; recurrence in later pregnancies is common.

stem: A 32-year-old male presents to your office with concern about progressive fatigue and lower extremity oedema. Past medical history is significant for sickle cell anaemia and diabetes mellitus. He has had multiple admissions to the hospital secondary to vasoocclusive crises since the age of three. Physical examination reveals a displaced PMI, but is otherwise unremarkable. ECG shows a first degree AV block and low voltage. Chest x-ray shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields. Which of the following would be the best initial diagnostic approach?

Order CT scan of the chest
Arrange for placement of a 24-hour ambulatory cardiac monitor
explanation: Multiply transfused patients develop iron-overload cardiomyopathy: check ferritin and transferrin saturation, then cardiac MRI T2*; chelation can reverse it.

stem: A 71-year-old woman is admitted with acute dyspnoea to the Emergency Department. Oxygen saturations are 94% on 28% supplementary oxygen and her respiratory rate is 30/min. A rapid B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) assay is reported as follows: BNP 62 pg/ml What is the best interpretation of this result?
options: No conclusion can be drawn from this result
Pulmonary embolism is the most likely cause of her symptoms
If a further BNP level is above 50 pg/ml after one hour then this is diagnostic of heart failure
Heart failure is unlikely to be the cause of her dyspnoea
Heart failure is highly likely to be the cause of her dyspnoea
explanation: BNP < 100 pg/mL (NT-proBNP < 300 acutely) has a high negative predictive value: acute heart failure is unlikely, so look for another cause.

stem: A 79-year-old man is admitted with congestive cardiac failure. Bloods on admission show: BNP 354 pg/ml Which one of the following would result from elevated BNP levels?
explanation: BNP causes natriuresis, vasodilatation and inhibits RAAS and sympathetic activity. Sacubitril raises natriuretic peptides by blocking neprilysin.

orig.stem: A 79-year-old man is admitted with congestive cardiac failure. Bloods on admission show: BNP 354 pg/ml Which one of the following would result from elevated BNP levels?
orig.explanation: Inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system BNP actions: natriuresis; vasodilation; RAAS and sympathetic inhibition. Does not reduce sodium diuresis or cause coronary vasoconstriction.

stem: Where is B-type natriuretic peptide mainly secreted from?
explanation: BNP/NT-proBNP is secreted mainly by ventricular myocytes in response to stretch; ANP comes from the atria.

orig.stem: Where is B-type natriuretic peptide mainly secreted from?
orig.explanation: Ventricular myocardium BNP mainly from ventricular myocardium under strain; rises in HF, ischemia, valvular disease, CKD; reduced by ACEi, ARB, diuretics; causes vasodilation and natriure sis.

stem: You have ordered a B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) test on a patient with suspected heart failure. It has come back as being slightly elevated. Which one of the following factors may account for a falsely elevated BNP?
explanation: BNP can be raised without LV failure in COPD (RV strain), PE, AF, sepsis, CKD, cirrhosis and age > 70. Obesity and HF drugs lower it.

orig.stem: You have ordered a B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) test on a patient with suspected heart failure. It has come back as being slightly elevated. Which one of the following factors may account for a falsely elevated BNP?

explanation: Hypertension in a young man with an arm BP difference suggests coarctation at or near the left subclavian origin (left arm lower). Check radiofemoral delay.

orig.stem: A 18-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension is noted to have a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg in the right arm and 120/80 mmHg in the left arm. What is the most likely underlying cause of his high blood pressure?

stem: An 18-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension has a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg in the right arm and 120/80 mmHg in the left arm. What best explains the difference between the two arms?
options: Atherosclerotic plaque in the left subclavian artery
Congenital anomaly of the brachial arteries
Coarctation of the aorta causing decreased flow to one arm
Incorrect cuff size on the left arm
explanation: Coarctation at or around the origin of the left subclavian artery reduces flow and pressure in the left arm, while the right arm, supplied from the brachiocephalic trunk proximal to the narrowing, remains hypertensive. More commonly the coarctation is distal to the left subclavian, and then both arms are hypertensive with weak, delayed femoral pulses. Subclavian stenosis from atheroma causes an arm difference in older smokers.

orig.stem: In the same patient, what best explains the difference between the blood pressure readings in the two arms?
options: Atherosclerotic plaque in the left subclavian artery
Congenital anomaly of the brachial arteries
Coarctation of the aorta causing decreased flow to one arm
Incorrect cuff size on the left arm
orig.explanation: Coarctation of the aorta causing decreased flow to one arm In coarctation of the aorta, the narrowing (usually just distal to the left subclavian artery) results in lower pressures in the left arm compared to the right.

stem: Which chest X-ray finding is most typically associated with coarctation of the aorta?
explanation: Inferior rib notching (ribs 3–8) from dilated intercostal collaterals is classic of coarctation, rarely before age 8; the '3 sign' is another clue.

orig.stem: Which chest X-ray finding is most typically associated with coarctation of the aorta?

stem: What is the definitive treatment for significant coarctation of the aorta (with hypertension or a large gradient)?

explanation: Significant coarctation (gradient ≥ 20 mmHg or hypertension) is repaired: stenting in suitable adults, surgery in infants. Lifelong follow-up for recoarctation.

stem: Which of the following best describes the second heart sound (S2) in patients with an ASD?

Loud S2 with a prominent P2
explanation: In ASD the shunt keeps RV volume high throughout respiration, so S2 is widely split with a fixed interval. Paradoxical splitting = LBBB or severe AS.

stem: Which of the following is true of Eisenmenger’s syndrome?

It occurs in patients with patent foramen ovale
Left to right shunting occurs because of pulmonary hypertension
Patients are peripherally but not centrally cyanosed
explanation: Eisenmenger syndrome: shunt reversal causes cyanosis, clubbing and erythrocytosis; life expectancy is markedly reduced and pregnancy is very high-risk.

stem: A 48 year old woman registers with a new family physician. She tells the doctor she had a small hole in her heart from birth but that it did not require any treatment. stem: You are working in a rural health clinic in Northern India. You evaluate an 8-year-old boy who has never seen a physician. His mother tells you that he is unable to keep up with his peers in terms of physical activity. On your initial examination of his skin, you notice clubbing and cyanosis in his feet, but his hands appear normal. Without any further examination, you suspect that he has which of the following congenital abnormalities?
options: Patent ductus arteriosus with secondary pulmonary hypertension
explanation: Clubbing and cyanosis of toes but not fingers (differential cyanosis) is PDA with pulmonary hypertension and shunt reversal.

stem: Mrs. Hellwig is a 25-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) complicated by nephropathy, hemolytic anaemia, and pleuritis. Her disease is well controlled on therapy. She recently discovered that she is pregnant, and presents today for prenatal counseling. She specifically is concerned about the effect her autoimmune disease may have on the infant. You tell her that the most common cardiac complication in children born to mothers with SLE is:
options: Pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular (RV) failure
explanation: Maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies damage the fetal conduction system, causing congenital complete heart block; monitor the fetal heart from 16 weeks.

options: Pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular (RV) failure
orig.explanation: AV block Congenital AV block is the most common cardiac manifestation in infants of mothers with SLE.

stem: A 37-year-old woman with no significant past medical history except for a childhood murmur is evaluated for sudden-onset severe pain in her right lower extremity. Examination is notable for pallor distal to the right knee, a cold leg, and absent dorsalis pedis pulse on the right, with the left leg being normal. Which of the following studies is likely to diagnose the underlying reason for the patient’s presentation?
options: Venous ultrasound of right upper extremity
explanation: Limb ischaemia in a young woman with a childhood murmur suggests paradoxical embolism through an ASD/PFO; echo with bubble study shows the shunt.
