orig.explanation: Continue observation Accelerated idioventricular rhythm post-reperfusion is benign and requires no treatment.

stem: A 73-year-old woman has chest discomfort and a slow pulse of 53/min with occasional pauses. Her ECG shows sinus bradycardia with intermittent pauses of 3 seconds in which no P wave appears. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sinus pauses with absent P waves plus bradycardia in an older person is sick sinus syndrome. In AV block P waves are present but not conducted.

orig.stem: A 73-year-old woman complains of suddenonset chest pain. On examination you note her pulse is regular at 53 beats/min. You request an electrocardiogram (ECG) which demonstrates a time interval of 3 seconds between each consecutive P wave. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Sick sinus syndrome Sick sinus syndrome is characterized by a prolonged interval between P waves, indicating sinoatrial node dysfunction.

stem: A 63-year-old man complains of gradual-onset chest pain. On examination you note his pulse is regular at 60 beats/min. You request an ECG which demonstrates an increasing PR interval which eventually culminates in an absent QRS complex after the P wave. What is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 63-year-old man complains of gradual-onset chest pain. On examination you note his pulse is regular at 60 beats/min. You request an ECG which demonstrates an increasing PR interval which eventually culminates in an absent QRS complex after the P wave. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Mobitz type 1 block Mobitz type 1 block (Wenckebach phenomenon) is characterized by progressively lengthening PR intervals until a beat is dropped.

stem: A 28-year-old man with no past medical history and not on medications presents to the emergency department with palpitations for several hours and was found to have supraventricular tachycardia. Carotid massage was attempted without success. What is the treatment of choice to stop the attack?
explanation: If vagal manoeuvres fail, adenosine (6 mg rapid bolus, then 12 and 18 mg) terminates AV-node-dependent SVT; verapamil if asthmatic.

orig.stem: A 28-year-old man with no past medical history and not on medications presents to the emergency department with palpitations for several hours and was found to have supraventricular tachycardia. Carotid massage was attempted without success. What is the treatment of choice to stop the attack?
orig.explanation: IV adenosine IV adenosine is the treatment of choice for terminating supraventricular tachycardia.

stem: A 75-year-old smoker with ischaemic heart disease and previous heart failure presents with a 6-hour history of palpitations and increasing breathlessness. He is alert, BP 128/76 mmHg, SpO2 94% on air, with no chest pain, and his chest is clear. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 160/min, and vagal manoeuvres have had no effect. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Slow the heart rate with IV atenolol to help identify the rhythm
IV lidocaine 50 mg bolus followed by an infusion of 4 mg/min
IV adenosine to terminate the rhythm or reveal the underlying atrial activity
Immediate DC cardioversion, because the rhythm may be ventricular tachycardia
Withhold oxygen because he is a smoker
explanation: Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: after vagal manoeuvres give adenosine, which ends AVNRT/AVRT or unmasks flutter waves. Cardiovert only if adverse features.

orig.stem: A 75-year-old cigarette smoker with known ischaemic heart disease and a history of cardiac failure presents to the emergency department with a 6-hour history of increasing dyspnoea. His ECG shows a narrow complex regular tachycardia with a rate of 160 beats/min. What is the most appropriate initial step in patient care?
options: His heart rate should be slowed using IV atenolol to aid in the diagnosis of the rhythm
He should be given a single IV dose of lignocaine (50 mg) followed by an infusion at 4 mg/ min
He should be given IV adenosine to aid in the diagnosis of the rhythm
His rhythm may represent a ventricular tachycardia and he should be immediately cardioverted
He should not be given high flow oxygen
orig.explanation: He should be given IV adenosine to aid in the diagnosis of the rhythm IV adenosine can help to slow the heart rate and unmask the underlying rhythm in narrow complex tachycardias.

stem: A 57-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of a strong family history of heart disease. An ECG shows sinus rhythm with a constant PR interval of 300 ms (0.3 s), and every P wave is followed by a QRS complex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: PR > 200 ms with every P conducted is first-degree AV block (ageing, vagal tone, AV-nodal drugs, inferior MI); no treatment needed alone.

orig.stem: A 57-year-old man comes to his general practitioner (GP) concerned about his general health. He is particularly worried as there is a strong family history of heart disease. The GP performs an ECG which shows a prolonged PR interval of 0.3 seconds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: First-degree AV block A prolonged PR interval of 0.3 seconds is indicative of first-degree AV block.

stem: A 75-year-old man is referred by the GP to the cardiology outpatient clinic. The patient has atrial fibrillation (AF) and hypertension. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 124/80 mmHg and his pulse varies between 90 and 130 beats/min. His last echocardiogram (done 1 month ago) revealed left atrial chamber dimensions that are increased above normal. What is the most effective management?

orig.stem: A 75-year-old man is referred by the GP to the cardiology outpatient clinic. The patient has atrial fibrillation (AF) and hypertension. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 124/80 mmHg and his pulse varies between 90 and 130 beats/min. His last echocardiogram (done 1 month ago) revealed left atrial chamber dimensions that are increased above normal. What is the most effective management?
orig.explanation: Digoxin, with warfarin Rate control with digoxin and anticoagulation with warfarin is appropriate given the risk of thromboembolism in AF with enlarged atria.

stem: You are the junior doctor on call and a nurse asks you to review an ECG. It shows regular P waves with a constant PR interval in the conducted beats, but some P waves are not followed by a QRS complex; there is no progressive PR prolongation before the dropped beats. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Dropped P waves with a fixed PR in conducted beats is Mobitz II: infranodal, can progress abruptly to complete block, so pace permanently.

orig.stem: You are a house officer on call when a nurse bleeps you to review an ECG. The ECG demonstrates an intermittent absence of the QRS complex but no evidence of progressive PR interval increase. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Mobitz type 2 block Mobitz type 2 block is characterized by intermittent non-conducted P waves without prior PR prolongation.

stem: You are a house officer on call when you are bleeped to see a patient complaining of dizziness. On further questioning the patient comments that he has blacked out on several occasions in the past. You perform an ECG which shows regular P and QRS complexes occurring independently of one another. What is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: You are a house officer on call when you are bleeped to see a patient complaining of dizziness. On further questioning the patient comments that he has blacked out on several occasions in the past. You perform an ECG which shows regular P and QRS complexes occurring independently of one another. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Complete heart block Complete heart block with dissociation between atrial and ventricular activity can cause blackouts and dizziness, often requiring pacemaker insertion.

stem: You are a house officer on call when you are asked to see a 48-year-old man who is found to be unresponsive by the nursing staff. You cannot obtain a palpable carotid pulse and the cardiac monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the first appropriate measure?
explanation: Pulseless VF is a shockable rhythm: defibrillate immediately, then 2 min CPR. Adrenaline is given after the third shock; bicarbonate and calcium are not routine.

orig.stem: You are a house officer on call when you are asked to see a 48-year-old man who is found to be unresponsive by the nursing staff. You cannot obtain a palpable carotid pulse and the cardiac monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the first appropriate measure?
options: One ampoule injection of IV calcium chloride
One ampoule injection of IV adrenaline
orig.explanation: Defibrillation with 200 J In ventricular fibrillation, immediate defibrillation is the first step according to advanced life support guidelines.

stem: At an ECG teaching session, a consultant describes a patient admitted to the coronary care unit with a regular atrial rate of 300/min and a regular ventricular rate of 150/min. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Atrial rate 300/min with ventricular rate 150/min is atrial flutter with 2:1 block; suspect it in any regular narrow tachycardia near 150/min.

orig.stem: A medical student attending a teaching session on ECG interpretation. The consultant tells you that a patient was admitted to the coronary care unit with an atrial rate of 300 beats/min and a ventricular rate of 150 beats/min. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Atrial flutter Atrial flutter with a 2:1 block typically presents with an atrial rate of 300 and a ventricular rate of 150.

stem: A patient on the coronary care unit develops new atrial flutter with an atrial rate of 300/min and a ventricular rate of 150/min; it began about 6 hours ago. He is haemodynamically stable, and a rhythm-control strategy is chosen. What is the most effective first-line treatment to restore sinus rhythm?
explanation: Synchronised DC cardioversion restores sinus rhythm in > 90% of flutter (drugs work poorly); anticoagulate as for AF. CTI ablation prevents recurrence.

orig.stem: You are a house officer on call when you are asked to review a patient in the coronary care unit. You note that the patient has an atrial rate of 300 beats/ min and a ventricular rate of 150 beats/min. The nurse says this is of new onset. Which management plan would you instigate first?
orig.explanation: Electrical cardioversion Electrical cardioversion is the initial management for new onset atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response.

stem: A previously well 36-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 2-month history of attacks of palpitations and sweating. The attacks come on suddenly and are unrelated to food, posture or exercise. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Which of the following investigations is the LEAST useful in evaluating her?
explanation: Paroxysmal palpitations with sweating: check TFTs, metanephrines (phaeochromocytoma), ambulatory ECG and echo. An upper GI study has no role.

orig.stem: A previously fit and well 36-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 2-month history of palpitations and sweats. These attacks come on suddenly and are unrelated to food intake, supine posture or exercise. She is a nonsmoker and does not drink alcohol. Which of the following investigations is the LEAST useful to evaluate this patient?
orig.explanation: Upper gastrointestinal study An upper gastrointestinal study is not useful in evaluating palpitations unrelated to gastrointestinal symptoms.

stem: A 57-year-old Bangladeshi patient is admitted to accident and emergency (AE) with palpitations. He speaks very little English but tells you he has a ‘heart problem’. On examination you note his pulse is irregular at 145 beats/min. An ECG is performed which demonstrates no P waves. Which management plan would you instigate first?
explanation: Irregular tachycardia without P waves is AF; first-line rate control in a stable patient is a beta-blocker (bisoprolol). Flecainide is for rhythm control.

orig.stem: A 57-year-old Bangladeshi patient is admitted to accident and emergency (AE) with palpitations. He speaks very little English but tells you he has a ‘heart problem’. On examination you note his pulse is irregular at 145 beats/min. An ECG is performed which demonstrates no P waves. Which management plan would you instigate first?
orig.explanation: Bisoprolol Beta-blockers like bisoprolol are the initial management for rate control in atrial fibrillation.

stem: A 37-year-old woman develops palpitations after recent surgery. Her pulse is regular at 175/min and BP is 125/70 mmHg; she is otherwise well. She has asthma. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
explanation: Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: vagal manoeuvres first (carotid massage if young, no bruit); then adenosine, or verapamil if asthmatic.

orig.stem: A 37-year-old woman is complaining of palpitations following recent surgery. On examination her pulse rate is regular at 175 beats/min and blood pressure is stable at 125/70 mmHg. She tells you she was seen the night before by the on-call cardiologist for the same problem. Her past medical history includes asthma. You request an ECG which shows normal-shaped QRS complexes but no P waves. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
orig.explanation: Carotid sinus massage Carotid sinus massage is a useful non-pharmacological maneuver to manage SVT, especially when adenosine is contraindicated due to asthma.

stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after collapsing during football training. He is now alert and orientated, and his vital signs and examination are normal. He remembers feeling dizzy before collapsing but recalls little else. He is normally healthy and takes no regular medication. Blood tests have been sent. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Syncope during exercise is a cardiac red flag (HCM, long QT, WPW, Brugada, ARVC); a 12-lead ECG is the essential first test.

orig.stem: A 16-year-old boy athlete is brought to AE after he collapsed during football training. On arrival, he appears alert and orientated. His vital signs and physical examination are normal. He remembers feeling dizzy prior to collapsing but cannot recall much else. He is normally healthy and not on any regular medications. Blood tests have been sent. What is the most appropriate next step for this patient?
orig.explanation: Order an ECG An ECG is essential in evaluating syncope in an athlete to rule out cardiac causes.

stem: An otherwise healthy 50-year-old man presents to his GP with palpitations and is found to have an irregularly irregular pulse. The episode lasts less than 2 hours in total and resolves without treatment. Full blood count, biochemistry, thyroid function, ECG and echocardiogram are all normal. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Brief self-terminating AF with CHA2DS2-VASc 0 and a normal heart needs no anticoagulation; antiplatelets are never used for AF stroke prevention.

orig.stem: An otherwise healthy 50-year-old male presents to the GP with palpitations and is noted to have an irregular heartbeat. He is otherwise fit and healthy. This resolves without treatment. Total duration was less than 2 hours. Full blood count, metabolic profile, thyroid studies, ECG and echocardiogram were all normal. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate treatment?
orig.explanation: Do nothing In the absence of document ed arrhythmia and with normal investigations, no treatment is necessary.

stem: A 79-year-old woman is admitted to the coronary care unit with unstable angina and started on appropriate antiplatelet and anti-anginal therapy. She has hypertension; fasting glucose is normal and total cholesterol is 5.2 mmol/L. She is found to be in atrial fibrillation. What is the most appropriate treatment to reduce her risk of stroke?
explanation: CHA2DS2-VASc 5: oral anticoagulation. After ACS with AF: brief triple therapy (≤ 1 week), then DOAC + clopidogrel to 12 months, then DOAC alone.

orig.stem: A 79-year-old woman is admitted to the coronary care unit (CCU) with unstable angina. She is started on appropriate medication to reduce her cardiac risk. She is hypertensive, fasting glucose is normal and cholesterol is 5.2. She is found to be in atrial fibrillation. What is the most appropriate treatment?
orig.explanation: Warfarin Anticoagulation with warfarin is indicated in high-risk patients with atrial fibrillation to reduce stroke risk.

stem: A 21-year-old man is on his way home from a party when he experiences the sudden onset of rapid palpitations. He feels uncomfortable but not short of breath and has no chest pain. He goes to the nearest accident and emergency department, where he is found to have a supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) at a rate of 170/ minute. Carotid sinus massage produced transient reversion to sinus rhythm, after which the tachycardia resumed. What would be the next step in your management?

orig.stem: A 21-year-old man is on his way home from a party when he experiences the sudden onset of rapid palpitations. He feels uncomfortable but not short of breath and has no chest pain. He goes to the nearest accident and emergency department, where he is found to have a supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) at a rate of 170/ minute. Carotid sinus massage produced transient reversion to sinus rhythm, after which the tachycardia resumed. What would be the next step in your management?
orig.explanation: IV adenosine IV adenosine is the drug of choice for terminating SVT due to its rapid onset and offset.

stem: A 29-year-old woman sees her GP with fatigue, palpitations and weight loss without dieting. Her pulse is about 120/min and irregularly irregular, BP 142/89 mmHg and BMI 19 kg/m2; there are no added heart sounds. An ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. What is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: Weight loss, fatigue and new AF in a young woman suggest hyperthyroidism: check TSH and free T4 (recommended in all new AF).

orig.stem: A 29-year-old woman goes to see her GP complaining of fatigue and palpitations. She says she has also lost weight, though without dieting. On examination, her pulse rate is approximately 120/min and irregularly irregular. Her blood pressure is 142/89 mmHg and her body mass index is 19. There are no added cardiac sounds. The ECG confirms the diagnosis of atrial fibrillation. What would you suggest as the most useful next investigation?
orig.explanation: Thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4) Thyrotoxicosis is a common cause of new-onset atrial fibrillation in young patients.

stem: A 62-year-old man with a previous myocardial infarction presents with palpitations that began 3 hours ago; this is his first known episode. The ECG shows atrial fibrillation at about 130/min without acute ischaemic changes. He has mild central chest discomfort, but BP is 128/80 mmHg and he is not distressed. A rhythm-control strategy is preferred. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Heparin and digoxin at the standard daily dose
Heparin followed by synchronised DC cardioversion
Wait for spontaneous reversion to sinus rhythm
explanation: AF < 48 h can be cardioverted once heparin is started. Prior MI contraindicates flecainide, so use DC cardioversion (or amiodarone).

orig.stem: A 62-year-old male presents with palpitations, which are shown on ECG to be atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of approximately 130/minute. He has mild central chest discomfort but is not acutely distressed. He first noticed these about 3 hours before coming to hospital. As far as is known this is his first episode of this kind. Which of the following would you prefer as first-line therapy?
options: Anticoagulate with heparin and start digoxin at standard daily dose
Administer bisoprolol and verapamil, and give warfarin
Wait to see if there is spontaneous reversion to sinus rhythm
orig.explanation: Attempt DC cardioversion Acute onset favors DC cardioversion without prior anticoagulation.

stem: In the ICU, a patient suddenly becomes pulseless and unresponsive, with cardiac monitor indicating ventricular tachycardia. The crash cart is immediately available. What is the best first therapy?

orig.stem: In the ICU, a patient suddenly becomes pulseless and unresponsive, with cardiac monitor indicating ventricular tachycardia. The crash cart is immediately available. What is the best first therapy?
orig.explanation: Defibrillation Defibrillation is the standard first-line treatment for ventricular fibrillation or unstable VT.

stem: A 36-year-old man presents with the sensation of a racing heart. His blood pressure is 110/70, respiratory rate 14/minute, and O2 saturation 98%. His ECG shows a narrow QRS complex tachycardia with rate 180, which you correctly diagnose as paroxysmal atrial tachycardia. Carotid massage and Valsalva maneuver do not improve the heart rate. Which of the following is the initial therapy of choice?
options: Verapamil 2.5 to 5 mg IV over 1 to 2 minutes

orig.stem: A 36-year-old man presents with the sensation of a racing heart. His blood pressure is 110/70, respiratory rate 14/minute, and O2 saturation 98%. His ECG shows a narrow QRS complex tachycardia with rate 180, which you correctly diagnose as paroxysmal atrial tachycardia. Carotid massage and Valsalva maneuver do not improve the heart rate. Which of the following is the initial therapy of choice?
options: Verapamil 2.5 to 5 mg IV over 1 to 2 minutes
orig.explanation: Adenosine 6-mg rapid IV bolus Adenosine is the drug of choice for SVT due to its safety and short half-life.

stem: A 60-year-old woman develops chest pain, respiratory distress, and confusion after right hip replacement surgery. She is confused and appears in respiratory distress. Blood pressure is 80/50, heart rate of 155/minute. ECG reveals atrial fibrillation. Which of the following is the best management of this patient’s arrhythmia?

orig.stem: A 60-year-old woman develops chest pain, respiratory distress, and confusion after right hip replacement surgery. She is confused and appears in respiratory distress. Blood pressure is 80/50, heart rate of 155/minute. ECG reveals atrial fibrillation. Which of the following is the best management of this patient’s arrhythmia?
orig.explanation: Immediate electric cardioversion Immediate synchronized cardioversion is indicated in hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation.

stem: A 69-year-old woman with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and asthma is evaluated. Episodes are infrequent, and echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart. Which statement regarding her management is correct?
options: Digoxin effectively prevents recurrences of the arrhythmia
Sotalol is a suitable choice to prevent recurrences
Oral flecainide taken as needed may be an effective way to terminate an attack
explanation: Infrequent paroxysmal AF in a normal heart: 'pill-in-the-pocket' flecainide with an AV-nodal blocker. Sotalol is contraindicated in asthma.

orig.stem: A 69-year-old woman with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and asthma is evaluated. Which statement regarding her management is correct?
options: Digoxin effectively prevents recurrence of the arrhythmia
Flecainide orally may be an effective as-needed treatment to abort an attack
orig.explanation: Flecainide orally may be an effective as-needed treatment to abort an attack Flecainide is recommended as an as-needed treatment; other agents are either ineffective or contraindicated in her context.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of shortness of breath. His pulse is irregular at 140/min, and the ECG shows atrial fibrillation. What would you expect to see in the jugular venous pulse?
explanation: The a wave is atrial contraction, so it is absent in AF. Cannon a waves = AV dissociation; large v waves = tricuspid regurgitation.

orig.stem: A 67-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of shortness of breath. On exam, his pulse is irregular at 140 bpm. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. What JVP finding would you expect?
orig.explanation: Absent ‘a waves’ Atrial fibrillation results in absent ‘a waves’ due to loss of effective atrial contraction.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with exertional chest tightness relieved by rest. ECG reveals first degree heart block. Which ECG finding is typical?

orig.stem: A 56-year-old man presents with exertional chest tightness relieved by rest. ECG reveals first degree heart block. Which ECG finding is typical?
orig.explanation: PR interval > 200 ms First degree heart block is defined by a PR interval >200 ms.

stem: An 82-year-old woman is admitted for observation after presenting with dizziness, and the rhythm strip shown is recorded on the monitor. She has no history of cardiac disease, diabetes or hypertension. On questioning she reports several previous episodes of transient dizziness and one brief syncope. Examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the best plan of care?
options: Reassurance; this is a benign condition and needs no treatment
Reassurance and advice not to drive until symptom-free; no other treatment
Nuclear cardiac stress testing, with treatment depending on the result
explanation: Rapid SVT ending in a long pause with dizziness/syncope is tachy–brady sick sinus syndrome: permanent pacemaker, then rate-control drugs safely.

orig.stem: An 82-year-old white female is admitted to the hospital for observation after presenting to the emergency department with dizziness. After being placed on a cardiac monitor in the ER, the rhythm strip below was recorded. There is no past history of cardiac disease, diabetes, or hypertension. With prompting, the patient discloses several prior episodes of transient dizziness and one episode of brief syncope in the past. Physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the best plan of care?
options: Reassurance. This is a benign condition, and no direct therapy is needed.
Reassurance. The patient may not drive until she is symptom free, but otherwise no direct therapy is needed.
Nuclear cardiac stress testing; treatment depending on results.
Arrange placement of a permanent pacemaker.
orig.explanation: Arrange placement of a permanent pacemaker. Tachy-brady syndrome with symptomatic pauses → pacemaker; may still need antiarrhythmic for tachy; consider anticoagulation; aspirin in sufficient.

stem: A 30-year-old female presents with a chief complaint of palpitations. A 24-hour Holter monitor shows occasional unifocal premature ventricular contractions and premature atrial contractions. Which of the following is the best management for this patient?

orig.stem: A 30-year-old female presents with a chief complaint of palpitations. A 24-hour Holter monitor shows occasional unifocal premature ventricular contractions and premature atrial contractions. Which of the following is the best management for this patient?
orig.explanation: Reassurance, no medication Isolated PVCs without structural disease are benign; no therapy; beta-blocker if symptomatic; avoid class I drugs; digoxin not useful.

stem: An active 78-year-old woman with hypertension presents with a new left hemiparesis; CT excludes haemorrhage, and cardiac monitoring shows atrial fibrillation. She was in sinus rhythm at a check-up 3 months earlier. Optimal management at discharge includes review of her antihypertensive therapy, a ventricular rate-control agent and which of the following?
options: An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator/permanent pacemaker to avoid the need for anticoagulation
Antiplatelet therapy such as aspirin, without anticoagulation
Antiplatelet therapy plus warfarin with a target INR of 1.5
Long-term oral anticoagulation (a DOAC, or warfarin with a target INR of 2.0–3.0)
explanation: Ischaemic stroke with AF (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 6): lifelong anticoagulation, DOAC preferred (or warfarin INR 2–3), started within days depending on infarct size.

orig.stem: An active 78-year-old female with history of hypertension presents with the new onset of left hemiparesis. Cardiac monitoring reveals atrial fibrillation. She had been in sinus rhythm on checkup 3 months earlier. Optimal manage ment at discharge includes a review of antihypertensive therapy, a ventricular rate control agent, and which of the following?
options: Automated implanted cardioverter-defibrillator (AICD)/permanent pacemaker to avoid the need for anticoagulation
Antiplatelet therapy such as aspirin, without warfarin
Antiplatelet therapy plus warfarin with a target INR of 1.5
Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0.
orig.explanation: Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0. AF with stroke risk → warfarin INR 2–3 (mechanical valve 2.5–3.5); anticoagulate before cardioversion or TEE-guided; AICD is for ventricular arrhythmias.

stem: A 72-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension develops a viral upper respiratory infection. On the second day he has palpitations and attends the emergency department. His BP is 118/78 mmHg and he is otherwise well. The rhythm strip (lead V1) is shown. What is the best next step in management?
options: Initiation of chest compressions and preparation for semielective intubation
explanation: Flutter waves ~250/min with 2:1 block in a stable patient: rate control first with IV metoprolol, then anticoagulation and elective cardioversion/ablation.

orig.stem: A 72-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled hypertension develops a viral upper respiratory infection. On his second day of symptoms he experiences palpitations and presents to the emergency room. His blood pressure is 118/78. The following rhythm strip is obtained. What is the best next step in the management of this patient?
options: Initiation of chest compressions and preparation for semielective intubation
orig.explanation: Administration of intravenous metoprolol Atrial flutter with RVR: if stable, rate control via AV nodal blockade (metoprolol). Adenosine diagnostic only; amiodarone for maintenance; no CPR.

stem: An asymptomatic 65-year-old man with diabetes attends the emergency department with a sports-related right shoulder injury. His pulse is irregular, and the rhythm strip shown is recorded; BP and the rest of the examination are normal. What is the best immediate management?
explanation: Progressive PR lengthening until a dropped beat is Mobitz I (AV-nodal, benign): observe and review AV-nodal drugs if asymptomatic.

orig.stem: An otherwise asymptomatic 65-year-old man with diabetes presents to the ER with a sports-related right shoulder injury. His heart rate is noted to be irregular, and this ECG is obtained. Which of the following is the best immediate therapy?
orig.explanation: Observation AV block types; tracing = Mobitz I (Wenckebach) with progressive PR then dropped beat; usually benign, often drug or inferior MI; rarely needs pacing.

stem: In the intensive care unit, a monitored patient suddenly becomes unresponsive and pulseless, and the monitor shows ventricular tachycardia. A defibrillator is immediately available. What is the best first treatment?
explanation: Pulseless VT is managed exactly like ventricular fibrillation: in a monitored, witnessed arrest with a defibrillator at hand, give an immediate unsynchronised shock (biphasic 120–200 J; up to three successive shocks may be given in this setting), then resume CPR. Synchronised cardioversion is for VT with a pulse – in pulseless VT, attempting to synchronise only delays the shock. Adrenaline 1 mg is given after the third shock and then every 3–5 minutes, with amiodarone 300 mg (or lidocaine) after the third shock.

orig.stem: In the ICU, a patient suddenly becomes pulseless and unresponsive, with cardiac monitor indicating ventricular tachycardia. The crash cart is immediately available. What is the best first therapy?
orig.explanation: Defibrillation at 200 J VF/unstable VT → defibrillate, epinephrine as needed, then amiodarone/lidocaine/procainamide; magnesium for torsades/hypomagnesemia.

stem: A 36-year-old male presents with the sensation of a racing heart. His blood pressure is 110/70, respiratory rate 14/minute, and O2 saturation 98%. His ECG shows a narrow QRS complex tachycardia with rate 180, which you correctly diagnose as paroxysmal atrial tachycardia. Carotid massage and Valsalva maneuver do not improve the heart rate. Which of the following is the initial therapy of choice?
options: Verapamil 2.5 to 5 mg IV over 1 to 2 min

orig.stem: A 36-year-old male presents with the sensation of a racing heart. His blood pressure is 110/70, respiratory rate 14/minute, and O2 saturation 98%. His ECG shows a narrow QRS complex tachycardia with rate 180, which you correctly diagnose as paroxysmal atrial tachycardia. Carotid massage and Valsalva maneuver do not improve the heart rate. Which of the following is the initial therapy of choice?
options: Verapamil 2.5 to 5 mg IV over 1 to 2 min
orig.explanation: Adenosine 6-mg rapid IV bolus Stable SVT: adenosine 6 mg then 12 mg; verapamil next; diltiazem/digoxin slower; cardioversion if unstable; lidocaine for ventricular rhythms.

stem: A patient has been on the coronary care unit for 24 hours with an acute anterior myocardial infarction. He develops the rhythm shown, although his BP remains stable at 110/68 mmHg. What is the best next step in management?
options: Pacing (temporary transvenous, then assessment for a permanent pacemaker)
explanation: Complete heart block after anterior MI is infranodal with an unreliable escape rhythm: pace (temporary, then assess permanent) even if BP is stable.

orig.stem: A patient has been in the coronary care unit for the past 24 hours with an acute anterior myocardial infarction. He develops the abnormal rhythm shown below, although blood pressure remains stable at 110/68. Which of the following is the best next step in therapy?
orig.explanation: Arrange for pacemaker placement. Complete heart block in MI: AV dissociation → temporary then likely permanent pacing; atropine temporizes; avoid AV-nodal blockers and lidocaine.

stem: A 62-year-old man with COPD develops a viral upper respiratory infection and starts an over-the-counter decongestant. Shortly afterwards he has palpitations and attends the emergency department, where the rhythm strip shown is recorded. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Regular saw-tooth waves ~300/min with a QRS after every fourth is atrial flutter with 4:1 block; decongestants and lung disease are triggers.

orig.stem: A 62-year-old male with underlying COPD develops a viral upper respiratory infection and begins taking an over-the-counter decongestant. Shortly thereafter he experiences palpitations and presents to the emergency room, where the following rhythm strip is obtained. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Paroxysmal atrial tachycardia with 2:1 atrioventricular block
Complete heart block with 2:1 atrioventricular block
orig.explanation: Atrial flutter with 4:1 atrioventricular block Atrial flutter with 4:1 conduction: atrial ~300, ventricular 75; sawtooth waves; excludes PAT/ junctional.

stem: An 80-year-old woman is admitted with dizziness. Monitoring shows atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, which is controlled with a beta-blocker. Echocardiography shows an enlarged left atrium, an ejection fraction of 50% and no diastolic dysfunction. She is now asymptomatic, with BP 130/80 mmHg and an irregularly irregular pulse of about 80/min. What is the best management strategy for her arrhythmia?
options: Continued rate control plus prolonged anticoagulation
explanation: Older patient with dilated LA, now rate-controlled and asymptomatic: continue rate control plus long-term anticoagulation (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 3).

orig.stem: An 80-year-old woman was admitted to your service for dizziness. Cardiac monitoring initially revealed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Her ventricular rate was controlled with beta-blocker. An echocardiogram revealed an enlarged left atrium and an ejection fraction of 50%. No evidence of diastolic heart dysfunction was noted. She is now asymptomatic, with blood pressure 130/80, heart rhythm irregularly irregular, and heart rate around 80/minute. Which of the following is the best management strategy of this patient’s arrhythmia?
options: Continued rate control plus prolonged anticoagulation
orig.explanation: Continued rate control plus prolonged anticoagulation AF strategy: rate control first; cardiovert only if symptomatic despite control; large LA predicts relapse; continue long-term anticoagulation.

stem: During medical screening of new military recruits, an 18-year-old man reports several episodes of palpitations and syncope over the past few years. Examination is unremarkable. Excerpts from his ECG are shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Previous myocardial infarction secondary to coronary artery disease
explanation: Short PR, delta wave and wide QRS is pre-excitation (WPW); palpitations or syncope warrant an EP study and pathway ablation.

orig.stem: You are performing medical screening of new military recruits when an 18-year-old male reports several episodes of palpitation and syncope over the past several years. Physical examination is unremarkable. An ECG is obtained with excerpts shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Prior myocardial infarction secondary to coronary artery disease
orig.explanation: Preexcitation syndrome (Wolff-Parkinson-White) WPW: short PR + delta wave + wide QRS; can mimic Q waves; not MI or MS; HOCM shows LVH changes.

stem: A 38-year-old man with no past medical history is referred after an abnormal preoperative ECG, and long QT syndrome is confirmed on repeat ECGs. His father had a heart condition diagnosed in his 20s, and he himself has had episodes of syncope after exertion. He is started on a beta-blocker and an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is planned. Loss of function of which of the following is most commonly associated with his condition?
explanation: Congenital long QT is most often loss of potassium-channel function (KCNQ1 LQT1, hERG LQT2); treat with nadolol/propranolol and avoid QT drugs.

orig.stem: A 38-year-old with no past medical history is referred to the clinic after an abnormal ECG finding is identified as part of a preoperative workup. Long QT syndrome is identified on repeat ECGs. On further questioning, the patient reports his father had a heart condition identified in his 20s, although he is unsure of the specific diagnosis, and he has experienced previous episodes of syncope following exertion. The patient is started on a beta-blocker and a plan to insert an implantable cardioverter defibrillator is made. A loss of what function is associated with this patient’s condition?
orig.explanation: Potassium channels Long QT usually from K+ channel loss or drugs or electrolytes; affects ventricular repolarization. AV node disease changes PR not QT. Brugada and early repolarization ≠ LQTS. SA node issues affect P waves. Na+ channel loss less typical than K+ in LQTS.

stem: A 55-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease presents with palpitations for the past 10 days. His pulse is 130/min and irregularly irregular. He had one previous episode of atrial fibrillation 3 months ago, which was terminated by elective cardioversion after anticoagulation with warfarin. Which term best describes his arrhythmia?
explanation: AF lasting > 7 days (or needing cardioversion after 7 days) is persistent; paroxysmal ends within 7 days, permanent means rhythm control abandoned.

orig.stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of ischaemic heart disease presents to the Emergency Department with palpitations for the past 10 days. Examination of his pulse reveals a rate of 130 bpm which is irregularly irregular. He has had one previous episode of atrial fibrillation 3 months ago which was terminated by elective cardioversion following warfarinisation. What term best describes his arrhythmia?
orig.explanation: Persistent atrial fibrillation AF patterns: first detected; paroxysmal <7 days; persistent >7 days; permanent when accepted or non-cardiovertible. Goals: rate control and anticoagulation as indicated.

stem: A 72-year-old man with hypertension and ischaemic heart disease presents with light-headedness. He takes bisoprolol, amlodipine and aspirin. Heart rate is 38/min, BP 96/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on air and temperature 37.1 °C. The ECG shows regular P–P and R–R intervals with no relationship between the P waves and the QRS complexes. What would you expect to hear on auscultation of the heart?
explanation: In complete heart block the varying AV interval makes S1 intensity vary (with intermittent cannon a waves). Stop bisoprolol and pace.

orig.stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with lightheadedness. He has a past medical history of hypertension and ischaemic heart disease. His medications include bisoprolol, amlodipine, and aspirin. Observations: - Heart rate 38 beats per minute - Blood pressure 96/54 mmHg - Respiratory rate 18/minute - Oxygen saturations 97% on room air - Temperature 37.1°C An ECG demonstrates a regular P-P interval and a regular R-R interval but there is no apparent relationship between the P waves and the QRS complexes. When auscultating this patient’s heart sounds, what is an expected finding?
orig.explanation: Variable intensity of S1 Complete heart block → variable S1 intensity. Loud S1: MS or TS. Soft S1: MR, severe HF, LBBB, 1° AV block. Loud S2: systemic HTN. Soft S2: severe AS.

stem: A 56-year-old man is brought in by paramedics after fainting this morning; he is now conscious but pale and light-headed, with no injuries. His heart rate is 37/min, respiratory rate 16/min and BP 105/70 mmHg. The ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a prolonged PR interval. What is the initial management?
explanation: Bradycardia with an adverse feature (syncope): IV atropine 500 µg, repeat to 3 mg; then transcutaneous pacing or isoprenaline/adrenaline infusion.

orig.stem: A 56-year-old gentleman is brought in by paramedics. The patient fainted this morning and has not regained consciousness. No injuries reported from his faint. On examination his heart rate is 37 beats/minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths/minute, blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg. You order an ECG: The ECG shows prolonged PR interval. What would be the initial management?
orig.explanation: IV atropine Symptomatic bradycardia with adverse features → give IV atropine first; adenosine treats SVT; escalate to pacing if no response.

stem: A 75-year-old woman is admitted to the acute medical unit with pneumonia. Her only past history is a transient ischaemic attack 2 months ago. On admission the ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 103/min. She is treated with IV fluids and antibiotics and improves; two further ECGs overnight show sinus rhythm, and next day she is medically fit for discharge. What is the single most appropriate management of her atrial fibrillation?
explanation: CHA2DS2-VASc 5 (age 75 = 2, female, prior TIA = 2): anticoagulate (DOAC); AF during acute illness often recurs. Aspirin is not used.

orig.stem: A 75-year-old woman was admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with pneumonia. Her only past medical history of note is transient ischaemic attack 2 months previously. On initial assessment, ECG revealed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 103. She was treated with intravenous fluids and antibiotics. She improved significantly. Two further ECGs overnight revealed normal sinus rhythm. The following day, she was deemed medically fit for discharge. What is the single most appropriate management option regarding her episode of atrial fibrillation?
orig.explanation: Oral anticoagulation Single paroxysmal AF episode still needs anticoagulation if CHA₂DS₂- VASc high; aspirin not used; Holter not required before starting OAC.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with sudden-onset palpitations. BP is 124/84 mmHg and pulse 150/min. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia. Vagal manoeuvres fail, IV access is obtained and adenosine 6 mg is given with no effect. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Adenosine is given 6 mg, then 12 mg, then 18 mg by rapid bolus with flush; repeating 6 mg rarely works. Verapamil if adenosine fails.

orig.stem: A 30-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department following the acute onset of palpitations. Blood pressure is 124/84 mmHg and her pulse is 150/min. An ECG shows a narrow complex tachycardia. Intravenous access is gained and 6mg of adenosine is given with no effect. What is the most appropriate next step?
orig.explanation: Intravenous adenosine 12 mg SVT unresponsive to first adenosine dose → give next dose per protocol.

stem: Each of the following may cause left bundle branch block EXCEPT:
explanation: LBBB occurs with IHD, hypertension/LVH, AS, cardiomyopathy and conduction fibrosis. Secundum ASD causes RBBB with right axis deviation.

orig.stem: Each one of the following may cause left bundle branch block, except:
orig.explanation: Atrial septal defect (ostium secundum) LBBB: WiLLiaM pattern (W in V1, M in V6). New LBBB is pathologic; causes include MI, HTN, AS, cardiomyopathy; also fibrosis, digoxin toxicity, hyperkalemia.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department after an episode of syncope. The ECG shows sinus rhythm at 85/min, QRS duration 110 ms, PR interval 180 ms and corrected QT interval 500 ms. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the ECG abnormality?
explanation: QTc 500 ms is prolonged (high torsades risk); hypokalaemia (flat T, U waves) is a common cause. Hypercalcaemia and digoxin shorten the QT.

orig.stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department following an episode of syn cope. An ECG is performed, which demonstrates sinus rhythm at rate 85 bpm. The QRS duration is 110 ms, PR interval is 180 ms and corrected QT interval is 500 ms. Of the following, what is the cause for the abnormality seen on the ECG?
orig.explanation: Hypokalaemia Long QT from hypokalemia; normal QTc <430 ms men, <450 ms women. Other acquired causes: hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, many drugs, CNS injury, malnutrition, hypothermia.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is admitted after a collapse, and the ECG shows polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Which one of the following is NOT associated with an increased risk of torsades de pointes?
explanation: Torsades needs a long QT: TCAs, SAH, hypothermia, congenital LQTS, low K/Mg/Ca. Hypercalcaemia shortens the QT. Treat with IV magnesium 2 g.

orig.stem: A 34-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department following a collapse. An ECG shows a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Which one of the following is not associated with an increased risk of developing torsade de pointes?
orig.explanation: Hypercalcaemia Hypocalcemia prolongs QT and risks torsades; hypercalcemia shortens QT.

topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a 4-day history of palpitations and increasing breathlessness on exertion. The ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 118/min. He has brittle asthma, hypertension and heart failure, and a recent echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 32%. What is the most appropriate drug to control his heart rate?
explanation: AF with HFrEF and brittle asthma: rate-limiting CCBs are negatively inotropic and beta-blockers are precluded, so digoxin is used.

orig.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a 4-day history of palpitations and increased breathlessness on exertion. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a rate of 118 beats per minute. His past medical history includes brittle asthma, hypertension, and congestive cardiac failure, and his recent echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 32%. What is the most appropriate medication to control the heart rate in this man?
orig.explanation: Digoxin AF with HFrEF: avoid rate-limiting CCBs; beta-blockers usual but avoid if brittle asthma; digoxin reasonable for rate control in sedentary HF.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents with lethargy and palpitations for the past 4–5 days. His pulse is 123/min and irregularly irregular, BP 118/70 mmHg, and his chest is clear. An ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. What is the most appropriate drug to control his heart rate?
explanation: For stable AF without heart failure, first-line rate control is a beta-blocker such as bisoprolol or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil), aiming initially for a resting rate below 110/min. Digoxin monotherapy is reserved for sedentary patients or when other agents are contraindicated, because it controls the rate poorly on exertion. Amiodarone and flecainide are rhythm-control drugs, and amlodipine is a dihydropyridine that does not slow AV-nodal conduction. He also needs CHA2DS2-VASc assessment for anticoagulation.

orig.stem: A 72-year-old man presents with lethargy and palpitations for the past four or five days. On examination his pulse is 123 bpm irregularly irregular, blood pressure is 118/70 mmHg and his chest is clear. An ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. What is the appropriate drug to control his heart rate?
orig.explanation: Bisoprolol AF long-term rate control: beta-blocker or rate-limiting CCB preferred to digoxin in most; choose rate control based on age and symptoms.

stem: Which one of the following is NOT an indication for insertion of a temporary pacemaker?
options: Complete heart block after an inferior MI, with normal blood pressure
Complete heart block after an anterior MI, with normal blood pressure
Bradycardia-dependent torsades de pointes recurring despite IV magnesium
Mobitz type II heart block after an anterior MI, with normal blood pressure
Symptomatic bradycardia not responding to drug treatment
explanation: CHB after inferior MI is nodal (narrow escape, atropine-responsive, usually resolves), so pacing is not needed if stable; after anterior MI it is.

orig.stem: Which one of the following is not an indication for insertion of a temporary pacemaker?
options: Complete heart block following an inferior MI - blood pressure normal
Complete heart block following an anterior MI - blood pressure normal
Mobitz type II heart block following an anterior MI - blood pressure normal
Symptomatic bradycardia not responding to drug treatment
orig.explanation: Complete heart block following an inferior MI - blood pressure normal Post-inferior MI complete heart block often transient; if stable, no pacing. Temporary pacing for unstable bradycardia unresponsive to atropine and for anterior MI high-grade block.

stem: A 71-year-old man with rheumatic heart disease for 20 years presents with breathlessness on exertion. BP is 128/78 mmHg. On examination the apex beat is displaced, the first heart sound is soft and the second heart sound is normal. Which valvular lesion is most likely?
explanation: A displaced apex with a soft S1 in rheumatic disease is mitral regurgitation (LV volume overload). MS gives a loud S1 and tapping undisplaced apex.

orig.stem: A 71-year-old man with history of rheumatic heart disease for 20 years presents with breathlessness on exertion. On auscultation, the first heart sound is soft, the second heart sound is normal, the apex beat is displaced. Which valvular lesion is most likely?
orig.explanation: Mitral regurgitation A soft S1 and displaced apex beat suggest MR rather than MS.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with breathlessness and chest discomfort. There is a loud first heart sound, an opening snap after S2 and a low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. Which valve lesion is most likely?
explanation: Loud S1, opening snap and an apical mid-diastolic rumble are mitral stenosis, usually rheumatic. Tricuspid stenosis is at the lower left sternal edge; aortic stenosis is systolic.

orig.stem: A 42-year-old female presents with shortness of breath and chest discomfort. On physical exam, a mid-diastolic murmur was heard at the left sternal border with an opening snap after S2. Which valvular lesion is suspected?
orig.explanation: Mitral stenosis , Mitral stenosis is classically associated with a mid-diastolic murmur and an opening snap after S2, best heard at the apex or left sternal border. The opening snap is due to sudden tensing of the stenotic mitral valve leaflets during diastole.

stem: A 66-year-old man presents with shortness-of-breath on exertion. On examination his blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, pulse 78/min and regular. Auscultation of his chest reveals an early diastolic murmur Which one of the following conditions is most associated with this kind of murmur?

orig.stem: A 66-year-old man presents with shortness-of-breath on exertion. On examination his blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, pulse 78/min and regular. Auscultation of his chest reveals an early diastolic murmur Which one of the following conditions is most associated with this kind of murmur?
orig.explanation: Aortic regurgitation An early diastolic murmur is most associated with aortic regurgitation.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with known rheumatic mitral stenosis presents with progressive breathlessness, ankle swelling and abdominal distension. She is in sinus rhythm. Examination shows a raised JVP, a left parasternal heave, tender hepatomegaly and pitting oedema to the knees. What is the most likely cause of her new symptoms?
options: Progression to pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure
explanation: Long-standing MS causes pulmonary hypertension and RV failure (raised JVP, RV heave, hepatomegaly, oedema); this indicates valvotomy or surgery.

orig.stem: A 62-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic mitral stenosis now presents with progressive dyspnea and signs of congestion. What is the most likely underlying cause of her new symptoms?
orig.explanation: Progression to pulmonary hypertension In rheumatic mitral stenosis, progression to pulmonary hypertension is a common cause of worsening symptoms.

stem: What is the typical character of the apex beat in a patient with mitral stenosis?
explanation: In MS the apex is undisplaced and tapping (a palpable loud S1) because the LV is protected from overload.

orig.stem: On physical examination of a patient with mitral stenosis, what is the typical character of the apex beat?
orig.explanation: Tapping only In mitral stenosis, the apex beat is typically localized and tapping in character, due to a palpable first heart sound (loud S1) caused by the stiff mitral valve snapping shut. This tapping apex beat is a classic clinical finding and more specific than simply saying “soft.”

stem: Which auscultatory finding most suggests pulmonary hypertension in a patient with mitral stenosis?
explanation: Pulmonary hypertension causes a loud (even palpable) P2, often with an RV heave. The opening snap and loud S1 come from the mitral valve itself.

orig.stem: Which auscultatory finding is most indicative of pulmonary hypertension in a patient with mitral stenosis?
orig.explanation: Loud P2 component of S2 A loud P2 (ac centuated pulmonary component of S2) is a key sign of pulmonary hypertension.

stem: In which patient with mitral stenosis is percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy indicated?
options: Symptomatic patients with favorable valve morphology and minimal mitral regurgitation
All patients with any degree of stenosis
Only in patients with associated atrial fibrillation
explanation: Balloon mitral commissurotomy: symptomatic MS (area ≤ 1.5 cm²) with pliable non-calcified leaflets, ≤ mild MR and no LA thrombus on TOE.

orig.stem: Percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy is indicated in which patient with mitral stenosis?
options: Symptomatic patients with favorable valve morphology and minimal mitral regurgitation
All patients with any degree of stenosis
Only in patients with associated atrial fibrillation
orig.explanation: Symptomatic patients with favorable valve morphology and minimal mitral regurgitation This procedure is reserved for symptomatic patients who have pliable valves without significant regurgitation.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with a past history of rheumatic fever presents with breathlessness on exertion and a malar flush. She is in sinus rhythm, and echocardiography confirms mitral stenosis. Which physical sign is she likely to have?
explanation: In MS with sinus rhythm, atrial contraction causes pre-systolic accentuation of the rumble; it disappears when AF develops.

orig.stem: A 34 year old woman presents with symptoms of breathlessness on exertion, a malar flush and has a past history of rheumatic fever. She is in sinus rhythm and has an echocardiogram that confirms mitral stenosis. Which physical sign is she likely to have?
orig.explanation: Pre-systolic accentuation Mitral stenosis is typically associated with a mid-diastolic murmur that has pre-systolic accentuation.

stem: An 80-year-old man is found to have an incidental ejection systolic murmur, and his family physician feels a systolic thrill at the base of the heart. What is the most likely cause of the thrill?
explanation: A basal systolic thrill with an ejection murmur in an elderly man is most likely calcific aortic stenosis; echo grades severity.

orig.stem: An 80 year old man presents with an incidental ejection systolic murmur. His family physician notices a parasternal thrill. What is the likely underlying reason for the thrill?
orig.explanation: Aortic stenosis A parasternal thrill is most commonly associated with aortic stenosis.

stem: A 43-year-old man has a routine health check at work. He has a murmur, isolated systolic hypertension (180/60 mmHg) and left ventricular hypertrophy on his ECG. Echocardiography shows significant regurgitant flow across the aortic valve. Which clinical sign is he likely to have?
options: Head nodding in time with the heartbeat (de Musset sign)
explanation: Pulse pressure 120 mmHg with significant AR gives hyperdynamic signs: collapsing pulse, Corrigan, de Musset (head nodding), Quincke and Duroziez.

orig.stem: A 43 year old man undergoes a routine health check with his employers. He is found to have a murmur, isolated systolic hypertension (180/60 mmHg) and left ventricular hypertrophy on his ECG. A significant regurgitant blood flow is noticed across the aortic valve on echocardiogram. Which of the following clinical signs is likely to be observed?
options: Palpable thrill in the aortic area
Prominent pulsation in the neck (de Musset’s sign)
orig.explanation: Prominent pulsation in the neck (de Musset’s sign) De Musset’s sign (neck pulsations) is characteristic of severe aortic regurgitation.

stem: An 84-year-old woman with diabetes and hyperlipidaemia had an anterior STEMI 3 weeks ago, treated with primary PCI and a drug-eluting stent to the left anterior descending artery. She has been well since on metoprolol, aspirin, clopidogrel, rosuvastatin, lisinopril and insulin. Her ophthalmologist has scheduled elective cataract surgery for next week but considers the bleeding risk too high while she takes both antiplatelet drugs, and asks your advice. What should you recommend?
options: Stop aspirin, continue clopidogrel and proceed with surgery
Stop clopidogrel, continue aspirin and proceed with surgery
Stop both antiplatelet drugs and proceed with surgery
Postpone surgery for at least 6 months, preferably 12, when clopidogrel can be stopped
Proceed with surgery on both drugs, as she will never be able to stop either
explanation: After ACS with a drug-eluting stent, DAPT continues ~12 months; stopping clopidogrel at 3 weeks risks fatal stent thrombosis. Defer elective surgery (≥ 6, ideally 12 months).

orig.stem: An 84-year-old woman with a history of diabetes and hyperlipidemia presented to the emergency department 3 weeks ago with an ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. She underwent emergent primary percutaneous coronary intervention to an acutely occluded left anterior descending artery. A 3.5 × 24 mm everolimus-eluting stent was placed with excellent angiographic result and complete resolution of her symptoms. She has been feeling excellent since then. Her discharge medications were metoprolol, aspirin, clopidogrel, rosuvastatin, lisinopril, and sliding scale insulin. She recently went to see her ophthalmologist who noted a right eye cataract. The ophthalmologist has contacted your office asking about your opinion on discontinuing her aspirin and/or clopidogrel to reduce bleeding risk during her cataract surgery, which has been scheduled for next week. She feels the bleeding risk on both medications is too high to perform the surgery. Which of the following should you recommend?
options: “Discontinue aspirin, continue clopidogrel, and proceed with cataract surgery.”
“Discontinue clopidogrel, continue aspirin, and proceed with cataract surgery.”
“Discontinue both aspirin and clopidogrel and proceed with cataract surgery.”
“Postpone the surgery for at least 6 months, and preferably 12 months, at which time the clopidogrel can be discontinued.”
“I advise to perform the surgery while she is on both aspirin and clopidogrel as she will never be able to stop either medication.”
orig.explanation: Postpone the surgery for at least 6 months, and preferably 12 months, at which time the clopidogrel can be discontinued. Postponing elective surgery minimizes the risk of stent thrombosis by allowing completion of dual antiplatelet therapy.

stem: An 87-year-old woman with severe COPD (FEV1 0.76 L), poorly controlled diabetes and stage 3 chronic kidney disease presents with exertional chest pressure, leg swelling, breathlessness and rapidly worsening fatigue. There is a harsh late-peaking systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids, an inaudible S2 and slow-rising, delayed carotid pulses. Echocardiography confirms aortic stenosis with a valve area of 0.59 cm². The cardiothoracic surgeon declines surgical aortic valve replacement because her predicted in-hospital mortality exceeds 15%. Which statement to her is reasonable?
options: For this condition, medications have been shown to reduce the risk of death
It does not matter that you are not a surgical candidate: your condition carries a low 1- and 5-year mortality, and medication can control your symptoms
Percutaneous balloon aortic valvotomy is a good non-surgical option with excellent short- and long-term results
As you are not a surgical candidate, no other procedure can replace your valve, so we should consider hospice care
We should refer you for assessment for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI)
explanation: Symptomatic severe AS has ~50% 2-year mortality without replacement; at prohibitive surgical risk, refer for TAVI (heart-team assessment).

orig.stem: Mrs. Edwards is an 87-year-old woman with a history of extensive tobacco abuse and resultant COPD with a forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) of 0.76 L, poorly controlled diabetes, and stage III chronic kidney disease. She was previously your patient, but has not followed up with you for the preceding 8 years. However, she comes to your clinic today complaining of chest pressure with exertion, leg swelling, shortness of breath, and accelerating fatigue with even minimal exertion. On examination, you quickly note a harsh, late-peaking systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating the carotid arteries and with a musical quality at the apex. You cannot appreciate a second heart sound, and the carotid impulses are muted and arrive late compared to the PMI on palpation. You suspect severe aortic stenosis, and indeed, an echocardiogram later that day confirms aortic stenosis with a valve area of 0.59 cm2. You refer Mrs. Edwards to a cardiothoracic surgeon who informs you that Mrs. Edwards is much too high risk for a surgical aortic valve replacement, citing a higher than 15% risk of in-hospital mortality. You are due to see Mrs. Edwards tomorrow. Which of the following statements to her would be rea sonable?
options: “For this condition, medications have been shown to reduce the risk of mortality.”
“It is okay that you are not a surgical candidate. Your condition carries a low risk of 1- and 5-year mortality, and we can control your symptoms with medications.”
“Percutaneous aortic balloon valvotomy is a good nonsurgical treatment option and has been found to have excellent short- and long-term outcomes.”
“Since you are not a surgical candidate, no other procedure exists for aortic valve replacement for you. We should consider hospice options.”
“We should consider referring you for further testing to see if you are a candidate for transcatheter aortic valve replacement.”
orig.explanation: We should consider referring you for further testing to see if you are a candidate for transcatheter aortic valve replacement. TAVR is now a viable option for high-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and haemoptysis. On examination there is a loud first heart sound and a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A loud S1 and a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex are the hallmarks of mitral stenosis, usually rheumatic; there may also be an opening snap and, in sinus rhythm, pre-systolic accentuation. Haemoptysis results from raised pulmonary venous pressure (rupture of bronchial veins, pulmonary oedema or infarction). MR and AS cause systolic murmurs, AR an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, and tricuspid stenosis a mid-diastolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that increases on inspiration.

orig.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and haemoptysis. On examination you note a loud first heart sound (HS) and a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Mitral stenosis The clinical findings are typical of mitral stenosis, often presenting with a loud first heart sound and diastolic rumble.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath on exertion and fatigue. On examination you note a soft first HS and a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to her axilla. What is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath on exertion and fatigue. On examination you note a soft first HS and a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to her axilla. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Mitral regurgitation Mitral regurgitation typically presents with a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with angina and breathlessness. On examination there is an ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the carotids is aortic stenosis; angina, dyspnoea and syncope signal severe disease.

orig.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with angina and dyspnoea. On examination you note an ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal border radiating to his neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Aortic stenosis Aortic stenosis often presents with an ejection systolic murmur that radiates to the neck.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with dyspnoea and orthopnoea. On examination you note a blowing early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with dyspnoea and orthopnoea. On examination you note a blowing early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Aortic regurgitation A blowing early diastolic murmur is characteristic of aortic regurgitation.

stem: A 42-year-old man is reviewed in the cardiology clinic after an echocardiogram showing right ventricular dysfunction. He has a raised JVP and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge louder on inspiration, with a raised JVP and large v waves, is tricuspid regurgitation.

orig.stem: A 42-year-old man is reviewed in the outpatient cardiology department following a recent echocardiogram (echo). The echo demonstrates right ventricular dysfunction. On examination you note an elevated JVP in addition to a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Tricuspid regurgitation Tricuspid regurgitation presents with an elevated JVP and a pansystolic murmur along the lower left sternal border.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with angina and breathlessness. There is an ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the neck. Which investigation is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
explanation: Transthoracic echo with Doppler confirms AS and grades it (velocity, gradient, area) with LV function; angiography is done before surgery.

orig.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with angina and dyspnoea. On examination you note a murmur at the upper right sternal border radiating to his neck. Which investigation is most likely to lead to a diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Echocardiogram An echocardiogram is the first-line investigation for cardiac murmurs.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and haemoptysis. There is a loud first heart sound and a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. An echocardiogram and chest X-ray are requested. All of the following are chest X-ray features of this condition EXCEPT:
explanation: In MS the enlarged LA straightens the left heart border, gives a double right border and splays (widens) the carina; upper-lobe diversion and Kerley B lines.

orig.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and haemoptysis. On examination you note a loud first HS and a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. You request an echocardiogram and a CXR. The following are all features of the CXR in this condition EXCEPT?
orig.explanation: Narrowed carina A narrowed carina is not a typical feature of the CXR in mitral stenosis.

stem: A 20-year-old student sees his GP with blurred vision; a year ago he had a dislocated lens. On examination he has pectus excavatum, a high-arched palate and joint hypermobility. Which cardiac disorder is often associated with his condition?
explanation: Ectopia lentis, pectus, high palate and hypermobility suggest Marfan syndrome, commonly with MVP; aortic root dilatation is the dangerous lesion.

orig.stem: A 20-year-old student sees his GP for blurred vision. On further questioning, he reports he had a ‘lens problem’ a year ago. On examination he also has pectus excavatum, a high arched palate and signs of hypermobility. Which of the following cardiac disorders is often associated with this patient’s condition?
orig.explanation: Mitral valve prolapse Mitral valve prolapse is commonly associated with connective tissue disorders, as seen in this patient.

stem: A 65-year-old man has 3 months of exertional central chest pain and breathlessness that settle with rest, and lately dizziness on exertion. There is an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. ECG shows tall R waves in I, aVL and V4–V6 with deep S waves in V1–V3. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Exertional angina, dyspnoea and dizziness/syncope with an ejection murmur and LVH on ECG is severe aortic stenosis. HCM is younger, and its murmur does not radiate to the carotids.

orig.stem: A 65-year-old man sees his GP with worsening central chest pain and breathlessness following exertion for 3 months. These symptoms usually resolve with rest. Lately he has also been feeling dizzy. On examination a systolic murmur is heard. ECG shows large R waves in leads I, aVL and V4–6, and large R waves in leads V1–3. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Aortic stenosis Aortic stenosis in the elderly can present with angina, syncope, and heart failure symptoms along with LVH on ECG.

stem: A 32-year-old woman attends her GP for a routine medical examination and is noted to have a mid-diastolic murmur with an opening snap. Her blood pressure is 118/71 mmHg and pulse is 66/min. She is entirely asymptomatic and her chest x-ray and ECG are normal. What would be the most appropriate investigation at this point?

orig.stem: A 32-year-old woman attends her GP for a routine medical examination and is noted to have a mid-diastolic murmur with an opening snap. Her blood pressure is 118/71 mmHg and pulse is 66/min. She is entirely asymptomatic and her chest x-ray and ECG are normal. What would be the most appropriate investigation at this point?
orig.explanation: Echocardiography Echocardiography is the investigation of choice in suspected mitral stenosis.

stem: A patient admitted with pneumonia is found to have a heart murmur. Which finding points to mitral regurgitation?
options: Murmur louder with patient in left lateral position
Murmur louder over the right 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line
explanation: Mitral murmurs are loudest at the apex with the patient in the left lateral position; MR is pansystolic, radiates to the axilla, louder in expiration.

orig.stem: A patient is admitted with pneumonia. A murmur is heard on examination. What finding points to mitral regurgitation?
options: Murmur louder with patient in left lateral position
Murmur louder over the right 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line
orig.explanation: Murmur louder with patient in left lateral position Mitral regurgitation is best heard at the apex and accentuated in the left lateral decubitus position.

stem: A 49-year-old woman presents with increasing shortness of breath on exertion over the past three months, with no chest pain, cough, or ankle swelling. On examination, BP is 158/61 mmHg, pulse 88/min, and crackles are present at both lung bases. A decrescendo diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 49-year-old woman presents with increasing shortness of breath on exertion over the past three months, with no chest pain, cough, or ankle swelling. On examination, BP is 158/61 mmHg, pulse 88/min, and crackles are present at both lung bases. A decrescendo diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Aortic regurgitation Aortic regurgitation typically presents with a decrescendo diastolic murmur and wide pulse pressure.

stem: A 59-year-old man attends for a routine check-up. He is asymptomatic, and examination reveals a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur at the apex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Mid-systolic click then late systolic murmur is mitral valve prolapse (Barlow); standing/Valsalva bring the click earlier, squatting delays it.

orig.stem: A 59-year-old man presents for a routine check-up. Examination reveals a mid systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur at the apex, but he is asymptomatic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Barlow syndrome The mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur is characteristic of mitral valve prolapse (Barlow syndrome).

stem: A 57-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic fever and essential hypertension presents with worsening breathlessness and reduced exercise tolerance. Which of the following is NOT a clinical sign of mitral stenosis?
options: Pan-systolic murmur which radiates to axilla
explanation: MS signs: malar flush, AF, tapping apex, loud S1, opening snap, RV heave. A pansystolic murmur to the axilla is mitral regurgitation.

orig.stem: A 57-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic fever and essential hypertension presents with worsening shortness of breath and decreased exercise tolerance. Which of the following is NOT a clinical sign associated with mitral stenosis?
options: Pan-systolic murmur which radiates to axilla
orig.explanation: Pan-systolic murmur which radiates to axilla Mitral stenosis is associated with malar flush, atrial fibrillation, a tapping apex beat, and right ventricular heave; a pan-systolic murmur is not typical.

stem: An asymptomatic 31-year-old woman is told she has mitral valve prolapse after an echocardiogram. Which statement is correct?
options: One or both leaflets of the mitral valve are pushed back into the left atrium during systole
Significant mitral regurgitation will eventually develop
explanation: MVP is systolic displacement of a leaflet > 2 mm into the LA; most are asymptomatic and need no drugs, but echo follow-up is advised.

orig.stem: An asymptomatic 31-year-old woman is told she has mitral valve prolapse after an ECG. Which statement is correct?
options: One or both leaflets of the mitral valve are pushed back into the left atrium during systole
Significant mitral regurgitation will eventually develop
orig.explanation: One or both leaflets of the mitral valve are pushed back into the left atrium during systole Mitral valve prolapse is defined by the systolic displacement of one or both leaflets into the left atrium; no specific therapy is indicated in asymptomatic patients.

options: Mid-diastolic murmur best heard at the apex
Crescendo systolic murmur best heard at the right sternal edge
Diastolic murmur best heard at the left sternal edge
Pan-systolic murmur best heard at the apex
Pan-systolic murmur best heard at the left sternal edge

options: Mid-diastolic murmur best heard at the apex
Crescendo systolic murmur best heard at the right sternal edge

Pan-systolic murmur best heard at the apex
Pan-systolic murmur best heard at the left sternal edge
orig.explanation: Crescendo systolic murmur best heard at the right sternal edge This presentation is classic for aortic stenosis, which produces a harsh systolic murmur best heard at the right sternal border.

options: A systolic ejection murmur at the apex that diminishes with squatting/handgrip and increases with Valsalva/standing
A systolic murmur with a mid to late systolic click at the apex, with the click and murmur occurring earlier with squatting/handgrip and delayed with Valsalva/standing

options: A systolic ejection murmur at the apex that diminishes with squatting/handgrip and increases with Valsalva/standing
A systolic murmur with a mid to late systolic click at the apex, with the click and murmur occurring earlier with squatting/handgrip and delayed with Valsalva/standing
A holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla that increases with squatting/handgrip and diminishes with Valsalva/standing
A blowing holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border which increases with squatting/ handgrip and diminishes with Valsalva/standing
