orig.explanation: A systolic murmur with a mid to late systolic click at the apex, with the click and mur mur occurring earlier with squatting/handgrip and delayed with Valsalva/standing Although the explanation provided discusses paradoxical embolism, the answer given is the murmur of mitral valve prolapse with the characteristic mid to late systolic click.

stem: A 75-year-old patient presents to the ER after a syncopal episode with occasional substernal chest pressure and exertional dyspnea. BP is 110/80 with bibasilar rales. Which auscultatory finding best explains his symptoms?
options: A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border
A diastolic decrescendo murmur heard at the mid-left sternal border
A holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex

orig.stem: A 75-year-old patient presents to the ER after a syncopal episode with occasional substernal chest pressure and exertional dyspnea. BP is 110/80 with bibasilar rales. Which auscultatory finding best explains his symptoms?
options: A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border
A diastolic decrescendo murmur heard at the mid-left sternal border
A holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex
orig.explanation: A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border This finding is classic for aortic stenosis, which is associated with syncope.

stem: A 78-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of productive cough, leg swelling and fatigue; he has been afebrile throughout. He had a porcine (bioprosthetic) mitral valve replacement for severe mitral regurgitation 12 years ago. Examination shows bibasal crackles, a laterally displaced apex beat and a grade 3/6 low-pitched diastolic murmur at the apex. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
options: Structural degeneration of the bioprosthetic valve
explanation: Bioprosthetic valves degenerate after ~10 years (earlier in mitral position); a new apical diastolic murmur means prosthetic MS. Exclude endocarditis; redo or valve-in-valve.

orig.stem: A 78-year-old man is brought to the ED with a 3-week history of productive cough, leg swelling, and fatigue. He had a porcine valve replacement for severe mitral regurgitation 12 years ago. Examination reveals bilateral basilar rales, a laterally displaced apical beat, and a grade 3/6 decrescendo-crescendo diastolic murmur at the apex. Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
orig.explanation: Valve Degeneration Biological valves degenerate over time, leading to dysfunction and heart failure.

stem: A 75-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a 50-year smoking history presents with progressive shortness of breath and fatigue. Physical exam shows weak peripheral pulses. Which diagnosis is most likely?

orig.stem: A 75-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a 50-year smoking history presents with progressive shortness of breath and fatigue. Physical exam shows weak peripheral pulses. Which diagnosis is most likely?
orig.explanation: Aortic stenosis Aortic stenosis causes a narrow pulse pressure and weak peripheral pulses due to LV outflow obstruction.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue and dyspnea for 2 months, with nocturnal dyspnea and occasional palpitations. He has type 2 diabetes and peripheral arterial disease. Examination shows bilateral basilar rales. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue and dyspnea for 2 months, with nocturnal dyspnea and occasional palpitations. He has type 2 diabetes and peripheral arterial disease. Examination shows bilateral basilar rales. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: MR The auscultatory findings are indicative of mitral regurgitation, a common cause of left-sided heart failure.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. He is now alert and, in retrospect, describes occasional substernal chest pressure and breathlessness on exertion. His BP is 110/80 mmHg and there are a few bibasal crackles. Which auscultatory finding would best explain his presentation?
options: A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border
A diastolic decrescendo murmur heard at the mid-left sternal border
A holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex
explanation: Exertional syncope, angina and breathlessness in an older patient with a narrow pulse pressure (110/80 mmHg) form the classic triad of severe aortic stenosis, whose murmur is a harsh crescendo–decrescendo (ejection) systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the carotids, often with a soft A2 and a slow-rising pulse. Once symptoms develop, survival without valve replacement is only a few years (shortest with heart failure), so urgent echocardiography and referral for AVR or TAVI follow. An early diastolic murmur indicates AR, an apical holosystolic murmur MR, a midsystolic click MVP and a rub pericarditis.

orig.stem: 1. A 75-year-old patient presents to the ER after a syncopal episode. He is again alert and in retrospect describes occasional substernal chest pressure and shortness of breath on exertion. His blood pressure is 110/80 and lungs have a few bibasilar rales. Which auscultatory finding would best explain his findings?
options: A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border
A diastolic decrescendo murmur heard at the mid-left sternal border
A holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex
orig.explanation: A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border Aortic stenosis triad: dyspnea, angina, syncope; narrow pulse pressure; systolic ejection murmur. Other listed murmurs ≠ this triad.

stem: A 72-year-old man has intermittent breathlessness on exertion, palpitations and a cough occasionally productive of blood. On auscultation, a low-pitched diastolic rumbling murmur is faintly heard at the apex. What is the most likely cause of the murmur?
options: A silent MI within the past year
explanation: Dyspnoea, AF and haemoptysis with an apical diastolic rumble is mitral stenosis, usually a late consequence of childhood rheumatic fever.

orig.stem: 2. A 72-year-old male comes to the office with intermittent symptoms of dyspnea on exertion, palpitations, and cough occasionally productive of blood. On cardiac auscultation, a low-pitched diastolic rumbling murmur is faintly heard at the apex. What is the most likely cause of the murmur?
options: A silent MI within the past year
orig.explanation: Rheumatic fever as a youth Mitral stenosis: dyspnea, palpitations, hemoptysis; diastolic rumble ± opening snap, loud S1; rheumatic origin; HTN gives S4, MI causes MR (systolic), anemia causes flow murmur.

stem: A 68-year-old man is intubated in the emergency department because of pulmonary oedema. His BP is 150/90 mmHg. Urgent echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 45% and severe mitral regurgitation. Despite aggressive diuresis with furosemide, he still requires mechanical ventilation for pulmonary oedema. What is the best next step?
options: Start IV afterload reduction (e.g. nitroprusside or IV enalaprilat)
explanation: Severe MR with pulmonary oedema and adequate BP: IV afterload reduction (nitroprusside/nitrates) increases forward flow; IABP if hypotensive; then surgery.

orig.stem: 3. A 68-year-old male was intubated in the emergency room because of pulmonary edema. Stat echocardiogram reveals an ejection fraction of 45% and severe mitral regurgitation. In spite of aggressive diuresis with furosemide, the patient continues to require mechanical ventilation secondary to pulmonary edema. What is the best next step in treating this patient?
options: Arrange for mitral valve replacement surgery.
orig.explanation: Begin intravenous enalapril. Acute severe MR with pulmonary edema → reduce afterload (ACEi/hydralazine/nitroprusside); plan MV surgery after stabilization; IABP/extra diuretic/BB not helpful.

stem: A nurse at a community clinic has listed patients scheduled for a dental extraction who may need antibiotic prophylaxis. Which of these patients is most likely to benefit from antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent infective endocarditis?
options: 17-year-old boy with coarctation of the aorta
26-year-old woman with a ventricular septal defect repaired in childhood
65-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve
explanation: Dental prophylaxis (AHA/ESC) only for highest risk: prosthetic valves, previous IE, unrepaired cyanotic CHD. NICE does not recommend it routinely.

orig.stem: 4. You are volunteering with a dental colleague in a community indigent clinic. A nurse has prepared a list of patients who are scheduled for a dental procedure and may need antibiotic prophylaxis beforehand. Of the patients listed below, who would be most likely to benefit from antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent infective endocarditis?
options: 17-year-old male with coarctation of the aorta
26-year-old female with a ventricular septal defect repaired in childhood
orig.explanation: 65-year-old male with prosthetic aortic valve IE prophylaxis only for highest risk: prior IE, prosthetic valves, unrepaired cyanotic CHD, graft <6 mo; dental prophylaxis amoxicillin 2 g 30–60 min pre-procedure; many procedures need none.

stem: A 62-year-old man who had a mechanical mitral valve replacement 4 years ago is reviewed. Which long-term antithrombotic therapy is he likely to be taking?
options: Aspirin + clopidogrel for the first 12 months
explanation: Mechanical valves need lifelong warfarin (INR ~2.5–3.5 mitral, 2.0–3.0 bileaflet aortic). DOACs are contraindicated (RE-ALIGN).

orig.stem: 5. A 62-year-old man who had a mechanical mitral valve replacement four years ago is reviewed. What long term antithrombotic therapy is he likely to be taking?
options: Aspirin + clopidogrel for the first 12 months
orig.explanation: Warfarin Prosthetic valves: mechanical → warfarin ± aspirin if other indication; bioprosthetic → aspirin; DOACs contraindicated in mechanical valves.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to his GP with fatigue and exertional breathlessness. He has no significant past history, takes no medication, and does not smoke or drink alcohol. He is very tall (2.08 m) and thin, with a high-arched palate. Auscultation reveals a pansystolic murmur that is loudest in inspiration. What is the most likely explanation for his symptoms?
explanation: A pansystolic murmur louder on inspiration (Carvallo) is tricuspid regurgitation; in Marfan it may follow tricuspid prolapse.

orig.stem: 6. A 34-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with fatigue and exertional shortness of breath. He has no significant past medical history and is on no medications. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. On examination, he is of tall stature (2.08 metres) and thin. A high arched palate is noted on examination. Auscultation of the precordium reveals a pansystolic murmur, heard loudest in inspiration. From the options listed below, what is the most likely explanation for his symptoms?
orig.explanation: Tricuspid regurgitation Tricuspid regurgitation: pansystolic; louder on inspiration; fits Marfan’s clues. MR louder on expiration; MS diastolic rumble; PR diastolic decrescendo.

stem: A 45-year-old woman who injects drugs presents with breathlessness and bilateral leg swelling. Her pulse is regular, there is a pansystolic murmur heard loudest at the lower left sternal edge, and there is shifting dullness in the abdomen. What is the most likely finding in her jugular venous pulse?
explanation: TR (e.g. right-sided IE in drug users) gives giant v (cv) waves in the JVP and a pulsatile liver. Cannon a waves mean AV dissociation.

orig.stem: 7. A 45-year-old female who has a background of intravenous drug abuse presented with difficulty in breathing and bilateral lower leg swelling. Upon examination, it was found she had a regular pulse with a pansystolic murmur heard lowest over the left lower sternal edge. There was shifting dullness when assessing her abdomen. What is the most likely finding when evaluating her jugular venous pressure (JVP)?
orig.explanation: Prominent V waves Prominent V waves on JVP indicate tricuspid regurgitation. Cannon A: complete heart block. Absent A: AF. X descent patterns fit tamponade or AF, not this case.

stem: Which one of the following conditions is most associated with a bisferiens pulse?
explanation: A bisferiens (double-peaked) pulse occurs in mixed aortic valve disease with predominant AR, severe AR and HOCM. Pure AS gives a slow-rising pulse.

orig.stem: 8. Which one of the following conditions is most associated with a bisferiens pulse?
orig.explanation: Mixed aortic valve disease Bisferiens pulse → mixed aortic valve disease. Not typical for tamponade, severe LV failure, isolated AS, or PDA.

stem: Which one of the following is a cause of a soft second heart sound?
explanation: Severe calcific AS gives a soft or absent A2 (and reversed splitting). Pulmonary hypertension gives a loud P2; ASD gives fixed splitting.

orig.stem: 9. Which one of the following is a cause of a soft second heart sound?
orig.explanation: Aortic stenosis S2 patterns: loud in HTN; soft in severe AS; fixed split in ASD; reversed split in LBBB.

stem: Which of the following conditions is NOT associated with the development of aortic regurgitation?
explanation: AR arises from leaflet disease (rheumatic, IE, bicuspid) or root dilatation (Marfan, ankylosing spondylitis, syphilis). DCM causes functional MR/TR.

orig.stem: 10. Which of the following conditions is not associated with the development of aortic regurgitation?
orig.explanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy Dilated cardiomyopathy causes functional MR, not AR. AR causes: valve disease like rheumatic or calcific; root disease like bicuspid or spondyloarthropathy.

stem: A 2-year-old boy is seen by his GP because his parents are concerned that he is struggling to gain weight and is excessively breathless on exertion. He has known congenital pulmonary stenosis, managed conservatively so far, and the parents ask whether intervention may be needed. What murmur is likely to be heard on examination?
explanation: Pulmonary stenosis: ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge, louder on inspiration, with click and soft P2; balloon valvuloplasty if severe.

orig.stem: 11. A 2-year-old boy is seen by the general practitioner as his parents are concerned that he is struggling to gain weight and is excessively short of breath on exertion. He was previously diagnosed with congenital pulmonary stenosis which was managed conservatively; however, the parents are now questioning whether surgical intervention may be required. What murmur is likely to be heard on examination?
orig.explanation: Ejection systolic, louder on inspiration Pulmonary stenosis: ejection systolic murmur louder on inspiration. MR: holosystolic louder on expiration. TR: holosystolic louder on inspiration. MVP: late systolic click. Aortic stenosis: ejection systolic louder on expiration.

stem: Which of the following is not a feature of cardiac tamponade?

orig.stem: Which of the following is not a feature of cardiac tamponade?
orig.explanation: Loud heart sounds Tamponade typically features distant or muffled heart sounds, not loud heart sounds.

stem: A patient with acute myocardial infarction came with repeated severe dyspnea. On examination PR was 112 beats/min with pulsus paradoxus, BP 90/55 mmHg, JVP was elevated, and heart sounds were muffled. The next day, what is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A patient with acute myocardial infarction came with repeated severe dyspnea. On examination PR was 112 beats/min with pulsus paradoxus, BP 90/55 mmHg, JVP was elevated, and heart sounds were muffled. The next day, what is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Cardiac tamponade Muffled heart sounds, elevated JVP, and pulsus paradoxus strongly suggest tamponade post-MI.

stem: A middle-aged woman presents with fatigue, abdominal distension and light-headedness. Constrictive pericarditis is suspected. Which of the following findings would be LEAST typical of this diagnosis?
explanation: Constriction gives a raised JVP with rapid y descent, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock and ascites. Pulsus paradoxus is the hallmark of tamponade.

orig.stem: A middle-aged lady presents with fatigue, abdominal distension, and lightheadedness. On examination, a pericardial knock was heard, a loud P2, and a diastolic rumble. A diagnosis of constrictive pericarditis was made. Which of the following finding(s) is against this diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Pulsus paradoxus Pulsus paradoxus is more commonly seen in tamponade, not typically in constrictive pericarditis.

stem: A 55-year-old man has progressive shortness of breath and ankle oedema. He is originally from Africa and probably had tuberculosis many years ago. His BP is 105/55 mmHg, the JVP is raised 5 cm with a rapid y descent, and there is marked ankle oedema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Right-sided congestion with a steep y descent after previous TB is constrictive pericarditis; CT/MRI shows thickening or calcification.

orig.stem: A 55 year old man has progressive shortness of breath and ankle oedema. He has come from Africa originally and gives a history of probably tuberculosis many years ago. On examination, he has a blood pressure of 105/55 mmHg: raised J VP +5 cm with a rapid y descent and significant ankle oedema What is the likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Pericardial constriction Rapid y descent is indicative of pericardial constriction.

stem: Dressler syndrome results from which of the following?
explanation: Dressler syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis weeks after MI (antimyocardial antibodies); treat with aspirin/NSAID plus colchicine.

orig.stem: Dressier’s syndrome results from:
orig.explanation: Autoimmune response Dressler’s syndrome is an autoimmune response following myocardial infarction.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with chest pain following a week of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Her cardiac examination reveals distant heart sounds and her chest X-ray shows an increased cardiac silhouette. What is the most likely cause of the increased cardiac silhouette?
explanation: Distant heart sounds with a newly enlarged globular silhouette after a viral illness is pericardial effusion (> 200–250 mL); echo confirms and checks for tamponade.

orig.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with chest pain following a week of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Her cardiac examination reveals distant heart sounds and her chest X-ray shows an increased cardiac silhouette. What is the most likely cause of the increased cardiac silhouette?
orig.explanation: Pericardial effusion An enlarged cardiac silhouette in this context suggests a pericardial effusion, often seen with pericarditis.

stem: Based on her history and exam, what is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: Based on her history and exam, what is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Acute pericarditis with effusion The combination of chest pain, recent infection symptoms, distant heart sounds, and enlarged cardiac silhouette points to acute pericarditis with effusion.

stem: Which investigation is most important to confirm the diagnosis?

orig.stem: Which investigation is most important to confirm the diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Echocardiography An echocardiogram is the key investigation to visualize a pericardial effusion and assess its hemodynamic impact.

stem: In a patient with a life-threatening pericardial effusion causing hemodynamic compromise, what is the best mode of therapy?

orig.stem: In a patient with a life-threatening pericardial effusion causing hemodynamic compromise, what is the best mode of therapy?
orig.explanation: Urgent pericardiocentesis Urgent pericardiocentesis is indicated to relieve cardiac tamponade from a large pericardial effusion.

stem: A 21-year-old man has a recent influenza-like illness with fever, myalgia and headache. He then develops pleuritic-type chest discomfort and breathlessness. His pulse is 105/min and regular and BP is 105/60 mmHg; the JVP is not raised. The first and second heart sounds are normal, and a loud, harsh to-and-fro sound is heard in both systole and diastole. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A to-and-fro scratchy sound in systole and diastole after a viral illness is a pericardial rub (acute viral pericarditis); treat with NSAID plus colchicine.

orig.stem: A 21 year old man presents with a recent history of an influenza-like illness initially characterised by fever, myalgia and headache. He develops pleuritic-type chest discomfort and breathlessness. On examination, pulse is 105 beats/min and regular; BP 105/60 mmHg. The JVP is not elevated. Heart sounds 1 and 2 are present with a loud to-and-fro harsh sound present in systole and diastole. Which of the following conditions explains this clinical presentation?
orig.explanation: Acute viral pericarditis The clinical picture is most compatible with acute pericarditis following a viral illness.

stem: What is the appropriate initial treatment for the symptoms of acute pericarditis?
explanation: Acute pericarditis: high-dose aspirin or ibuprofen tapered over 1–2 weeks plus colchicine for 3 months (halves recurrence). Steroids are second line.

orig.stem: What is the appropriate initial treatment for the symptoms of acute pericarditis?
orig.explanation: Oral aspirin Aspirin is effective as an initial anti-inflammatory treatment for pericarditis.

stem: Which of the following conditions may result in chronic pericardial constriction?
explanation: TB is the commonest cause of constriction worldwide; others are cardiac surgery, radiotherapy, viral/idiopathic pericarditis and connective tissue disease.

orig.stem: Which of the following conditions may result in chronic pericardial constriction?
orig.explanation: Tuberculosis Tuberculosis is a recognized cause of chronic pericardial constriction.

stem: A 75-year-old male smoker has a 6-week history of progressive exertional breathlessness and fatigue, and recently his ankles swell in the afternoon. His pulse is 100/min and regular and BP is 92/60 mmHg. The JVP is raised and rises on inspiration, the heart sounds are quiet with no added sounds, and there is bilateral pitting oedema to the knees. The chest X-ray shows apparent cardiomegaly with a globular cardiac silhouette. A pericardial effusion is suspected. Which of the following statements is true?
options: A large effusion can be a sign of malignancy
A pericardial rub is always heard if the effusion is large
An ECG is the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis
High-dose diuretic therapy will resolve the pericardial effusion
In symptomatic patients, cardiac surgery is required to remove the pericardial fluid
explanation: A large effusion in an older smoker suggests malignancy; a rub is often absent, echo confirms, and diuretics do not help. Drain and send cytology.

orig.stem: A 75 year old male smoker presents with a 6-week history of progressive exertional breathlessness and fatigue. Latterly he has noticed his ankles swelling in the afternoon. On examination, pulse is 100 beats/min and regular; BP 92/60 mmHg. The JVP is elevated and rises on inspiration. Heart sounds are quiet and there are no added sounds. There is bilateral pitting oedema to the knees. A chest X-ray is requested, which shows apparent cardiomegaly with a globular cardiac silhouette. You suspect a possible pericardial effusion. Which of the following statements is true?
options: A large effusion can be a sign of malignancy
A pericardial rub is always heard if the effusion is large
An ECG is the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis
High-dose diuretic therapy will resolve the pericardial effusion
In symptomatic patients, cardiac surgery is required to remove the pericardial fluid
orig.explanation: A large effusion can be a sign of malignancy A large pericardial effusion may indicate an underlying malignancy.

stem: An 18-year-old man has sudden-onset sharp chest pain that is worse on deep inspiration or lying flat and relieved by sitting forward and taking shallow breaths. Acute pericarditis is suspected. What is the most specific ECG change in acute pericarditis?
explanation: PR depression (with PR elevation in aVR) is the most specific ECG sign of pericarditis; ST elevation is diffuse, concave and without reciprocal change.

orig.stem: An 18 year old man presents with sudden onset of sharp chest pain. The pain is made worse by deep inspiration or lying down flat. It is relieved by sitting forward and taking shallow breaths. He presents to the emergency de partment and an ECG is recorded because the attending doctor suspects acute pericarditis. What is the most specific ECG change in pericarditis?
orig.explanation: PR segment depression PR segment depression is highly specific for acute pericarditis.

stem: In patients with a pericardial effusion, what is the most important clinical sign to determine whether there is cardiac tamponade?
explanation: Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory SBP fall > 10 mmHg) is the key bedside sign that an effusion is causing tamponade; echo confirms.

orig.stem: In patients with a pericardial effusion, what is the most important clinical sign to determine whether there is cardiac tamponade?
orig.explanation: Pulsus paradoxus Pulsus paradoxus is a key sign indicating cardiac tamponade.

stem: A 75-year-old woman with widely metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer is admitted to intensive care with BP 73/52 mmHg after 3–5 days of fatigue and worsening breathlessness. Her neck veins are distended, and the chest X-ray shows a massive, water-bottle-shaped heart shadow without new pulmonary infiltrates. Which additional finding is most likely on examination?
options: Fall in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg with inspiration
Lack of fall of the jugular venous pressure with inspiration
Late diastolic murmur with opening snap
Rapid y-descent of jugular venous pressure tracing
explanation: Hypotension, distended neck veins and a water-bottle heart in lung cancer is malignant tamponade, so pulsus paradoxus is expected. Kussmaul sign suggests constriction.

orig.stem: A 75-year-old woman with widely metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer is admitted to the intensive care unit with a systolic blood pressure of 73/52 mmHg. She presented complaining of fatigue and worsening dyspnea over the last 3-5 days. Her physical examination shows elevated neck veins. Chest radiograph shows a massive, water bottle-shaped heart shadow and no new pulmonary infiltrates. Which of the following additional findings is most likely present on physical examination?
options: Fall in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg with inspiration
Lack of fall of the jugular venous pressure with inspiration
Late diastolic murmur with opening snap
Rapid y-descent of jugular venous pressure tracing
orig.explanation: Fall in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg with inspiration In cardiac tamponade, an exaggerated fall in systolic blood pressure (pulsus paradoxus) is observed.

stem: A 27-year-old doctor has had 1 week of cough, coryza and low-grade fever. Today he develops rapidly escalating chest pain that is worse on deep inspiration. His 12-lead ECG is shown. His BP is normal, he is now afebrile, and the JVP is not raised, but he is uncomfortable from the pain. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Administer aspirin, intravenous heparin, sublingual nitroglycerin, and clopidogrel
Emergently obtain transthoracic echocardiogram with possible pericardiocentesis
Emergently perform coronary angiography to evaluate for acute myocardial infarction
explanation: Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression after a viral illness, no high-risk features: outpatient ibuprofen plus colchicine.

orig.stem: You are asked to evaluate a 27-year-old internal medicine resident reporting 1 week of cough, coryza, and a low-grade fever. Today, he has developed rapidly escalating chest discomfort while in clinic. He notes that the pain becomes more intense when he takes a deep breath. You perform a standard 12-lead ECG (see Figure V-18). On examination, his blood pressure is normal, he is afebrile, and his jugular venous pulse is not elevated. However, he appears mildly uncomfortable from the chest pain. The next most appropriate step would be which of the following?
options: Administer aspirin, intravenous heparin, sublingual nitroglycerin, and clopidogrel.
Emergently obtain transthoracic echocardiogram with possible pericardiocentesis.
Emergently perform coronary angiography to evaluate for acute myocardial infarction.
orig.explanation: Prescribe ibuprofen and colchicine. The presentation and ECG are most consistent with pericarditis, best managed with NSAIDs and colchicine.

stem: A 23-year-old man who has recently recovered from an upper respiratory tract infection presents to the AE department with chest pain made worse on breathing. On examination he is febrile, and has a ‘scratchy’ sound heard on auscultation in systole and diastole. ECG reveals widespread saddle-shaped ST segment elevation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 23-year-old man who has recently recovered from an upper respiratory tract infection presents to the AE department with chest pain made worse on breathing. On examination he is febrile, and has a ‘scratchy’ sound heard on auscultation in systole and diastole. ECG reveals widespread saddle-shaped ST segment elevation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Acute pericarditis The presentation is consistent with acute pericarditis, especially following a viral infection.

What additional feature is most likely to be present in this patient?
options: Diastolic murmur over the praecordium radiating towards the left axilla
An 18-mmHg blood pressure drop during inspiration
An 18-mmHg blood pressure drop during expiration

orig.stem: A previously fit and well 30-year-old gym instructor is admitted to hospital following a stab wound to the left side of his chest. He has a blood pressure of 80/45 mmHg and heart rate of 125 beats/min. Breath sounds are present throughout but his HSs are muffled. His JVP appears raised. What additional feature is most likely to be present in this patient?
options: Diastolic murmur over the praecordium radiating towards the left axilla
An 18-mmHg blood pressure drop during inspiration
An 18-mmHg blood pressure drop during expiration
orig.explanation: An 18-mmHg blood pressure drop during inspiration An 18-mmHg drop in systolic blood pressure during inspiration (pulsus paradoxus) is indicative of cardiac tamponade.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with chest pain. She comments that the pain is worse on inspiration but is relieved by leaning forward. Her past medical history includes breast carcinoma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward is acute pericarditis; with breast cancer consider malignant involvement and check echo.

orig.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with chest pain. She comments that the pain is worse on inspiration but is relieved by leaning forward. Her past medical history includes breast carcinoma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Acute pericarditis The clinical picture is classic for acute pericarditis, with pain relieved by leaning forward.

stem: A 43-year-old woman with known breast cancer has increasing breathlessness. Heart sounds are soft and the apex beat cannot be felt. Which investigation is most likely to make the diagnosis?
explanation: Soft heart sounds and an impalpable apex in a patient with cancer suggest a malignant pericardial effusion; echocardiography confirms it and shows tamponade physiology.

orig.stem: A 43-year-old obese woman with known breast cancer complains of shortness of breath. On examination you note soft HSs and obscuration of the apex beat. Which investigation is most likely to lead to a diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Echocardiogram An echocardiogram is the most sensitive investigation for detecting pericardial effusion.

stem: A 55-year-old man attends the emergency department with a dry cough and severe chest pain that began this morning. Two months ago he had an inferior myocardial infarction treated with a right coronary artery stent. He has hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia and takes aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin and enalapril. Temperature 38.5 °C, pulse 92/min, respiratory rate 22/min, BP 130/80 mmHg. A high-pitched scratching sound is heard best with him leaning forward in expiration; the rest of the examination is normal. The ECG shows diffuse ST elevation and troponin I is 0.2 µg/L (0.2 ng/mL). What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: Fever, pleuritic pain, rub and diffuse ST elevation weeks after MI is Dressler syndrome; early infarct pericarditis occurs within 1–3 days.

orig.stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a dry cough and severe chest pain beginning that morning. Two months ago, he was diagnosed with inferior wall myocardial infarction and was treated with stent implantation of the right coronary artery. He has a history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. His medications include aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin, and enalapril. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 92/ min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a high-pitched scratching sound best heard while sitting upright and during expiration. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An ECG shows diffuse ST elevations. Serum studies show a troponin I of 0.2 ng/mL. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
orig.explanation: Dressler syndrome Dressler syndrome (post-MI syndrome) is an immune-mediated pericarditis occurring weeks after infarction.

stem: Two weeks after hospital discharge for documented myocardial infarction, a 65-year-old returns to your office concerned about low-grade fever and pleuritic chest pain. There is no associated shortness of breath. Lungs are clear to auscultation and the heart is free of murmur, gallop, or rub. ECG is unchanged from the last one in the hospital. Which therapy is most likely to be effective?
explanation: Fever and pleuritic pain 2 weeks after MI with no new ECG change is Dressler syndrome: aspirin/NSAID plus colchicine. Anticoagulation risks haemopericardium.

orig.stem: Two weeks after hospital discharge for documented myocardial infarction, a 65-year-old returns to your office concerned about low- grade fever and pleuritic chest pain. There is no associated shortness of breath. Lungs are clear to auscultation and the heart is free of murmur, gallop, or rub. ECG is unchanged from the last one in the hospital. Which therapy is most likely to be effective?
orig.explanation: An anti-inflammatory agent Post–cardiac injury (Dressler): days–6 w after MI/surgery; fever + pleuritic pain; treat NSAIDs or steroids; not PE, pneumonia, or ACS.

stem: A 35-year-old man has substernal chest pain aggravated by inspiration and relieved by sitting up. The lung fields are clear and the heart sounds are somewhat distant. The chest X-ray shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette. What is the best next step in evaluation?
explanation: Pericarditic pain with distant heart sounds and an enlarged cardiac silhouette suggests pericarditis with an effusion, and transthoracic echocardiography is the investigation of choice: it confirms and sizes the effusion and shows whether there is tamponade physiology. A lateral decubitus film is used for pleural, not pericardial, fluid, and serial ECGs are non-specific. Cardiac catheterisation and stress imaging are for coronary disease and have no role here.

orig.stem: A 35-year-old male complains of substernal chest pain aggravated by inspiration and relieved by sitting up. Lung fields are clear to auscultation, and heart sounds are somewhat distant. Chest x-ray shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Which of the following is the best next step in evaluation?
orig.explanation: Echocardiogram Pericarditis with effusion: pleuritic pain better sitting up; echo confirms fluid; CXR may show enlarged silhouette; no role for cath or stress test.

stem: A 42-year-old female with acute pericarditis develops jugular venous distention and hypotension. The ECG shows electrical alternans. Which of the following is the most likely additional physical finding?
options: Basilar rales halfway up both posterior lung fields

orig.stem: A 42-year-old female with acute pericarditis develops jugular venous distention and hypotension. The ECG shows electrical alternans. Which of the following is the most likely additional physical finding?
options: Basilar rales halfway up both posterior lung fields
orig.explanation: Pulsus paradoxus Cardiac tamponade: hypotension, JVP, clear lungs, pulsus paradoxus; urgent echo and pericardiocentesis; RUQ tenderness from hepatic congestion.

stem: A 77-year-old man is under review on the ward after having a pacemaker inserted earlier that day. He initially presented to the emergency department two days ago with recurrent episodes of collapse, leading to a diagnosis of sick sinus syndrome. In the past hour, he has reported increasing chest discomfort and developed hypotension. On examination, he is cool and clammy peripherally, his jugular venous pressure (JVP) is at 5 cm above the sternal angle, and his heart sounds are indistinct. His current heart rate is 72 bpm with a blood pressure of 88/56 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Chest discomfort, hypotension, raised JVP and quiet heart sounds hours after pacing suggest lead perforation with haemopericardium/tamponade.

orig.stem: A 77-year-old man is under review on the ward after having a pacemaker inserted earlier that day. He initially presented to the emergency department two days ago with recurrent episodes of collapse, leading to a diagnosis of sick sinus syndrome. In the past hour, he has reported increasing chest discomfort and developed hypotension. On examination, he is cool and clammy peripherally, his jugular venous pressure (JVP) is at 5 cm above the sternal angle, and his heart sounds are indistinct. His current heart rate is 72 bpm with a blood pressure of 88/56 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Haemopericardium Post-pacemaker tamponade from myocardial perforation → Beck’s triad; treat with urgent pericardiocentesis. Lead fracture presents as device malfunction, not tamponade.

stem: A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes attends the emergency department with increasing breathlessness over 7 days, much worse in the last 24 hours, and light-headedness. He has left shoulder pain and mild ongoing chest pain that improves on sitting up. Five weeks ago he had an anterior STEMI treated with a stent to the left anterior descending artery. The JVP is raised, peripheral pulses are weak and the heart sounds are muffled; the chest is clear with good air entry. Pulse 101/min regular, BP 89/50 mmHg (equal in both arms), temperature 36.0 °C, SpO2 95% on air, respiratory rate 20/min. The ECG shows Q waves in V1–V3 without ST change and small-amplitude complexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds and low voltages weeks after MI is tamponade from a post-MI effusion: urgent echo and pericardiocentesis.

orig.stem: A 65-year-old male presents to the emergency department with increased shortness of breath and a light-headed feeling. He reports some left shoulder pain and some ongoing mild chest pain, which improved when sitting up. The patient reports that the breathlessness has been increasing over the last 7 days, but has been significantly worse over the last 24 hours. The patient reports having had a STEMI (ST elevation myocardial infarction) 5 weeks ago with a stent inserted into the left anterior descending artery. The patient has a past medical history of type II diabetes mellitus. On examination, the patient is found to have a raised jugular venous pressure. Peripheral pulses are weak and the patient is tachycardic with a regular rhythm. The chest is clear on examination with good air entry throughout, and the heart sounds are muffled. Observations: - Heart rate: 101 bpm - Blood pressure: 89/50 mmHg - Temperature: 36.0°C - Oxygen saturations: 95% on air - Respiratory Rate: 20 bpm There is no discrepancy between the blood pressures in each arm. An ECG is done which shows Q waves in V1-V3 with no ST change. The complexes are small amplitude. What is the most likely diagnosis for the patient’s symptoms?
orig.explanation: Cardiac tamponade Beck’s triad after recent STEMI → tamponade; PE would desaturate and not muffle heart sounds; dissection has tearing pain; small QRS voltage also supports effusion.

stem: A 30-year-old woman attends the emergency department with a 1-day history of severe, non-radiating central chest pain that eases on expiration. Cardiorespiratory examination is normal apart from a heart rate of 96/min. The ECG shows widespread ST elevation in the anterior, inferior and lateral leads. FBC and U&E are normal; troponin I is 0.8 µg/L (reference < 0.2 µg/L). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Multi-territory ST elevation with pleuritic pain in a young woman is pericarditis; a small troponin rise means myopericarditis, not ACS.

orig.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a one-day history of central chest pain. The pain is described as severe, non-radiating and eases on expiration. Clinical examination of her cardiorespiratory system is unremarkable other than a heart rate of 96/min. An ECG shows widespread ST elevation in the anterior, inferior and lateral leads. Bloods show the following: Full blood count: Normal Urea and electrolytes: Normal Troponin I: 0.8 ng/mL (< 0.2 ng/mL) What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Acute pericarditis Acute pericarditis: sharp central pain better when sitting forward; widespread ST elevation; troponin may be mildly raised; ACS usually territorial.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with several days of progressive chest pain, pleuritic in nature and worse on lying down. He achieves some relief from the pain by sitting forward. On examination, a pericardial rub is noted when leaning forward. Given the most likely diagnosis, which of the following electrocardiogram (ECG) findings is most specific?

orig.stem: A 30-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with several days of progressive chest pain, pleuritic in nature and worse on lying down. He achieves some relief from the pain by sitting forward. On examination, a pericardial rub is noted when leaning forward. Given the most likely diagnosis, which of the following electrocardiogram (ECG) findings is most specific?
orig.explanation: PR depression Acute pericarditis ECG: most specific sign is PR depression; ST elevation is diffuse; QRS widening suggests other pathology.

stem: Which of the following is bad prognostic sign regarding acute rheumatic fever:

orig.stem: Which of the following is bad prognostic sign regarding acute rheumatic fever:
orig.explanation: Old age. Old age is considered a bad prognostic sign in acute rheumatic fever.

stem: A patient with history of mitral valve replacement 3 weeks ago developed infective endocarditis. Which of the following microorganisms is responsible for this endocarditis?

orig.stem: A patient with history of mitral valve replacement 3 weeks ago developed infective endocarditis. Which of the following microorganisms is responsible for this endocarditis?
orig.explanation: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (Staphylococcus epidermidis) Coagulase-negative staphylococci are a common cause of early prosthetic valve endocarditis.

stem: Which manifestation of acute rheumatic fever is responsible for its long-term organ damage?
explanation: Carditis is the only rheumatic fever manifestation causing permanent damage (chronic rheumatic valve disease); arthritis, rash and chorea resolve.

orig.stem: In rheumatic fever, the most condition considered as a sequel and end damage for organ is
orig.explanation: Carditis Carditis is the most significant sequelae in rheumatic fever.

stem: Which of the following conditions carries the LOWEST risk of infective endocarditis?
options: Rheumatic heart disease with mitral regurgitation
explanation: MVP without regurgitation has near-population endocarditis risk. Prosthetic valves and previous IE carry the highest risk.

orig.stem: The lower risk condition for infective endocarditis is
orig.explanation: Mitral valve prolapse without regurgitation Mitral valve prolapse without regurgitation carries a lower risk for infective endocarditis.

stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted with pyrexia and found to have infective endocarditis. Which one of the following is most associated with a good prognosis?
explanation: Viridans streptococcal native-valve IE is usually penicillin-sensitive with > 90% cure. S. aureus, prosthetic and culture-negative IE do worse.

orig.stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted with pyrexia and found to have infective endocarditis. Which one of the following is most associated with a good prognosis?
orig.explanation: Streptococcus viridans infection Streptococcus viridans endocarditis generally has a favorable prognosis.

stem: Which one of the following is bad prognostic sign of rheumatic fever

orig.stem: which one of the following is bad prognostic sign of rheumatic fever
orig.explanation: Old age Old age is considered a bad prognostic sign in rheumatic fever.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with a history of fever, chills, night sweats, and a pansystolic murmur over the apex radiating to the axilla. What is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with a history of fever, chills, night sweats, and a pansystolic murmur over the apex radiating to the axilla. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Infective endocarditis The prolonged fever with a new murmur, particularly a pansystolic murmur at the apex, is highly suggestive of infective endocarditis.

stem: Which investigation is most indicated to confirm the diagnosis of infective endocarditis in this patient?

orig.stem: Which investigation is most indicated to confirm the diagnosis of infective endocarditis in this patient?
orig.explanation: Blood cultures and echocardiography Blood cultures combined with echocardiography are the mainstays in diagnosing infective endocarditis.

stem: Which of the following clinical signs is characteristically associated with infective endocarditis?
explanation: Janeway lesions (painless palmar/plantar haemorrhagic macules from septic emboli) are characteristic of endocarditis; a minor Duke criterion.

orig.stem: Which clinical sign is often associated with infective endocarditis?
orig.explanation: Janeway lesions Janeway lesions (non-tender, erythematous lesions on the palms and soles) are a well-known sign of infective endocarditis.

stem: A 32-year-old woman has fever, chills, night sweats and a new apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Infective endocarditis is suspected and three sets of blood cultures have been taken. She is unwell but haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy tailored after culture results
explanation: After blood cultures, start empirical high-dose IV bactericidal antibiotics, then tailor to the organism for 4–6 weeks. Surgery only for specific indications.

orig.stem: What is the most appropriate initial treatment approach for infective endocarditis in this patient?
options: Empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy tailored after culture results
orig.explanation: Empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy tailored after culture results Early initiation of empirical IV antibiotics—later tailored to culture results—is crucial in the treatment of infective endocarditis.

stem: A 50-year-old man has 3 weeks of fever and influenza-like symptoms. He has a heart rate of 105/min and a wide pulse pressure (BP 140/45 mmHg). A murmur was suspected but is not heard on repeat examination. There is no evidence of chest or urinary infection. What are these findings most compatible with?
options: Infective endocarditis affecting the aortic valve
Infective endocarditis affecting the tricuspid valve
explanation: Prolonged fever with a new wide pulse pressure suggests aortic valve endocarditis with acute AR; its soft short murmur is easily missed.

orig.stem: A 50 year old man is assessed because of 3 weeks of fever and influenza-like symptoms. Examination findings are tachycardia (heart rate 105 beats/min), and a large pulse pressure, BP 140/45 mmHg. Initially it was thought a murmur was present but repeat examination reveals no murmur. Investigations reveal no evidence of chest or urinary infection. What are these findings most compatible with?
options: Infective endocarditis affecting the aortic valve
Infective endocarditis affecting the tricuspid valve
orig.explanation: Infective endocarditis affecting the aortic valve A wide pulse pressure suggests aortic incompetence, which can be seen in infective endocarditis of the aortic valve.

stem: An 18 year old woman presents with a sore throat and suspected acute rheumatic fever. Which of the following is a minor manifestation of acute rheumatic fever?
explanation: Jones minor criteria: fever, arthralgia, raised ESR/CRP, prolonged PR. Carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum and nodules are major.

orig.stem: An 18 year old woman presents with a sore throat and suspected acute rheumatic fever. Which of the following is a minor manifestation of acute rheumatic fever?
orig.explanation: Raised C-reactive protein Raised C-reactive protein is a minor criterion in the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever.

stem: An 18 year old woman has a raised C-reactive protein, a rash consistent with erythema marginatum and pyrexia. However, the clinician remains uncertain about the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever. Rapid response to which treatment will help to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation: Rheumatic arthritis responds dramatically to aspirin within 24–48 h; a rapid response supports the diagnosis.

orig.stem: An 18 year old woman has a raised C-reactive protein, a rash consistent with erythema marginatum and pyrexia. However, the clinician remains uncertain about the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever. Rapid response to which treatment will help to confirm the diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Aspirin A rapid clinical response to high- dose aspirin supports the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever.

stem: A 65-year-old man has a 4-week history of general malaise and lethargy. Two courses of antibiotics have temporarily improved his symptoms, but overall he continues to deteriorate, and his GP notes that he has become anaemic. He is admitted with fever; blood cultures are taken and an echocardiogram shows a mass on the mitral valve. Which organism is most likely to grow from his blood cultures?
explanation: An indolent illness with anaemia and partial response to antibiotics is subacute native-valve IE, classically viridans streptococci.

orig.stem: A 65 year old man presents with a 4-week history of general malaise and lethargy. He has had two courses of antibiotics that have temporarily improved his symptoms but he continues to feel worse over time. His family physician notices he has become anaemic. He attends the emergency department and he is admitted to hospital with a fever. He has some blood cultures taken and he undergoes an echocardiogram, which shows a mass on his mitral valve. What is the most likely organism that will be grown from his blood cultures?
orig.explanation: Viridans streptococci Viridans streptococci are the most common cause of native valve endocarditis.

stem: A 65-year-old man with a 4-week illness of malaise, anaemia and fever has a mitral valve mass on echocardiography. Before the blood culture results are known, a junior doctor examines him for signs of endocarditis. Which of the following is the commonest finding?
explanation: Microscopic haematuria (glomerulonephritis or renal emboli) is commoner in IE than splinters, Osler nodes or Roth spots; dipstick the urine.

orig.stem: Considering the patient in Question 16.72, before the blood culture results are known, the junior doctor reviews the 65 year old man and examines him for evidence of endocarditis. What is the commonest sign that the doctor is likely to find?
orig.explanation: Haematuria Haematuria, often microscopic, is the most common sign in endocarditis.

stem: A 45-year-old man attends the emergency department with worsening breathlessness and fevers. The medical team suspects a diagnosis of infective endocarditis. Which of the following is the most suggestive feature of infective endocarditis?
explanation: A new or changing regurgitant murmur with fever is the most suggestive feature of IE; new regurgitation on echo is a major Duke criterion.

orig.stem: A 45-year-old man attends the emergency department with worsening breathlessness and fevers. The medical team suspects a diagnosis of infective endocarditis. Which of the following is the most suggestive feature of infective endocarditis?
orig.explanation: Appearing and changing murmurs A new or changing murmur is a major criterion for infective endocarditis.

stem: A 35-year-old man who injects drugs has night sweats and weight loss. He is febrile (38.5 °C) and infective endocarditis is suspected. Which organism is most likely responsible?
explanation: In people who inject drugs, S. aureus is the commonest cause of IE, usually tricuspid with septic pulmonary emboli; cover MRSA where prevalent.

orig.stem: A 35-year-old IV drug abuser presents with night sweats and weight loss. On examination he is pyrexial with a temperature of 38.5°C. You suspect a diagnosis of infective endocarditis. Which of the following organisms is most likely to account for his condition?
orig.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of infective endocarditis in IV drug abusers.

stem: A 31-year-old woman presents with night sweats. On examination you detect a systolic murmur. She has severe gum and tooth decay and has recently had two teeth taken out. Which of the following organisms is most likely to account for her condition?

orig.stem: A 31-year-old woman presents with night sweats. On examination you detect a systolic murmur. She has severe gum and tooth decay and has recently had two teeth taken out. Which of the following organisms is most likely to account for her condition?
orig.explanation: Streptococcus mutans Streptococcus mutans, associated with dental infections, is a likely cause of endocarditis in this context.

stem: A 40-year-old man with an underlying cardiac condition is about to have root canal treatment and a new crown fitted. For which of the following conditions is antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis recommended?
options: Previous coronary artery bypass grafting involving the use of the internal mammary arteries
Presence of a dual chamber pacemaker
explanation: Prophylaxis only for highest risk (prosthetic valves, previous IE, unrepaired cyanotic CHD). ASD, VSD, CABG and pacemakers do not qualify.

orig.stem: A 40-year-old man with an underlying cardiac condition is about to undergo a root canal treatment with a new crown to be fitted in the dentist’s office. Which one of the following conditions strongly warrants antibiotics prophylaxis?
options: Previous coronary artery bypass grafting involving the use of the internal mammary arteries
Presence of a dual chamber pacemaker
orig.explanation: None of the above Current guidelines do not recommend antibiotic prophylaxis for these conditions.

stem: Some clinical features of infective endocarditis result from immune-complex deposition. Which of the following is NOT an immune-complex phenomenon?
explanation: Immune-complex phenomena: Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis, rheumatoid factor. Splenic abscess is embolic (vascular), like Janeway lesions.

orig.stem: You are attending a seminar on infective endocarditis. The lecturer comments that some clinical features of the condition result from immune complex deposition. The following features are all the result of immune complex deposition EXCEPT?
orig.explanation: Splenic abscess Splenic abscess is not a result of immune complex deposition in infective endocarditis.

stem: A 35-year-old man complains of fatigue, night sweats and weight loss. On examination you note a systolic murmur and evidence of splenomegaly. Which investigation is most likely to lead to a diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 35-year-old man complains of fatigue, night sweats and weight loss. On examination you note a systolic murmur and evidence of splenomegaly. Which investigation is most likely to lead to a diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Blood cultures Blood cultures are essential in the diagnosis of infective endocarditis.

stem: A previously well 45-year-old man has fevers and malaise. He has multiple splinter haemorrhages and a systolic murmur, and infective endocarditis is suspected. Regarding the modified Duke criteria, which statement is INCORRECT?
options: The presence of Osler's nodes is a minor criterion
A positive rheumatoid factor is a minor criterion
Echocardiographic evidence of new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve is a major criterion
A single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetii or a phase I IgG titre > 1:800 is a major criterion
A definite diagnosis can be made with three minor criteria
explanation: Definite IE (modified Duke): 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor. Three minor criteria give only 'possible' endocarditis.

orig.stem: A previously fit and well 45-year-old man presents to AE with fevers and malaise. On examination he has multiple splinter haemorrhages and a systolic murmur. A diagnosis of infective endocarditis is suspected. Dukes criteria is used to help with the diagnosis of the condition. Which of the following statements is INCORRECT in Dukes criteria?
options: Presence of Osler nodes is a minor criterion
Positive blood for rheumatoid factor is a minor criterion
Echocardiographic evidence of prosthetic valve dehiscence is a major criterion
Serological evidence of active infection with an organism consistent with infective endocarditis (IE)
Definite diagnosis can be made with three minor criteria
orig.explanation: Definite diagnosis can be made with three minor criteria A definite diagnosis of IE requires either two major, or one major and three minor, or five minor criteria; three minor criteria alone are not sufficient.

stem: A 45-year-old teacher with known mitral valve prolapse presents to his GP with a 2-week history of fevers, rigors, chest pain and breathlessness. He recently underwent a tooth extraction. On examination he is febrile with multiple splinter haemorrhages. A systolic murmur is heard and appears to have increased in intensity since his last GP visit. What is the most likely causative agent in this case?
explanation: Subacute IE on a prolapsing mitral valve after dental work is most likely viridans streptococci from the mouth; benzylpenicillin-based treatment.

orig.stem: A 45-year-old teacher with known mitral valve prolapse presents to his GP with a 2-week history of fevers, rigors, chest pain and breathlessness. He recently underwent a tooth extraction. On examination he is febrile with multiple splinter haemorrhages. A systolic murmur is heard and appears to have increased in intensity since his last GP visit. What is the most likely causative agent in this case?
orig.explanation: Streptococcus viridans Streptococcus viridans, a normal oral flora, is the most common cause of endocarditis following dental procedures.

stem: A 41-year-old man with fever and transient pain in both knees and elbows. The right knee was red and swollen for 1 day during the week prior to presentation. The following laboratory values are obtained: Hct 42%, WBC 12,000/µL with 80% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 20% lymphocytes, ESR 60 mm/h. On physical examination, the patient has a low-grade fever. He has a III/ VI, high-pitched, apical systolic murmur with radiation to the axilla, as well as a soft, mid-diastolic murmur heard at the base.
