orig.explanation: Antistreptolysin O antibody An elevated ASO titer is needed to confirm a recent streptococcal infection in rheumatic fever.

stem: A 12-year-old girl has high fever and swelling of the left ankle and knee 3 weeks after a sore throat. Two years ago she developed breathlessness and a generalised rash when given dicloxacillin for a skin infection. Temperature 38.8 °C, pulse 87/min, BP 98/62 mmHg. The left ankle and knee are swollen and tender with limited movement, and a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the apex. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
explanation: Rheumatic fever: eradicate group A strep with penicillin/amoxicillin; with penicillin anaphylaxis use a macrolide (clarithromycin/azithromycin).

orig.stem: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of high fever and left ankle and knee joint swelling. She had a sore throat 3 weeks ago. There is no family history of serious illness. Her immunizations are up-to- date. She had an episode of breathlessness and generalized rash when she received dicloxacillin for a skin infection 2 years ago. She appears ill. Her temperature is 38.8°C (102.3°F), pulse is 87/min, and blood pressure is 98/62 mm Hg. Examination shows left ankle and knee joint swelling and tenderness with limited range of motion. Breath sounds are normal. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the apex. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
orig.explanation: Clarithromycin Clarithromycin is the antibiotic of choice for patients with beta-lactam allergy in the treatment of rheumatic fever.

stem: A 25-year-old woman with mitral valve prolapse develops low grade fever, malaise, and night sweats after a dental procedure. Which investigation is most likely to provide a definitive diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 25-year-old woman with mitral valve prolapse develops low grade fever, malaise, and night sweats after a dental procedure. Which investigation is most likely to provide a definitive diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Blood culture Blood cultures are definitive in diagnosing subacute bacterial endocarditis.

stem: A nurse prepares a list of patients for dental procedures. Which patient is most likely to ben efit from antibiotic prophylaxis?

orig.stem: A nurse prepares a list of patients for dental procedures. Which patient is most likely to ben efit from antibiotic prophylaxis?
orig.explanation: 65-year-old man with prosthetic aortic valve Only patients with prosthetic valves, prior IE, or unrepaired cyanotic heart disease require prophylaxis.

stem: A 43-year-old man with HIV who injects drugs presents with fever, night sweats and a holosystolic murmur that increases on inspiration. Which complication of his condition is most likely?
options: Painful nodules on the finger pads
Painless haemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles
explanation: IE in people who inject drugs is usually tricuspid (murmur louder on inspiration) and embolises to the lungs as septic pulmonary emboli.

orig.stem: A 43-year-old man with HIV and IV drug use presents with fever, night sweats, and a holosystolic murmur. What is the most likely sequela of his condition?
options: Asymptomatic hemorrhages on palms and soles
orig.explanation: Pulmonary embolism IV drug users with IE are at high risk for septic emboli to the lungs.

stem: Blood cultures and TEE in a patient with tricuspid vegetations reveal the organism responsible for IE. Which organism is most likely?

orig.stem: Blood cultures and TEE in a patient with tricuspid vegetations reveal the organism responsible for IE. Which organism is most likely?
orig.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus S. aureus is the most common cause of acute IE in IV drug users.

stem: A 34-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve has fatigue, exertional breathlessness, low-grade fevers and splinter haemorrhages. He was started on empirical IV vancomycin, and blood cultures now grow Cardiobacterium hominis. What is the next step in management?
explanation: Cardiobacterium hominis is a HACEK organism, often beta-lactamase-producing: switch to ceftriaxone for 4 weeks (6 for prosthetic valves).

orig.stem: A 34-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve presents with fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, low-grade fevers, and nail hemorrhages. Blood cultures grow Cardiobacterium hominis. What is the next step in management?
orig.explanation: Switch to IV ceftriaxone Targeted therapy with ceftriaxone is indicated for Cardiobacterium hominis, a HACEK organism.

stem: A 64-year-old man admitted 7 days ago with pancreatitis after abdominal trauma develops fever, breathlessness and a new holosystolic murmur. There is purulent discharge from his central venous catheter site. Which organism is most likely responsible?
explanation: Line-associated healthcare IE is most often S. aureus; remove the line, take cultures and give vancomycin until MRSA is excluded.

orig.stem: A 64-year-old man, 7 days post-admission for traumatic pancreatitis, develops fever, dyspnea, and a new holosystolic murmur. There is purulent discharge at his central line site. Which organism is most likely responsible?
orig.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus Healthcare-associated IE is most commonly caused by S. aureus.

stem: A 41-year-old man with IV drug use presents with a 10-day history of weakness, headache, and night sweats, and a holosystolic murmur on exam. What is the most likely consequence of his condition?
options: Painless macules and papules on palms and soles

orig.stem: A 41-year-old man with IV drug use presents with a 10-day history of weakness, headache, and night sweats, and a holosystolic murmur on exam. What is the most likely consequence of his condition?
options: Painless macules and papules on palms and soles
orig.explanation: Pulmonary embolism Right-sided IE in IV drug users commonly leads to septic pulmonary emboli.

stem: At autopsy, multiple small sterile nodules composed of immune complexes, fibrin and thrombus are found on both surfaces of the mitral valve, including the ventricular side. In which patient would these findings most likely be found?
options: A 71-year-old man with acute high fever and nail-bed haemorrhages
A 41-year-old woman with a facial rash and non-erosive arthritis
A 28-year-old HIV-positive woman who injects drugs
A 6-year-old girl with subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum
explanation: Sterile vegetations on both sides of the mitral leaflets are Libman–Sacks endocarditis of SLE (malar rash, non-erosive arthritis), especially with antiphospholipid antibodies.

orig.stem: An autopsy shows multiple nodules on the ventricular side of the mitral valve composed of immune complexes and thrombi. In which patient would these findings most likely be found?
options: A 71-year-old male with acute high fever and nail-bed hemorrhages
A 41-year-old female with a facial rash and nonerosive arthritis
A 28-year-old HIV-positive female IV drug user
A 6-year-old female with subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum
orig.explanation: A 41-year-old female with a facial rash and nonerosive arthritis These findings are characteristic of Libman-Sacks endocarditis seen in SLE.

stem: Three weeks after a transurethral resection of the prostate, a 70-year-old man has fever, malaise and limb pain. He has subungual petechiae, tender red papules on the fingers and a new holosystolic murmur. Blood cultures grow a non-haemolytic, PYR-positive Gram-positive coccus. Which organism is most likely responsible?
explanation: IE after a urological procedure with a non-haemolytic, PYR-positive Gram-positive coccus is Enterococcus faecalis: amoxicillin plus ceftriaxone or gentamicin ~6 weeks.

orig.stem: Three weeks after transurethral prostate resection, a 70-year-old man presents with fever, malaise, and extremity pain. He has subungual petechiae and tender red papules, with a new holosystolic murmur. The organism does not cause hemolysis and is PYR positive. Which organism is most likely responsible?
orig.explanation: Enterococcus faecalis Enterococcus faecalis, a PYR positive, gram-positive coccus, is known to cause endocarditis post GU procedures.

stem: An 18-year-old man has fever and flitting pain in both knees and elbows; the right knee was red and swollen for 1 day during the previous week. He has a low-grade fever, a grade III/VI high-pitched apical systolic murmur radiating to the axilla and a soft mid-diastolic murmur at the base. A tender nodule is felt over an extensor tendon of the hand, and there are pink erythematous lesions on the abdomen, some with central clearing. Haematocrit 0.42, WBC 12 × 10⁹/L (80% neutrophils, 20% lymphocytes), ESR 60 mm/h. His ECG is shown. Which test is most critical to the diagnosis?
explanation: Migratory arthritis, carditis, nodules and erythema marginatum meet Jones criteria, which also need evidence of recent strep infection: a raised ASO (or anti-DNase B) titre.

orig.stem: An 18-year-old male complains of fever and transient pain in both knees and elbows. The right knee was red and swollen for 1 day during the week prior to presentation. On physical examination, the patient has a low-grade fever. He has a III/VI, high pitched, apical systolic murmur with radiation to the axilla, as well as a soft, mid-diastolic murmur heard at the base. A tender nodule is palpated over an extensor tendon of the hand. There are pink erythematous lesions over the abdomen, some with central clearing. The following laboratory values are obtained: Hct: 42, WBC: 12,000/μL with 80% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 20% lymphocytes, ESR: 60 mm/h. The patient’s ECG is shown below. Which of the following tests is most critical to diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Antistreptolysin O antibody Acute rheumatic fever per Jones: prior strep + carditis/MR, arthritis, fever, erythema marginatum, nodules, PR prolongation; send ASO; DDx IE/SLE/MI less likely.

stem: Which one of the following features is not part of the modified Duke criteria used in the diagnosis of infective endocarditis?
explanation: A prolonged PR is a Jones (rheumatic fever) criterion, not a Duke criterion; in IE new conduction block may signal an aortic root abscess.

orig.stem: Which one of the following features is not part of the modified Duke criteria used in the diagnosis of infective endocarditis?
orig.explanation: Prolonged PR interval Rheumatic fever may prolong PR. IE diagnosis per modified Duke/ESC: pathology OR 2 major OR 1 major + 3 minor OR 5 minor; majors = typical positive blood cultures or echo/endocardial involvement; minors = risk, fever, vascular, immunologic, microbiologic not meeting major.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is due to have a tooth extracted next week. She had an aortic valve replacement 2 years ago. According to current ESC guidance, what antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended before this procedure?
explanation: A prosthetic valve is highest risk: ESC/AHA advise single-dose oral amoxicillin 2 g 30–60 min before extraction. NICE advises against routine prophylaxis.

orig.stem: A 72-year-old woman is due to have a tooth extracted next week. Her past medical history is significant for an aortic valve replacement 2 years previously. What antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended prior to this procedure?
orig.explanation: General oral hygiene advice No routine IE prophylaxis for dental work; emphasize oral hygiene. Chlorhexidine and pre-procedure antibiotics not recommended without specific indications.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of fevers, night sweats and lethargy. On examination, you note several Janeway lesions on his hands. There is a collapsing pulse and you note an early diastolic murmur. You take multiple sets of blood cultures and commence the patient on broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for presumed infective endocarditis. A trans-thoracic echo identifies large vegetation on the aortic valve with associated aortic regurgitation. You note the patient has a background of metastatic colorectal cancer and is currently receiving palliative chemotherapy. In light of the patient’s past medical history, which of the following organisms are most likely to be responsible?
explanation: Streptococcus gallolyticus (S. bovis) IE is strongly linked to colorectal neoplasia, so isolating it should prompt colonoscopy.

orig.stem: A 75-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of fevers, night sweats and lethargy. On examination, you note several Janeway lesions on his hands. There is a collapsing pulse and you note an early diastolic murmur. You take multiple sets of blood cultures and commence the patient on broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for presumed infective endocarditis. A trans-thoracic echo identifies large vegetation on the aortic valve with associated aortic regurgitation. You note the patient has a background of metastatic colorectal cancer and is currently receiving palliative chemotherapy. In light of the patient’s past medical history, which of the following organisms are most likely to be responsible?
orig.explanation: Streptococcus gallolyticus Streptococcus gallolyticus (S. bovis group) IE strongly linked to colorectal cancer; S. viridans common after dental sources.

stem: A 60-year-old man who had a mitral valve replacement 3 years ago presents acutely with high fever, rigors and fatigue 1 week after a large boil (furuncle) on his thigh. Echocardiography shows a new vegetation on the prosthetic valve, and three sets of blood cultures are taken. Which organism is most likely to be responsible?
explanation: Late prosthetic valve IE (> 1 year) resembles native IE; an acute illness after a furuncle points to S. aureus, which usually needs rifampicin and early surgery.

orig.stem: A 60-year-old male who recently underwent cardiac surgery presents with fever, fatigue, and weight loss. The patient was discharged after a successful mitral valve replacement 4 months ago and as such an urgent echocardiogram is performed. The echo confirms the presence of a new valvular lesion, and a diagnosis of endocarditis is made. Three sets of blood cultures are taken. Which organism is most likely to be responsible for the patient’s diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus Most IE now S. aureus; early post-valve (<2 mo) S. epidermidis dominates; >2 mo reverts to usual spectrum; S. bovis group links to colon cancer.

stem: Which one of the following conditions is most associated with aortic dissection?
explanation: Bicuspid aortic valve has an associated aortopathy and raises dissection risk. Others: hypertension (commonest), Marfan, Loeys–Dietz, coarctation, Turner, pregnancy, cocaine.

orig.stem: Which one of the following conditions is most associated with aortic dissection?
orig.explanation: Bicuspid aortic valve Bicuspid aortic valve is most associated with aortic dissection.

stem: A 63-year-old man with hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset tearing chest pain radiating to the back. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sudden tearing pain radiating to the back in a hypertensive patient is aortic dissection until proved otherwise; confirm with CT aortography and control BP and heart rate.

orig.stem: A 63-year-old man with a history of high blood pressure presents in AE with suddenonset tearing chest pain radiating to the back.
orig.explanation: Aortic dissection Tearing chest pain radiating to the back is indicative of aortic dissection.

stem: A 70-year-old hypertensive man presents with sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back and a weak right radial pulse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sudden, severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back in a hypertensive patient, with a pulse deficit or blood-pressure difference between the arms, is aortic dissection until proved otherwise; other clues are aortic regurgitation, a widened mediastinum and neurological deficits. MI causes crushing pain without pulse deficits, pulmonary embolism causes pleuritic pain and hypoxia, and oesophageal rupture follows vomiting.

orig.stem: A 70-year-old hypertensive man presents with sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back and a weak right radial pulse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Aortic dissection The described “tearing” chest pain with pulse deficit is most consistent with an aortic dissection.

stem: Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis of aortic dissection?
explanation: CT angiography of the whole aorta confirms dissection in a stable patient; TOE if unstable. Chest X-ray and transthoracic echo cannot exclude it.

orig.stem: Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis of aortic dissection?
orig.explanation: CT angiography of the aorta CT angiography is the gold standard for diagnosing aortic dissection in hemodynamically stable patients.

stem: What is the best treatment strategy for a patient with aortic dissection (Type A) presenting in this manner?
options: Urgent surgical repair after blood pressure control
explanation: Type A dissection (ascending aorta) kills 1–2%/hour untreated: emergency surgery after IV beta-blocker BP/HR control. Type B is usually medical.

orig.stem: What is the best treatment strategy for a patient with aortic dissection (Type A) presenting in this manner?
options: Urgent surgical repair after blood pressure control
orig.explanation: Urgent surgical repair after blood pressure control Type A aortic dissection requires urgent surgical intervention along with aggressive blood pressure management.

stem: Which of the following is a common complication of aortic dissection?
explanation: Proximal dissection can rupture into the pericardium causing tamponade, a leading cause of death; also acute AR, coronary occlusion and branch ischaemia.

orig.stem: Which of the following is a common complication of aortic dissection?
orig.explanation: Cardiac tamponade Aortic dissection may lead to rupture into the pericardial space, causing cardiac tamponade.

stem: A 55 year old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents with a history of sudden-onset central chest pain. There are no diagnostic electrocardiogram (ECG) abnormalities, and an interval troponin concentration is not diagnostic of myocardial infarction. What diagnosis should be confirmed or excluded next?
explanation: Sudden severe chest pain in a hypertensive with no MI on ECG/troponin: exclude aortic dissection before antithrombotics or thrombolysis, which could be fatal.

orig.stem: A 55 year old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents with a history of sudden-onset central chest pain. There are no diagnostic electrocardiogram (ECG) abnormalities, and an interval troponin concentration is not diagnostic of myocardial infarction. What diagnosis should be confirmed or excluded next?
orig.explanation: Aortic dissection Aortic dissection should be considered in hypertensive patients with acute chest pain because antithrombotic drugs given before excluding it may cause fatal bleeding.

stem: Which of the following pathologies can be associated with an early diastolic murmur?
explanation: An early diastolic murmur is aortic regurgitation; in Marfan syndrome aortic root dilatation stretches the valve ring. MVP gives a click and late systolic murmur.

orig.stem: Which of the following pathologies can be associated with an early diastolic murmur?
orig.explanation: Marfan’s syndrome Marfan’s syndrome predisposes to aortic regurgitation, which produces an early diastolic murmur.

stem: A 75 year old man is incidentally found to have a pulsatile swelling in his abdomen on a routine health check. He is sent for an abdominal ultrasound scan, which confirms the presence of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Which risk factor is protective against the formation and expansion of an abdominal aortic aneurysm?
explanation: Diabetes is consistently linked to fewer and slower-growing AAAs. Smoking is the strongest risk factor; also male sex, age, family history and hypertension.

orig.stem: A 75 year old man is incidentally found to have a pulsatile swelling in his abdomen on a routine health check. He is sent for an abdominal ultrasound scan, which confirms the presence of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Which risk factor is protective against the formation and expansion of an abdominal aortic aneurysm?
orig.explanation: Diabetes mellitus Diabetes mellitus has been shown to be protective against AAA formation and expansion.

stem: A 65 year old smoker with hypertension is found to have an abdominal aortic aneurysm on population screening with ultrasound. Which intervention will most reduce his future risk of aortic aneurysm rupture?
explanation: Stopping smoking slows AAA growth and lowers rupture risk; drugs (ACEi, beta-blocker, statin) have not been shown to slow growth.

orig.stem: A 65 year old smoker with hypertension is found to have an abdominal aortic aneurysm on population screening with ultrasound. Which intervention will most reduce his future risk of aortic aneurysm rupture?
orig.explanation: Smoking cessation Smoking cessation is the most effective intervention to reduce the risk of aneurysm rupture.

stem: A 65 year old man with known hypertension presents with severe central chest pain that radiates between his shoulder blades. He is sweaty with a BP of 200/100 mmHg in his right arm, a pale left arm and an ECG showing sinus tachycardia. His chest X-ray shows mediastinal widening and a computed tomography scan shows a type A aortic dissection. Which of the following is known to reduce mortality?
options: Emergency repair of the ascending aorta
Prevention of limb or renal ischaemia

orig.stem: A 65 year old man with known hypertension presents with severe central chest pain that radiates between his shoulder blades. He is sweaty with a BP of 200/100 mmHg in his right arm, a pale left arm and an ECG showing sinus tachycardia. His chest X-ray shows mediastinal widening and a computed tomography scan shows a type A aortic dissection. Which of the following is known to reduce mortality?
options: Emergency repair of the ascending aorta
Prevention of limb or renal ischaemia
orig.explanation: Emergency repair of the ascending aorta Surgical repair of the ascending aorta is the definitive treatment to reduce mortality in type A dissection.

stem: A short young woman presents with severe chest pain, vomiting and a sinus tachycardia. She is in the last trimester of pregnancy and has had normal blood pressure and observations at antenatal care. She is admitted for observation but is later found collapsed and in cardiac arrest. Despite attempts at resuscitation, mother and child die. Postmortem reveals an aortic dissection. What is the most likely underlying cause for the dissection?
explanation: Pregnancy (third trimester/peripartum) predisposes to dissection through medial hormonal change and high cardiac output; this woman had no Marfan features.

orig.stem: A short young woman presents with severe chest pain, vomiting and a sinus tachycardia. She is in the last trimester of pregnancy and has had normal blood pressure and observations at antenatal care. She is admitted for observation but is later found collapsed and in cardiac arrest. Despite attempts at resuscitation, mother and child die. Postmortem reveals an aortic dissection. What is the most likely underlying cause for the dissection?
orig.explanation: Pregnancy Pregnancy-associated dissection, though rare, can occur in the third trimester.

stem: A 23 year old woman is referred for evaluation because she is very tall, has problems with her vision and has a heart murmur. Her family physician is concerned that she may have Marfan’s syndrome. What structural gene is associated with an abnormality in Marfan’s syndrome?
explanation: Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant, due to FBN1 (fibrillin-1) mutations: tall, ectopia lentis, aortic root dilatation and MVP. Sarcomere genes cause HCM.

orig.stem: A 23 year old woman is referred for evaluation because she is very tall, has problems with her vision and has a heart murmur. Her family physician is concerned that she may have Marfan’s syndrome. What structural gene is associated with an abnormality in Marfan’s syndrome?
orig.explanation: Fibrillin Marfan’s syndrome is caused by mutations in the fibrillin gene.

stem: Four days after an open aortobifemoral bypass, a CT scan shows a pseudoaneurysm just proximal to the aortic origin of the graft. Which of the following best defines a pseudoaneurysm?
options: A focal dilation in a vessel in which the intimal and medial layers are disrupted and the dilated segment is lined by adventitia only
A focal dilation of a vessel only involving one portion of the circumference
Apparent dilation of a vessel due to intrinsic narrowing proximal and distal to the point of apparent narrowing
Dilation of a vessel, though not to the size necessary to be diagnosed as a true aneurysm
The appearance of an aneurysmal dilation of a vessel on imaging due to the angulation of the artery and imaging technique
explanation: A pseudoaneurysm is a contained rupture held only by adventitia or surrounding tissue (after puncture, surgery, trauma). A true aneurysm involves all three layers.

orig.stem: A 67-year-old former heavy smoker is postoperative day 4 from an open aortobifemoral bypass operation for severe claudication. On routine postoperative CT scan prior to discharge, a pseudoaneurysm is noted just proximal to the aortic origin of the bypass grafts. Which of the following best defines a pseudoaneurysm?
options: A focal dilation in a vessel in which the intimal and medial layers are disrupted and the dilated segment is lined by adventitia only
A focal dilation of a vessel only involving one portion of the circumference
Apparent dilation of a vessel due to intrinsic narrowing proximal and distal to the point of apparent narrowing
Dilation of a vessel, though not to the size necessary to be diagnosed as a true aneurysm
The appearance of an aneurysmal dilation of a vessel on imaging due to the angulation of the artery and imaging technique
orig.explanation: A focal dilation in a vessel in which the intimal and medial layers are disrupted and the dilated segment is lined by adventitia only This definition describes a pseudoaneurysm, where the vessel wall is disrupted and only the adventitia contains the dilation.

stem: All of the following factors are associated with elevated risk for the development of an aortic aneurysm EXCEPT:
explanation: Degenerative aortic aneurysms are several times commoner in men, so female sex is not a risk factor. Age, smoking, hypertension and family history are.

orig.stem: All of the following factors are associated with elevated risk for the development of an aortic aneurysm EXCEPT:
orig.explanation: Female sex Female sex is not a risk factor; in fact, males are at higher risk for degenerative aortic aneurysms.

stem: You are seeing Mr. Walker in clinic for follow-up. He is a 22-year-old man with a family history of sudden death and arterial aneurysms. He is quite tall with widely spaced eyes and a broad uvula. On his first visit, you order a transthoracic echocardiogram to investigate a diastolic murmur and note an aortic root aneurysm of 4.9 cm. He most likely has a mutation in which of the following genes?
explanation: Aortic root aneurysm with hypertelorism, bifid uvula and familial sudden death is Loeys–Dietz (TGFBR1/2); aneurysms dissect smaller, so repair earlier than Marfan.

orig.stem: You are seeing Mr. Walker in clinic for follow-up. He is a 22-year-old man with a family history of sudden death and arterial aneurysms. He is quite tall with widely spaced eyes and a broad uvula. On his first visit, you order a transthoracic echocardiogram to investigate a diastolic murmur and note an aortic root aneurysm of 4.9 cm. He most likely has a mutation in which of the following genes?
orig.explanation: TGF-B receptor Loeys-Dietz syndrome is associated with mutations in the TGF-B receptor genes.

stem: Which of the following patients with aortic dissection or hematoma is best managed without surgical therapy?
options: A 45-year-old female with a dissection involving the aorta distal to the great vessel origin but cephalad to the renal arteries
A 74-year-old male with a dissection involving the root of the aorta
A 58-year-old male with aortic dissection involving the distal aorta and the bilateral renal arteries
A 69-year-old male with an intramural hematoma within the aortic root
All of the above patients require surgical management of their aortic disease
explanation: Uncomplicated type B dissection (beyond the left subclavian) is treated medically with IV beta-blockade. Malperfusion, rupture or expansion need repair; any ascending involvement needs surgery.

orig.stem: Which of the following patients with aortic dissection or hematoma is best managed without surgical therapy?
options: A 45-year-old female with a dissection involving the aorta distal to the great vessel origin but cephalad to the renal arteries
A 74-year-old male with a dissection involving the root of the aorta
A 58-year-old male with aortic dissection involving the distal aorta and the bilateral renal arteries
A 69-year-old male with an intramural hematoma within the aortic root
All of the above patients require surgical management of their aortic disease.
orig.explanation: A 45-year-old female with a dissection involving the aorta distal to the great vessel origin but cephalad to the renal arteries Uncomplicated distal dissections can be managed medically.

stem: An incidental CT finding in a 32-year-old woman is dilatation of the ascending aorta to 4.3 cm. All of the following are recognised causes of this finding EXCEPT:
explanation: Ascending aortic dilatation: GCA, Takayasu, syphilis, spondyloarthritis, Marfan/Loeys–Dietz/EDS, bicuspid valve. SLE is not a recognised cause.

orig.stem: A 32-year-old woman is seen in the emergency department for acute shortness of breath. A helical CT shows no evidence of pulmonary embolus, but incidental note is made of dilatation of the ascending aorta to 4.3 cm. All the following are associated with this finding EXCEPT:
orig.explanation: Systemic lupus erythematosus SLE is not typically associated with ascending aortic dilation.

stem: A 46-year-old man develops sudden severe central chest pain after lifting heavy cases while moving house. The pain radiates to the back and both shoulders but not to either arm. His BP is 155/90 mmHg, pulse rate is 92 beats per minute and the ECG is normal. He is distressed and sweaty, but not nauseated. What would you consider the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 46-year-old man develops sudden severe central chest pain after lifting heavy cases while moving house. The pain radiates to the back and both shoulders but not to either arm. His BP is 155/90 mmHg, pulse rate is 92 beats per minute and the ECG is normal. He is distressed and sweaty, but not nauseated. What would you consider the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Aortic dissection The most likely diagnosis – and the one that must be urgently excluded – is an aortic dissection. The other options do not fit the clinical picture.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents to accident and emergency with a 3-day history of increasingly severe chest pain. The patient describes the pain as a sharp, tearing pain starting in the centre of his chest and radiating straight through to his back between his shoulder blades. The patient looks in pain but there is no pallor, heart rate is 95, respiratory rate is 20, temperature 37°C and blood pressure is 155/95 mmHg. The most likely diagnosis is:

orig.stem: A 60-year-old man presents to accident and emergency with a 3-day history of increasingly severe chest pain. The patient describes the pain as a sharp, tearing pain starting in the centre of his chest and radiating straight through to his back between his shoulder blades. The patient looks in pain but there is no pallor, heart rate is 95, respiratory rate is 20, temperature 37°C and blood pressure is 155/95 mmHg. The most likely diagnosis is:
orig.explanation: Aortic dissection The description is typical of an aortic dissection, which presents with a severe, tearing pain radiating to the back.

stem: A 67-year-old male presents to your office after community ultrasound screening revealed an aortic aneurysm measuring 3.0 × 3.5 cm. Physical examination confirms a palpable, pulsatile, nontender abdominal mass just above the umbilicus. The patient’s medical conditions include hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and tobacco use. What is the best recommendation for the patient to consider?
options: Watchful waiting is the best course until the first onset of abdominal pain
Surgery is indicated except for the excess operative risk represented by the patient’s risk factors
Serial follow-up with ultrasound, CT, or MRI is indicated, with the major determinant for surgery being aneurysmal size greater than 5 to 6 cm
Serial follow-up with ultrasound, CT, or MRI is indicated, with the major determinant for surgery being involvement of a renal artery
Unlike stents in coronary artery disease, endovascular stent grafts have proven unsuccessful in the management of AAAs
explanation: A 3.0–3.5 cm AAA is monitored with ultrasound while treating risk factors; repair at ≥ 5.5 cm, growth > 1 cm/year or symptoms. EVAR is an alternative to open repair.

orig.stem: A 67-year-old male presents to your office after community ultrasound screening revealed an aortic aneurysm measuring 3.0 × 3.5 cm. Physical examination confirms a palpable, pulsatile, nontender abdominal mass just above the umbilicus. The patient’s medical conditions include hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and tobacco use. What is the best recommendation for the patient to consider?
options: Watchful waiting is the best course until the first onset of abdominal pain.
Surgery is indicated except for the excess operative risk represented by the patient’s risk factors.
Serial follow-up with ultrasound, CT, or MRI is indicated, with the major determinant for surgery being aneurysmal size greater than 5 to 6 cm.
Serial follow-up with ultrasound, CT, or MRI is indicated, with the major determinant for surgery being involvement of a renal artery.
Unlike stents in coronary artery disease, endovascular stent grafts have proven unsuccessful in the management of AAAs.
orig.explanation: Serial follow-up with ultrasound, CT, or MRI is indicated, with the major determinant for surgery being aneurysmal size greater than 5 to 6 cm. AAA: smoking/HTN risk; rupture risk by size; repair if >5.5 cm, rapid growth, or symptoms; endovascular option; renal artery involvement complicates repair only.

stem: A 70-year-old female has been healthy except for hypertension treated with a thiazide diuretic. She presents with sudden onset of a severe, tearing chest pain, which radiates to the back and is associated with dyspnoea and diaphoresis. Blood pressure is 210/94. Lung auscultation reveals bilateral basilar rales. A faint murmur of aortic insufficiency is heard. The BNP level is elevated at 550 pg/mL (Normal < 100). ECG shows nonspecific ST-T changes. Chest x-ray suggests a widened mediastinum. Which of the following choices represents the best initial management?
options: IV furosemide plus IV loading dose of digoxin
Percutaneous coronary intervention with consideration of angioplasty and/or stenting
Blood cultures and rapid initiation of vancomycin plus gentamicin, followed by echocardiography
IV beta-blocker to control heart rate, IV nitroprusside to control blood pressure, transesophageal echocardiogram
IV heparin followed by CT pulmonary angiography
explanation: Tearing back pain, severe hypertension, new AR and widened mediastinum is proximal dissection: IV beta-blocker, then nitroprusside, urgent TOE/CT and surgery.

orig.stem: A 70-year-old female has been healthy except for hypertension treated with a thiazide diuretic. She presents with sudden onset of a severe, tearing chest pain, which radiates to the back and is associated with dyspnea and diaphoresis. Blood pressure is 210/94. Lung auscultation reveals bilateral basilar rales. A faint murmur of aortic insufficiency is heard. The BNP level is elevated at 550 pg/mL (Normal < 100). ECG shows nonspecific ST-T changes. Chest x-ray suggests a widened mediastinum. Which of the following choices represents the best initial management?
options: IV furosemide plus IV loading dose of digoxin
Percutaneous coronary intervention with consideration of angioplasty and/or stenting
Blood cultures and rapid initiation of vancomycin plus gentamicin, followed by echocardiography
IV beta-blocker to control heart rate, IV nitroprusside to control blood pressure, transesophageal echocardiogram
IV heparin followed by CT pulmonary angiography
orig.explanation: IV beta-blocker to control heart rate, IV nitroprusside to control blood pressure, transesophageal echocardiogram Aortic dissection with AR and HTN → IV beta-blocker first, then nitroprusside; diagnose by TEE/MRA/CTA; urgent surgery for Type A; avoid anticoagulation and digoxin.

stem: A 67-year-old male presents to your clinic to establish primary care; he is asymptomatic. He has a history of hypertension for which he takes hydrochlorothiazide. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 62. The patient smoked until 5 years ago, but has been abstinent from tobacco since then. His blood pressure in the office today is 132/78. Aside from being overweight, the remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following preventive health interventions would be most appropriately offered to him today?
options: Carotid ultrasound to evaluate for carotid ar tery stenosis
Abdominal ultrasound to evaluate for aortic aneurysm
Lipoprotein(a) assay to evaluate coronary heart disease risk
Exercise (treadmill) stress testing to evaluate for coronary artery disease
Homocysteine level to evaluate coronary heart disease risk
explanation: One-off ultrasound AAA screening is offered to men 65–75 who have ever smoked (all men at 65 in the UK); it reduces aneurysm deaths.

orig.stem: A 67-year-old male presents to your clinic to establish primary care; he is asymptomatic. He has a history of hypertension for which he takes hydrochlorothiazide. options: Carotid ultrasound to evaluate for carotid ar tery stenosis
Abdominal ultrasound to evaluate for aortic aneurysm
Lipoprotein(a) assay to evaluate coronary heart disease risk
Exercise (treadmill) stress testing to evaluate for coronary artery disease
Homocysteine level to evaluate coronary heart disease risk
orig.explanation: Abdominal ultrasound to evaluate for aortic aneurysm USPSTF: one-time AAA ultrasound for men 65–75 who ever smoked; no carotid US/ treadmill screening in asymptomatic; do not order Lp(a)/homocysteine.

stem: A 38-year-old lady presents to the emergency department with increased shortness of breath for the last 5 days. On full history taking, you find she has also recently had some episodes of chest pain on exertion. She is normally fit and well but does report generalized aching and a high temperature approximately 2 weeks ago. On examination you find that she is haemodynamically stable with a blood pressure on 100/65 mmHg in the right arm and a heart rate of 95 bpm. The radial pulse on the right side is absent. Heart sounds are normal and the apex beat is non displaced. Her oxygen saturations are 95% on air and her respiratory rate at rest is 20 breaths per minute. Given the history and examination findings given, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A young woman with prior systemic illness, chest pain and an absent radial pulse has Takayasu arteritis (large-vessel vasculitis); diagnose by CT/MR angiography, treat with steroids.

orig.stem: A 38-year-old lady presents to the emergency department with increased shortness of breath for the last 5 days. Heart sounds are normal and the apex beat is non displaced. Her oxygen saturations are 95% on air and her respiratory rate at rest is 20 breaths per minute. Given the history and examination findings given, what is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Takayasu’s arteritis Absent radial pulse + systemic features best explained by Takayasu arteritis; alternatives each miss key findings.

stem: Which of the following drugs is not first line antihypertensive?

orig.stem: Which of the following drugs is not first line antihypertensive?
orig.explanation: Beta blockers Beta blockers are no longer considered first-line for primary hypertension in many guidelines.

stem: Which of the following is not considered as a first line treatment for hypertension?

orig.stem: Which of the following is not considered as a first line treatment for hypertension?
orig.explanation: Beta blockers Beta blockers are not considered first line treatment for hypertension.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is reviewed in the diabetes clinic. Her blood pressure was 145/95 mmHg and lisinopril was started. Baseline blood tests showed potassium 4.5 mmol/L, creatinine 159 µmol/L (1.8 mg/dL) and eGFR 47 mL/min/1.73 m². Three months later, potassium is 4.9 mmol/L, creatinine 177 µmol/L (2.0 mg/dL) and eGFR 44 mL/min/1.73 m². What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Stop lisinopril and arrange investigations to exclude renal artery stenosis
explanation: A creatinine rise < 30% (eGFR fall < 25%) with K⁺ < 6 after an ACE inhibitor is expected; continue the drug and monitor.

orig.stem: A 45-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is reviewed in the diabetes clinic. Blood pressure was 145/95 mmHg. Lisinopril was started to treat her hypertension. Her blood tests were S.K 4.5 mmol/l, Creatinine 1.8 mg/ dl and eGFR was 47 ml/min. Three months later S.K 4.9 mmol/l, screatinine 2 mg/dl and eGFR was 44 ml/min. Which of the following options is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Stop lisinopril and arrange investigations to exclude renal artery stenosis
orig.explanation: No action No action is appropriate as the changes in renal parameters are minimal.

stem: A 42-year-old man with known hypertension who ran out of his medication presents with a blood pressure of 230/140 mmHg, severe headache, dizziness and blurred optic disc margins (papilloedema) on fundoscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Severe hypertension with papilloedema (acute organ damage) is a hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension): admit for controlled IV treatment.

orig.stem: A 42-year-old man with known hypertension who ran out of his medication presents with a blood pressure of 230/140 mmHg, severe headache, dizziness, and blurred disc margins on fundoscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Hypertensive emergency The very high blood pressure with end-organ damage (blurred disc margins) indicates a hypertensive emergency.

stem: How would you best label this patient’s hypertensive state?

orig.stem: How would you best label this patient’s hypertensive state?
orig.explanation: Hypertensive emergency End-organ damage (e.g., retinal changes) in the context of severely elevated blood pressure defines a hypertensive emergency.

stem: A 42-year-old man with known hypertension who ran out of his medication presents with a blood pressure of 230/140 mmHg, severe headache, dizziness and papilloedema on fundoscopy. Which of the following is an appropriate first-line antihypertensive in this situation?
explanation: Hypertensive emergency needs a titratable IV drug (labetalol, nicardipine or nitroprusside); lower MAP by ≤ 20–25% over the first hours.

orig.stem: Which of the following is an appropriate first-line intravenous antihypertensive agent in this scenario?
orig.explanation: Intravenous nitroprusside IV nitroprusside (or alternatively IV labetalol) is often used for rapid blood pressure control in hypertensive emergencies.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with headache. On auscultation he has a loud second heart sound. Which of the following could explain this finding?
explanation: Systemic hypertension makes the aortic valve close forcefully, giving a loud A2. Aortic regurgitation softens A2.

orig.stem: A 56 year old man presents with a history of headache. He is noted to have a loud second heart sound on auscultation. Which of the following pathologies could explain this finding?
orig.explanation: Essential hypertension A loud second heart sound may result from high diastolic pressures as seen in essential hypertension.

stem: A 35-year-old executive has a reproducible blood pressure of 180/100 mmHg and is referred to clinic to look for an underlying cause. What is the commonest cause of secondary hypertension?
explanation: Renal disease (parenchymal and renovascular) is the commonest secondary cause; primary aldosteronism is the commonest endocrine cause.

orig.stem: A 35 year old executive has a reproducible BP of 180/100 mmHg. She is referred for assessment in the clinic. You perform a range of tests to determine whether there is an underlying cause for her hypertension. What is the commonest cause of secondary hypertension?
orig.explanation: Renal disease Renal disease is the most common cause of secondary hypertension.

stem: A 60-year-old man is referred by his family doctor because his blood pressure remains uncontrolled despite four drugs, and a secondary cause is suspected. What is the commonest cause of poorly controlled hypertension?
explanation: Apparent resistant hypertension is most often non-adherence (pseudo-resistance); exclude it, white-coat effect and NSAIDs before seeking secondary causes.

orig.stem: A 60 year old man is referred by his family physician because despite four drugs he continues to have uncontrolled blood pressure. The doctor feels that the patient needs further investigation for a potential secondary cause of hypertension. What is the commonest cause of poorly controlled hypertension?
orig.explanation: Poor adherence with medication Poor adherence to antihypertensive therapy is the most common cause of uncontrolled blood pressure.

stem: All of the following statements regarding the epidemiology of hypertension are true EXCEPT:
options: Among people aged 60 years or older, average systolic blood pressure is higher in women than in men
Diastolic blood pressure increases steadily with age throughout life
Systolic blood pressure continues to rise with age throughout adult life
In industrialised nations, blood pressure rises steadily during the first two decades of life
Worldwide, around one-third of adults aged 30–79 years have hypertension
explanation: Systolic BP rises throughout life; diastolic plateaus or falls after 50–60 as arteries stiffen, hence isolated systolic hypertension in the elderly.

orig.stem: All of the following statements regarding the epidemiology of hypertension are true EXCEPT:
options: Among individuals age 60 years or older, average systolic blood pressure is higher in women.
Diastolic blood pressure increases steadily with age throughout life.
Hypertension prevalence is lower in Mexican Americans than non-Hispanic whites.
In industrialized nations, blood pressure increases steadily during the first two decades of life.
In the United States, approximately 30% of adults have hypertension.
orig.explanation: Diastolic blood pressure increases steadily with age throughout life Diastolic BP actually declines after age 55, making this statement false.

stem: Disease of which organ is the most common cause of mortality in hypertensive patients?
explanation: Heart disease (CHD, LVH, heart failure) is the commonest cause of death in hypertension; stroke is most tightly linked to BP level.

orig.stem: Disease of which organ is the most common cause of mortality in hypertensive patients?
orig.explanation: Heart Heart disease is the leading cause of death in hypertensive patients.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has had hypertension that is difficult to control since the age of 26 years, requiring increasing doses of medication. Her current regimen is labetalol 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 40 mg once daily, clonidine 0.1 mg twice daily and amlodipine 5 mg once daily. She appears well; blood pressure is 168/100 mmHg and heart rate 84 bpm. Cardiac examination is unremarkable, peripheral pulses are good and there is no oedema. There is no hirsutism, abnormal fat distribution or genital abnormality. Serum potassium is 2.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 32 mmol/L and fasting glucose 6.3 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia and alkalosis despite an ACE inhibitor suggests primary aldosteronism (Conn's); check aldosterone:renin ratio.

orig.stem: A 28-year-old woman has hypertension that is difficult to control. She was diagnosed at age 26. Since that time, she has been on increasing amounts of medication. Her current regimen consists of labetalol 1000 mg twice a day, lisinopril 40 mg once a day, clonidine 0.1 mg twice a day, and amlodipine 5 mg once a day. On physical examination, she appears without distress. Blood pressure is 168/100 mmHg, and heart rate is 84 bpm. Cardiac examination is unremarkable. She has good peripheral pulses and no edema. Her physical appearance does not reveal any hirsutism, fat maldistribution, or abnormalities of genitalia. Laboratory studies reveal a potassium of 2.8 mEq/dL and a serum bicarbonate of 32 mEq/dL. Fasting blood glucose is 114 mg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Conn syndrome Resistant hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis suggests primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome).

stem: A 28-year-old woman has resistant hypertension despite four antihypertensive drugs. She has no cushingoid features. Serum potassium is 2.8 mmol/L and bicarbonate 32 mmol/L. What is the best initial test to establish the diagnosis?
explanation: Screen for primary aldosteronism with the aldosterone:renin ratio (correct K⁺ first); confirm by suppression test, then adrenal CT and venous sampling.

orig.stem: What is the best way to diagnose the disease in the patient described in Question V-143?
orig.explanation: Plasma aldosterone/renin ratio The plasma aldosterone/renin ratio is the preferred diagnostic test for Conn syndrome.

stem: A 65-year-old engineer who never sees a doctor and takes no medications is brought to the emergency department with a headache that has worsened over the past day and confusion that began an hour ago. Blood pressure is 230/140 mmHg, heart rate 90 bpm and oxygen saturation 95%. He moves all limbs equally and has no cranial nerve deficit but is clearly delirious. The apex beat is forceful and displaced with an S4 gallop; the lungs are clear. Creatinine is 212 µmol/L (2.4 mg/dL), urine shows 2+ protein and haematuria, haematocrit is 0.32 with a normal platelet count, and the blood film shows schistocytes. Urgent brain MRI shows old microvascular changes but no acute infarct or haemorrhage. Which is the most reasonable approach to his blood pressure?
options: Intravenous labetalol 20 mg followed by a continuous infusion, aiming for a mean arterial pressure of about 125 mmHg in the first hour
explanation: Malignant hypertension with encephalopathy and AKI: IV labetalol infusion, lowering MAP by no more than 20–25% in the first hour.

orig.stem: Mr. Wilkins is a 65-year-old aeronautics engineer who has never been to the doctor and takes no medications. He is brought to the emergency department by his wife for worsening headache over the last day and confusion starting about an hour ago. His blood pressure on presentation is 230/140 mmHg, and heart rate is 90 bpm. Arterial oxygen saturation is 95%. On examination, he is moving all extremities equally, and there are no obvious cranial nerve deficits, but he is clearly delirious. Cardiac examination reveals an enlarged and forceful PMI and an S4 gallop; his lungs are clear to auscultation. Laboratory studies show a creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL, 2+ protein in his urine with hematuria, and a hematocrit of 32% with normal platelet count. Peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes. Emergent brain MRI shows old microvascular changes but no acute infarct or hemorrhage. Regarding his blood pressure management, which of the following would be the most reasonable therapeutic course?
options: 20 mg of IV labetalol and initiation of a continuous parenteral drip for goal mean arterial pressure of 125 mmHg in the first hour
orig.explanation: 20 mg of IV labetalol and initiation of a continuous parenteral drip for goal mean arterial pressure of 125 mmHg in the first hour In malignant hypertension, rapid yet controlled blood pressure reduction using IV agents is warranted.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the physiology of renal perfusion is true?
options: Because of tight precapillary regulation, the glomerular capillary endothelium is relatively shielded from pressure injury
Renal cortical blood flow is less than renal medullary blood flow, and together with the high metabolic needs of the cortex this leaves the cortex bordering on hypoxia
Renal perfusion is tightly matched to the metabolic needs of the kidney
Urinary albumin excretion predicts systemic atherosclerotic events and can appear years before clinical atherosclerotic disease
Venous blood returning from the renal cortex has a lower oxygen content than venous blood returning from the renal medulla
explanation: Albuminuria reflects generalised endothelial dysfunction and predicts CV events years ahead; hence urine ACR in the hypertension work-up.

orig.stem: Which of the following statements regarding the physiology of renal perfusion is true?
options: Due to tight precapillary regulation, the glomerular capillary endothelium is relatively shield ed from pressure injury.
Renal cortical blood flow is less than renal medullary blood flow, and coupled with the high metabolic needs of the renal cortex, this leaves that region bordering on hypoxemia.
Renal perfusion is tightly regulated to the metabolic needs of the kidney.
Urinary albumin excretion is predictive of systemic atherosclerotic events and can present years in advance of clinical atherosclerotic disease.
Venous blood returning from the renal cortex has a lower oxygen content than venous blood returning from the renal medulla.
orig.explanation: Urinary albumin excretion is predictive of systemic atherosclerotic events and can present years in advance of clinical atherosclerotic disease. Increased urinary albumin excretion is an early marker for systemic atherosclerotic events.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding renal artery stenosis is true?
options: An abnormally reduced renal artery flow velocity by Doppler ultrasound is predictive of haemodynamically significant stenosis
Early in the course of renal artery stenosis, elevated systemic renin levels are typical
In the general population, the presence of fibromuscular dysplasia is rare (<1% prevalence)
Levels of renin activity observed in renal artery stenosis are predictive of response to medical therapy
Usually the first clinical presentation of renal stenosis due to fibromuscular dysplasia is reduced renal function
explanation: Early renal artery stenosis raises renin (renin-dependent hypertension); a significant stenosis increases peak Doppler velocity.

orig.stem: Which of the following statements regarding renal artery stenosis is true?
options: An abnormally reduced renal artery flow velocity by Doppler ultrasound is predictive of hemodynamically significant stenosis.
Early in the course of renal artery stenosis, elevated systemic renin levels are typical.
In the general population, the presence of fibromuscular dysplasia is rare (<1% prevalence).
Levels of renin activity observed in renal artery stenosis are predictive of response to medical therapy.
Usually the first clinical presentation of renal stenosis due to fibromuscular dysplasia is reduced renal function.
orig.explanation: Early in the course of renal artery stenosis, elevated systemic renin levels are typical. Elevated renin levels are an early indicator of hemodynamically significant renal artery stenosis.

stem: A man has been diagnosed with essential hypertension by his GP and is about to start treatment. Which of the following statements about the treatment of essential hypertension is true?
options: Alpha-blockers such as prazosin rarely cause postural hypotension
Patients of African-Caribbean origin respond well to ACE inhibitor monotherapy
ACE inhibitors are safe in bilateral renal artery stenosis
Treatment with bendroflumethiazide may cause hypokalaemia
ACE inhibitors commonly cause ankle swelling
explanation: Thiazides cause hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, gout and hyperglycaemia. Ankle swelling is from dihydropyridine CCBs, not ACE inhibitors.

orig.stem: A man has been diagnosed with essential hypertension by his GP and needs to commence on the appropriate treatment. In the treatment of essential hypertension, which of the following statements is true?
options: Alpha-blockers such as prazosin are unlikely to cause postural hypotension
Patients of Afro-Caribbean descent respond well to ACE inhibitors
ACE inhibitors are indicated if there is unilateral renal artery stenosis
Treatment with bendrofluazide may result in hypokalaemia
ACE inhibitors may cause ankle swelling as a side effect
orig.explanation: Treatment with bendrofluazide may result in hypokalaemia Thiazide diuretics like bendrofluazide can cause hypokalaemia.

stem: A 50-year-old man has a persistently raised blood pressure of about 185/110 mmHg. He has had headaches for a few weeks but is otherwise well. His ECG shows increased QRS voltages with ST depression in the left ventricular leads, and fundoscopy shows arteriovenous nipping without haemorrhages or papilloedema. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Advise weight loss and see again in 2 months
Hospitalize and give urgent IV antihypertensive medication
Begin oral antihypertensives and see in 2 months
Begin oral antihypertensives and see in 3 days
explanation: Grade 3 hypertension with LVH and grade 2 retinopathy but no acute features: start oral treatment now and review within days.

orig.stem: A 50-year-old man has persistently elevated blood pressure of about 185/110 mmHg. He has been complaining of headaches for a few weeks but otherwise well. ECG reveals abnormal voltage changes and ST segment depression in the left ventricular leads. He was also found to have evidence of arteriovenous nipping on fundoscopy. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Advise weight loss and see again in 2 months
Hospitalize and give urgent IV antihypertensive medication
Begin oral antihypertensives and see in 2 months
Begin oral antihypertensives and see in 3 days
orig.explanation: Begin oral antihypertensives and see in 3 days This is hypertensive urgency with minor end-organ damage; blood pressure should be reduced over hours using oral agents.

stem: A 50-year-old white man sees his GP for a blood pressure check, having recently been diagnosed with essential hypertension. His only other condition is type 2 diabetes mellitus without end-organ damage, well controlled on oral hypoglycaemic agents. His blood pressure has remained about 145/90 mmHg despite 3 months of diet and exercise. Which is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive?
explanation: In type 2 diabetes NICE starts an ACE inhibitor at any age (ARB if Black or ACEi-intolerant); add CCB or thiazide-like diuretic next.

orig.stem: A 50-year-old Caucasian man sees his GP for a blood pressure check as he has recently been diagnosed with essential hypertension. His only other medical history is type II diabetes mellitus with no end-organ damage, which is well controlled on oral hypoglycaemic agents. His blood pressure has been 145/90 mmHg persistently despite diet and exercise for 3 months. Which of the following is the first-line medication for blood pressure control in this patient?
orig.explanation: Start on enalapril ACE inhibitors like enalapril are first-line in hypertensive diabetic patients.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a mild headache. He is known to have poorly controlled hypertension and is on multiple antihypertensive medications. On examination his blood pressure is 205/110 mmHg and there is no evidence of end-organ involvement. His headache is still present but there is no focal neurology identified. Which of the following is the least appropriate in the management of this patient’s blood pressure?
options: Rapidly lowering blood pressure in the emergency department
Adjust treatment and follow-up within 24 to 48 hours of presentation in the community
Initiate a maintenance dose of an oral medication before discharge
Consider a short observation period before discharge
Discharge the patient, emphasizing the importance of close follow-up and compliance with medications
explanation: Hypertensive urgency (no acute organ damage) is lowered gradually with oral drugs; rapid ED reduction risks stroke and ischaemia.

orig.stem: A 50-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a mild headache. He is known to have poorly controlled hypertension and is on multiple antihypertensive medications. On examination his blood pressure is 205/110 mmHg and there is no evidence of end-organ involvement. His headache is still present but there is no focal neurology identified. Which of the following is the least appropriate in the management of this patient’s blood pressure?
options: Rapidly lowering blood pressure in the emergency department
Adjust treatment and follow-up within 24 to 48 hours of presentation in the community
Initiate a maintenance dose of an oral medication before discharge
Consider a short observation period before discharge
Discharge the patient, emphasizing the importance of close follow-up and compliance with medications
orig.explanation: Rapidly lowering blood pressure in the emergency department Rapid lowering of blood pressure in asymptomatic hypertensive patients may be harmful and is not recommended.

stem: A 55-year-old man has been recently diagnosed with hypertension and commenced on treatment. He attends his GP to find out more about the condition. Which of the following is the commonest cause of hypertension?
explanation: About 90–95% of hypertension is primary (essential) with no single cause; secondary causes make up only 5–10%.

orig.stem: A 55-year-old man has been recently diagnosed with hypertension and commenced on treatment. He attends his GP to find out more about the condition. Which of the following is the commonest cause of hypertension?
orig.explanation: Undetermined cause Primary or essential hypertension, with an undetermined cause, accounts for the majority of cases.

stem: A 63-year-old retired doctor presents with nausea and headaches. His past medical history includes type II diabetes mellitus. On examination you note his blood pressure is 165/76 mmHg. What is the next most appropriate step in management?

orig.stem: A 63-year-old retired doctor presents with nausea and headaches. His past medical history includes type II diabetes mellitus. On examination you note his blood pressure is 165/76 mmHg. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
orig.explanation: ACE inhibitors ACE inhibitors are the first- line treatment for hypertension in diabetic patients.

stem: A 65-year-old hypertensive patient is reviewed in the outpatient clinic complaining of visual disturbances. On examination you note flame-shaped haemorrhages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Keith–Wagener: 1 narrowing/silver wiring, 2 AV nipping, 3 flame haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots, 4 papilloedema.

orig.stem: A 65-year-old hypertensive patient is reviewed in the outpatient clinic complaining of visual disturbances. On examination you note flame-shaped haemorrhages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Grade 3 retinal disease Flame-shaped haemorrhages are characteristic of Grade 3 hypertensive retinal changes.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with lethargy and a blood pressure of 250/150 mmHg. Her family say she complained of severe headache and visual disturbance earlier in the day. She has a history of asthma but no known kidney disease. Fundoscopy shows retinal haemorrhages. Which of the following is the best approach?
explanation: Hypertensive emergency with asthma: avoid labetalol; use a nitroprusside (or nicardipine) infusion, lowering MAP ≤ 25% in the first hour.

orig.stem: A 55-year-old African American female presents to the ER with lethargy and blood pressure of 250/150. Her family members indicate that she was complaining of severe headache and visual disturbance earlier in the day. They report a past history of asthma but no known kidney disease. On physical examination, retinal hemorrhages are present. Which of the following is the best approach?
options: Clonidine by mouth to lower blood pressure
Nifedipine sublingually to lower blood pressure
orig.explanation: Continuous-infusion nitroprusside Hypertensive emergency with encephalopathy → ICU IV nitroprusside or alternatives; avoid labetalol in asthma; no SL nifedipine; clonidine too slow; loops not acute control.

stem: A 50-year-old construction worker continues to have a blood pressure of 160/95 mmHg even after a third agent is added to his antihypertensive regimen. Physical examination is normal, electrolytes are normal and he takes no over-the-counter medications. Which of the following is the best next step?
options: Check chest x-ray for coarctation of the aorta
explanation: Before calling hypertension resistant, exclude non-adherence (pill count, drug levels) and confirm with ABPM; then seek secondary causes.

orig.stem: A 50-year-old construction worker continues to have elevated blood pressure of 160/95 even after a third agent is added to his antihypertensive regimen. Physical examination is normal, electrolytes are normal, and the patient is taking no over-the-counter medications. Which of the following is the best next step for this patient?
options: Check chest x-ray for coarctation of the aorta.
orig.explanation: Check pill count. Resistant HTN most often nonadherence; check history/pill count; also salt, alcohol, sleep apnea; secondary causes less likely without clues.

stem: You see a 45-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus for the first time in clinic. Her systolic blood pressure was above 140 mmHg at each of her last two clinic appointments, home blood pressure monitoring over the past week averaged 150/90 mmHg, and her clinic blood pressure today is 164/92 mmHg. What is the best next step in her blood pressure management?
options: Ask her to keep a written record of her home blood pressure and bring it to a return appointment
Advise a heart-healthy, low-sodium diet and refer her to a dietitian
Prescribe an ACE inhibitor in addition to a heart-healthy diet
Prescribe a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker in addition to a heart-healthy diet
Arrange an echocardiogram to assess for end-organ damage
explanation: In diabetes with confirmed hypertension, start an ACE inhibitor alongside lifestyle advice (reduces albuminuria and nephropathy).

orig.stem: You are seeing a 45-year-old female patient of your partner for the first time in your clinic. A quick review of the patient’s medical record shows that her systolic blood pressure was greater than 140 mm Hg at both of her last clinic appointments. Her medical history is otherwise significant only for diabetes mellitus. Her blood pressure today is 164/92. What is the best next step in her blood pressure management?
options: Ask the patient to keep a written record of her blood pressure and bring with her to a return appointment.
Advise the patient to begin a heart healthy, low sodium diet and refer to a nutritionist.
Prescribe an ACE inhibitor in addition to heart healthy diet.
Prescribe a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker in addition to a heart healthy diet.
Arrange for echocardiogram to assess for end-organ damage.
orig.explanation: Prescribe an ACE inhibitor in addition to heart healthy diet. Diabetes + HTN target ≤130/80; start ACEi (renal benefit) over lifestyle alone; thiazides are general first line; CCB acceptable but not preferred initially.

stem: A 45-year-old man with hypertension attends his GP for review. His last clinic reading was 156/80 mmHg, and ambulatory blood pressure monitoring shows a daytime average of 138/85 mmHg. He is already taking the maximum dose of ramipril. Which agent would be most appropriate to add?
explanation: Daytime ABPM 138/85 is above the < 135/85 target on maximum ACEi: step 2 adds a CCB or thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide).

orig.stem: A 45-year-old man with high blood pressure attends his GP practice for a review. His blood pressure readings have been persistently raised. His blood pressure on the previous clinic reading was 156/80 so the GP organised for him to have ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, which revealed a daytime average blood pressure of 138/85 mmHg. He is on the maximum dose of ramipril. Which second-line agent would be most appropriate to add?
orig.explanation: Indapamide ACEi + uncontrolled HTN → add CCB or thiazide-like diuretic; resistant HTN 4th line: K>4.5 bisoprolol or doxazosin; K<4.5 spironolactone; avoid verapamil for primary HTN.

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding hypertension in pregnancy is NOT correct?
options: A rise above booking readings of more than 30 mmHg systolic or 15 mmHg diastolic suggests hypertension
Pre-eclampsia occurs in around 5% of pregnancies
A urine dipstick showing protein + is consistent with gestational hypertension
A rise in blood pressure before 20 weeks suggests pre-existing hypertension
In gestational hypertension the blood pressure rises in the second half of pregnancy
explanation: Gestational hypertension is new BP ≥ 140/90 after 20 weeks without proteinuria; proteinuria makes it pre-eclampsia. Labetalol is first line.

orig.stem: Which one of the following statements is not correct regarding hypertension in pregnancy?
options: An increase above booking readings of > 30 mmHg systolic or > 15 mmHg diastolic suggests hypertension
Pre-eclampsia occurs in around 5% of pregnancies
Urine dipstick showing protein + is consistent with gestational hypertension
A rise in blood pressure before 20 weeks suggests pre-existing hypertension
With gestational hypertension the blood pressure rises in the second half of pregnancy
orig.explanation: Urine dipstick showing protein + is consistent with gestational hypertension Proteinuria suggests pre-eclampsia not gestational HTN. Gestational HTN = ≥20 w high BP without protein. Rise >30 systolic or >15 diastolic from booking suggests HTN. Pre-eclampsia ~2–8%. BP rise before 20 w = chronic HTN.

stem: All of the fallowing drugs improve the prognosis in heart failure Except:

orig.stem: All of the fallowing drugs improve the prognosis in heart failure Except:
orig.explanation: Diguxin. Diguxin does not improve prognosis in heart failure.

stem: Digoxin toxicity may be precipitated by all of the following EXCEPT:
explanation: Digoxin is renally excreted, so hepatic impairment matters little. Renal impairment, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia and amiodarone/verapamil precipitate toxicity.

orig.stem: Digitalis toxicity may be precipitated by all except one:
orig.explanation: Hepatic impairment Hepatic impairment does not precipitate digitalis toxicity as the liver plays a minimal role in its elimination.

stem: A 47-year-old man is admitted with an acute coronary syndrome. He has a history of peptic ulcer disease, and his cardiologist decides to use clopidogrel. What is the mechanism of action of clopidogrel?
options: Blocks ADP binding to its platelet P2Y12 receptor
explanation: Clopidogrel is a prodrug (CYP2C19) that irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor. Omeprazole may reduce its activation; prefer lansoprazole.

orig.stem: A 47-year-old man is admitted to hospital following an acute coronary syndrome. He has a history peptic ulcer disease and his cardiologist decides to use clopidogrel. What is the mechanism of action of clopidogrel?
options: Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor
orig.explanation: Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor Clopidogrel works by inhibiting ADP binding to its platelet receptor.

stem: Loop diuretics such as furosemide and bumetanide have which of the following effects?
options: Diuresis due to inhibition of potassium and water reabsorption
Diuresis due to inhibition of sodium and water reabsorption
Diuresis due to inhibition of water reabsorption only
Increased serum potassium levels due to enhanced distal tubule function
explanation: Loop diuretics block the Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ co-transporter in the thick ascending limb, the most potent diuresis; they cause hypokalaemia and alkalosis.

orig.stem: Loop diuretics such as furosemide and bumetanide have which of the following effects?
options: Diuresis due to inhibition of potassium and water reabsorption
Diuresis due to inhibition of sodium and water reabsorption
Diuresis due to inhibition of water reabsorption only
Increased serum potassium levels due to enhanced distal tubule function
orig.explanation: Diuresis due to inhibition of sodium and water reabsorption Loop diuretics act in the loop of Henle to inhibit sodium and water reabsorp tion.

topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
stem: In which of the following situations are beta-adrenoceptor antagonists (beta-blockers) indicated?
explanation: Evidence-based beta-blockers cut mortality by about a third in chronic HFrEF (start low when euvolaemic). They are harmful in acute LVF and cardiogenic shock.

orig.stem: B-Adrenoceptor antagonists (B-blockers) are used in which of the following situations?
orig.explanation: Chronic left ventricular systolic dysfunction Beta blockers improve survival in chronic LV dysfunction but are contraindicated in acute failure or shock.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with hypertension presents with fatigue and rapid, irregular palpitations. She normally takes enalapril. Her pulse is irregularly irregular at 125 beats/min and her blood pressure is 128/86 mmHg; cardiovascular examination is otherwise normal. A 12-lead ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a poorly controlled ventricular rate and no other abnormality. Which of the following drugs is most suitable to control her heart rate?
explanation: AF rate control without heart failure: a beta-blocker or rate-limiting CCB first (target < 110/min). Her CHA2DS2-VASc is 3, so anticoagulate too.

orig.stem: A 71 year old woman with a history of hypertension presents with fatigue and rapid, irregular palpitations. She normally takes enalapril for blood pressure control. Clinical examination reveals an irregularly irregular pulse, rate 125 beats/min, and BP 128/86 mmHg. Cardiovascular examination is otherwise normal. A 12- lead ECG is performed, which shows atrial fibrillation with poor ventricular rate control, but no other abnormality. Which of the following drugs is the most suitable agent to control heart rate in this patient?
orig.explanation: B-blocker B-blockers are the first-line therapy for rate control in atrial fibrillation.

stem: Which of the following drugs is known to be effective in preventing stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation?
explanation: Oral anticoagulants cut AF stroke by ~two-thirds; apixaban beat warfarin with less bleeding (ARISTOTLE). Aspirin is not recommended.

orig.stem: Which of the following drugs is known to be effective in preventing stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation?
orig.explanation: Apixaban Apixaban, an oral factor Xa inhibitor, has been shown to prevent stroke in AF patients.

stem: Which of the following antiplatelet drugs is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor?
explanation: Dipyridamole inhibits platelet phosphodiesterase and adenosine reuptake (raises cAMP). Clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor block P2Y12.

orig.stem: Which of the following antiplatelet drugs is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor?
orig.explanation: Dipyridamole Dipyridamole works by inhibiting phosphodiesterase, thereby increasing cAMP in platelets.

stem: A 58-year-old man with known mitral valve prolapse presents with 4 weeks of fever, malaise and weight loss after a dental extraction. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a vegetation on his native mitral valve with no abscess, and he has no embolic complications. Blood cultures grow viridans streptococci fully sensitive to penicillin, and his renal function is normal. What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen to start?
explanation: Penicillin-sensitive streptococcal native-valve IE: IV benzylpenicillin 4 weeks (or 2 weeks with gentamicin if uncomplicated). Vancomycin is for allergy.

orig.stem: Considering the patient in Questions 16.72 and 16.73, blood cultures demonstrate viridans streptococci. What is the most appropriate antibiotic regime to commence the patient on?
orig.explanation: Intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin Benzylpenicillin combined with gentamicin is the recommended regimen for viridans streptococcal endocarditis.

topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
stem: Which of the following beta-blockers has been shown to reduce mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)?
explanation: Mortality benefit in HFrEF is proven for bisoprolol, carvedilol and metoprolol succinate (MERIT-HF); short-acting metoprolol tartrate was inferior.

orig.stem: The B-blockers represent the most-studied drug in the history of HFrEF. Initially avoided for their negative inotropic and chronotropic effects, they now form the foundation of neurohormonal-targeted therapy in the treatment of chronic HFrEF. However, the benefit of B-blockers is not a blanket class effect and indeed has only been demonstrated for three drugs in the numerous clinical trials: metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol, and carvedilol. Importantly, metoprolol tartrate has never been found to have mortality benefit in HFrEF, nor have B-blockers with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (nebivolol, xamoterol).
orig.explanation: Answer: C. Metoprolol succinate. The B-blockers represent the most-studied drug in the history of HFrEF. Initially avoided for their negative inotropic and chronotropic effects, they now form the foundation of neurohormonal-targeted therapy in the treatment of chronic HFrEF. However, the benefit of B-blockers is not a blanket class effect and indeed has only been demonstrated for three drugs in the numerous clinical trials: metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol, and carvedilol.
