stem: All of the following drugs used in the acute management of ST-elevation myocardial infarction are correctly matched to their mechanism of benefit EXCEPT:
options: Abciximab – inhibition of the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor
Beta-adrenergic antagonists – reduced myocardial oxygen consumption
Clopidogrel – inhibition of the platelet adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor
explanation: GTN is mainly a venodilator: its benefit is preload (not afterload) reduction. Avoid in hypotension, RV infarction and after PDE-5 inhibitors.

orig.stem: All of the following medications used in the acute management of ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction are appropriately matched to their mechanism of effect EXCEPT:
options: Abciximab – inhibition of the glycoprotein IIb/ IIIa receptor
B-Adrenergic antagonists – reduced myocardial oxygen consumption
Clopidogrel – inhibition of the platelet adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor
orig.explanation: Nitroglycerin – reduced cardiac afterload Nitroglycerin primarily reduces preload rather than afterload.

stem: A 64-year-old female comes to your surgery with a past medical history of hypertension. She is on an ACE inhibitor as well as on a range of other medications. Which one of the following would be most likely to blunt the antihypertensive effects of an ACE inhibitor?
explanation: NSAIDs block renal prostaglandins, causing salt retention that blunts ACEi; with a diuretic they form the 'triple whammy' for AKI.

orig.stem: A 64-year-old female comes to your surgery with a past medical history of hypertension. She is on an ACE inhibitor as well as on a range of other medications. Which one of the following would be most likely to blunt the antihypertensive effects of an ACE inhibitor?
orig.explanation: Ibuprofen Ibuprofen, an NSAID, can blunt the antihypertensive effects of ACE inhibitors by reducing renal excretion.

stem: A 48-year-old woman who has been treated for essential hypertension for 3 months presents with a persistent dry cough that has not responded to linctus or antibiotics. Which antihypertensive is most likely responsible?
explanation: ACE inhibitors cause dry cough in 10–15% (bradykinin accumulation), often weeks after starting; switch to an ARB.

orig.stem: A 48-year-old woman with essential hypertension, treated for 3 months, presents with a persistent dry cough despite linctus and antibiotics. Which antihypertensive is responsible?
orig.explanation: Lisinopril ACE inhibitors like lisinopril are known to cause a dry cough.

stem: A 66-year-old man is diagnosed with a transient ischaemic attack and commenced on clopidogrel. He already takes a statin. After a week of treatment, he presents to his GP complaining of severe diarrhoea. His GP suspects that clopidogrel is the cause and decides to switch him to combination antiplatelet treatment. This includes modified-release dipyridamole. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
explanation: Dipyridamole is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that also blocks adenosine reuptake; MR dipyridamole + aspirin is used after TIA/stroke if clopidogrel is not tolerated.

orig.stem: A 66-year-old man is diagnosed with a transient ischaemic attack and commenced on clopidogrel. He already takes a statin. After a week of treatment, he presents to his GP complaining of severe diarrhoea. His GP suspects that clopidogrel is the cause and decides to switch him to combination antiplatelet treatment. This includes modified-release dipyridamole. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
orig.explanation: Phosphodiesterase inhibitor Dipyridamole: non-specific PDE inhibitor; decreases adenosine uptake; antiplatelet with aspirin if clopidogrel intolerant. GP IIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen; tirofiban blocks it. GPIb binds vWF. P2Y12 blocked by clopidogrel.

stem: A 60-year-old man is admitted following an acute coronary syndrome. He receives aspirin, clopidogrel, nitrates and morphine. His 6-month risk score is high and percutaneous coronary intervention is planned. He is therefore given intravenous tirofiban. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
options: Inhibits the production of thromboxane A2
explanation: Tirofiban (like eptifibatide, abciximab) blocks platelet GP IIb/IIIa, the final common pathway of aggregation; now mainly bail-out during PCI.

orig.stem: A 60-year-old man is admitted following an acute coronary syndrome. He receives aspirin, clopidogrel, nitrates and morphine. His 6-month risk score is high and percutaneous coronary intervention is planned. He is therefore given intravenous tirofiban. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
options: Inhibits the production of thromboxane A2
orig.explanation: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist Tirofiban is GP IIb/IIIa antagonist that blocks fibrinogen binding and platelet aggregation; not COX-1 inhibition; not AT-III activation; not a vasodilator.

stem: A 78-year-old man presents with a hot, red, swollen leg. On examination, the left leg is tender and hot to touch, with evidence of a recent superficial laceration he sustained whilst gardening. His blood tests show raised inflammatory markers and a negative D-dimer. He is treated for cellulitis with clarithromycin due to being penicillin-allergic. Which of his regular medications should be concurrently suspended?
explanation: Clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4, raising simvastatin levels and risking rhabdomyolysis; withhold the statin during the course.

orig.stem: A 78-year-old man presents with a hot, red, swollen leg. On examination, the left leg is tender and hot to touch, with evidence of a recent superficial laceration he sustained whilst gardening. His blood tests show raised inflammatory markers and a negative D-dimer. He is treated for cellulitis with clarithromycin due to being penicillin-allergic. Which of his regular medications should be concurrently suspended?
orig.explanation: Simvastatin Clarithromycin increases simvastatin exposure → myopathy risk; notable interactions of clarithromycin with SSRIs etc; no key interaction with aspirin or clopidogrel.

stem: A 24-year-old man with no prior medical problems faints while having exercise. He has a quick recovery and has no neurologic deficits. ECG shows a normal sinus rhythm. Which of the following is the most useful diagnostic test?

orig.explanation: Echocardiogram. Echocardiogram is used to detect underlying structural heart issues.

orig.stem: Common causes of empyema are the following EXCEPT:

stem: In the management of cardiac arrest, which of the following most accurately describes basic life support (BLS)?
options: Administration of intravenous drugs and external defibrillation (the two ‘D’s)
Support of airway, breathing and circulation (ABC)
Support of airway, breathing and circulation, and assessment of disability and exposure (ABCDE)
Support of airway, breathing and circulation, and assessment of disability and exposure, treatment of fibrillation (ABCDEF)
explanation: BLS is support of airway, breathing and circulation without equipment: call for help, CPR 30:2 and early AED. Drugs belong to ALS.

orig.stem: In the management of cardiac arrest, which of the following most accurately describes basic life support (BLS)?
options: Administration of intravenous drugs and external defibrillation (the two ‘D’s)
Support of airway, breathing and circulation (ABC)
Support of airway, breathing and circulation, and assessment of disability and exposure (ABCDE)
Support of airway, breathing and circulation, and assessment of disability and exposure, treatment of fibrillation (ABCDEF)
orig.explanation: Support of airway, breathing and circulation, and assessment of disability and exposure (ABCDE) BLS involves ensuring airway, breathing, circulation and a quick assessment of disability and exposure.

stem: Which of the following statements is true of a pulseless electrical activity (PEA) cardiac arrest?
options: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be carried out for 1 minute before the rhythm is reassessed
Intravenous amiodarone will restore cardiac output
It is initially managed with immediate defibrillation
Reversible causes include hyperthyroidism and hypercalcaemia
Reversible causes include hypothermia and hypoxia
explanation: PEA is non-shockable: CPR, adrenaline 1 mg ASAP then every 3–5 min, and treat the 4 Hs and 4 Ts (e.g. hypoxia, hypothermia).

orig.stem: Which of the following statements is true of a pulseless electrical activity (PEA) cardiac arrest?
options: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be carried out for 1 minute before the rhythm is reassessed
Intravenous amiodarone will restore cardiac output
It is initially managed with immediate defibrillation
Reversible causes include hyperthyroidism and hypercalcaemia
Reversible causes include hypothermia and hypoxia
orig.explanation: Reversible causes include hypothermia and hypoxia PEA is associated with reversible causes such as hypothermia and hypoxia; defibrillation is not effective.

stem: Atrial myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumour. Which of the following is true of atrial myxoma?
options: It occurs more commonly in the right atrium than in the left atrium
Surgery is not indicated because atrial myxomas are benign
Surgery is usually indicated to prevent embolic complications such as stroke
The tumour commonly obstructs the aortic valve
explanation: Atrial myxoma (75% left atrial, from the septum) can obstruct the mitral valve, embolise and cause fever/high ESR (IL-6); excise surgically.

orig.stem: Atrial myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumour. Which of the following is true of atrial myxoma?
options: It occurs more commonly in the right atrium than in the left atrium
Surgery is not indicated because atrial myxomas are benign
Surgery is usually indicated to prevent embolic complications such as stroke

orig.explanation: Surgery is usually indicated to prevent embolic complications such as stroke Although benign, atrial myxomas require surgical removal to prevent embolism.

stem: A patient presents with an incidental finding of a mass in the left atrium whilst undergoing an echocardiogram for hypertension. What is the most likely cardiac tumour in this situation?
explanation: The commonest primary cardiac tumour in adults is myxoma, a pedunculated LA mass on the septum; metastases are commoner overall.

orig.stem: A patient presents with an incidental finding of a mass in the left atrium whilst undergoing an echocardiogram for hypertension. What is the most likely cardiac tumour in this situation?
orig.explanation: Atrial myxoma Atrial myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumour.

stem: A country with a population and environment very similar to China is moving from the first stage of the epidemiological transition ('pestilence and famine') to the second ('receding pandemics'). Regarding the expected pattern of cardiovascular disease (CVD) in this country, which of the following is true?
options: As this nation enters the stage of receding pandemics, you would expect the majority of CVD morbidity and mortality to be due to cardiomyopathies secondary to infectious agents
Each nation or geographical location progresses through the five stages of epidemiologic transition identically in regard to CVD risk
In this nation, when CVD mortality peaks, you would expect stroke mortality to be greater than coronary heart disease mortality
One would expect a very homogeneous epidemiologic pattern of CVD risk throughout this nation over time
You anticipate that CVD mortality will inexorably climb as this nation progresses through the five stages of the epidemiologic transition
explanation: In China-like populations, as CVD peaks, stroke mortality exceeds coronary mortality (high hypertension and salt intake).

orig.stem: You are appointed as a cardiac epidemiologist advisor on an international committee setting global health policy. Your committee is assigned to predict health trends in a Pacific East Asian nation with a population and environment very similar to China. At this point in history, the nation is just moving from the first classic stage in the epidemiologic transition (“pestilence and famine”) to the second classic stage (“receding pandemics”). In regard to the anticipated patterns of cardiovascular disease (CVD) in this nation, which of the following is true?
options: As this nation enters the stage of receding pandemics, you would expect the majority of CVD morbidity and mortality to be due to cardiomyopathies secondary to infectious agents.
Each nation or geographical location progresses through the five stages of epidemiologic transition identically in regard to CVD risk.
In this nation, when CVD mortality peaks, you would expect stroke mortality to be greater than coronary heart disease mortality.
One would expect a very homogeneous epidemiologic pattern of CVD risk throughout this nation over time.
You anticipate that CVD mortality will inexorably climb as this nation progresses through the five stages of the epidemiologic transition.
orig.explanation: In this nation, when CVD mortality peaks, you would expect stroke mortality to be greater than coronary heart disease mortality. Epidemiologic transition studies show that in countries similar to China, stroke mortality predominates over CHD at the peak of CVD mortality.

stem: A 67-year-old man complains of exertional breathlessness, leg oedema and waking at night acutely short of breath. You assess his volume status by examining the jugular venous pulse (JVP). Which of the following statements about JVP measurement is true?
options: If done properly, the angle of inclination matters little to the measurement of JVP
In normal patients, the JVP rises with inspiration due to the augmented volume loading of the right heart
Measurement of the elevation of the top of the JVP and the sternal inflection point (angle of Louis) will provide a highly accurate measurement of central venous pressure
The external jugular is preferred over the internal jugular vein due to its ease of visibility
Venous pulsations above the clavicle in the sitting position are abnormal
explanation: The RA lies ~5 cm below the sternal angle, so venous pulsation above the clavicle when sitting upright means a raised JVP.

orig.stem: You are evaluating Mr. Estebez, a 67-year- old owner of a wildly successful chain of sushi restaurants. He complains of shortness of breath with exertion, lower extremity edema, and awakening at night feeling acutely short of breath. You wish to assess his volume status, and know that jugular venous pulse (JVP) assessment is the single most important physi cal examination measurement to aid you in this component of your evaluation. Which of the following statements regarding JVP measurement is true?
options: If done properly, the angle of inclination matters little to the measurement of JVP.
In normal patients, the JVP rises with inspiration due to the augmented volume loading of the right heart.
Measurement of the elevation of the top of the JVP and the sternal inflection point (angle of Louis) will provide a highly accurate measurement of central venous pressure.
The external jugular is preferred over the internal jugular vein due to its ease of visibility.
Venous pulsations above the clavicle in the sitting position are abnormal.
orig.explanation: Venous pulsations above the clavicle in the sitting position are abnormal. Because the internal jugular is the true reflection of right atrial pressure, visible pulsations above the clavicle indicate abnormal elevation.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding blood pressure measurements is true?
options: Systolic pressure increases and diastolic pressure decreases when measured in more distal arteries
Systolic leg blood pressures are usually as much as 20 mmHg lower than arm blood pressures
The concept of 'white coat hypertension' (pressures measured in clinical settings significantly higher than elsewhere) has been shown to be a myth
An inter-arm systolic difference of 25 mmHg is within normal limits
Using a blood pressure cuff that is too small results in a marked underestimation of the true blood pressure
explanation: Pulse amplification makes systolic pressure higher and diastolic lower in distal arteries (leg SBP > arm, basis of the ABPI).

orig.stem: Which of the following statements regarding blood pressure measurements is true?
options: Systolic pressure increases and diastolic pressure decreases when measured in more distal arteries.
Systolic leg blood pressures are usually as much as 20 mmHg lower than arm blood pressures.
The concept of “white coat hypertension” (blood pressures measured in office or hospital settings significantly higher than in nonclinical settings) has been shown to be a myth.
The difference in blood pressure measured in both arms should be less than 20mmHg.
Using a blood pressure cuff that is too small will result in a marked underestimation of the true blood pressure.
orig.explanation: Systolic pressure increases and diastolic pressure decreases when measured in more distal arteries. The blood pressure changes with distance from the heart due to pulse pressure amplification and damping of diastolic pressure.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding normal depolarization patterns of the heart is true?
options: Each normal sinus beat is initiated by spontaneous depolarization in the atrioventricular (AV) node
The normal order of depolarization is as follows: sinoatrial (SA) node - atrial myocardium - AV node - His bundle - Purkinje fibers - ventricular myocardium
The right bundle branch bifurcates into an anterior and posterior fascicle
The SA node is unique in its ability to spontaneously depolarize, a quality known as automaticity
Within the ventricular myocardium, depolarization sweeps from epicardium to endocardium
explanation: Normal conduction: SA node → atria → AV node → His bundle → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricles (endocardium to epicardium).

orig.stem: Which of the following statements regarding normal depolarization patterns of the heart is true?
options: Each normal sinus beat is initiated by spontaneous depolarization in the atrioventricular (AV) node.
The normal order of depolarization is as follows: sinoatrial (SA) node - atrial myocardium - AV node - His bundle - Purkinje fibers - ventricular myocardium.
The right bundle branch bifurcates into an anterior and posterior fascicle.
The SA node is unique in its ability to spontaneously depolarize, a quality known as automaticity.
Within the ventricular myocardium, depolarization sweeps from epicardium to endocardium.
orig.explanation: The normal order of depolarization is as follows: sinoatrial (SA) node - atrial myocardium - AV node - His bundle - Purkinje fibers - ventricular myocardium. This reflects the normal conduction sequence initiating at the SA node and propagating through the specialized conduction system.

stem: All of the following ECG waveforms are matched correctly to the cardiac cycle that they represent EXCEPT:
options: PR interval – conduction from the atria through the AV node and His–Purkinje system
explanation: The P wave is atrial depolarisation; atrial repolarisation is hidden in the PR segment/QRS. T = ventricular repolarisation.

orig.stem: All of the following ECG waveforms are matched correctly to the cardiac cycle that they represent EXCEPT:
orig.explanation: P wave - atrial repolarization Atrial repolarization is typically not visible on the ECG, making this pairing incorrect.

stem: Which of the following mean QRS vectors in the frontal electrocardiographic plane is matched appropriately to its designation?
options: All of the above are incorrect
explanation: Normal QRS axis is −30° to +90°, so −20° is normal; −30° to −90° is left axis deviation.

orig.stem: Which of the following mean QRS vectors in the frontal electrocardiographic plane is matched appropriately to its designation?
options: All of the above are incorrect.
orig.explanation: -20 degrees - normal axis A normal QRS axis is generally defined between -30° and +90°; -20° falls within this range.

stem: What is the primary finding on the ECG shown?
options: ST elevation in the anterior precordial leads; suspect anterior myocardial ischaemia
explanation: Sinus rhythm with normal axis, intervals, R-wave progression and no ST shift or tall T waves: a normal ECG.

orig.stem: Which of the following options describes the primary finding in the ECG shown in Figure V-14?
options: ST elevation in the anterior precordial leads; suspect anterior myocardial ischemia

stem: The SA node serves as the dominant pacemaker of the heart in normal sinus rhythm. What property of SA nodal cells allows it to act as the primary pacemaker?
options: Location near the superior lateral area of the right atrium
More numerous intercalated discs of any other myocardial tissue
Only cells with the ability to spontaneously depolarize
Spontaneous depolarization during phase 4 of the action potential at a more rapid rate than any other myocardial cells
explanation: SA node cells depolarise spontaneously in phase 4 (funny current) faster than any other tissue, so they reach threshold first and dominate.

orig.stem: The SA node serves as the dominant pacemaker of the heart in normal sinus rhythm. What property of SA nodal cells allows it to act as the primary pacemaker?
options: Location near the superior lateral area of the right atrium
More numerous intercalated discs of any other myocardial tissue
Only cells with the ability to spontaneously depolarize
Spontaneous depolarization during phase 4 of the action potential at a more rapid rate than any other myocardial cells
orig.explanation: Spontaneous depolarization during phase 4 of the action potential at a more rapid rate than any other myocardial cells The SA node’s intrinsic automaticity during phase 4 is the key factor in pacemaking.

stem: A 76-year-old woman with hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes mellitus and osteoporosis is brought to the emergency department after a fall at home, followed immediately by intense left hip pain. She was found by a neighbour after several hours and cannot remember whether she lost consciousness. She is exquisitely tender over the left hip, and the leg is shortened and externally rotated. Her mucous membranes are dry and skin turgor is reduced. Blood pressure is 170/80 mmHg and heart rate 130 beats/min. Her rhythm strip is shown (arrows mark P waves). What is the most appropriate first step for her tachycardia?
explanation: Multifocal/sinus tachycardia driven by pain, dehydration and hypoxia after a hip fracture: treat the cause (analgesia, IV fluids, oxygen).

orig.stem: A 76-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes mellitus, and osteoporo sis presents to the emergency department after a fall at home followed immediately by intense left hip pain. She was found by a neighbor after several hours. The patient cannot remember if she lost consciousness. She is exquisitely tender to palpation over the left hip, and her leg is shortened and externally rotated. Her mucous membranes are dry, and her skin tents easily. Blood pressure is 170/80 mmHg and heart rate is 130 bpm. Her rhythm strip is shown in Figure V-39. What is the most appropriate first step for her tachycardia?
orig.explanation: Pain control and IV hydration Tachycardia in this setting is most likely secondary to pain and dehydration; supportive care is appropriate.

stem: After a snowstorm has kept people indoors for 4 days, a middle-aged woman is brought to the emergency department obtunded. Her neighbours had not seen her since the snow started, and the police found her unconscious on the floor. A radial pulse is barely palpable and blood pressure is 60 mmHg systolic. She has an arteriovenous dialysis fistula in the left arm. Her ECG is shown. What electrolyte abnormality do you expect?
explanation: Missed dialysis with a sine-wave ECG is pre-terminal hyperkalaemia: IV calcium, insulin–glucose and salbutamol, then urgent dialysis.

orig.stem: You are having a quiet shift in the local emergency department. For the past 4 days, there has been a large snowstorm limiting traffic, and people have generally stayed indoors and out of harm’s way. Suddenly, the emergency medical personnel arrive with a middle-aged woman who is obtunded. Her downstairs neighbors noted that they had not seen her for the past 4 days (since the snow started) and alerted the police who found her unconscious on her floor. On your assessment, you can barely feel a radial pulse. You note a dialysis fistula graft in her left arm. Blood pressure is 60/palp, and her ECG tracing is shown in Figure V-43. You rapidly set up for defibrillation and request a full chemistry panel. What electrolyte abnormality do you expect to find?
orig.explanation: Hyperkalemia The sinusoidal, bizarre ECG pattern is characteristic of severe hyperkalemia in a dialysis patient.

stem: An 87-year-old man with an orthotopic heart transplant presents with a mild resting tachycardia. Which of the following best explains his heart rate response?
options: The denervated donor heart lacks resting vagal tone and responds only to circulating catecholamines
The transplant procedure permanently damages the SA node
explanation: A denervated transplanted heart lacks vagal tone, so it runs at its intrinsic rate (~90–110/min) and responds only to circulating catecholamines.

orig.stem: An 87-year-old man with an orthotopic heart transplant presents with a mild resting tachycardia. Which of the following best explains his heart rate response?
options: The denervated donor heart responds only to circulating catecholamines.
The heart rate is due to rejection.
The transplant procedure damages the SA node permanently.
orig.explanation: The transplant heart is denervated and thus relies on circulating catecholamines for rate response. After transplant, the donor heart lacks autonomic innervation, causing a higher resting rate and delayed response to stress.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with breathlessness on exertion. For the past 3 months, he has become limited by breathlessness on progressively less exertion. He is adamant that he has no chest pain or pressure. He takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and low-dose prednisolone and is fully adherent. Echocardiography shows normal LV function and wall thickness, and his resting ECG shows sinus rhythm at 80 beats/min. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: Late after transplant, breathlessness without angina suggests cardiac allograft vasculopathy (denervated heart); diagnose by angiography.

orig.stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department for dyspnea on exertion. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
orig.explanation: specifically cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV), a common long-term complication after heart transplantation. It causes diffuse, progressive narrowing of coronary arteries, often without angina due to cardiac denervation. Symptoms like exertional dyspnea are typical and may be the only sign.

stem: A 19-year-old woman attending a travel clinic complains of a painless swelling of one leg. What cause do you suspect?
options: Cancer involving the inguinal lymph nodes
explanation: Lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti) is the commonest cause of secondary lymphoedema worldwide; cancer treatment in high-income countries.

stem: A woman has chronic lymphoedema of the leg following recurrent streptococcal lymphangitis in childhood. She finds the swelling unsightly and asks about treatment. All of the following are reasonable treatments for chronic lymphoedema EXCEPT:
explanation: Lymphoedema is protein-rich fluid, so diuretics do not help. Use decongestive therapy, compression, skin care and exercise.

orig.stem: You are taking care of a patient who suffers from chronic lymphedema due to recurrent streptococcal lymphangitis in childhood. She finds her leg swelling unsightly and asks about therapeutic options. All of the following are reasonable therapeutic options for chronic lymphedema EXCEPT:
orig.explanation: Diuretic therapy Diuretics are contraindicated in lymphedema as they may lead to intravascular depletion and metabolic disturbances.

stem: While on call, you are bleeped to see a man who has had a massive rectal bleed. He is drowsy, with a blood pressure of 65/40 mmHg and a pulse of 130 beats/min. While IV access is obtained, he arrests and CPR is started. The monitor shows organised QRS complexes, but there is no pulse. CPR continues and adrenaline 1 mg IV has just been given. What is the most important next step in management?
options: Rapid IV infusion of blood products via the major haemorrhage protocol
explanation: PEA from massive haemorrhage will not reverse without volume: give blood products rapidly via the major haemorrhage protocol during CPR.

orig.explanation: Administration of colloid In pulseless elec trical activity due to hypovolaemia, volume resuscitation with colloid is the next appropriate step.

explanation: Sharp localised pain reproduced by palpation with normal ECG and CXR is musculoskeletal (costochondritis); no further tests, reassure and analgesia.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% has NYHA class II symptoms. She takes lisinopril 40 mg daily, carvedilol 25 mg twice daily and spironolactone 25 mg daily. Blood pressure is 102/82 mmHg and she is in sinus rhythm at 60 beats/min. explanation: HFrEF on ACEi, beta-blocker and MRA: add an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin), which cuts CV death and admissions with or without diabetes.

stem: A 57-year-old man had a large anterior myocardial infarction 8 months ago, treated with primary PCI with an excellent result despite a late presentation. explanation: EF ≤ 30% > 40 days after MI: a primary-prevention ICD reduces mortality (MADIT-II). CRT needs LBBB with QRS ≥ 150 ms.

explanation: A resting rate of ~90/min in a well heart-transplant recipient is expected (denervation); reassure.

stem: A government committee on organ transplantation is considering a nationwide sharing strategy for donor hearts in a large country. Why is such a strategy not beneficial?
options: Blood groups are distributed non-randomly across the country, preventing true nationwide sharing
Regions use highly variable criteria for grading severity of illness
The financial structure of reimbursement would not allow it
The tolerable cold ischaemic time of a harvested heart is too short to allow nationwide sharing
explanation: A donor heart tolerates only about 4 h of cold ischaemia, so it must be allocated within a limited radius of the donor.

stem: A 68-year-old woman with chemotherapy-related cardiomyopathy (EF 15%) has frequent admissions with acute decompensated heart failure despite optimal therapy. She is not a candidate for heart transplantation. Which of the following statements about other options to prolong her life is correct?
options: Continuous infusion of milrinone will improve cardiac function and survival
A left ventricular assist device can improve quality of life but provides no survival benefit over optimal medical care
A left ventricular assist device can improve survival over the initial 2–5 years more than optimal medical therapy
Stem cell implantation has been shown to prolong life in patients with end-stage cardiomyopathy
There are no other options for prolonging life, and we should consider palliative measures in the future
explanation: In transplant-ineligible stage D heart failure, a durable LVAD (destination therapy) improves survival; inotropes do not.

stem: A 62-year-old man is being assessed for mitral valve surgery for severe mitral regurgitation. Transoesophageal echocardiography shows a small jet of right-to-left flow across the atrial septum, occurring when a small flap of tissue swings open (less than 1 mm). Which of the following explains this finding?
explanation: A flap that opens intermittently between atria is a PFO (~25% of adults), allowing paradoxical embolism; no treatment if incidental.

orig.explanation: Patent foramen ovale A patent foramen ovale is characterized by a small, flap-like opening in the atrial septum.

stem: A 21-year-old man has a newly diagnosed ventricular septal defect (VSD). Echocardiography confirms a 5-mm VSD in the muscular interventricular septum. Right heart catheterisation shows a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 20 mmHg, pulmonary vascular resistance of 2 Wood units and systemic vascular resistance of 6 Wood units, with a Qp:Qs of 1.25. What do you recommend?
options: Cardiopulmonary exercise testing to define peak oxygen consumption
Closure with a percutaneously deployed septal occluder device
Consideration of heart and lung transplant
No intervention now; annual cardiology assessments and reimaging if any new symptoms emerge
Surgical correction via open heart surgery and patch repair
explanation: A small restrictive VSD with Qp:Qs < 1.5 and normal pulmonary pressures needs no closure; review periodically and maintain dental hygiene.

stem: A 52-year-old patient presents with chest pain and raised cardiac enzymes. A superficial continuous murmur, not previously documented, is heard at the mid-sternal level. Echocardiography shows normal valves. Right heart catheterisation gives these oxygen saturations: superior vena cava 58%, right atrium 60%, mid-coronary sinus 91%, right ventricle 70%, pulmonary artery 70%. What abnormality accounts for these findings?
options: Anomalous left coronary artery off the main pulmonary artery
Coronary arteriovenous fistula to the coronary sinus
explanation: A coronary sinus saturation of 91% (normally ~30–40%) means arterial blood is entering it: a coronary AV fistula, causing a continuous murmur and steal.

stem: A 40-year-old man has a congenital bicuspid aortic valve. Which other structure is important to follow on his regular echocardiograms?
explanation: Bicuspid aortic valve carries an aortopathy, so measure the aortic root/ascending aorta on every echo; repair at 55 mm (50 mm with risk factors).

stem: All of the following are classic defining features of tetralogy of Fallot EXCEPT:
explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot: VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction and RV hypertrophy. Tricuspid atresia is a separate cyanotic lesion.
