orig.explanation: Tricuspid atresia Tetralogy of Fallot does not include tricuspid atresia; it consists of RV outflow obstruction, overriding aorta, VSD, and RV hypertrophy.

stem: A 78-year-old man with a history of tobacco abuse, obesity, and diabetes mellitus is evaluated for dyspnoea on exertion. Echocardiography confirms severe aortic stenosis. Which of the following most likely contributed to the development of his lesion?
explanation: Calcific AS of a trileaflet valve at 78 shares atherosclerotic risk factors: age, diabetes, hypertension, smoking, lipids, CKD.

orig.stem: A 78-year-old man with a history of tobacco abuse, obesity, and diabetes mellitus is evaluated for dyspnea on exertion. Echocardiography confirms severe aortic stenosis. Which of the following most likely contributed to the development of his lesion?
orig.explanation: Diabetes mellitus Diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for calcific aortic stenosis in the elderly.

stem: A 63-year-old man presents with new exertional syncope and is found to have severe aortic stenosis. What is the average life expectancy of untreated patients with this presentation?
explanation: Untreated severe AS: average survival ~5 years after angina, 3 after syncope and 2 after heart failure; any symptom means valve replacement.

orig.stem: A 63-year-old man presents with new-onset exertional syncope and is found to have aortic stenosis. Untreated patients with his presentation have a predicted average life span of:
orig.explanation: 3 years Exertional syncope in aortic stenosis is associated with a poor prognosis, with an average lifespan of about 3 years if untreated.

stem: An 82-year-old man with severe calcific aortic stenosis, who previously deferred surgery, now presents with hypotension, tachycardia, and signs of multi-organ dysfunction. Which of the following would be a reasonable therapeutic option to improve his short-term perfusion to permit aortic valve replacement?
options: Digoxin 250 µg IV once and 125 µg orally daily thereafter
Metoprolol 5 mg IV serial dosing targeting a resting heart rate of 60–70 bpm
Phenylephrine continuous IV infusion titrated to a mean arterial pressure of >65
explanation: Cardiogenic shock from critical AS: balloon aortic valvuloplasty temporarily relieves obstruction as a bridge to AVR/TAVI (restenosis within months).

orig.stem: An 82-year-old man with severe calcific aortic stenosis, who previously deferred surgery, now presents with hypotension, tachycardia, and signs of multi-organ dysfunction. Which of the following would be a reasonable therapeutic option to improve his short-term perfusion to permit aortic valve replacement?
options: Digoxin 250 µg IV once and 125 µg orally daily thereafter
Metoprolol 5 mg IV serial dosing targeting a resting heart rate of 60–70 bpm
Phenylephrine continuous IV infusion titrated to a mean arterial pressure of >65
orig.explanation: Percutaneous aortic balloon valvuloplasty Balloon valvuloplasty can temporarily improve perfusion in severe aortic stenosis.

stem: An 85-year-old man presents with increasing breathlessness and leg oedema. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 25% with global hypokinesis, a calculated aortic valve area of 0.8 cm² and a mean gradient of 25 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step to determine whether he would benefit from aortic valve replacement?
options: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to evaluate ventricular scar and aortic valve mor phology
Cardiac positron emission tomography (PET) to determine ventricular viability
Coronary angiography to evaluate for the presence of obstructive coronary disease
Right heart catheterization to document cardiac output and filling pressures
explanation: Low-flow low-gradient AS with poor EF: dobutamine stress echo separates true severe AS (gradient rises, area stays ≤ 1 cm²) from pseudo-severe and shows contractile reserve.

orig.stem: An 85-year-old former lawyer presents with accelerating dyspnea and lower extremity edema. Echocardiogram reveals an ejection fraction of 25% with global hypokinesis, a calculated aortic valve area of 0.8 cm2, and a mean gradient of 25 mmHg. What is the next most reasonable step to determine whether this patient would benefit from aortic valve replacement?
options: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to evaluate ventricular scar and aortic valve mor phology
Cardiac positron emission tomography (PET) to determine ventricular viability
Coronary angiography to evaluate for the presence of obstructive coronary disease
Right heart catheterization to document cardiac output and filling pressures
orig.explanation: Dobutamine stress echocardiography Dobutamine stress echo helps differentiate true severe AS from pseudo-severe AS in low-flow states.

stem: Which of the following parameters is typically reduced in chronic severe aortic regurgitation?
explanation: In chronic severe AR diastolic pressure falls and pulse pressure widens; LV end-diastolic volume, stroke volume and afterload all increase.

orig.stem: Which of the following parameters is typically reduced in chronic severe aortic regurgitation?
orig.explanation: Diastolic blood pressure Chronic aortic regurgitation leads to a decrease in diastolic blood pressure due to regurgitant flow.

stem: A 21-year-old woman with a connective tissue disease presents with acute breathlessness and pulmonary oedema. Echocardiography shows severe aortic regurgitation with an avulsed right coronary cusp. While awaiting emergency surgery, which intervention is most likely to help maintain her end-organ perfusion?
options: Esmolol continuous IV infusion titrated to a heart rate of 60–70 bpm
explanation: Acute severe AR: nitroprusside (± dobutamine) increases forward flow as a bridge to surgery. IABP is contraindicated; beta-blockers lengthen diastole.

orig.stem: A 21-year-old woman with connective tissue disease presents with acute shortness of breath and pulmonary edema. Echocardiogram shows severe aortic regurgitation with an avulsed right coronary cusp. While awaiting emergent surgery, what intervention is most likely to help maintain her end-organ perfusion?
options: Esmolol continuous IV infusion titrated to a heart rate of 60–70 bpm
orig.explanation: IV nitroprusside Nitroprusside reduces afterload and regurgitant flow, improving effective stroke volume.

stem: What is the most common cause of obstruction to left ventricular inflow worldwide?
options: Infective endocarditis with large mitral valve vegetations
explanation: Rheumatic heart disease is by far the commonest cause of mitral stenosis/LV inflow obstruction worldwide; annular calcification in the elderly.

orig.stem: What is the most common cause of obstruction to left ventricular inflow?
options: Infective endocarditis with large mitral valve vegetations
orig.explanation: Rheumatic mitral disease Rheumatic fever is the leading cause of mitral stenosis, which obstructs LV inflow.

stem: In cases of severe mitral stenosis, which of the following parameters is typically increased?
explanation: In MS left atrial pressure rises to drive flow across the valve; LV end-diastolic pressure is normal or low and output falls.

orig.stem: In cases of severe mitral stenosis, which of the following parameters is typically increased?
orig.explanation: Left atrial pressure Mitral stenosis leads to elevated left atrial pressure to maintain cardiac output.

stem: In a patient with mitral stenosis, all of the following will raise left atrial pressure and may worsen pulmonary congestion EXCEPT:
explanation: Anything raising heart rate or output raises LA pressure in MS. Beta-blockers (metoprolol) lengthen diastole and lower LA pressure.

orig.stem: All of the following will result in an elevation of left atrial pressure and potential worsening of lung function EXCEPT:
orig.explanation: Metoprolol Metoprolol, a beta-blocker, does not increase left atrial pressure.

stem: An 84-year-old woman with severe mitral stenosis develops new-onset atrial fibrillation. Which of the following interventions will NOT help lower her left atrial pressure?
options: Transvenous pacemaker placement and pacing at a heart rate of 90 bpm
All of the above will help lower left atrial pressure
explanation: In MS, LA pressure falls with diuretics, valvotomy, cardioversion or rate control. Pacing at 90/min shortens diastole and raises it.

orig.stem: Mrs. Bream, an 84-year-old woman with severe mitral stenosis, develops new onset atrial fibrillation. Which of the following therapeutic interventions will NOT help lower her left atrial pressure?
options: Transvenous pacemaker placement and pacing at a heart rate of 90 bpm
All of the above will help lower left atrial pressure
orig.explanation: Transvenous pacemaker placement and pacing at a heart rate of 90 bpm Increasing the heart rate with pacing can worsen the elevated left atrial pressure in mitral stenosis.

stem: A 34-year-old man with rheumatic mitral stenosis is asymptomatic, with a mitral valve area of 1.7 cm². On exercise his pulmonary artery systolic pressure reaches 40 mmHg. What management do you recommend?
options: Periodic cardiology assessments and echocardiographic monitoring
explanation: MVA 1.7 cm² is moderate MS; asymptomatic with exercise PASP < 60 mmHg, so review and serial echo every 1–2 years.

orig.stem: A 34-year-old man with rheumatic mitral stenosis is asymptomatic with a mitral valve area of 1.7 cm2. On exercise, his pulmonary artery systolic pressure reaches 40 mmHg. What treatment plan do you recommend?
options: Periodic cardiology assessments and echocardiographic monitoring
orig.explanation: Periodic cardiology assessments and echocardiographic monitoring Asymptomatic moderate mitral stenosis is managed conservatively with regular monitoring.

stem: A 65-year-old man with a 15-year history of non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30%) has severe functional (secondary) mitral regurgitation. He remains in NYHA class III despite optimal guideline-directed medical therapy and cardiac resynchronisation. He asks whether fixing his valve would improve his survival. What is the most accurate response?
options: Valve repair is only needed if you develop pulmonary hypertension or atrial fibrillation
Neither surgical nor percutaneous valve repair has ever been shown to improve survival in patients like you
Surgery should be considered only if repair is possible, because replacement would not improve survival
Surgical repair has not been shown to improve survival, but in selected patients like you transcatheter edge-to-edge repair has been shown to reduce mortality
Yes, your valve should have been fixed years ago
explanation: In secondary (functional) MR surgery does not improve survival, but transcatheter edge-to-edge repair reduced mortality in selected patients (COAPT).

orig.stem: A 65-year-old man with a 15-year history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy and severe mi tral regurgitation asks whether his valve should be fixed to improve survival. What is your response?
options: If you were to have high pulmonary artery pressures or develop new atrial fibrillation, we would move forward with valve repair.
In patients like you, valve repair has never been shown to improve survival.
We should consider valve surgery only if repair is possible. Replacement would not improve your survival.
While surgical methods have not shown survival benefit, percutaneous mitral valve repair has been shown to reduce mortality in patients like you.
Yes, your valve should have been fixed years ago.
orig.explanation: In patients like you, valve repair has never been shown to improve survival. Repair of functional mitral regurgitation in the setting of dilated cardiomyopathy has not demonstrated a survival benefit.

stem: During right and left heart catheterisation of a patient with stenosis of two valves, the following pressures are recorded: right atrium (mean) 15 mmHg; right ventricle 25/6 mmHg; pulmonary artery 25/12 mmHg; pulmonary artery wedge pressure 12 mmHg; left ventricle 105/6 mmHg; aorta 105/75 mmHg. Which two valves are stenosed?
explanation: Diastolic gradients RA > RVEDP and wedge > LVEDP mean tricuspid and mitral stenosis; no systolic gradients exclude pulmonary and aortic stenosis.

orig.stem: You are performing a right and left heart catheterization on a patient with stenosis involving two valves. Based on the pressure readings, which two valves are involved?
orig.explanation: Mitral and tricuspid The pressure gradients indicate combined stenosis of the mitral and tricuspid valves, commonly seen in rheumatic disease.

stem: You are evaluating a 50-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension. She has severe tricuspid regurgitation, a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle, and signs of right heart failure. What is the best treatment for her severe tricuspid regurgitation?
options: Diuretics and salt restriction accompanied by medical therapy targeting her elevated pulmonary artery pressures
explanation: Functional TR from pulmonary hypertension is treated by diuretics, salt restriction and pulmonary vasodilator therapy; valve surgery is high-risk.

orig.stem: You are evaluating a 50-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension. She has severe tricuspid regurgitation, a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle, and signs of right heart failure. What is the best treatment for her severe tricuspid regurgitation?
options: Diuretics and salt restriction accompanied by medical therapy targeting her elevated pulmonary artery pressures
orig.explanation: Diuretics and salt restriction accompanied by medical therapy targeting her elevated pulmonary artery pressures Management of functional tricuspid regurgitation in the setting of pulmonary hypertension is primarily medical.

stem: A 21-year-old woman who has never seen a doctor is found to have an ejection systolic murmur in the left second intercostal space, preceded by an ejection click. Echocardiography confirms pulmonary stenosis with a peak gradient of 70 mmHg and a doming pulmonary valve without regurgitation. What is the best treatment?
explanation: Doming pulmonary valve with peak gradient > ~64 mmHg is congenital pulmonary stenosis: percutaneous balloon valvotomy.

orig.stem: You are seeing a 21-year-old woman in primary care who has never seen a physician before. She is found to have a systolic murmur in the left second interspace preceded by a presystolic click. Echocardiogram confirms pulmonic stenosis with a peak gradient of 60 mmHg and doming of the pulmonic valve without regurgitation. What is her best treatment option?
orig.explanation: Percutaneous balloon valvotomy Percutaneous balloon valvotomy is the treatment of choice for symptomatic pulmonic stenosis.

stem: A 77-year-old patient with severe aortic stenosis develops signs of acute pulmonary oedema and is found to have a new soft, short apical systolic murmur consistent with acute severe mitral regurgitation due to ruptured chordae. Which parameter will likely increase as a result of the new severe mitral regurgitation?
explanation: New severe MR gives the LV a low-pressure outlet, so EF rises while forward flow and the aortic gradient fall.

orig.stem: A 77-year-old patient with severe aortic stenosis develops signs of acute pulmonary edema and is found to have a new soft, short apical systolic murmur consistent with acute severe mitral regurgitation due to ruptured chordae. Which parameter will likely increase as a result of the new severe mitral regurgitation?
orig.explanation: Ejection fraction The ejection fraction may increase due to a reduction in afterload when regurgitation occurs.

stem: A man with rheumatic heart disease and moderate mitral stenosis presents with atrial fibrillation at a ventricular rate of 60 beats/min. Which of the following is the appropriate thromboembolic prophylaxis?
options: More information is needed prior to initiating thromboembolic prophylaxis
explanation: AF with moderate–severe rheumatic MS needs warfarin (INR 2–3) regardless of CHA2DS2-VASc; rivaroxaban was inferior (INVICTUS).

orig.stem: Mr. Milsap, a patient with a history of rheumatic heart disease, presents with atrial fibrillation at a rate of 60 bpm. Which of the following options for thromboembolic prophylaxis is appropriate?
options: More information is needed prior to initiating thromboembolic prophylaxis
orig.explanation: Warfarin Warfarin remains the recommended anticoagulant for valvular atrial fibrillation.

stem: All of the following are risk factors for the development of peripartum cardiomyopathy EXCEPT:
explanation: Peripartum cardiomyopathy risk factors: older age, multiparity, twins, pre-eclampsia/hypertension, African ancestry. Primiparity is not one.

orig.stem: All of the following are risk factors for the development of peripartum cardiomyopathy EXCEPT:
orig.explanation: Primiparous Primiparity is not a risk factor for peripartum cardiomyopathy; multiparity is more common.

stem: A 25-year-old man with a diagnosis of heart failure has used a wheelchair for many years and has severe scoliosis. His ECG shows tall R waves in V1 and V2 with deep Q waves in V5 and V6, and echocardiography shows severe global left ventricular dysfunction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A wheelchair-bound young man with scoliosis and DCM has Duchenne muscular dystrophy (X-linked dystrophin); tall R in V1–V2 is typical.

orig.stem: You are evaluating a 25-year-old patient diagnosed with “heart failure” who has been wheelchair-bound for many years and has severe scoliosis. His ECG shows tall R waves in V1 and V2 with deep Qs in V5 and V6, and echocardiogram reveals severe global left ventricular dysfunction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy The patient’s longstanding neuromuscular issues and characteristic ECG findings point to Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

stem: Which of the following is the most common inheritance pattern for familial cardiomyopathies?
options: Autosomal dominant driven by exon duplication
Autosomal dominant driven by missense mutations
Autosomal recessive driven by exon deletion
Autosomal recessive driven by exon duplication
explanation: Most familial cardiomyopathies are autosomal dominant missense mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3, TTN, LMNA); offer cascade screening.

orig.stem: Which of the following is the most common inheritance pattern for familial cardiomyopathies?
options: Autosomal dominant driven by exon duplication
Autosomal dominant driven by missense mutations
Autosomal recessive driven by exon deletion
Autosomal recessive driven by exon duplication
orig.explanation: Autosomal dominant driven by missense mutations Familial cardiomyopathies are most commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with missense mutations.

stem: A 45-year-old man with obesity presents with several months of breathlessness, fatigue and a nocturnal cough. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with a globally reduced ejection fraction of 25%. Which blood test is routinely recommended in all patients with newly diagnosed heart failure to identify a reversible cause?
explanation: TSH is part of routine tests in new heart failure, as hypo- and hyperthyroidism are reversible causes.

orig.stem: A 45-year-old man with obesity presents with dyspnea, fatigue, and a nocturnal cough over several months. Echocardiography reveals a globally depressed left ventricular ejection fraction of 25% with a dilated left ventricle. Which of the following tests is a Level I recommendation for further workup?
orig.explanation: Thyroid-stimulating hormone level TSH level is a Level I recommended test in the workup of new cardiomyopathy.

stem: A 22-year-old student presents with lethargy and fatigue 3 days after a viral upper respiratory illness. He is obtunded, tachycardic and hypotensive, with cool peripheries and a raised jugular venous pressure. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 30% with mild mitral regurgitation, and endomyocardial biopsy shows lymphocytic myocarditis. Which of the following statements about his prognosis and treatment is true?
options: His chance of survival is <10% without cardiac transplantation. Emergent transplant listing is warranted

His chance of survival is >50%, with many similar patients having a full recovery in left ventricular function over the ensuing weeks to months. Aggressive pharmacologic and mechanical haemodynamic support is warranted
Immunosuppression with high-dose systemic steroids will increase his chance of survival
The presence and titer of anti-heart antibodies can help provide prognostic information for this patient
explanation: Fulminant lymphocytic myocarditis has a good outcome if supported (inotropes, ECMO/VAD); LV function often recovers fully.

orig.stem: A 22-year-old college student presents with lethargy and fatigue 3 days after a viral upper respiratory illness. He is obtunded, tachycardic, hypotensive, with cool extremities and elevated jugular venous pressure. Echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 30% and mild mitral regurgitation. Endomyocardial biopsy reveals lymphocytic myocarditis. Which of the following statements regarding his prognosis and implications for therapy is true?
options: His chance of survival is <10% without cardiac transplantation. Emergent transplant listing is warranted.

His chance of survival is >50%, with many similar patients having a full recovery in left ventricular function over the ensuing weeks to months. Aggressive pharmacologic and mechanical hemodynamic support is warranted.
Immunosuppression with high-dose systemic steroids will increase his chance of survival.
The presence and titer of anti-heart antibodies can help provide prognostic information for this patient.
orig.explanation: His chance of survival is >50%, with many similar patients having a full recovery in left ventricular function over the ensuing weeks to months. Aggressive pharmacologic and mechanical hemodynamic support is warranted. Fulminant viral myocarditis can have a good prognosis with aggressive support, with many patients recovering LV function.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis is brought in after collapsing at home. She reports several days of worsening lethargy and chest discomfort. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 15%, and endomyocardial biopsy shows diffuse inflammatory infiltrates with multinucleated giant cells and myocyte necrosis. Which of the following statements about her diagnosis is true?
options: Most patients with this form of cardiomyopathy recover with supportive care
Steroids alone are highly effective in treating this form of cardiomyopathy
The course is often rapidly progressive, with deterioration requiring urgent transplantation
Ventricular tachyarrhythmias are rare in this disease
None of the above is true
explanation: Giant cell myocarditis (with autoimmune disease) progresses rapidly with heart block and VT; immunosuppression helps but many need urgent transplant.

orig.stem: You are evaluating a 42-year-old woman with a history of Hashimoto thyroiditis treated with radioactive iodine. She presents after passing out at home and reports several days of worsening lethargy and chest discomfort. Echocardiogram reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction of 15%, and endomyocardial biopsy shows diffuse granulomatous lesions with inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following statements is true regarding her diagnosis?
options: Most patients with this etiology of cardiomyopathy recover with supportive care.
Steroids are highly effective in treating this form of cardiomyopathy.
The course of this cardiomyopathy is dire, often with rapid deterioration requiring urgent transplantation.
While seen occasionally, ventricular tachyar rhythmias are rare in this disease.
None of the above is true.
orig.explanation: The course of this cardiomyopathy is dire, often with rapid deterioration requiring urgent transplantation. Giant cell myocarditis presents with a fulminant course and often requires urgent transplantation.

stem: All of the following are associated with an elevated risk for development of cardiomyopathy during anthracycline chemotherapy EXCEPT:
options: All of the above are associated with elevated risk
explanation: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity rises with cumulative dose (> 400–450 mg/m²), chest radiotherapy, heart disease, age extremes and trastuzumab.

orig.stem: All of the following are associated with an elevated risk for development of cardiomyopathy during anthracycline chemotherapy EXCEPT:
options: All of the above are associated with elevated risk
orig.explanation: All of the above are associated with elevated risk of cardiomyopathy due to anthracyclines. Each listed factor increases the risk of anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents with chest pain after a week of coryza, cough, fever and muscle aches. The pain is constant, radiates to his left shoulder, and is worse lying flat and on deep inspiration. There is a scratchy extracardiac sound with three components per heartbeat. His ECG is shown, and troponin I is undetectable. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Aspirin 75 mg daily, metoprolol 25 mg twice daily and atorvastatin 80 mg daily
High-dose aspirin (750 mg–1 g every 8 hours) plus colchicine, with proton pump inhibitor cover
Heparin, aspirin and clopidogrel with immediate coronary angiography
Prednisolone 40 mg daily for 2 weeks, then tapered over 2 months
explanation: Viral pericarditis (rub, diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression, normal troponin): high-dose aspirin or NSAID with PPI plus colchicine.

orig.stem: Mr. Kia is a 32-year-old bass guitarist who presents with chest pain after a week of coryza, cough, fever, and muscle aches. His pain is constant, radiates to his left shoulder, and is exacerbated by lying flat and during deep breaths. Examination reveals a rasping extracardiac sound present in three components per heartbeat. His ECG is shown and troponin I levels are undetectable. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Aspirin 81 mg daily, metoprolol 25 mg twice daily, and atorvastatin 80 mg daily
Aspirin 1 g every 8 hours with omeprazole 20 mg daily
Heparin, aspirin, clopidogrel, and immediate coronary angiography
Prednisone 40 mg daily for 2 weeks followed by a taper over 2 months
orig.explanation: Aspirin 1 g every 8 hours with omeprazole 20 mg daily This presentation is consistent with acute pericarditis, for which high-dose aspirin is indicated.

stem: You are caring for a 45-year-old man in the cardiac intensive care unit who was initially treated for acute coronary syndrome but is now diagnosed with acute pericarditis. Shortly after admission, he becomes hypotensive with elevated neck veins and cool extremities. What is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: You are caring for a 45-year-old man in the cardiac intensive care unit who was initially treated for acute coronary syndrome but is now diagnosed with acute pericarditis. Shortly after admission, he becomes hypotensive with elevated neck veins and cool extremities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Cardiac tamponade The clinical findings of hypotension, elevated JVP, and pulsus paradoxus are indicative of cardiac tamponade.

stem: In a patient with cardiac tamponade, which of the following is likely to be increased during inspiration compared to expiration?
explanation: In tamponade inspiration increases RV filling (tricuspid inflow) while LV filling and SBP fall (pulsus paradoxus).

orig.stem: In a patient with cardiac tamponade, which of the following is likely to be increased during inspiration compared to expiration?
orig.explanation: Tricuspid inflow velocity In cardiac tamponade, tricuspid inflow velocity increases during inspiration due to ventricular interdependence.

stem: All of the following ECG characteristics aid in differentiating acute pericarditis from acute myocardial infarction EXCEPT:
options: Absence of the development of Q waves
T-wave inversions after return of the ST segments to baseline
explanation: Pericarditis: diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression, no reciprocal change or Q waves. ST elevation in V2 occurs in both, so it does not help.

orig.stem: All of the following ECG characteristics aid in differentiating acute pericarditis from acute myocardial infarction EXCEPT:
options: Absence of the development of Q waves
T-wave inversions after return of the ST segments to baseline
orig.explanation: ST elevation in V2 ST elevation in V2 is not a distinguishing feature between pericarditis and MI.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with a history of Hodgkin disease treated with chemotherapy and mediastinal irradiation presents with signs of constrictive pericarditis. Echocardiogram shows pericardial thickening and an abrupt cessation of ventricular filling in early diastole. What is the best approach for treatment?
explanation: Post-radiotherapy constriction (knock, dip-and-plateau) is treated definitively by pericardiectomy; diuretics give only temporary relief.

orig.stem: A 35-year-old woman with a history of Hodgkin disease treated with chemotherapy and mediastinal irradiation presents with signs of constrictive pericarditis. Echocardiogram shows pericardial thickening and an abrupt cessation of ventricular filling in early diastole. What is the best approach for treatment?
orig.explanation: Pericardial resection Pericardial resection is the definitive treatment for constrictive pericarditis.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a 3-month history of fevers, symmetrical arthralgia and fatigue develops sudden left hand weakness that resolves within 1 hour. Echocardiography shows a solitary 2-cm pedunculated mass in the left atrium arising from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Cardiothoracic surgical removal of the mass
Repeat blood cultures and evaluation for HACEK organisms
Serologies for ANAs, anti-DNA, and anticardiolipin antibodies
Whole-body PET scan to evaluate for malignancy
explanation: A pedunculated LA mass at the fossa ovalis with fever, arthralgia and TIA is myxoma: surgical excision without delay.

orig.stem: A 45-year-old accountant with a 3-month history of fevers, symmetric arthralgias, and fatigue experiences sudden left hand weakness that resolves within 1 hour. Echocardiogram shows a solitary 2-cm mass in the left atrium arising from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis that appears pedunculated. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Cardiothoracic surgical removal of the mass
Repeat blood cultures and evaluation for HACEK organisms
Serologies for ANAs, anti-DNA, and anticardiolipin antibodies
Whole-body PET scan to evaluate for malignancy
orig.explanation: Cardiothoracic surgical removal of the mass The mass is most consistent with an atrial myxoma, which should be surgically removed.

stem: Which of the following malignancies carries the highest relative risk of metastasis to the heart?
explanation: Melanoma has the highest propensity for cardiac metastasis; lung and breast cancer are commonest by number.

orig.stem: Which of the following malignancies carries the highest relative risk of metastasis to the heart?
orig.explanation: Malignant melanoma Malignant melanoma has the highest relative risk of cardiac metastases.

stem: At a children's baseball game, a 12-year-old catcher is struck in the chest by a foul ball and immediately collapses in cardiac arrest. Which intervention is most critical for his survival?
options: Emergent transfer for percutaneous coronary intervention
Emergent transfer for repair of an acute aortic dissection
Prompt cardiac surgery to repair an avulsed aortic valve
explanation: Commotio cordis: a precordial blow on the T-wave upslope triggers VF in a normal heart; immediate CPR and defibrillation save life.

orig.stem: You are attending your 12-year-old son’s Little League baseball game when the catcher fouls the ball into his chest, leading to collapse and cardiac arrest. What intervention is most critical for his survival?
options: Emergent transfer for percutaneous coronary intervention
Emergent transfer for repair of an acute aortic dissection
Prompt cardiac surgery to repair an avulsed aortic valve
orig.explanation: Prompt defibrillation Immediate defibrillation is crucial in commotio cordis to restore normal rhythm.

stem: A 47-year-old woman with a BMI of 37 kg/m² and type 2 diabetes asks about her future risk of heart attack and stroke. What is the most common cause of death in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus?
explanation: Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of death in type 2 diabetes (2–4× risk, often silent ischaemia).

orig.stem: A 47-year-old woman with a BMI of 37 kg/ m2 and type 2 diabetes is informed about her future risk of heart attack and stroke. What is the most common cause of death in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus?
orig.explanation: Coronary artery disease Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of death in adults with type 2 diabetes.

stem: A 49-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol use presents with high-output heart failure. After treatment, his symptoms and left ventricular size improve rapidly. Which treatment most likely produced this improvement?
explanation: High-output heart failure in a heavy drinker that responds rapidly is wet beriberi from thiamine deficiency; give thiamine before glucose.

orig.stem: Mr. Daniels, a 49-year-old man with a history of alcohol abuse, presents with signs of high-output heart failure. After treatment, his symptoms and left ventricular size improve rapidly. Which of the following most likely caused this improvement?
orig.explanation: Thiamine Thiamine deficiency (wet beriberi) can cause high-output heart failure that improves rapidly with thiamine administration.

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, brittle hair and leg swelling. Her TSH is 79.4 mU/L. Which cardiovascular measurement is NOT expected to decrease?
explanation: Hypothyroidism lowers heart rate, stroke volume and output, raises SVR and prolongs (not shortens) the QT.

orig.stem: A 65-year-old former factory worker with rheumatoid arthritis presents with fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, brittle hair, and lower extremity swelling. Her TSH is 79.4 mIU/L. In regard to her cardiovascular system, which measurement is NOT expected to decrease?
orig.explanation: QT interval In hypothyroidism, most parameters decrease except the QT interval, which is often prolonged.

stem: In the current model describing the steps of atherosclerosis initiation and evolution, which of the following constitutes the first step?
options: Arterial endothelial cells overexpress adhesion receptors for leukocytes
Low-density lipoproteins accumulate within the arterial intima
Macrophages and other leukocytes are recruited to the arterial intima
Macrophages become lipid-laden foam cells via endocytosis
explanation: Atherogenesis begins with LDL retention in the intima; oxidation, endothelial activation, monocyte recruitment and foam cells follow.

orig.stem: In the current model describing the steps of atherosclerosis initiation and evolution, which of the following constitutes the first step?
options: Arterial endothelial cells overexpress adhesion receptors for leukocytes.
Low-density lipoproteins accumulate within the arterial intima.
Macrophages and other leukocytes are recruited to the arterial intima.
Macrophages become lipid-laden foam cells via endocytosis.
orig.explanation: Low-density lipoproteins accumulate within the arterial intima. The initial step in atherosclerosis is the accumulation of LDL within the arterial intima.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the pathophysiologic consequences of an atheroma is true?
options: An atheroma resulting in total vascular occlusion invariably causes infarction
An enlarging atheroma does not generally encroach on the arterial lumen until the plaque exceeds 40% of the internal elastic lamina
Most atheromas will eventually produce symptoms in the patient
Upon initial formation, the atheromatous plaque usually grows inward toward the vessel lumen
Vessels affected by atherogenesis tend to contract and get smaller in diameter
explanation: Arteries remodel outward, so a plaque does not narrow the lumen until it exceeds ~40% of the area within the internal elastic lamina (Glagov).

orig.stem: Which of the following statements regarding the pathophysiologic consequences of an atheroma is true?
options: An atheroma resulting in total vascular occlusion invariably causes infarction.
An enlarging atheroma does not generally encroach on the arterial lumen until the plaque exceeds 40% of the internal elastic lamina.
Most atheromas will eventually produce symptoms in the patient.
Upon initial formation, the atheromatous plaque usually grows inward toward the vessel lumen.
Vessels affected by atherogenesis tend to contract and get smaller in diameter.
orig.explanation: An enlarging atheroma does not generally encroach on the arterial lumen until the plaque exceeds 40% of the internal elastic lamina. Compensatory enlargement prevents luminal narrowing until advanced stages.

stem: Under the 2013 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline (whose statin benefit groups were retained in 2018), all of the following are statin benefit groups EXCEPT:
options: All individuals with clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD)
Individuals with a raised high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP) regardless of LDL cholesterol or ASCVD risk
Individuals with LDL cholesterol of 4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL) or more without a secondary cause
Individuals aged 40–75 years without ASCVD or diabetes, with LDL 1.8–4.9 mmol/L (70–189 mg/dL) and a 10-year ASCVD risk of 7.5% or more
Individuals aged 40–75 years with diabetes but no ASCVD, with LDL 1.8–4.9 mmol/L (70–189 mg/dL)
explanation: Statin benefit groups: clinical ASCVD, LDL ≥ 4.9 mmol/L, diabetes aged 40–75, 10-year risk ≥ 7.5%. Raised hs-CRP alone is not one.

orig.stem: Based on the 2013 cholesterol guidelines from the ACC/AHA, all of the following groups are a definite statin benefit group EXCEPT:
options: All individuals who have clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD)
Individuals with an elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP) regardless of LDL cholesterol level or ASCVD risk
Individuals with LDL cholesterol ≥190 mg/dL without a secondary cause
Individuals without established ASCVD or diabetes who are 40–75 years old with LDL 70–189 mg/dL and ASCVD risk ≥7.5%
Patients with diabetes without established cardiovascular disease who are 40–75 years old and have LDL 70–189 mg/dL
orig.explanation: Individuals with an elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP) regardless of LDL cholesterol level or ASCVD risk Elevated hsCRP alone is not an indication for statin therapy per the guidelines.

stem: A 50-year-old man with obesity attends his annual check-up. He has no known vascular disease and a 10-year ASCVD risk of 6%. His lipid profile shows total cholesterol 5.7 mmol/L (220 mg/dL), triglycerides 3.2 mmol/L (283 mg/dL), HDL cholesterol 0.75 mmol/L (29 mg/dL) and LDL cholesterol 3.4 mmol/L (132 mg/dL). He is concerned about his low HDL. Which intervention aimed at his low HDL has been shown to lower his cardiovascular risk?
options: A cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibitor
Weight loss and regular physical activity
explanation: HDL-raising drugs (CETP inhibitors, niacin, fibrates) did not cut events; weight loss and exercise improve HDL and overall risk.

orig.stem: A 50-year-old man presents for his yearly check-up. He has a history of vascular disease, obesity, and an ASCVD risk of 6%. He is concerned about his low HDL cholesterol. What can definitively lower his cardiovascular risk the most regarding his HDL?
options: An agonist of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor B
An inhibitor of cholesteryl ester transfer protein
orig.explanation: Weight loss and physical activity Lifestyle modifications remain the most effective means to improve HDL levels and reduce cardiovascular risk.

stem: All of the following are major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand EXCEPT:
options: All of the above are major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand
explanation: Myocardial oxygen demand depends on heart rate, contractility and wall stress (preload and afterload); rhythm itself is not a primary determinant.

orig.stem: All of the following are major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand EXCEPT:
options: All of the above are major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand.
orig.explanation: Heart rhythm Heart rhythm is not a primary determinant of myocardial oxygen demand.

stem: During an exercise stress test, how does the normal heart meet its increased oxygen demand?
options: Increased myocardial oxygen extraction during near-constant coronary blood flow
Increased oxygen extraction from the ventricular chambers
Relative expansion of the diastolic time period allowing increased coronary flow
Vasodilation of epicardial coronary arteries leading to decreased resistance and increased flow
Vasodilation of intramyocardial coronary vessels leading to increased coronary flow
explanation: The heart already extracts ~70–75% of oxygen at rest, so extra demand is met by arteriolar dilatation and increased coronary flow.

orig.stem: Mr. Jackson is undergoing an exercise stress test. How does the normal heart respond to meet its higher oxygen demand?
options: Increased myocardial oxygen extraction during near-constant coronary blood flow
Increased oxygen extraction from the ventricular chambers
Relative expansion of the diastolic time period allowing increased coronary flow
Vasodilation of epicardial coronary arteries leading to decreased resistance and increased flow
Vasodilation of intramyocardial coronary vessels leading to increased coronary flow
orig.explanation: Vasodilation of intramyocardial coronary vessels leading to increased coronary flow The primary mechanism is vasodilation of intramyocardial vessels to increase blood flow.

stem: A man develops angina during an exercise stress test. Which of the following biochemical changes would NOT be expected in his ischaemic myocardium?
options: A shift from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism
Depletion of myocardial stores of high-energy phosphates
explanation: Ischaemia shifts to anaerobic glycolysis: lactate and H⁺ accumulate (pH falls), ATP depletes, calcium rises and potassium leaks out.

orig.stem: As Mr. Jackson continues his exercise stress test and experiences angina, which of the following biochemical changes in his ischemic myocardium would NOT be observed?
options: A shift from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism
Depletion of myocardial stores of high-energy phosphates
orig.explanation: An increase in intracellular pH During ischemia, intracellular pH decreases due to anaerobic metabolism.

stem: Which of the following is an unusual site for radiation of anginal pain?
explanation: Angina radiates to arms, neck, jaw, epigastrium and back; radiation to the trapezius ridge is characteristic of pericarditis.

orig.stem: Which of the following sites is an unusual anatomic location for anginal pain radiation?
orig.explanation: Trapezius muscle Anginal pain rarely radiates to the trapezius muscle.

stem: Ms. Wilson is a 66-year-old postmenopausal postal employee who experiences chest pressure and dyspnea while walking her mail route. What term and CCS functional class best describe her angina?

orig.stem: Ms. Wilson is a 66-year-old postmenopausal postal employee who experiences chest pressure and dyspnea while walking her mail route. What term and CCS functional class best describe her angina?
orig.explanation: Stable angina – CCS class II Her predictable symptoms at a certain level of exertion classify her as CCS class II stable angina.

stem: A 50-year-old accountant with a history of cigarette use completes an exercise treadmill ECG stress test. He develops upsloping ST depressions in leads II, III, and aVF. His peak heart rate is 130 bpm, and his blood pressure increases from 120/80 to 155/95 mmHg. What is the appropriate interpretation of this stress test?
options: Negative stress test; inappropriate hypertensive response to exercise
Negative stress test; nonspecific ST changes
Nondiagnostic stress test; normal blood pressure response
Positive stress test; inappropriate hypertensive response to exercise
Positive stress test; normal blood pressure response

orig.stem: A 50-year-old accountant with a history of cigarette use completes an exercise treadmill ECG stress test. He develops upsloping ST depressions in leads II, III, and aVF. His peak heart rate is 130 bpm, and his blood pressure increases from 120/80 to 155/95 mmHg. What is the appropriate interpretation of this stress test?
options: Negative stress test; inappropriate hypertensive response to exercise
Negative stress test; nonspecific ST changes
Nondiagnostic stress test; normal blood pressure response
Positive stress test; inappropriate hypertensive response to exercise
Positive stress test; normal blood pressure response
orig.explanation: Positive stress test; normal blood pressure response The ST changes and blood pressure response are consistent with a positive stress test.

stem: Mr. Brian, a 57-year-old hockey team coach with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and tobacco abuse, presents with chest discomfort that initially occurred with vigorous exertion but now at rest. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
options: More information is required before making a diagnosis

orig.stem: Mr. Brian, a 57-year-old hockey team coach with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and tobacco abuse, presents with chest discomfort that initially occurred with vigorous exertion but now at rest. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
options: More information is required before making a diagnosis.
orig.explanation: Unstable angina The progression of symptoms from exertional to rest suggests unstable angina. E. Hepatopulmonary syndrome

stem: A 70-year-old man with mild chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus and heart failure is admitted with reduced urine output, weakness and breathlessness. He takes several medications but cannot remember their names. Blood results are pending, and his ECG is shown. Based on the information available, what is the best initial step in management?
options: Administration of oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate
explanation: Peaked T waves with flat P waves are hyperkalaemia: give IV calcium gluconate first, then insulin–glucose and salbutamol.

orig.stem: A 70-year-old male with a history of mild chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, and CHF is admitted to your inpatient service with decreased urine output, weakness, and shortness of breath. He takes several medications but cannot remember their names. Labs are pending; his ECG is shown below. Based on the information available, what is the best initial step in management?
options: Administration of oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate
orig.explanation: Administration of intravenous calcium gluconate Hyperkalemia ECG: peaked T, PR/QRS prolongation → sine wave risk; treat now with IV calcium, insulin ± glucose, ± bicarbonate; then remove K⁺; check glucose/renal status.

stem: A surgical colleague asks you to review a 54-year-old woman with ECG abnormalities the day after a subtotal thyroidectomy for toxic multinodular goitre. Her only medication is fentanyl for postoperative pain. She has no history of syncope and no family history of sudden cardiac death. Examination is unremarkable apart from a clean incision at the base of the neck. Her ECG is shown. What is the best next step?
options: Stat noncontrast CT scan of the brain
Reassure the patient that her ECG is normal for a woman her age
explanation: Long QT from ST-segment lengthening the day after thyroidectomy suggests hypocalcaemia (parathyroid injury): measure ionised calcium.

orig.stem: You are called by a surgical colleague to evaluate a 54-year-old woman with ECG abnormalities one day after a subtotal thyroidectomy for a toxic multinodular goiter. Her only medication is fentanyl for postoperative pain control. The patient denies any history of syncope, and has no family history of sudden cardiac death. Physical examination is unremarkable except for a clean postoperative incision at the base of the neck. Her ECG is reproduced below. What is the best next step in evaluation and management of this patient?
options: Stat noncontrast CT scan of the brain
Reassure the patient that her ECG is normal for a woman her age
orig.explanation: Measurement of serum ionized calcium Prolonged QT post-thyroid surgery → suspect hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism; check ionized calcium; magnesium for torsades only.

stem: A 56-year-old man attends his GP surgery for a routine blood pressure check and examination. He has no immediate concerns and his past medical history includes hypertension and asthma. He feels well in himself. On examination, he appears well and observa tions are normal except for a raised blood pressure of 155/87 mmHg. Upon auscultation of the heart, the GP notices an S4 heart sound. The GP then requests an ECG recording. Which part of the ECG does this sound coincide with?
explanation: S4 is atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, so it falls just after the P wave; S1 coincides with QRS. No S4 in AF.

orig.stem: A 56-year-old man attends his GP surgery for a routine blood pressure check and examination. He has no immediate concerns and his past medical history includes hypertension and asthma. He feels well in himself. On examination, he appears well and observa tions are normal except for a raised blood pressure of 155/87 mmHg. Upon auscultation of the heart, the GP notices an S4 heart sound. The GP then requests an ECG recording. Which part of the ECG does this sound coincide with?
orig.explanation: P wave S4 = atrial kick against stiff ventricle; aligns with ECG P wave; not QRS, ST, T, or U.

stem: Asthma is characterized by all the following EXCEPT:
options: The patient can be completely free between the episodes
The disease can start at any age
In adults it is more common and more severe in men than women

orig.stem: Asthma is characterized by all the following EXCEPT:
options: The patient can be completely free between the episodes.
The disease can start at any age.
In adults it is more common and more severe in men than women.
orig.explanation: In adults it is more common and more severe in men than women. Asthma in adulthood is more common in women.

stem: Dyspnea that associate with wheezing can be caused by the following EXCEPT:

orig.stem: Dyspnea that associate with wheezing can be caused by the following EXCEPT:
orig.explanation: Pneumothorax. Pneumothorax usually does not present with wheezing.

stem: All of the following are characteristic of asthma EXCEPT:
options: It is rare before 5 years of age
It can be seasonal or perennial
It can start at any age
The patient can be completely free of symptoms between episodes
explanation: Asthma often begins before age 5 (most persistent cases), can start at any age, and is characteristically variable.

orig.stem: Asthma is characterized by all the following EXCEPT:
options: Rare before five years of age.
The disease can start at any age.
The patient can be completely free between the episodes.
orig.explanation: Rare before five years of age. Asthma can occur before five years of age, hence this statement is incorrect.

stem: Which feature is incorrect regarding asthma
options: Patient can be complete free between episodes
In adults it is more severe in male than female

orig.stem: which feature is incorrect regarding asthma
options: Patient can be complete free between episodes
In adults it is more severe in male than female
orig.explanation: In adults it is more severe in male than female Asthma in adults is typically more severe in females.

stem: A 53-year-old woman with a 30-year history of asthma has worsening control despite maximal inhaled therapy, a chronic cough productive of green sputum, breathlessness and wheeze. A CT scan of her chest is shown. What does it show?
explanation: Dilated thick-walled central upper-lobe bronchi (signet ring) in a long-standing asthmatic suggest ABPA with bronchiectasis; check IgE and Aspergillus serology.

orig.stem: A 53 year old woman with a 30-year history of asthma, now with worsening control despite maximal inhaled therapy, chronic productive cough of green sputum, breathlessness and wheeze is sent for a CT scan. What is shown on the image?
orig.explanation: Bronchiectasis CT demonstrates bilateral, proximal bronchiectatic changes consistent with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

stem: A 37 year old asthmatic woman presents with difficult asthma control that worsens in April and May. Serum allergy testing reveals: Total IgE 1241 kU/L; Specific IgE to dog 24 kU/L; cat

orig.stem: A 37 year old asthmatic woman presents with difficult asthma control that worsens in April and May. Serum allergy testing reveals: Total IgE 1241 kU/L; Specific IgE to dog 24 kU/L; cat
orig.explanation: The patient’s asthma is triggered by seasonal pollens (specific IgE to oilseed rape and grass positive) Seasonal allergens are implicated given the positive specific IgE and seasonal pattern.

stem: A 37-year-old woman with asthma has difficult asthma control that worsens every April and May. Serum allergy testing shows: total IgE 1241 kU/L; specific IgE to dog 24 kU/L, cat 4 kU/L, tree pollen 0.2 kU/L, oilseed rape 34 kU/L and grass pollen 25 kU/L. What is the most likely explanation for her presentation?
options: She has exercise-induced asthma, so IgE testing is irrelevant
She has concealed exposure to animals, as dog and cat specific IgE are raised
She is non-adherent to medication, as total IgE remains high
She is sensitised to montelukast, and the IgE results represent cross-reactivity
Her asthma is triggered by seasonal pollens (oilseed rape and grass)
explanation: Worsening every April–May with sensitisation to oilseed rape and grass pollen is seasonal allergic asthma; optimise ICS before the season.

orig.stem: 4 kU/L; tree pollen 0.2 kU/L; oilseed rape 34 kU/L; grass pollen 25 kU/L. What is the likely explanation for her presentation?
options: The patient has exercise-induced asthma (IgE testing irrelevant)
The patient has lied about exposure to animals (specific IgE to cats and dogs elevated)
The patient is non-adherent with medication (total IgE remains high)
The patient is sensitised to montelukast (IgE results represent cross-reactivity)
The patient’s asthma is triggered by seasonal pollens (specific IgE to oilseed rape and grass positive)
orig.explanation: Low dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) Asthma with reversible obstruction after SABA failure → start low-dose ICS; COPD less likely given minimal pack-years; LABA/LAMA, LABA alone, omalizumab, and oral steroids are not first-line maintenance.

stem: A 45-year-old smoker with cough, wheeze and productive sputum undergoes pulmonary function testing. Pre-bronchodilator: FEV1 2.6 L, FVC 4.4 L, FEV1/FVC 0.59. Post-bronchodilator: FEV1 3.2 L, FVC 4.4 L, FEV1/FVC 0.73. What does the testing show?
options: A mixture of obstruction and restriction
explanation: FEV1 rises 600 mL (23%) and the ratio normalises: a reversible obstructive defect; ≥ 400 mL strongly favours asthma.

orig.stem: A 45 year old smoker with cough, wheeze and productive sputum undergoes pulmonary function testing. Spirometry pre-bronchodilator: FEV1 2.6 L, FVC 4.4 L, FEV1/FVC 0.59. Post-bronchodilator: FEV1 3.2 L, FVC 4.4 L, FEV1/FVC 0.73. What does the testing reveal?
options: A mixture of obstruction and restriction
orig.explanation: A reversible obstructive defect The marked reversibility confirms an asthma diagnosis despite a smoking history.

stem: A 27-year-old woman with severe atopic asthma, who is 26 weeks pregnant, presents with worsening nocturnal cough and breathlessness. PEF is 240 L/min (best 450 L/min). Her medications are high-dose ICS/LABA, oral montelukast and an as-needed SABA. What should be the next step in her management?
explanation: PEF 53% of best with nocturnal symptoms in pregnancy is an exacerbation: prednisolone 40–50 mg ≥ 5 days; continue all asthma drugs.

orig.stem: A 27 year old woman with severe atopic asthma, 26 weeks pregnant, presents with worsening nocturnal cough and breathlessness. PEFR is 240 L/min (best 450 L/min). Her medications include high-dose ICS/LABA, oral montelukast, and as-needed SABA. What should be the next step in her management?
orig.explanation: Oral prednisolone The patient is experiencing a significant asthma exacerbation; systemic steroids are indicated.

stem: A 48-year-old man with asthma has increasingly frequent exacerbations, nocturnal cough and blood eosinophilia. He uses fluticasone–salmeterol twice daily (good adherence and technique) and salbutamol as required, and has just started a 5-day course of prednisolone for the current exacerbation. According to current BTS/NICE/SIGN guidance, what is the most appropriate change to his maintenance therapy?
options: Switch to budesonide–formoterol as maintenance and reliever therapy (MART)
explanation: Uncontrolled on fixed ICS/LABA + SABA: switch to ICS–formoterol MART; if still uncontrolled with eosinophilia, refer for a biologic.

orig.stem: A 48 year old asthmatic with increased exacerbations, nocturnal cough, and eosinophilia is on Flixotide/salmeterol and salbutamol as required. He has started a 5-day course of prednisolone. In line with BTS guidelines, what should be added to step-up therapy?
orig.explanation: Add montelukast Montelukast is recommended as an add-on therapy for difficult-to-control asthma.

stem: A 43-year-old woman who smokes and works in a bakery presents with cough, breathlessness and wheeze, which deteriorate after 3 weeks back at work. Which test is most helpful to assess for occupational asthma?
explanation: Serial PEF (≥ 4×/day for 3–4 weeks, at and away from work) is the first-line test for occupational asthma.

orig.stem: A 43 year old woman presents with cough, shortness of breath and wheeze. A smoker working in a bakery, she experiences deterioration after 3 weeks back at work. To assess for occupational asthma, which test is most helpful?
orig.explanation: Peak expiratory flow rate diary A detailed PEFR diary over several weeks is key for diagnosing occupational asthma.

stem: Which of the following is the major risk factor for asthma?
explanation: Atopy (IgE sensitisation to common allergens) is the strongest identifiable risk factor for asthma.

orig.stem: Which of the following is the major risk factor for asthma?
orig.explanation: Atopy Atopy is the strongest risk factor for asthma development.

stem: A 24-year-old woman with eczema and allergic rhinitis has asthma. Which statement regarding her disease is true?
options: Confirmation of the diagnosis requires methacholine challenge testing
Mortality due to the disease has been increasing over the past decade
The most common risk factor in individuals with the disorder is genetic predisposition
The prevalence of the disorder has not changed in the past several decades
The severity of the disease does not vary significantly within a given patient with the disease
explanation: Asthma severity tends to stay constant within an individual (mild rarely becomes severe), though control fluctuates.

orig.stem: A 24-year-old woman with eczema and allergic rhinitis has asthma. Which statement regarding her disease is true?
options: Confirmation of the diagnosis requires methacholine challenge testing.
Mortality due to the disease has been increasing over the past decade.
The most common risk factor in individuals with the disorder is genetic predisposition.
The prevalence of the disorder has not changed in the past several decades.
The severity of the disease does not vary significantly within a given patient with the disease.
orig.explanation: The severity of the disease does not vary significantly within a given patient with the disease Individuals with mild disease generally stay mild, and severe disease remains severe over time.

stem: A 38-year-old woman dies of status asthmaticus. All of the following pathologic findings are likely EXCEPT:
options: Infiltration of the airway mucosa with eosinophils and activated T lymphocytes
Infiltration of the alveolar spaces with eosinophils and neutrophils
Occlusion of the airway lumen by mucous plugs
Thickening and oedema of the airway wall
Thickening of the basement membrane of the airways with subepithelial collagen deposition
explanation: Fatal asthma shows mucus plugs, eosinophilic airway inflammation, oedema, smooth-muscle hypertrophy and basement membrane thickening; alveoli are spared.

orig.stem: A 38-year-old woman dies of status asthmaticus. All of the following pathologic findings are likely EXCEPT:
options: Infiltration of the airway mucosa with eosinophils and activated T lymphocytes
Infiltration of the alveolar spaces with eosinophils and neutrophils
Occlusion of the airway lumen by mucous plugs
Thickening and edema of the airway wall
Thickening of the basement membrane of the airways with subepithelial collagen deposition
orig.explanation: Infiltration of the alveolar spaces with eosinophils and neutrophils Asthma is primarily an airway (bronchial) disease; alveolar spaces are usually spared.

stem: Which of the following patients is appropriately diagnosed with asthma?
options: A 24-year-old with cough and wheeze for 6 weeks after a viral respiratory infection
A 26-year-old with cough and occasional wheeze when exercising in cold weather
A 34-year-old with chronic cough whose FEV1 increases from 1.68 L to 1.98 L (18%) after salbutamol
A 44-year-old laboratory worker who handles mice and has cough and wheeze towards the end of each working week
A 60-year-old heavy smoker with chronic breathlessness and airway hyperreactivity
explanation: Asthma needs symptoms plus objective variability: FEV1 rise ≥ 12% and ≥ 200 mL after bronchodilator (here 300 mL, 18%).

orig.stem: Which of the following patients is appropriately diagnosed with asthma?
options: A 24-year-old with cough and wheeze 6 weeks after a viral infection
A 26-year-old with cold-exercise cough and occasional wheeze
A 34-year-old with chronic cough and FEV1 increasing from 1.68 L to 1.98 L (18%) after albuterol
A 44-year-old with workplace mouse allergen exposure only at week’s end
A 60-year-old heavy smoker with airway hyperreactivity and chronic dyspnea
orig.explanation: A 34-year-old with chronic cough and an 18% improvement in FEV1 after albuterol Diagnosis requires reversible airflow obstruction (≥12% and 200 mL improvement in FEV1).

stem: A 24-year-old woman with mild asthma uses her salbutamol inhaler 4–7 times a week and takes no other treatment. What do you advise?
explanation: SABA-only treatment is no longer advised; mild asthma uses as-needed low-dose budesonide–formoterol (cuts severe exacerbations by ~two-thirds).

orig.stem: A 24-year-old woman with mild intermittent asthma uses albuterol 4-7 times/week. What do you advise?
options: Add inhaled salmeterol twice a day
Think of a new name for the goldfish
orig.explanation: Add inhaled beclomethasone Using a rescue inhaler more than twice per week indicates the need for a low-dose inhaled steroid.

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman with mild persistent asthma is well controlled on an inhaled corticosteroid and salbutamol as needed. Which statement is correct?
options: She should continue her current therapy and follow symptoms
She should switch to inhaled tiotropium as needed
She should switch from inhaled beclomethasone to salmeterol
There is >70% chance her asthma will lessen in pregnancy
There is >70% chance her asthma will worsen in pregnancy
explanation: Asthma in pregnancy follows the rule of thirds; continue ICS and relievers, as uncontrolled asthma is the real fetal risk.

orig.stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman with mild persistent asthma is on inhaled corticosteroids and albuterol prn. Which statement is correct?
options: She should continue her current therapy and follow symptoms.
She should switch to inhaled tiotropium as needed.
She should switch from inhaled beclomethasone to salmeterol.
There is >70% chance her asthma will lessen in pregnancy.
There is >70% chance her asthma will worsen in pregnancy.
orig.explanation: She should continue her current therapy and follow symptoms. Inhaled steroids and short-acting B-agonists are safe and effective in pregnancy.

stem: A 34-year-old man with severe persistent asthma expectorates brown mucus plugs and has marked blood eosinophilia. Which test is indicated next?
explanation: Brown mucus plugs with eosinophilia in severe asthma suggest ABPA: total IgE (often > 1000) with Aspergillus-specific IgE first.

orig.stem: A 34-year-old man with severe persistent asthma, brown mucous plugs, and high eosinophils. Which test is indicated next?
orig.explanation: Serum immunoglobulin (Ig) E level Evaluation for ABPA requires checking total serum IgE and Aspergillus sensitivity.

stem: A known asthmatic presents to the GP complaining of gradually worsening of her symptoms. She is already taking a regular B2 agonist inhaler. What is the next most appropriate step in management?

orig.stem: A known asthmatic presents to the GP complaining of gradually worsening of her symptoms. She is already taking a regular B2 agonist inhaler. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
orig.explanation: Low-dose inhaled steroid The next step in the management plan is to add on a low- dose inhaled steroid. If this is inadequate, then a long-acting B2 agonist is added. Further escalation may involve high-dose inhaled steroids or additional therapies.

stem: A woman is admitted to hospital with acute severe asthma. Her respiratory rate is greater than 25 breaths/min and peak flow is less than 50% of her predicted value. What is the next most appropriate step in management?

orig.stem: A woman is admitted to hospital with acute severe asthma. Her respiratory rate is greater than 25 breaths/min and peak flow is less than 50% of her predicted value. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
orig.explanation: Nebulized salbutamol Nebulized salbutamol or terbutaline in addition to oral steroids are the initial treatment of acute severe asthma. Intravenous magnesium is added in life-threatening exacerbation.

stem: A 30-year-old woman known to have asthma presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of worsening breathlessness and chest tightness despite regular salbutamol inhalers. She has been suffering from an upper respiratory tract infection for the past few days. Which of the following findings on clinical examination would be an ominous sign for an impending respiratory failure in this patient?
explanation: A silent chest means almost no airflow: a life-threatening feature signalling impending respiratory failure; urgent ICU review.

orig.stem: A 30-year-old woman known to have asthma presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of worsening breathlessness and chest tightness despite regular salbutamol inhalers. She has been suffering from an upper respiratory tract infection for the past few days. Which of the following findings on clinical examination would be an ominous sign for an impending respiratory failure in this patient?
orig.explanation: Silent chest A silent chest (absence of wheezing) is an ominous sign indicating severe airway obstruction and impending respiratory failure in asthma.

stem: A 36-year-old woman with a history of moderate persistent asthma presents to the emergency department with progressive worsening of SOB, wheezing and cough over 3 days. She has been compliant with her maintenance asthma regimen, which consists of an inhaled corticosteroid and a leukotriene receptor antagonist for maintenance therapy and salbutamol as rescue therapy. Which one of the following is most consistent with a diagnosis of asthma?
options: Reduced FEV1 and reduced FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FEV1 and normal FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FEV1 and increased FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FVC and normal FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FVC and increased FEV1:FVC ratio
explanation: Asthma is obstructive: FEV1 falls more than FVC (ratio < 0.70), with reversibility. Low FVC with normal ratio means restriction.

orig.stem: A 36-year-old woman with a history of moderate persistent asthma presents to the emergency department with progressive worsening of SOB, wheezing and cough over 3 days. She has been compliant with her maintenance asthma regimen, which consists of an inhaled corticosteroid and a leukotriene receptor antagonist for maintenance therapy and salbutamol as rescue therapy. Which one of the following is most consistent with a diagnosis of asthma?
options: Reduced FEV1 and reduced FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FEV1 and normal FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FEV1 and increased FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FVC1 and normal FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FVC1 and increased FEV1:FVC ratio
orig.explanation: Reduced FEV1 and reduced FEV1:FVC ratio Asthma is typically associated with an obstructive impairment that is reversible with bronchodilators; a reduced FEV1 and FEV1:FVC ratio indicates airflow obstruction.

stem: A 28-year-old male with a long history of severe asthma presents to the emergency room with shortness of breath. He has previously required admission to the hospital and was once intubated for asthma. Which of the following findings on physical examination would predict a benign course?
explanation: Pulsus paradoxus up to 10 mmHg is normal, so 5 mmHg predicts a benign course; silent chest, hypercapnia and confusion are ominous.

orig.stem: A 28-year-old male with a long history of severe asthma presents to the emergency room with shortness of breath. He has previously required admission to the hospital and was once intubated for asthma. Which of the following findings on physical examination would predict a benign course?
orig.explanation: Pulsus paradoxus of 5 mm Hg Severe asthma red flags: silent chest, hypercapnia, thoracoabdominal paradox, AMS; these warrant ventilatory support; pulsus paradoxus 5 mmHg is normal.

stem: A 30-year-old athlete presents with intermittent wheezing that begins shortly after running. He smokes 20–40 cigarettes a day and has done so for 5 years. Which finding would be consistent with asthma?
options: Low oxygen saturation on finger oximetry
Dyspnoea on assuming a supine position
explanation: Asthma's defining feature is reversible obstruction: FEV1 rise ≥ 12% and ≥ 200 mL after bronchodilator.

stem: A 28-year-old builder attends the respiratory clinic with a 6-month history of progressive exertional breathlessness and cough. stem: A 50-year-old woman has breathlessness on exertion that has been worsening for a year, with wheeze that is worse with exercise and during the summer, when she also has severe hay fever. stem: A 25-year-old man presents with breathlessness. Lung function tests show a PEFR of 300 L/min and a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio. He is otherwise healthy, smokes five cigarettes a day and keeps a pet cat. What is the most likely diagnosis?

stem: Cough productive of sputum on most days for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years is the clinical definition of which condition?

orig.stem: Common stage of disease is one sees cough and sputum as an important feature in ? (filled with standard approach)

stem: Regarding treatment of acute exacerbation of COPD, the following are true EXCEPT:
options: When sputum is purulent, simple antibiotic regimens such as amoxicillin or a macrolide are advised
Oral prednisolone reduces symptoms but cannot improve lung function
Mechanical ventilation may be considered in those with a reversible cause for deterioration (e.g. pneumonia) or no prior history of respiratory failure
Nebulised short-acting beta2-agonists can be combined with an anticholinergic agent
explanation: Steroids in a COPD exacerbation do improve FEV1 and shorten recovery, so that statement is false; antibiotics for purulent sputum.

stem: A 66-year-old heavy smoker presents with chronic productive cough, progressive dyspnoea, pursed-lip breathing, and a barrel chest. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Chronic productive cough, dyspnoea, pursed-lip breathing and barrel chest in a heavy smoker is COPD; confirm FEV1/FVC < 0.70.

orig.stem: A 66-year-old heavy smoker presents with chronic productive cough, progressive dyspnea, pursed-lip breathing, and a barrel chest. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) The history and physical findings (smoking history, barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing) are typical for COPD.

stem: Which pulmonary function test finding is most consistent with COPD?
options: Increased diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide
Isolated reduced FVC with normal FEV1
explanation: COPD is obstructive: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70, with gas trapping (raised RV/TLC) and low DLCO in emphysema. A low TLC means restriction.

orig.stem: Which pulmonary function test finding is most consistent with COPD?
options: Increased diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide
Isolated reduced FVC with normal FEV1
orig.explanation: Reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (obstructive pattern) COPD is characterized by an obstructive pattern with a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio.

stem: A 55-year-old taxi driver has smoked 30 cigarettes a day since the age of 15 and is increasingly breathless on exertion. SpO2 is 98% on air. Examination shows tracheal tug, a reduced cricosternal distance, a barrel chest, reduced cardiac dullness and symmetrically reduced air entry. The chest X-ray shows hyperinflation and spirometry shows moderate airflow obstruction. He walks 300 m on an incremental shuttle walk test before becoming breathless, and his saturations are maintained. Which pathological change best explains why he is breathless on exertion?
explanation: Emphysema destroys elastin; loss of elastic recoil collapses small airways in expiration, causing dynamic hyperinflation on exertion.

orig.stem: A 55 year old man has smoked 30 cigarettes per day since he was 15 years old. He is a taxi driver. He finds he is increasingly breathless on exertion. Oxygen saturations are 98% on room air. Examination reveals tracheal tug, reduced cricosternal distance and a barrel chest. He has reduced cardiac dullness and symmetrically reduced air entry. CXR reveals hyperinflation and spirometry reveals moderate airways obstruction. The patient walks 300 m on an incremental walk test before becoming breathless; oxygen saturations are maintained. What pathological change best explains why he is breathless on exertion?
orig.explanation: Loss of elastic recoil Loss of elastin fibers in COPD cause dynamic hyperinflation on exertion.

stem: A 67-year-old woman, an ex-smoker, has progressive exertional breathlessness. Spirometry is normal (FEV1/FVC 0.74), but gas transfer (TLCO) is reduced to 55% of predicted. A CT scan of her chest is shown. What is the most likely cause of her breathlessness?
explanation: Upper-lobe low-attenuation areas without walls are centrilobular emphysema; it can cause breathlessness and low TLCO before spirometry changes.

orig.stem: A 67 year old ex-smoker woman with progressive exertional breathlessness, normal spirometry but CT showing emphysema is evaluated. What is the most likely cause of her breathlessness?

stem: A 65 year old man with known COPD and mild obstruction presents with increasing exertional breathlessness despite LAMA and SABA. He does not desaturate on walk test. What is a reasonable addition to escalate therapy?
explanation: Persistent breathlessness on a LAMA: escalate to LABA + LAMA (GOLD 2025). ICS only with exacerbations and eosinophils ≥ 300/µL.

orig.stem: A 65 year old man with known COPD and mild obstruction presents with increasing exertional breathlessness despite LAMA and SABA. He does not desaturate on walk test. What is a reasonable addition to escalate therapy?

explanation: Asbestosis is interstitial fibrosis causing restriction; asthma, bronchiectasis, chronic bronchitis and emphysema are obstructive.

stem: A 69-year-old man, an ex-smoker with COPD (FEV1 45% of predicted), has had three exacerbations in the past year despite good adherence and inhaler technique on triple therapy (LAMA/LABA/ICS) and completion of pulmonary rehabilitation. Resting SpO2 is 94% on air, PaCO2 is normal and his ECG shows a normal QT interval. Which treatment is most likely to reduce the frequency of his exacerbations?
explanation: Frequent exacerbator despite optimal inhalers: azithromycin 250 mg three times weekly (check ECG, LFTs, hearing). Roflumilast is the alternative.

orig.stem: A 69-year-old man with COPD has frequent exacerbations. Which treatment decreases exacerbation frequency?
orig.explanation: “Signet ring” sign. The signet ring sign is highly characteristic of bronchiectasis.

stem: All of the following are risk factors for COPD EXCEPT:
options: Use of biomass fuels in poorly ventilated areas
explanation: Smoking, occupational dust and biomass smoke cause COPD; adult respiratory infections trigger exacerbations but are not proven causes.

stem: A 65-year-old woman is suspected of COPD. What are the expected PFT findings?
options: Increased FEV1/FVC ratio, decreased TLC, decreased DLCO
Decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, increased TLC, increased RV, decreased DLCO
Normal FEV1/FVC ratio, decreased TLC, normal DLCO
Normal lung volumes, normal DLCO, normal FEV1/FVC ratio
Decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, normal TLC, increased DLCO
explanation: COPD is obstructive: FEV1 falls more than FVC, so the FEV1/FVC ratio is below 0.70. Loss of elastic recoil and airway collapse cause gas trapping (raised RV) and hyperinflation (raised TLC), and emphysematous alveolar destruction lowers DLCO. A reduced TLC with a normal or high ratio indicates restriction, a raised DLCO suggests alveolar haemorrhage, polycythaemia or asthma, and normal results would not fit symptomatic COPD. A low ratio with a normal or raised DLCO suggests asthma.

orig.stem: A 65-year-old woman is suspected of COPD. What are the expected PFT findings?
options: Increased FEV1/FVC ratio, decreased TLC, decreased DLCO
Decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, increased TLC, increased RV, decreased DLCO

Normal lung volumes, normal DLCO, normal FEV1/FVC ratio

orig.explanation: Decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, increased TLC, increased RV, decreased DLCO COPD is characterized by airflow obstruction with hyperinflation and air trapping.

stem: A 70-year-old man with moderate COPD on albuterol only. Next best step in management?
