She was initially complaining of pain in her right hip and ribs but has become increasingly drowsy since the paramedics administered 2 mg of morphine. She is brought to the emergency department by ambulance. Urgent X-rays reveal a pelvic fracture, and a single right-sided rib fracture. Having, initially been drowsy but responsive she is now unresponsive. Oxygen saturations are 87% on 2 L/min oxygen via nasal cannulae. She is apyrexial. BP is 110/66 mmHg, pulse is 65 beats/min. There are no new findings on examination. An urgent CT brain reveals only small vessel disease. Arterial blood gas: H+ 60 nmol/L (pH 7.22), PaO2 8.7 kPa (65 mmHg), PaCO2 10 kPa (75 mmHg), HCO3- 26 mmol/L. What is the most likely cause of her deteriorating conscious level?
options: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with oxygen toxicity – loss of hypoxic drive
Flail segment due to rib fracture – loss of elastic recoil
Opiate toxicity – suppression of the respiratory centre
Undetected fracture of C3 – diaphragmatic failure
orig.explanation: Undetected fracture of C3 – diaphragmatic failure A fracture at C3 can paralyse the diaphragm leading to type II respiratory failure with a normal A–a gradient.

stem: In which of the following conditions might acute type I respiratory failure be expected?
explanation: Lobar collapse causes a shunt with normal/low PaCO2 (type 1). Flail chest, OSA, myasthenia and opioids cause hypoventilation (type 2).

orig.stem: In which of the following conditions might acute type I respiratory failure be expected?
orig.explanation: Pneumothorax Increased resonance and reduced expansion suggest pneumothorax.

stem: A 25-year-old man is brought in unresponsive. Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.16, PaCO2 9.3 kPa (70 mmHg), PaO2 7.3 kPa (55 mmHg). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Acute respiratory acidosis with a normal A–a gradient (~7 mmHg) means pure hypoventilation, e.g. opioid overdose: give naloxone.

orig.stem: A 25-year-old man is brought in unresponsive with pH 7.16, PCO2 70 mmHg, and PO2 55 mmHg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Empyema The D-shaped opacity and clinical presentation are typical of an empyema requiring drainage.

stem: A patient with mild amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (motor neurone disease) has a PaCO2 of ≥6 kPa (45 mmHg). Which accompanying symptom is an indication for non-invasive ventilation?
options: Breathlessness on activities of daily living
explanation: In MND, NIV is offered when symptoms of hypoventilation (orthopnoea, poor sleep, morning headache, breathlessness) accompany hypercapnia.

orig.stem: A patient with mild ALS has PaCO2≥45 mmHg plus which symptom indicates NIV therapy?
orig.explanation: All of the above Any symptom of hypoventilation with hypercapnia warrants noninvasive ventilation.

stem: A 70-year-old patient with chronic obstructive lung disease requires 2 L/min of nasal O2 to treat his hypoxia, which is sometimes associated with angina. The patient develops pleuritic chest pain, fever, and purulent sputum. While using his oxygen at an increased flow of 5 L/min he becomes stuporous and develops a respiratory acidosis with CO2 retention and worsening hypoxia. What would be the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: Observe for 24 hours before changing therapy
explanation: High-flow oxygen caused CO2 narcosis; stuporous with acidosis and worsening hypoxia, he cannot protect his airway: intubate and ventilate.

orig.stem: A 70-year-old patient with chronic obstructive lung disease requires 2 L/min of nasal O2 to treat his hypoxia, which is sometimes associated with angina. The patient develops pleuritic chest pain, fever, and purulent sputum. While using his oxygen at an increased flow of 5 L/min he becomes stuporous and develops a respiratory acidosis with CO2 retention and worsening hypoxia. What would be the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: Observe patient 24 hours before changing therapy.
orig.explanation: Intubate and begin mechanical ventilation. Severe COPD with CO₂ narcosis after high O₂ → acute ventilatory failure; treat with ventilation (consider NIV if alert); bicarbonate not indicated.

stem: The following can cause exudative pleural effusion EXCEPT:

orig.stem: The following can cause exudative pleural effusion EXCEPT:
orig.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome. Nephrotic syndrome typically causes a transudative effusion.

stem: The following can cause exudative pleural effusion EXCEPT: A) Pulmonary infarction. B) Malignancies. C) Para-pneumonic effusion. D) Liver cirrhosis.

orig.stem: The following can cause exudative pleural effusion EXCEPT: A) Pulmonary infarction. B) Malignancies. C) Para-pneumonic effusion. D) Liver cirrhosis.
orig.explanation: Liver cirrhosis. Liver cirrhosis is typically associated with transudative pleural effusion.

stem: A 21-year-old high-jumper presents with acute-onset breathlessness and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Examination reveals increased percussion resonance and reduced expansion on the right side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sudden pleuritic pain in a tall young athlete with hyper-resonance and reduced expansion is primary spontaneous pneumothorax.

orig.stem: A 21-year-old high-jumper presents with acute-onset dyspnoea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Examination reveals increased resonance and reduced expansion on the right side.
orig.explanation: Hyper-resonance, decreased breath sounds in the left chest with trachea deviation to right PTX → hyperresonance, ↓breath sounds, ↓fremitus; tension shifts mediastinum away; rales/ wheeze suggest alternate pathology.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents with a 1-week history of fever, left-sided pleuritic chest pain and increasing shortness of breath. He has a history of alcohol dependency, alcoholic liver disease and chronic pancreatitis. He has smoked 10 cigarettes per day for 30 years and still drinks 28 units a week. In his 20s he worked as a labourer on building sites where asbestos was removed. His chest X-ray is shown. What is the most likely cause of the abnormality?
explanation: A large left effusion with a week of fever and pleuritic pain in a heavy drinker is most likely empyema; aspirate urgently.

orig.stem: A 52 year old man presents with a 1-week history of fever, left-sided pleuritic chest pain and increasing shortness of breath. He has a past history of alcohol dependency, alcoholic liver disease and chronic pancreatitis. He has smoked 10 cigarettes per day for 30 years and still drinks 28 units a week. He worked as a casual labourer on building sites where asbestos was removed in his 20s. What is most likely to be causing the CXR shown below?
orig.explanation: Stop smoking After spontaneous pneumothorax: stop smoking; fitness-to-fly typically 1–2 weeks post-resolution with clear CXR and no residual air.

stem: A 71 year old man presents with increasing breathlessness with no cough or systemic symptoms. He has atrial fibrillation and a recent echocardiogram with preserved LV function. What does his CXR show?
options: Right middle and lower lobe collapse
explanation: Homogeneous lower-zone opacity with a meniscus and lost costophrenic angle is a pleural effusion; unilateral with normal LV needs investigation.

orig.stem: A 71 year old man presents with increasing breathlessness with no cough or systemic symptoms. He has atrial fibrillation and a recent echocardiogram with preserved LV function. What does his CXR show?
options: Right middle and lower lobe collapse
orig.explanation: Right-sided pleural effusion The CXR demonstrates a homogenous right-sided opacification with a meniscus sign, typical of a pleural effusion.

stem: A 71-year-old man with atrial fibrillation on apixaban presents with increasing breathlessness but no cough or systemic symptoms. A recent echocardiogram showed preserved left ventricular function. His chest X-ray shows a moderate right-sided pleural effusion. What is the best next step in his management?
options: Bedside thoracic ultrasound and pleural aspiration
Thoracic ultrasound scan-guided intercostal chest drain
explanation: Unilateral effusion with normal LV function: bedside ultrasound and diagnostic aspiration; no need to stop apixaban (BTS 2023).

orig.stem: For the patient described in Question 17.11, what would be the best next step in his management?
options: Bedside thoracic ultrasound and pleural aspiration
Thoracic ultrasound scan-guided intercostal chest drain
orig.explanation: Stop apixaban The isolated effusion in a patient on apixaban requires cautious intervention; stopping the anticoagulant is necessary before aspiration.

stem: A 35 year old man has been unwell for a week with fever, productive cough, rhinitis and aching muscles. He now presents with left-sided pleuritic chest pain. His CXR is shown. What is shown on the CXR?
explanation: A visible pleural edge with no markings beyond and a hyperlucent hemithorax is a left pneumothorax.

orig.stem: A 35 year old man has been unwell for a week with fever, productive cough, rhinitis and aching muscles. He now presents with left-sided pleuritic chest pain. His CXR is shown. What is shown on the CXR?
orig.explanation: Ambulatory device Symptomatic primary pneumothorax without high-risk features → options: conservative care, needle aspiration, or ambulatory one-way valve device.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents with progressive shortness of breath over a week, new central chest discomfort and a productive cough. He is a heavy cannabis smoker with no significant past medical history. His chest X-ray (shown) shows large lucent upper-zone areas without lung markings, and it is unclear whether these are bullae or a pneumothorax. What is the next step in his management?
explanation: In a cannabis smoker, a large bulla can mimic pneumothorax; CT distinguishes them before any drain (risk of bronchopleural fistula).

orig.stem: A 29 year old man presents with progressive shortness of breath over a week, new central chest discomfort, and a productive cough. He is a cannabis smoker with no significant past medical history. His CXR is shown. What would be the next step in his management?
orig.explanation: B Chest drain insertion initially COPD with symptomatic pneumothorax, rim >2 cm → initial chest drain (no aspiration) per BTS.

stem: A 75 year old man with asbestos exposure presents with a large right-sided pleural effusion. Pleural aspiration is exudative but cytology is negative and CT shows circumferential pleural thickening. Which test is most likely to give a diagnosis?
explanation: Asbestos, cytology-negative exudate and circumferential thickening suggest mesothelioma; thoracoscopic biopsy (yield > 90%).

orig.stem: A 75 year old man with asbestos exposure presents with a large right-sided pleural effusion. Pleural aspiration is exudative but cytology is negative and CT shows circumferential pleural thickening. Which test is most likely to give a diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Thoracoscopy Direct visualisation and biopsy of pleural lesions via thoracoscopy is the gold standard.

stem: Which of the following is a cause of a transudative pleural effusion?
explanation: Hypothyroidism can cause a transudate; infarction, RA, TB and drugs cause exudates.

orig.stem: Which of the following is a cause of a transudative pleural effusion?
orig.explanation: Hypothyroidism Hypothyroidism can cause a transudative effusion.

stem: Which one of the following statements is true regarding Light’s criteria?
options: Pleural fluid LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH
Pleural fluid LDH < two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH
explanation: Light's exudate criteria: protein ratio > 0.5, LDH ratio > 0.6, or fluid LDH > 2/3 of the upper limit of serum LDH.

orig.stem: Which one of the following statements is true regarding Light’s criteria?
options: Pleural fluid LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH
Pleural fluid LDH < two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH
orig.explanation: Pleural fluid LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH Light’s criteria use thresholds of protein and LDH ratios to define an exudate.

stem: A 64 year old man presents with fever, sweats, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. He is an ex-smoker with a history of alcohol excess. Pleural fluid aspiration under ultrasound guidance is performed. Which value might be expected?
explanation: A septated effusion with fever means complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema: pH < 7.2 (here 6.9) with low glucose and high LDH.

orig.stem: A 64 year old man presents with fever, sweats, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. He is an ex-smoker with a history of alcohol excess. Pleural fluid aspiration under ultrasound guidance is performed. Which value might be expected?
orig.explanation: Pleural fluid pH 6.9 (H+ 126 nmol/L) The low pH with high LDH and protein is typical for empyema.

stem: A 34 year old man presents with acute-onset shortness of breath and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Examination reveals O2 saturations of 94% on room air and a hyper-resonant left chest. CXR shows a large left-sided pneumothorax. Therapeutic aspiration of 2.5 L of air is performed with no radiographic improvement. What should be the next step?
explanation: If needle aspiration fails to re-expand the lung, insert a chest drain (or ambulatory device); stop aspiration at 2.5 L.

orig.stem: A 34 year old man presents with acute-onset shortness of breath and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Examination reveals O2 saturations of 94% on room air and a hyper-resonant left chest. CXR shows a large left-sided pneumothorax. Therapeutic aspiration of 2.5 L of air is performed with no radiographic improvement. What should be the next step?
orig.explanation: Decreased TLC, decreased VC, decreased RV, increased FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP IPF is a restrictive disease with reduced lung volumes, but normal muscle strength, increasing the FEV1/FVC ratio.

stem: A 53-year-old man with pneumonia is found to have gross pus in the pleural space (empyema), and a chest tube is placed along with intravenous antibiotics. Which additional treatment improves pleural drainage and reduces the need for surgery?
explanation: In poorly draining pleural infection, intrapleural alteplase plus DNase improves drainage and reduces surgery (MIST-2).

orig.stem: A 53-year-old with pneumonia, gross pus in the pleural space (empyema). A large-bore chest tube is placed. What else helps?
orig.explanation: Intrapleural instillation of alteplase plus DNase Combination therapy improves drainage in empyema.

stem: A 44-year-old man on mechanical ventilation suddenly becomes hypotensive. The peak airway pressure has risen to 55 cmH2O and breath sounds are absent on the right. What is the next step?
options: Needle decompression of the right chest
explanation: Sudden hypotension, high airway pressure and absent breath sounds in a ventilated patient is tension pneumothorax: needle decompression.

orig.stem: A 44-year-old on mechanical ventilation has sudden hypotension, peak airway pressure 55, absent right breath sounds. Next step?
options: Needle decompression of the right chest
orig.explanation: Place a large-bore needle into the right second anterior intercostal space to alleviate a tension pneumothorax. High airway pressures, absent breath sounds, and hypotension indicate tension pneumothorax.

stem: A 62-year-old man with pneumonia has a pleural effusion. Which finding does NOT indicate a complicated parapneumonic effusion?
options: Positive pleural fluid Gram stain or culture
Reaccumulation of fluid after the initial thoracentesis
explanation: Complicated parapneumonic effusion: loculation, pus, positive Gram stain/culture, pH < 7.2 or glucose < 3.3 mmol/L. Reaccumulation alone is not one.

orig.stem: A 62-year-old with pneumonia and a pleural effusion. Which finding does NOT indicate a complicated effusion?
options: Recurrence of fluid after initial thoracentesis
orig.explanation: Recurrence of fluid following the initial thoracentesis Recurrence alone does not indicate complexity if pH, glucose, and loculation are not present.

stem: A patient has a moderate right-sided pleural effusion. The pleural fluid analysis is shown. Which of the following is NOT a likely cause of this effusion?
explanation: The fluid is a lymphocytic exudate (protein ratio 0.8, LDH ratio 0.89); cirrhosis causes a transudate, so it is not the cause.

orig.stem: A moderate right-sided pleural effusion is exudative. Which is NOT likely a cause of this pleural fluid?
orig.explanation: B Interstitial lung disease Systemic sclerosis may present first with lung disease; bibasal fine crackles; HRCT shows interstitial changes almost universally.

stem: A 28-year-old tall, thin man who smokes has a small right-sided primary spontaneous pneumothorax. Which statement is true?
options: Smoking does not affect his risk of recurrence
If it recurs, VATS pleurectomy or pleural abrasion reduces the recurrence rate to about 1–5%
Most patients need tube thoracostomy for the pneumothorax to resolve
The recurrence rate after a first episode is less than 5%
He can fly safely 24 hours after the pneumothorax resolves on X-ray
explanation: Recurrent primary pneumothorax is treated by VATS pleurectomy/abrasion (recurrence 1–5%); stopping smoking cuts recurrence.

orig.stem: A 28-year-old tall, thin male smoker has a 20% spontaneous pneumothorax on the right. Which statement is true?
options: CT scan is likely to show emphysematous changes.
If recurrent, thoracoscopy with pleural abrasion nearly 100% prevents recurrence.
Most patients need tube thoracostomy to resolve it.
Tall, thin habitus is the primary risk factor.
orig.explanation: If the patient were to develop recurrent pneumothoraces, thoracoscopy with pleural abrasion has a near 100% success rate for prevention of recurrence. Video-assisted thoracoscopic pleurodesis is highly effective in preventing recurrences.

stem: With regard to pleural fluid, which of the following is most important in determining whether an effusion is a transudate or exudate?
explanation: Protein separates transudate from exudate (ratio > 0.5, or > 35 g/L); Light's criteria are used when protein is 25–35 g/L.

orig.stem: With regard to pleural fluid, which of the following is most important in determining whether an effusion is a transudate or exudate?
orig.explanation: Protein levels Transudative effusions have low protein/albumin levels compared with exudative effusions, as determined by Light’s criteria.

stem: Which of the following typically causes a transudative pleural effusion?

orig.stem: Which of the following typically causes a transudative pleural effusion?
orig.explanation: Heart failure Heart failure is a common cause of transudative pleural effusions due to increased hydrostatic pressure.

stem: You are called to review a 70-year-old man admitted with pneumococcal pneumonia who has become more unwell, with swinging fevers, worsening breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. His inflammatory markers are rising and a repeat chest X-ray shows a new right-sided pleural effusion. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic investigation?
options: Recheck the sputum for resistant organisms
explanation: A new effusion with ongoing sepsis during pneumonia: ultrasound-guided diagnostic tap; pH < 7.2 or pus means a drain.

orig.stem: You are called to review a 70-year-old man admitted for treatment of pneumococcal pneumonia, who has become more unwell with swinging fevers, worsening breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. His inflammatory markers are rising and a repeat CXR shows a new right-sided pleural effusion. What is the next most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
options: Recheck the sputum for resistant organisms
orig.explanation: Ultrasound-guided diagnostic pleural tap Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis is diagnostic, as it yields pleural fluid for culture, Gram stain, and analysis, and reduces complications.

stem: A 76-year-old man with COPD is admitted to the emergency department with acute-on-chronic breathlessness and has a chest drain inserted for a pneumothorax. Which of the following is true of chest drain management?
options: He should have his drain clamped if he has to travel to the radiology department without a medical escort
The drain should only be removed when it has stopped bubbling
The drain may be clamped if it only bubbles on coughing
The drain should only be removed when it has stopped swinging
Pain relief is usually not necessary in the first few days after insertion
explanation: Remove a pneumothorax drain only when bubbling has stopped and the lung is re-expanded; never clamp a bubbling drain.

orig.stem: A 76-year-old man with COPD was admitted to accident and emergency department with acute on chronic SOB. He has a chest drain inserted for a pneumothorax. Which of the following is true of chest drain management?
options: He should have his drain clamped if he has to travel to the radiology department without a medical escort.
The drain should only be removed when it has stopped bubbling.
The drain may be clamped if it only bubbles on coughing.
The drain should only be removed when it has stopped swinging.
Pain relief is usually not necessary in the first few days after insertion.
orig.explanation: The drain should only be removed when it has stopped bubbling. The drain can only be removed when bubbling in the underwater seal has ceased, indicating resolution of the air leak.

stem: A 76-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit for intravenous potassium replacement. A central venous line is inserted via the subclavian vein, and during the procedure he becomes acutely breathless with falling oxygen saturation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: The guidewire has entered the right ventricle
His chronic obstructive airways disease has been exacerbated
A myocardial infarction has been induced
explanation: Sudden breathlessness and desaturation during subclavian line insertion is iatrogenic pneumothorax; urgent CXR.

orig.stem: A 76-year-old man is admitted to intensive care unit (ICU) for potassium replacement. A central venous line is inserted via the subclavian vein. During the procedure he becomes acutely breathless with decreasing oxygen saturation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: The wire has threaded into the left ventricle
His chronic obstructive airways disease has been exacerbated
A myocardial infarction has been induced
orig.explanation: A pneumothorax has been created Pneumothorax is a known complication of subclavian vein cannulation due to inadvertent lung puncture.

stem: A 58-year-old man with longstanding emphysema presents to the emergency department with sudden breathlessness and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. He is hypoxic, tachypnoeic, hypotensive and tachycardic. His trachea is deviated to the right and breath sounds are markedly reduced on the left. What is the next step in management?
options: Insert a large-bore cannula into the left second intercostal space
Insert a left-sided chest drain with suction
explanation: Hypotension and tracheal deviation away from a silent hemithorax is tension pneumothorax: immediate large-bore cannula decompression.

orig.stem: A 58-year-old man with longstanding emphysema presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of breathlessness and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. On arrival, he is hypoxic, tachypnoeic, hypotensive and tachycardic. His trachea is deviated to the right and breath sounds are markedly reduced on the left side of his chest. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
options: Insert large bore cannula into the left second intercostal space
Insert chest drain with negative suction on the left side
orig.explanation: Insert large bore cannula into the left second intercostal space The clinical picture is suggestive of a tension pneumothorax, which is an emergency treated with immediate needle decompression in the second intercostal space.

stem: A 40-year-old nonsmoker presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset breathlessness and left-sided chest pain. On examination, he is unable to complete sentences and has low oxygen saturation levels. He has diminished breath sounds on the left side with tracheal deviation towards the right. Heart sounds are normal. What is the most likely explanation for these findings?

orig.explanation: Pneumothorax Unilateral diminished breath sounds with tracheal deviation strongly indicate a pneumothorax.

stem: A 66-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of progressive shortness of breath and sharp right-sided chest pain that is worse on deep inspiration. She also has mild pain in the right leg. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are unremarkable; heart rate is 96/min and respiratory rate 12/min. She denies weight loss or long-haul flights but had a nasal polypectomy 3 weeks ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pleuritic pain and breathlessness with calf pain 3 weeks after surgery is PE: Wells score, CTPA and anticoagulate meanwhile.

orig.stem: A 66-year-old woman presents to accident and emergency with a 2-day history of shortness of breath. The patient notes becoming progressively short of breath as well as a sharp pain in the right side of the chest which is most painful when taking a deep breath. The patient also complains of mild pain in the right leg, though there is nothing significant on full cardiovascular and respiratory examination. Heart rate is 96 and respiratory rate is 12. The patient denies any weight loss or long haul flights but mentions undergoing a nasal polypectomy 3 weeks ago. The most likely diagnosis is:
orig.explanation: Pulmonary embolism Pulmonary embolism is most likely given the acute onset of pleuritic chest pain with associated leg pain and recent surgery; other options are less consistent with the clinical findings.

stem: A patient with low-grade fever and weight loss has poor excursion on the right side of the chest with decreased fremitus, flatness to percussion, and decreased breath sounds all on the right. The trachea is deviated to the left. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Stony dullness, reduced breath sounds and fremitus with the trachea pushed away is a large effusion (TB or malignancy here).

orig.stem: A patient with low-grade fever and weight loss has poor excursion on the right side of the chest with decreased fremitus, flatness to percussion, and decreased breath sounds all on the right. The trachea is deviated to the left. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Pleural effusion Poor excursion + dullness + ↓fremitus on right with contralateral tracheal shift → large right pleural effusion; not PTX (hyperresonant) or consolidation (↑fremitus).

explanation: All Light's criteria negative (protein 0.38, LDH 0.46, LDH < 127): a transudate, most commonly heart failure.

stem: A 50-year-old male with emphysema develops the sudden onset of shortness of breath and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Pneumothorax is suspected. Which of the following physical examination findings would be consistent with the diagnosis?

Hyper-resonance, decreased breath sounds in the left chest with trachea deviation to right

Decreased breath sounds on the left side with deviation of the trachea to the left
explanation: Pneumothorax: hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds on the affected side, with a large one pushing the trachea away.

stem: A 29-year-old man is admitted with sudden onset dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain. He is a smoker but has no history of respiratory disease. He considers himself healthy and regularly plays rugby. On admission he has a chest x-ray that shows a pneumothorax with a 3cm rim of air. Aspiration is successful and he is discharged. A follow-up chest x-ray two weeks later shows a complete resolution. What is the single most important piece of advice to reduce his risk of further pneumothoraces?
options: Arrange a course of respiratory physiotherapy
Seek prompt medical advice for potential respiratory infections
explanation: Smoking (including cannabis) is the main modifiable risk for pneumothorax recurrence: advise stopping.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is referred to ambulatory care with a 3-month history of increasing breathlessness. She has no significant respiratory history. On examination her observations are normal, with reduced air entry at the right base. Chest X-ray shows a large right-sided pleural effusion. Pleural aspiration results: pleural fluid protein 34 g/L (serum protein 61 g/L); white cell count 2500 cells/μL, predominantly lymphocytes; no organisms on microscopy; no growth on culture after 48 hours. What is the most likely cause of this effusion?
explanation: A lymphocytic sterile exudate with a 3-month history in an older woman suggests malignancy (lung cancer); cytology and CT.

orig.stem: A 72-year-old woman is referred to ambulatory care with a 3-month history of increasing breathlessness. She has no significant respiratory past medical history. On examination, observations are normal but there is decreased air entry to the right lung base. A chest x-ray confirms a large right-sided pleural effusion. The results of the pleural aspirate are shown below: Pleural fluid protein 134 g/L; Serum protein 61 g/L (60 - 80); White cell count 13,000 cells/ μL (< 1000); Microscopy No organisms seen; Culture No growth on routine culture after 48 hours. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s pleural effusion?
orig.explanation: Lung cancer Exudative pleural effusion with high protein and negative cultures in older adult → malignancy most likely (lung cancer common).

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath that began at the start of her menstrual period. A similar but milder episode occurred during her last period and resolved. The pain now radiates to her shoulder. She has two children, the second delivered by emergency caesarean section. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation: Recurrent right pneumothorax within 72 h of menstruation is catamenial pneumothorax from thoracic endometriosis.

orig.stem: A 35-year-old married woman presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath associated with the start of her menstrual period. This occurred during her last menstrual period but resolved. Now the pain is more severe with some radiation to her shoulder. She has two young children; first born via spontaneous vaginal delivery and the other by emergency caesarean section. What is the likely cause of the patient’s symptoms?
orig.explanation: Catamenial pneumothorax Catamenial pneumothorax: cyclical, right-sided, around menses due to thoracic endometriosis.

stem: A 32-year-old man with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset left-sided chest pain and breathlessness. There is no trauma or recent infection. Respiratory rate 21/min, SpO2 96% on air, BP 124/78 mmHg, heart rate 88/min, apyrexial. The trachea is central; the left side of the chest is hyper-resonant with reduced breath sounds. Chest X-ray shows a 2.5 cm apical rim of air. His pain and breathlessness are troubling him and he wants the air treated, but he strongly wishes to avoid hospital admission. What is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation: Symptomatic primary pneumothorax without high-risk features, wishing to avoid admission: ambulatory valve device (BTS 2023).

orig.stem: A 32-year-old man with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset left-sided chest pain. He denies any trauma or recent respiratory infections. His observations are as follows: respiratory rate 21 /min, sats 96% on room air, BP 124/78 mmHg, heart rate 88 bpm, and he is apyrexial. On examination, his trachea is central, the chest on the left side is hyper-resonant on percussion and there is reduced breath sound. The right side of the chest is normal. A chest x-ray reveals a 2.5cm apical rim of air. What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
orig.explanation: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis The HRCT features are classical for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

stem: A 70-year-old man with moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) attends the Emergency Department with increasing dyspnoea. He has been found to have a 3-cm pneumothorax. What would be the optimal management for this patient?
options: Chest drain insertion if needle aspiration fails
Conservative management, with observation and repeat chest X-ray after 4 hours
Conservative management, with observation and repeat chest X-ray after 12 hours
explanation: Secondary pneumothorax in COPD is high-risk; symptomatic or > 2 cm needs admission and a chest drain.

stem: A 43-year-old woman has a pleural effusion together with arthralgia and a photosensitive rash that has worsened after sun exposure over the past few months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Photosensitive rash, arthralgia and pleural effusion suggest SLE serositis; check ANA, anti-dsDNA and complement.

A few minutes later she becomes cyanosed and hypotensive; her trachea is deviated to the right and the left hemithorax is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Pneumothorax with cyanosis, hypotension and tracheal deviation away is tension pneumothorax: needle decompression then drain.

orig.explanation: E Tension pneumothorax Tension pneumothorax: rising intrapleural pressure with one-way air entry → rapid decompensation; immediate needle decompression then chest tube.

stem: Which of the following is not typically associated with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
explanation: IPF gives tachypnoea, crackles, clubbing and cyanosis; tremor and hyperreflexia are unrelated neurological signs.

orig.stem: Which of the following is not typically associated with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
orig.explanation: Tremor or hyperreflexia Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis commonly presents with tachypnea, fine crackles, clubbing, and may cause some shift; tremor or hyperreflexia is not typical.

stem: A 73-year-old woman has a 1-year history of progressive exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. She has finger clubbing and bibasal crackles. Her CT chest is shown. What is the most likely cause of the CT appearance?
explanation: Subpleural reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis on CT is a UIP pattern: IPF.

orig.stem: A 73 year old woman with a 1-year history of progressive exertional breathlessness and a dry cough, finger clubbing and bi-basal crackles is imaged with CT. What is the likely cause of the CT appearance?
orig.explanation: Extrinsic allergic alveolitis Upper-zone fibrosis + bird exposure → EAA (hypersensitivity pneumonitis); asbestosis, RA, nitrofurantoin usually lower-lobe.

stem: A 71-year-old man presents with increasing breathlessness. He has no relevant occupational or drug exposures and no features of connective tissue disease. HRCT shows bilateral subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis. Which statement about confirming the diagnosis is correct?
options: A typical CT appearance is sufficient for diagnosis
Blind transbronchial needle aspiration would likely give the diagnosis
Bronchoscopy with cytopathological analysis of washings would help
Endobronchial ultrasound of his subcarinal node would exclude more diffuse disease
Transbronchial lung biopsy would give a tissue diagnosis
explanation: A typical UIP pattern on HRCT in the right context is sufficient to diagnose IPF after MDT discussion (ATS/ERS 2022); no biopsy needed.

orig.stem: A 71 year old man presents with increasing breathlessness without cough. CT chest reveals bilateral diffuse fibrotic change with basal honeycombing. What does his CXR show?

orig.explanation: A typical CT appearance is sufficient for diagnosis A characteristic CT pattern in IPF permits diagnosis without biopsy in the appropriate clinical context.

explanation: FEV1/FVC 0.84 with normal volumes excludes obstruction and restriction; an isolated low TLCO needs Hb, HRCT and echo.

stem: A 79 year old woman with progressive exertional breathlessness, bilateral fine basal crackles and clubbing has an HRCT showing bilateral basal peripheral reticulation with honeycomb cysts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Basal, peripheral reticulation with honeycomb cysts is the usual interstitial pneumonia pattern, which in an older patient with clubbing and no alternative cause means IPF. Non-specific interstitial pneumonia gives more uniform ground-glass with fine reticulation, often with subpleural sparing and little honeycombing, in younger patients often with connective tissue disease. Acute interstitial pneumonia is a rapidly progressive ARDS-like illness; lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia causes ground-glass with thin-walled cysts (Sjögren's syndrome, HIV); fibrotic sarcoidosis is upper-zone and perihilar.

orig.stem: A 79 year old woman with progressive exertional breathlessness, bilateral fine basal crackles and clubbing has an HRCT showing bilateral basal peripheral reticulation with honeycomb cysts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Spontaneous resolution Sarcoidosis with Löfgren syndrome → good prognosis; many resolve without treatment; relapses less common.

stem: Respiratory bronchiolitis–interstitial lung disease (RBILD) is more common in which group?
explanation: RB-ILD is a smoking-related ILD of current heavy smokers; smoking cessation is the key treatment.

orig.stem: Respiratory bronchiolitis–interstitial lung disease (RBILD) is more common in which group?
orig.explanation: Monitoring Sarcoidosis often remits without therapy in the majority of patients.

stem: A 55 year old man with a 2-year history of increasing breathlessness and dry cough, with restrictive PFTs and HRCT showing bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, bronchovascular nodules and extensive fibrosis is evaluated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Scadding stage IV sarcoidosis is established fibrosis, even if hilar nodes remain; stage I (BHL alone) usually resolves.

orig.stem: A 55 year old man with a 2-year history of increasing breathlessness and dry cough, with restrictive PFTs and HRCT showing bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, bronchovascular nodules and extensive fibrosis is evaluated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Sarcoidosis stage IV The presence of extensive fibrosis with lymph node enlargement indicates end-stage (stage IV) sarcoidosis.

stem: A 26 year old non-smoking woman presents for the second time with pneumothorax. CT identifies multiple lung cysts and an upper pole abnormality of the right kidney. What diagnosis should be considered?
explanation: Recurrent pneumothorax with diffuse thin-walled cysts and a renal angiomyolipoma in a young woman is LAM; VEGF-D, sirolimus.

orig.stem: A 26 year old non-smoking woman presents for the second time with pneumothorax. CT identifies multiple lung cysts and an upper pole abnormality of the right kidney. What diagnosis should be considered?
orig.explanation: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis The combination of recurrent pneumothorax, cystic lung changes and a renal lesion is characteristic of LAM.

stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding progressive massive fibrosis (PMF)?
options: Finger clubbing and basal crackles are characteristic
It has no impact on lung function
It may progress even after exposure ceases
explanation: Progressive massive fibrosis (complicated CWP/silicosis) forms upper-zone conglomerate masses and can progress after exposure stops.

orig.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding progressive massive fibrosis (PMF)?
options: Finger clubbing and basal crackles are characteristic
It has no impact on lung function
It may progress even after exposure ceases
orig.explanation: It may progress even after exposure ceas es PMF may progress and lead to respiratory failure despite removal from exposure.

stem: A 41 year old stonemason with shortness of breath is found to have silicosis on imaging. Silicosis results from the inhalation of which substance?
explanation: Silicosis is caused by respirable crystalline silica (quartz) in stonemasonry, quarrying and sandblasting.

orig.stem: A 41 year old stonemason with shortness of breath is found to have silicosis on imaging. Silicosis results from the inhalation of which substance?
orig.explanation: Quartz Silicosis is caused by inhalation of crystalline silica (quartz).

stem: Which of the following pulmonary function test results is consistent with Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
options: Increased TLC, decreased vital capacity, decreased FEV1/FVC ratio
Decreased TLC, decreased VC, decreased RV, increased FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
Decreased TLC, increased RV, normal FEV1/FVC ratio, decreased MIP
Normal TLC, normal RV, normal FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
Normal TLC, decreased VC, increased RV, decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
explanation: IPF: all lung volumes fall (TLC, VC, RV) with a high FEV1/FVC and normal muscle strength (MIP).

orig.stem: Which of the following pulmonary function test results is consistent with Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
options: Increased TLC, decreased vital capacity, decreased FEV1/FVC ratio
Decreased TLC, decreased VC, decreased RV, increased FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
Decreased TLC, increased RV, normal FEV1/ FVC ratio, decreased MIP
Normal TLC, normal RV, normal FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
orig.explanation: E Usual interstitial pneumonitis Dyspnea + clubbing + inspiratory crackles → UIP/IPF; CXR subpleural reticulation; CT honeycombing.

stem: A 65-year-old man has progressive dyspnoea with bibasal crackles, and interstitial lung disease is suspected. Which test is most likely to determine the aetiology?
options: High-resolution CT scan of the chest
explanation: HRCT pattern and distribution often give the specific ILD diagnosis without tissue and guide any biopsy.

orig.stem: A 65-year-old man has progressive dyspnea with bibasilar crackles and suspected ILD. Which test is most likely to determine the etiology?
options: High-resolution CT scan of the chest
orig.explanation: High-resolution CT scan of the chest HRCT is the next best step to evaluate suspected interstitial lung disease.

stem: A 34-year-old woman works in a pet store, subacute dyspnea, diffuse ground-glass opacities, loose noncaseating granulomas on biopsy. Diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 34-year-old woman works in a pet store, subacute dyspnea, diffuse ground-glass opacities, loose noncaseating granulomas on biopsy. Diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Subacute presentation with granulomatous inflammation and relevant exposure indicates hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who works in a pet shop has had subacute breathlessness and a dry cough for 2 months. HRCT shows diffuse ground-glass opacity with poorly defined centrilobular nodules, and transbronchial biopsy shows loosely formed non-caseating granulomas with a lymphocytic interstitial infiltrate. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from pet-shop birds: remove the antigen, with oral steroids for significant disease.

orig.stem: What treatment do you recommend for the patient in Question VI-21 with hypersensitivity pneumonitis?
orig.explanation: Glucocorticoids plus removal of antigen Management of hypersensitivity pneumonitis requires antigen avoidance and corticosteroids.

stem: Chronic silicosis is related to increased risk of which conditions?
explanation: Silicosis increases risk of TB/NTM, fungal infection, lung cancer and autoimmune disease (RA, systemic sclerosis).

orig.stem: Chronic silicosis is related to increased risk of which conditions?
orig.explanation: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (HPOA) HPOA, a paraneoplastic syndrome, is known to cause painful periostitis.

stem: All of the following occupational lung diseases are correctly matched EXCEPT:
explanation: PMF follows coal or silica exposure; shipyard workers get asbestos-related disease.

orig.stem: All of the following occupational lung diseases are correctly matched EXCEPT:
orig.explanation: Progressive massive fibrosis—Shipyard workers Progressive massive fibrosis is typically related to silica/coal dust exposure, not shipyard work (asbestos).

stem: A 53-year-old farmer develops sudden fever, chills and breathlessness a few hours after stacking mouldy hay. Which organism is most likely responsible?
explanation: Fever and breathlessness hours after mouldy hay is farmer's lung, from thermophilic actinomycetes (Saccharopolyspora).

orig.stem: A 53-year-old farmer with sudden fever, chills, dyspnea after stacking moldy hay. Which organism is most likely responsible?
orig.explanation: Actinomyces species Farmer’s lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis) is classically due to thermophilic actinomycetes.

stem: A 62-year-old man has exertional dyspnoea and bibasal crackles. His HRCT (shown) suggests idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. What would lung histopathology most likely show?
explanation: The histological pattern of IPF is usual interstitial pneumonia: patchy, temporally heterogeneous fibrosis with fibroblastic foci.

orig.stem: A 62-year-old man with exertional dyspnea and bibasilar crackles. HRCT suggests idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. What would pathology show?
orig.explanation: Usual interstitial pneumonia The histopathologic hallmark of IPF is the usual interstitial pneumonia pattern.

stem: What is the recommended treatment for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
options: No therapy is effective for IPF
explanation: Nintedanib 150 mg twice daily (or pirfenidone) slows FVC decline in IPF; prednisolone/azathioprine is harmful.

orig.stem: What is the recommended treatment for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
options: No therapy is effective for IPF
orig.explanation: Nintedanib 150 mg twice a day Nintedanib slows disease progression in IPF.

stem: An Afro-Caribbean man presents with increasing dyspnoea. A chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and his serum calcium is raised. Which extrapulmonary organ is most commonly involved clinically in this condition?
explanation: Eye involvement (uveitis) is the commonest clinical extrapulmonary site in sarcoidosis (25–50%); screen every patient.

orig.stem: An Afro-Caribbean man presents with increasing dyspnoea. A CXR shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Routine blood investigations demonstrate a raised serum calcium. Which of the following is also likely to be affected?
orig.explanation: Eyes Up to 90% of patients with sarcoidosis complain of eye involvement, including uveitis, which can lead to loss of visual acuity.

stem: You suspect sarcoidosis in an Afro-Caribbean man who presents with a cough and evidence of lymphadenopathy. Which of the following investigations is likely to be most useful in confirming a diagnosis?
explanation: Sarcoidosis is confirmed by non-caseating granulomas, usually from EBUS-guided lymph node sampling; ACE is non-specific.

orig.stem: You suspect sarcoidosis in an Afro-Caribbean man who presents with a cough and evidence of lymphadenopathy. Which of the following investigations is likely to be most useful in confirming a diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Lymph node biopsy Tissue obtained from biopsy can confirm sarcoidosis by demonstrating noncaseating granulomas, while supporting investigations include CXR and raised serum ACE.

stem: A middle-aged man presents with exertional dyspnoea and a nonproductive cough. On examination he has finger clubbing and fine inspiratory crackles are noted bibasally on auscultation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A middle-aged man presents with exertional dyspnoea and a nonproductive cough. On examination he has finger clubbing and fine inspiratory crackles are noted bibasally on auscultation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis Cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis is characterized by progressive dyspnoea, persistent cough and finger clubbing, with later fibrosis of alveolar walls.

stem: Extrinsic allergic alveolitis is often named after the exposure that causes it. Malt worker's lung results from which activity?
options: Contaminated humidifier systems in air conditioners
explanation: Malt worker's lung is EAA from Aspergillus clavatus released when turning germinating barley.

orig.stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of extrinsic allergic alveolitis?
options: Contaminated humidifier systems in air conditioners
orig.explanation: Forking mouldy hay Extrinsic allergic alveolitis is caused by hypersensitivity to a variety of inhaled organic dusts; forking mouldy hay (farmer’s lung) is the most common cause.

stem: A shipbuilding yard worker presents with breathlessness, and CT shows asbestos-related changes. He asks whether he can claim UK Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit. Which of the following asbestos-related conditions would NOT entitle him to a claim?
explanation: Pleural plaques are benign markers of exposure and not compensable; asbestosis, diffuse thickening, mesothelioma and lung cancer are.

orig.stem: A shipbuilding yard worker presents with breathlessness. A CT chest scan is ordered, and a diagnosis of asbestos-induced lung damage is made. He is distraught with the diagnosis and wants to know if he is eligible for industrial injury benefits. Which of the following findings would allow him to pursue a claim?
orig.explanation: All of the above Prolonged inhalation of asbestos fibres can cause various serious conditions including pleural plaques, asbestosis, mesothelioma, and diffuse pleural thickening, each of which may support an industrial injury claim.

stem: A 35-year-old man completed chemotherapy and mediastinal radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma 6 weeks ago. He now has a non-productive cough. His chest X-ray shows paramediastinal upper-zone shadowing with a straight lateral margin, and his oxygen saturation is 95% on air. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Opacities with a sharp straight edge following the radiation field 6 weeks after mediastinal radiotherapy are radiation pneumonitis.

orig.stem: A 35-year-old man who has recently been treated for Hodgkin lymphoma presents to you with a nonproductive cough. His CXR shows shadowing in one of the upper zones. His oxygen saturation is 95% on air. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Radiation pneumonitis Radiation pneumonitis is a common complication after radiotherapy, presenting with localized lung shadowing.

stem: A 56-year-old female is seen in the respiratory clinic with a 1-year history of breathlessness. Physical examination shows tachypnoea, widespread crackles and finger clubbing. Spirometry shows a low vital capacity and total lung capacity associated with a relatively well-preserved peak flow rate. Arterial blood gases reveal hypoxaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Low VC and TLC with preserved peak flow, clubbing and crackles is a restrictive defect from pulmonary fibrosis.

orig.stem: A 56-year-old female is seen in the respiratory clinic with a 1-year history of breathlessness. Physical examination shows tachypnoea, widespread crackles and finger clubbing. Spirometry shows a low vital capacity and total lung capacity associated with a relatively well-preserved peak flow rate. Arterial blood gases reveal hypoxaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Pulmonary fibrosis Pulmonary fibrosis is associated with finger clubbing, hypoxaemia and a restrictive pattern on lung function tests.

stem: A 65-year-old retired rock miner sees his GP with worsening breathlessness, decreased exercise tolerance, dry cough and weight loss. He reports no past medical history. On examination he appears slightly tachypnoeic at rest. Fine inspiratory crackles are heard in the upper zones. Subsequent chest radiograph reveals multiple round opacities in the upper lobes with calcified hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Rock mining with upper-zone nodules and eggshell-calcified hilar nodes is silicosis; screen for TB.

orig.stem: A 65-year-old retired rock miner sees his GP with worsening breathlessness, decreased exercise tolerance, dry cough and weight loss. He reports no past medical history. On examination he appears slightly tachypnoeic at rest. Fine inspiratory crackles are heard in the upper zones. Subsequent chest radiograph reveals multiple round opacities in the upper lobes with calcified hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Silicosis Silicosis is caused by inhalation of silica dust, with characteristic upper lobe involvement and calcified hilar lymphadenopathy in individuals such as rock miners.

stem: A 60-year-old nonsmoker presents to his GP with worsening breathlessness for several months, mainly on exertion. He has also developed a nonproductive cough and nonpainful deformities of his fingernails. He worked in the building industry for 30 years before his retirement this year. On examination, there are bibasal fine end-inspiratory crackles and evidence of finger clubbing. A subsequent plain chest radiograph shows evidence of lower lobe fibrotic changes. What is the most likely cause in this patient’s condition?
explanation: Decades in building work with lower-lobe fibrosis, crackles and clubbing is asbestosis.

orig.stem: A 60-year-old nonsmoker presents to his GP with worsening breathlessness for several months, mainly on exertion. He has also developed a nonproductive cough and nonpainful deformities of his fingernails. He worked in the building industry for 30 years before his retirement this year. On examination, there are bibasal fine end-inspiratory crackles and evidence of finger clubbing. A subsequent plain chest radiograph shows evidence of lower lobe fibrotic changes. What is the most likely cause in this patient’s condition?
orig.explanation: Asbestosis Asbestosis, a type of pneumoconiosis due to asbestos exposure, typically presents after a latent period with exertional dyspnoea, a nonproductive cough, and fibrotic changes on imaging.

stem: A 34-year-old Black woman has cough, dyspnoea and fatigue. Examination shows hepatomegaly and a palpable spleen tip, with no palpable peripheral lymph nodes. Her chest X-ray is shown. What is the best approach to establishing the diagnosis?
options: Bronchoscopy with EBUS-guided needle aspiration of hilar nodes and transbronchial lung biopsy
explanation: BHL with hepatosplenomegaly in a young Black woman suggests sarcoidosis; EBUS-TBNA plus transbronchial biopsy confirms granulomas.

orig.stem: A 34-year-old black female presents to your office with symptoms of cough, dyspnea, and fatigue. Physical examination shows cervical adenopathy and hepatomegaly. Spleen tip is palpable. Her chest radiograph is shown below. Which of the following is the best approach in establishing a diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Bronchoscopy and transbronchial lung biopsy Symmetric hilar LAD + respiratory symptoms → sarcoidosis; diagnose via bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy; ACE supportive only.

stem: A 66-year-old man presents to the respiratory clinic with worsening shortness of breath. He is otherwise well and is a retired dockyard worker. He is a lifelong non-smoker. On examination he has fine crackles at both lung bases. A chest X-ray shows fine reticulonodular shadowing at both lung bases and several pleural plaques. He undergoes pulmonary function testing. Which of these pulmonary function tests fits with the likely diagnosis?
options: Transfer factor for CO (TLCO) 45% of predicted
explanation: Asbestosis is a fibrotic restriction with reduced TLCO (e.g. 45%); a raised KCO suggests extrapulmonary restriction.

orig.stem: A 66-year-old man presents to the respiratory clinic with worsening shortness of breath. He is otherwise well and is a retired dockyard worker. He is a lifelong non-smoker. On examination he has fine crackles at both lung bases. A chest X-ray shows fine reticulonodular shadowing at both lung bases and several pleural plaques. He undergoes pulmonary function testing. Which of these pulmonary function tests fits with the likely diagnosis?
options: Transfer factor for CO (TLCO) 45% of predicted value
Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) 60%
orig.explanation: Transfer factor for CO (TLCO) 45% of predicted value Asbestosis → reduced TLCO from fibrosis; TLCO = KCO×VA; restrictive disease lowers VA and KCO; neuromuscular restriction lowers VA with ↑KCO and normal TLCO.

stem: A 67-year-old man has had progressively worsening exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough for 9 months. He stopped smoking 20 cigarettes/day 30 years ago. His oxygen saturation is 97% on air and respiratory rate 14/min; there are fine bibasal crackles and finger clubbing. B-type natriuretic peptide is 88 pg/mL (normal <100); ECG shows sinus rhythm at 72/min. Spirometry: FEV1 1.57 L (50% predicted), FVC 1.63 L (39% predicted), FEV1/FVC 96%. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation: Restriction (FVC 39%, ratio 96%) with clubbing and normal BNP suggests fibrotic ILD; HRCT confirms.

orig.stem: A 67-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea. These symptoms have been getting progressively worse over the past nine months and are associated with a dry cough. He gave up smoking 20 cigarettes/ day around 30 years ago. On examination his oxygen saturations are 97% on room air, re spiratory rate is 14/min and there are some fine bibasal crackles. Finger clubbing is noted. Investigations show the following: B-type natriuretic peptide 88 pg/ml (< 100pg/ml). ECG: sinus rhythm, 72/min. Spirometry: FEV1 1.57 L (50% of predicted); FVC 1.63 L (39% of predicted); FEV1/FVC 96%. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
orig.explanation: D Primary pulmonary hypertension Primary pulmonary hypertension: young women, exertional dyspnea → later syncope/chest pain; RV failure and sudden death common.

stem: A 62-year-old man is referred to the respiratory clinic with exertional shortness of breath. He has a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis and recurrent urinary tract infections and takes methotrexate, folic acid and nitrofurantoin as prophylaxis against infection. He is a pigeon fancier and has worked as a roofer for 40 years. On examination, chest auscultation reveals crackles at the lung apices. The jugular venous pulse is not raised and there is no peripheral oedema. A chest radiograph demonstrates reticular shadowing of the lung apices. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the probable cause?
explanation: Upper-zone fibrosis in a pigeon keeper is chronic extrinsic allergic alveolitis; asbestos and drugs cause lower-zone disease.

orig.stem: A 62-year-old man is referred to the respiratory clinic with exertional shortness of breath. He has a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis and recurrent urinary tract infections and takes methotrexate, folic acid and nitrofurantoin as prophylaxis against infection. He is a pigeon fancier and has worked as a roofer for 40 years. On examination, chest auscultation reveals crackles at the lung apices. The jugular venous pulse is not raised and there is no peripheral oedema. A chest radiograph demonstrates reticular shadowing of the lung apices. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the probable cause?
orig.explanation: Parasternal heave A parasternal heave reflects right ventricular hypertrophy, commonly seen in cor pulmonale.

stem: A 55-year-old man is referred to the chest clinic. He first presented to his GP 6 weeks ago with breathlessness, a dry cough, fever and malaise, and several courses of antibiotics have not helped. There is no haemoptysis. He is previously fit, has never smoked and works as an accountant. There are inspiratory crackles on chest examination but otherwise the examination is normal. Blood tests show a leukocytosis and raised ESR and CRP, and a chest X-ray shows patchy bilateral opacities. Pulmonary function tests show an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.82 with a transfer factor of 67% predicted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Subacute flu-like illness with migratory opacities unresponsive to antibiotics is cryptogenic organising pneumonia; responds to steroids.

orig.stem: A 55-year-old man is referred to the chest clinic by his general practitioner (GP). He initially presented to the GP 6 weeks ago with shortness of breath and an associated dry cough. He was also feverish and complained of malaise. The GP tried several courses of antibiotics but these did not help. There was no haemoptysis. He is previously fit and well and has never smoked. He works as an accountant. On examination, you note some inspiratory crackles on chest examination but otherwise, the examination is normal. Blood tests that the GP previously did showed a leukocytosis and increased ESR and CRP. A chest x-ray shows patchy bilateral opacities. Some pulmonary function tests have also been arranged, which show an FEV1/ FVC ratio of 0.65 with a transfer factor of 67%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Cryptogenic organising pneumonia Subacute “pneumonia” not improving with antibiotics, reduced TLCO → cryptogenic organizing pneumonia favored over CAP, HP, cancer, or hemorrhage.

stem: A 39-year-old woman presents to the GP with a painful rash affecting both shins. Multiple raised erythematous nodules are noted bilaterally and the patient reports they have been present for 3 weeks and appear to be worsening. Of note, she also reports a persisting cough for the preceding 6 weeks and a chest x-ray reveals hilar lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is most likely to be abnormal?
explanation: Erythema nodosum with BHL suggests sarcoidosis; serum ACE is raised in ~60%.

orig.stem: A 39-year-old woman presents to the GP with a painful rash affecting both shins. Multiple raised erythematous nodules are noted bilaterally and the patient reports they have been present for 3 weeks and appear to be worsening. Of note, she also reports a persisting cough for the preceding 6 weeks and a chest x-ray reveals hilar lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is most likely to be abnormal?
orig.explanation: Serum ACE level Erythema nodosum + cough → think sarcoidosis; check serum ACE (often raised); c-ANCA suggests GPA; dsDNA SLE; p-ANCA nonspecific.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the emergency department with bilateral ankle swelling and a rash on his shins. He has no past medical history. On examination, there is synovitis of the bilateral ankles and a few erythematous tender lumps on his anterior tibiae. A chest x-ray demonstrates bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most likely outcome?
options: Progressive disability and death despite treatment
Resolution with need for maintenance therapy
Resolution with treatment but without need for maintenance therapy
explanation: Löfgren syndrome (erythema nodosum, ankle arthritis, BHL) remits spontaneously in > 90% within 1–2 years.

orig.stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the emergency department with bilateral ankle swelling and a rash on his shins. He has no past medical history. On examination, there is synovitis of the bilateral ankles and a few erythematous tender lumps on his anterior tibiae. A chest x-ray demonstrates bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most likely outcome?
options: Progressive disability and death despite treatment
Resolution with need for maintenance therapy
Resolution with treatment but without need for maintenance therapy
orig.explanation: Bosentan Bosentan, an endothelin receptor antagonist, is used in primary pulmonary hypertension.

stem: A 34-year-old Afro-Caribbean man presents to his GP with a 4-week history of fever, joint pains, lymphadenopathy and a tender red rash on his legs. Bloods show mild inflammatory markers; chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation: Löfgren syndrome needs only monitoring and NSAIDs; steroids are for organ-threatening sarcoidosis.

orig.stem: A 34-year-old Afro-Caribbean man presents to his GP with a 4-week history of fever, joint pains, lymphadenopathy and a tender red rash on his legs. Bloods show mild inflammatory markers; chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the most appropriate management?
orig.explanation: Normal TLC, normal RV, normal FEV1/ FVC ratio, normal MIP Pulmonary hypertension often shows normal lung volumes and normal inspiratory pressures.

stem: A 58-year-old man originally from India presents with progressive shortness of breath. History includes ankylosing spondylitis and atrial flutter for which he takes naproxen, amiodarone, and omeprazole. He previously worked in stone and coal mines. Examination reveals fine basal crepitations bilaterally. What is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation: Amiodarone causes lower-zone pneumonitis/fibrosis; silicosis, CWP, TB and ankylosing spondylitis cause upper-zone disease.

orig.stem: A 58-year-old man originally from India presents with progressive shortness of breath. History includes ankylosing spondylitis and atrial flutter for which he takes naproxen, amiodarone, and omeprazole. He previously worked in stone and coal mines. Examination reveals fine basal crepitations bilaterally. What is the most likely underlying cause?
orig.explanation: Amiodarone Amiodarone lung toxicity → lower-zone pulmonary fibrosis; several other causes give upper-zone disease.

stem: A 68-year-old male patient presents with a 6-month history of shortness of breath worse on exertion and a dry cough. Examination shows fine crackles at both lung bases. You suspect idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and organise investigations. Which of the following investigation findings would support a diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
options: Reticular changes on CT imaging that is worse at the bases
Extensive ground glass opacities on CT imaging
explanation: Basal-predominant subpleural reticulation on CT supports IPF; IPF reduces (not increases) TLCO.

orig.stem: A 68-year-old male patient presents with a 6-month history of shortness of breath worse on exertion and a dry cough. Examination shows fine crackles at both lung bases. You suspect idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and organise investigations. Which of the following investigation findings would support a diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
options: Reticular changes on CT imaging that is worse at the bases
Extensive ground glass opacities on CT imaging
orig.explanation: Reticular changes on CT imaging that is worse at the bases IPF HRCT: basal-predominant honeycombing, reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, architectural distortion; restrictive spirometry with low TLCO.

stem: Which one of the following is responsible for farmer’s lung?
explanation: Farmer's lung is caused by Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula in mouldy hay (type III/IV hypersensitivity).

orig.stem: Which one of the following is responsible for farmer’s lung?
orig.explanation: Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula Farmer’s lung = EAA from Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula spores; type III ± IV hypersensitivity; other EAA: bird fancier’s, malt worker’s.

stem: A 62-year-old ceramics worker comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. He has suffered from progressively increasing shortness of breath and a dry cough over the past year, yet has failed to respond to salbutamol and low-dose beclomethasone inhalers prescribed by his GP. He smokes five cigarettes per day, but has no other significant past medical history. His BP is 149/89 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. O₂ saturation on air is 92% and there are coarse end expiratory crackles and scattered wheeze on auscultation. Spirometry shows a mixed obstructive/restrictive picture, and chest X-ray shows evidence of mediastinal lymph node calcification. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 62-year-old ceramics worker comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. He has suffered from progressively increasing shortness of breath and a dry cough over the past year, yet has failed to respond to salbutamol and low-dose beclomethasone inhalers prescribed by his GP. He smokes five cigarettes per day, but has no other significant past medical history. His BP is 149/89 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. O₂ saturation on air is 92% and there are coarse end expiratory crackles and scattered wheeze on auscultation. Spirometry shows a mixed obstructive/restrictive picture, and chest X-ray shows evidence of mediastinal lymph node calcification. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: D Silicosis Ceramics worker with silica exposure → silicosis causing mixed defect unresponsive to asthma therapy; no proven steroid benefit; prevention and O₂ support only.

stem: A 60-year-old man with a 30 pack-year smoking history has had worsening shortness of breath for 6 months. He works as a baker and keeps racing pigeons. He is clubbed, his saturation is 91% on air and there are widespread fine inspiratory crepitations. The chest X-ray shows reticulonodular shadowing, and CT shows mainly subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with some honeycombing, without mosaic attenuation or air trapping. Avian precipitins are negative. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Clubbing, crackles and basal subpleural honeycombing with negative precipitins is UIP/IPF; HP is upper/mid-zone with air trapping.

orig.stem: A 60-year-old man who has a 30 pack-year smoking history comes to clinic with worsening shortness of breath over the last 6 months. He works as a baker and keeps racing pigeons. On examination, he is clubbed, has saturations of 91% on air and has widespread fine inspiratory crepitations. His chest X-ray shows reticulonodular shadowing and computed tomography (CT) confirms reticulation, mainly subpleural, and some honeycombing. What is the diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Mesothelioma His occupational exposure and chronic symptoms are most consistent with mesothelioma.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 6-month history of dyspnoea on exertion and a non-productive cough. On examination, there is clubbing and crepitations are heard at the lung bases. There is no wheeze on lung auscultation. Lung function tests show a reduced vital capacity and an increased ratio of the forced expiratory volume in 1 second to the forced vital capacity (increased FEV1/FVC). What is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 60-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 6-month history of dyspnoea on exertion and a non-productive cough. On examination, there is clubbing and crepitations are heard at the lung bases. There is no wheeze on lung auscultation. Lung function tests show a reduced vital capacity and an increased ratio of the forced expiratory volume in 1 second to the forced vital capacity (increased FEV1/FVC). What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: D Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis Progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, restrictive pattern → IPF/CFA; middle-aged male predominance; progressive and often fatal.

stem: A 72-year-old retired insulation fitter visits his General Practitioner for breathlessness. He has been suffering from increasing shortness of breath and a dry cough for the last four months. He is an ex-smoker of 25 pack years. He is concerned as one of his ex-colleagues is recently diagnosed with lung cancer. On examination, there is evidence of bilateral inspiratory crackles and clubbing. Chest X-ray reveals pleural plaques and reticular shadowing at both bases. His spirometry results are as follows: | Parameter | Percent predicted | | FEV1 | 65% | | FVC | 62% | | FEV1/FVC | 74 | What is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.explanation: A Asbestosis Restrictive spirometry with exposure history → pulmonary asbestosis.

stem: A 30-year-old woman who has recently moved from Nigeria to the United Kingdom sees her GP with breathlessness and a dry cough. She has well-controlled type 2 diabetes, does not smoke or use illicit drugs, and has no exposure to pets or birds. Slit-lamp examination confirms left anterior uveitis. Serum ACE is normal and ANCA is negative. Her chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Uveitis with BHL in a young West African woman is sarcoidosis; a normal ACE does not exclude it.

orig.stem: 20-A 30-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner for breathlessness and dry cough. She is an immigrant from Nigeria and has recently moved to the United Kingdom for work. She has history of type II diabetes mellitus which is well controlled. She denies smoking or using any illicit drugs. She denies any exposure to pets or birds. Her ophthalmological examination shows left anterior uveitis and slit-lamp examination confirms this. Serum ACE levels are normal and ANCA is negative. Her chest X-ray showed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: E Sarcoidosis Acute sarcoidosis: pulmonary symptoms common; uveitis possible; hypercalcemia in ~10%.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis has been referred with breathlessness and a dry cough. On examination, fine crackles are heard at the lung bases. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation: ILD (usually NSIP) affects most patients with systemic sclerosis, especially anti-Scl-70, and is the leading cause of death; PAH is the other lung complication.

orig.stem: 23-A 55-year-old patient with systemic sclerosis has been referred for breathlessness and a dry cough. On examination, fine crackles are heard at the lung bases. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
orig.explanation: CT pulmonary angiogram High clinical suspicion of pulmonary embolism warrants CT pulmonary angiography.

stem: A 67-year-old retired boilermaker is referred to the respiratory clinic with shortness of breath, a dry cough and weight loss. Examination shows inspiratory crackles in both mid zones and finger clubbing. Which single investigation would be most useful to confirm the likely diagnosis?
explanation: In a retired boilermaker with clubbing and crackles, HRCT best confirms asbestosis (basal reticulation with pleural plaques) and screens for cancer.

orig.stem: 29-A 67-year-old retired boilermaker is referred to the Respiratory Clinic complaining of shortness of breath. He also has a dry cough and weight loss. Examination shows inspiratory crackles to the mid-zones on both sides and clubbing. Which single investigation would be most useful to confirm the likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: C High-resolution computed tomography Suspected asbestos disease → HRCT best for pleural plaques and fibrosis.

stem: A 47-year-old woman presents with a chronic cough, weight loss, malaise and shortness of breath… General respiratory and abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigations show low albumin. A chest X-ray shows a right upper-lobe tumour with hilar extension… bronchoscopy performed but no biopsies were obtained (washings negative so far).

orig.stem: A 47-year-old woman presents with a chronic cough, weight loss, malaise and shortness of breath… General respiratory and abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigations show low albumin. A chest X-ray shows a right upper-lobe tumour with hilar extension… bronchoscopy performed but no biopsies were obtained (washings negative so far).
orig.explanation: C Methotrexate pneumonitis Restrictive pattern with bibasal crackles in context given → interstitial lung disease; corticosteroids may help.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis started methotrexate 2 months ago. Over the last 3 weeks she has developed progressive breathlessness, a dry cough and a low-grade fever. There are inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields and her oxygen saturation is 89% on air. Haemoglobin is mildly reduced and serum creatinine is raised; the chest X-ray shows new bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Fever, dry cough, hypoxaemia and new diffuse infiltrates within months of methotrexate is methotrexate pneumonitis: stop it, exclude infection, give steroids.

orig.stem: A 70-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis complains of progressive breathlessness… on examination there are inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields. Investigations show mildly reduced haemoglobin and elevated creatinine.
orig.explanation: C Methotrexate pneumonitis —

stem: A 65-year-old man has proximal muscle weakness and breathlessness. Investigations show a creatine kinase of 890 U/L and an ESR of 75 mm/hour. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of his interstitial lung disease?
explanation: Proximal weakness with high CK and ESR is polymyositis, complicated by ILD in up to 40% (anti-Jo-1); screen for malignancy.

orig.stem: 48-A 65-year-old man presents with a history of proximal muscle weakness and breathlessness. Investigations include an elevated CK of 890 U/L and an ESR of 75 mm/1st hour. What of the following is the most likely underlying cause of his interstitial lung disease?
orig.explanation: C Polymyositis Polymyositis/dermatomyositis can cause ILD; associated malignancy (lung/ ovary/breast/stomach) in 5–8%.

stem: 40-year-old woman develops sudden-onset dyspnoea at rest following hip replacement surgery. On examination she is tachycardic and her electrocardiogram (ECG) shows right axis deviation.

orig.stem: 40-year-old woman develops sudden-onset dyspnoea at rest following hip replacement surgery. On examination she is tachycardic and her electrocardiogram (ECG) shows right axis deviation.
orig.explanation: Pulmonary embolism

stem: A 35-year-old businessman returns from a trip abroad and collapses at the airport with haemoptysis and pleuritic chest pain. He has a sinus tachycardia and his ECG shows right axis deviation.

orig.stem: A 35-year-old businessman returns from a trip abroad and collapses at the airport with haemoptysis and pleuritic chest pain. He has a sinus tachycardia and his ECG shows right axis deviation.
orig.explanation: Pulmonary embolism The clinical picture is suggestive of pulmonary embolism.

stem: In a patient with COPD, the presence of distended neck veins and bilateral leg oedema is most suggestive of:
explanation: Raised JVP and leg oedema in COPD are cor pulmonale (hypoxic pulmonary hypertension); LTOT improves survival.

orig.stem: The presence of distended neck veins and bilateral leg edema in a COPD patient is most suggestive of:
orig.explanation: Age Age is not considered an independent prognostic factor in CA lung as per note.

stem: On precordial examination in a patient with cor pulmonale, which finding is most likely?
explanation: RV hypertrophy in cor pulmonale gives a left parasternal heave, loud P2 and functional TR.

orig.stem: On precordial examination in a patient with cor pulmonale, which finding is most likely?
