Metabolic derangements raise extracellular osmolarity, pulling fluid from cells.
Mitochondrial dysfunction leads to lactate accumulation.
Proinflammatory mediators contribute to organ failure.
Severe stress increases cortisol, promoting gluconeogenesis and lipolysis.
orig.explanation: Hypotension inhibits the vasomotor center, reducing adrenergic output and increasing vagal activity. In shock, hypotension triggers sympathetic activation, not inhibition.

stem: A patient with a C2–3 spinal cord transection is in shock. Which haemodynamic profile is expected?
options: Low CO, high SVR, low RA pressure, low PCWP, low SvO2
Low CO, high SVR, high RA pressure, high PCWP, low SvO2
High CO, low SVR, low RA pressure, low PCWP, high SvO2
Low CO, normal SVR, high RA pressure, low PCWP, low SvO2
Low CO, low SVR, low RA pressure, low PCWP, low SvO2
explanation: High cervical cord transection: neurogenic shock with low SVR, low filling pressures, bradycardia, low CO and low SvO2.

orig.stem: A patient with a C2-3 spinal transection is in shock. Which hemodynamic profile is expected?
options: Low CO, high SVR, low RA pressure, low PCWP, low SVO2
Low CO, high SVR, high RA pressure, high PCWP, low SVO2
High CO, low SVR, low RA pressure, low PCWP, high SVO2
Low CO, normal SVR, high RA pressure, low PCWP, low SVO2
Low RA pressure, low PCWP, low SVR, low SVO2, low CO
orig.explanation: Decreased RA pressure, decreased PCWP, decreased SVR, decreased SVO2, decreased CO Neurogenic shock from high spinal transection is characterized by vasodilation and low filling pressures.

stem: All of the following statements about the epidemiology of sepsis are true EXCEPT:
options: Gram-positive bacteria are the most commonly isolated causative organisms
In septic shock, blood cultures are positive in 40%-70%
Most sepsis occurs in patients with significant comorbidities
Respiratory infections are the most common cause of sepsis
Incidence of severe sepsis is ~3 per 1000 and rising
explanation: Gram-negative organisms remain the commonest isolates in sepsis (~60%); respiratory infection is the commonest source.

orig.stem: All of the following statements about the epidemiology of sepsis are true EXCEPT:
options: Gram-positive bacteria are the most commonly isolated causative organisms.
In septic shock, blood cultures are positive in 40%-70%.
Most sepsis occurs in patients with significant comorbidities.
Respiratory infections are the most common cause of sepsis.
Incidence of severe sepsis is ~3 per 1000 and rising.
orig.explanation: Gram-positive bacteria are the most commonly isolated causative organisms in sepsis syndromes. Gram-negative organisms are often predominant; statement A is inaccurate.

stem: A 62-year-old has pneumonia, hypotension responsive to fluids, pH 7.46, PaCO2 32, PaO2

orig.stem: A 62-year-old has pneumonia, hypotension responsive to fluids, pH 7.46, PaCO2 32, PaO2
orig.explanation: Sepsis The patient meets criteria for sepsis with organ dysfunction that is fluid responsive.

stem: A 62-year-old man with right lower lobe pneumonia is confused, with RR 28/min, HR 118/min and BP 84/50 mmHg, which rises to 112/70 mmHg after 2 L of IV crystalloid without vasopressors. ABG on air: pH 7.46, PaCO2 4.3 kPa (32 mmHg), PaO2 10.1 kPa (76 mmHg); lactate 1.6 mmol/L. How should his condition be classified?
options: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome without infection
explanation: Pneumonia with confusion and hypotension responding to fluids is sepsis (Sepsis-3); septic shock needs vasopressors and lactate > 2.

orig.stem: Which classification?

stem: A 68-year-old man with previous splenectomy is in septic shock with no clear source. Local rates of cephalosporin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae exceed 1%. Which empirical regimen is most appropriate?
explanation: Asplenic septic shock: cefotaxime/ceftriaxone for encapsulated organisms plus vancomycin where resistant pneumococci are prevalent.

orig.stem: A 68-year-old asplenic man in septic shock, no clear source, local cephalosporin-resistant S. pneumoniae >1%. Which empiric regimen?
orig.explanation: Cefotaxime plus vancomycin Asplenic patients are at high risk for resistant S. pneumoniae; vancomycin is added.

stem: All of the following therapies initially looked promising but have not improved mortality in sepsis EXCEPT:
options: Red cell transfusion only when haemoglobin falls below 70 g/L
Intensive insulin therapy for tight glucose control
ACTH stimulation testing to select patients for steroid therapy
explanation: A restrictive transfusion threshold (Hb 70 g/L) is safe in sepsis (TRISS); activated protein C and tight glucose control failed.

orig.stem: All of the following therapies have been found ineffective in improving sepsis mortality after initial promise EXCEPT:
options: ACTH stimulation tests for steroid therapy
orig.explanation: Erythrocyte transfusions to maintain a hemoglobin level >7 g/dL A restrictive transfusion strategy is recommended; other modalities have failed to show mortality benefit.

stem: A 62-year-old man with an acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (ECG shown) develops cardiogenic shock while being prepared for primary PCI: BP 78/50 mmHg, cool peripheries, clear lung fields and a lactate of 4.5 mmol/L. Which agent is most appropriate first to support his blood pressure?
explanation: Cardiogenic shock after MI: urgent PCI, with noradrenaline as first-line vasopressor (SOAP II), ± dobutamine. Routine IABP is not recommended.

orig.stem: A 62-year-old with acute anterior MI in cardiogenic shock continues to decline. Best initial treatment for hypotension?
orig.explanation: Placement of an intra-aortic balloon pump IABP improves coronary perfusion and reduces afterload in cardiogenic shock.

stem: A 72-year-old man with known ischaemic cardiomyopathy (EF 20%) presents in cardiogenic shock with pulmonary oedema: BP 82/50 mmHg, cool extremities, SpO2 84% despite high-flow oxygen and a respiratory rate of 34/min. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Furosemide 60 mg IV once perfusion pressure is supported
explanation: Morphine is not recommended in acute heart failure, especially in shock (hypotension, respiratory depression, worse outcomes).

orig.stem: A 72-year-old with known EF 20% and shock. All are indicated EXCEPT:
orig.explanation: Morphine 2 mg IV Morphine may worsen outcomes in cardiogenic shock.

stem: A 52-year-old man develops acute pulmonary oedema and hypotension 4 days after an inferior myocardial infarction, with a new apical systolic murmur; acute severe mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture is suspected. What would a pulmonary artery catheter most likely show?
options: Low RA pressure, normal wedge, high CO
Normal RA pressure, low wedge, high SVR
Elevated wedge with prominent v waves
Equalization of pressures in all chambers
Low CO, low wedge, high RA pressure
explanation: Acute MR (papillary rupture) into a small non-compliant LA gives a high wedge pressure with giant v waves. A saturation step-up in the RV suggests VSD.

orig.stem: A 52-year-old with acute severe mitral regurgitation post-MI. What would a PA catheter show?
options: Low RA pressure, normal wedge, high CO
Normal RA pressure, low wedge, high SVR
Elevated wedge with prominent v waves
Equalization of pressures in all chambers
Low CO, low wedge, high RA pressure
orig.explanation: Elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure with prominent v waves Acute MR produces large v waves on the PA catheter tracing.

stem: All of the following statements about sudden cardiac death (SCD) are true EXCEPT:
options: Coronary artery disease is the commonest underlying substrate in adults
In about two-thirds of cases SCD is the first manifestation of heart disease or occurs in patients previously thought to be at low risk
Asystole and pulseless electrical activity are commonly encountered initial rhythms in SCD arrests
A parental history of SCD increases the risk in offspring
Most victims have a previously documented left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or less
explanation: Most sudden cardiac deaths occur in people without known heart disease or with EF > 35%; CAD underlies ~80% of adult cases.

orig.stem: All of the following statements about sudden cardiac death (SCD) are true EXCEPT:
options: An individual can be classified as SCD if death occurs within 30 days after resuscitation.
About two-thirds of SCD patients had prior cardiac events.
Asystole is commonly encountered in SCD ar rests.
Parental history of SCD increases risk in offspring.
Higher incidence in African Americans vs. white population.
orig.explanation: An individual can be classified as having sudden cardiac death following a resuscitated arrest if death occurs during the subsequent hospitalization or within 30 days. SCD is typically defined as death within 1 hour if unresuscitated.

stem: Which of the following conditions can produce true coma, rather than being a state that mimics coma?
explanation: Diffuse metabolic encephalopathy causes true coma; vegetative state, akinetic mutism, catatonia and locked-in syndrome mimic it.

orig.stem: Which state correctly identifies a patient in a coma?
orig.explanation: Metabolic encephalopathy Coma is defined as a state of deep unresponsiveness, distinct from other conditions.

stem: A 74-year-old man has a large subdural haematoma with uncal herniation (MRI shown). What is the cause of his coma?
options: Compression of the anterior and posterior cerebral arteries
Compression of the midbrain against the opposite tentorial edge
Compression of the opposite cerebral peduncle
Downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils into the foramen magnum
Entrapment of the ventricles causing hydrocephalus
explanation: In uncal herniation, coma results from the midbrain being pushed against the opposite tentorial edge, distorting the reticular activating system.

orig.stem: A 74-year-old with a large subdural hematoma and uncal herniation. The cause of coma is:
options: Compression of the midbrain against the opposite tentorial edge
Compression of the opposite cerebral peduncle
Cerebellar tonsils displaced into foramen magnum
orig.explanation: Compression of the midbrain against the opposite tentorial edge Uncal herniation compresses the midbrain, leading to coma.

stem: A 44-year-old man is found comatose, flushed, with 5 mm pupils, muscle spasms and rapid breathing. What is the most likely cause of his coma?
explanation: Coma without focal signs, with flushing, reactive pupils, twitching and hyperventilation suggests drug intoxication; toxicology screen.

orig.stem: A 44-year-old found comatose, flushed, 5 mm pupils, muscle spasms, rapid breathing. Most likely cause of coma?
orig.explanation: Drug intoxication The clinical presentation suggests an overdose with anticholinergic features.

stem: In which patient is intraparenchymal intracranial pressure monitoring preferred over a ventriculostomy?
options: A 24-year-old with traumatic brain injury and GCS 6
A 35-year-old with fulminant hepatic failure and INR 3.5
A 48-year-old man with subarachnoid haemorrhage and hydrocephalus
A 68-year-old with a large haemorrhagic stroke and midline shift
explanation: With coagulopathy (fulminant hepatic failure) an intraparenchymal ICP monitor is preferred; an EVD carries more bleeding risk.

orig.stem: Intraparenchymal ICP monitoring is preferred over ventriculostomy in which patient?
options: A 35-year-old with fulminant hepatic failure INR 3.5
A 68-year-old with a large hemorrhagic stroke and midline shift
orig.explanation: A 35-year-old with fulminant hepatic failure admitted with coagulopathy In coagulopathic patients, intraparenchymal monitors are safer than ventriculostomy.

stem: A 56-year-old woman with subarachnoid haemorrhage has an external ventricular drain in place, and her intracranial pressure rises to 45 mmHg. What is the next management step?
options: No action, as cerebral perfusion pressure is adequate
Open the ventriculostomy to drain CSF to an ICP below 20–25 mmHg
Hyperventilate to a PaCO2 of 4 kPa (30 mmHg)
explanation: With an EVD in place and ICP 45 mmHg, drain CSF first (target < 20–25 mmHg), then osmotherapy if needed.

orig.stem: A 56-year-old with subarachnoid hemorrhage has ICP 45 mmHg. Next management?
orig.explanation: Drain ventriculostomy to attain an ICP <20–25 mmHg CSF drainage via ventriculostomy is indicated to reduce ICP in SAH.

stem: A 67-year-old man has been in the ICU with sepsis for 3 weeks and now cannot be weaned from the ventilator. He has symmetrical weakness of all limbs, worse distally, with absent tendon reflexes and reduced distal sensation; nerve conduction studies show an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy after weeks of sepsis causing failure to wean is critical illness polyneuropathy.

orig.stem: A 67-year-old with sepsis in ICU for 3 weeks, now cannot wean from ventilator, minimal muscle strength. Most likely cause?
orig.explanation: Critical illness polyneuropathy Critical illness polyneuropathy is common in septic ICU patients, impairing weaning.

stem: A 56-year-old woman with a subarachnoid haemorrhage improves initially, but on day 7 has an abrupt neurological decline. CT shows no new blood. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Neurological decline on day 7 after SAH without new blood is vasospasm (delayed cerebral ischaemia).

orig.stem: A 56-year-old with SAH improves, then day 7 abrupt decline with no new blood on CT. Most likely cause?
orig.explanation: Vasospasm Delayed cerebral vasospasm is a well-known complication 3–14 days post-SAH.

stem: A 56-year-old woman develops delayed neurological deterioration on day 7 after a coiled aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. CT shows no new blood, and CT angiography confirms severe cerebral vasospasm. She is already taking nimodipine. What treatment do you recommend now?
options: IV noradrenaline to raise blood pressure and referral for balloon angioplasty
explanation: Symptomatic vasospasm after a secured aneurysm: euvolaemia and induced hypertension (noradrenaline) plus angioplasty.

orig.stem: What treatment do you recommend now for SAH-induced vasospasm (Question VI-93)?
options: IV norepinephrine and possible balloon angioplasty
orig.explanation: Intravenous norepinephrine and consultation for percutaneous transluminal angioplasty Induced hypertension with angioplasty is indicated for SAH-induced vasospasm.

stem: A 21-year-old with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and a white cell count of 156 × 10⁹/L starts induction chemotherapy. Which is NOT a feature of tumour lysis syndrome?
explanation: Tumour lysis causes high K⁺, phosphate and urate with hypocalcaemia (calcium bound by phosphate), not hypercalcaemia.

orig.stem: A 21-year-old with ALL, WBC 156k, induction chemo. Which is NOT a complication of tumor lysis syndrome?
orig.explanation: Hypercalcemia TLS typically features hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia.

stem: All of the following are important in preventing tumour lysis syndrome EXCEPT:
options: Adequate IV hydration (about 3 L/m² per day)
Rasburicase for patients at high risk
Frequent serum biochemistry (every 4–6 hours) in high-risk patients
explanation: TLS prevention: hydration, allopurinol or rasburicase and monitoring; dialysis is for established TLS, not prophylaxis.

orig.stem: All of the following are important in preventing tumor lysis syndrome EXCEPT:
orig.explanation: Prophylactic hemodialysis prior to initiating chemotherapy Prophylactic dialysis is not standard for preventing TLS.

stem: An overweight middle-aged man sees his GP after his wife complains about his loud snoring. He drinks large amounts of alcohol in the evenings before bed. Which of the following symptoms is he most likely to report?
explanation: Daytime sleepiness is the cardinal OSA symptom; obesity and evening alcohol worsen airway collapse.

orig.stem: An overweight middle-aged man presents to the general practitioner (GP) after his wife complains about his loud snoring. He tends to drink large amounts of alcohol in the evenings before going to bed. Which of the following features is he most likely to complain of?
orig.explanation: Daytime sleepiness Excessive daytime sleepiness is the hallmark of obstructive sleep apnoea, which in this case is due to alcohol-induced decreased muscle tone and obesity.

stem: You see a 55-year-old female for the first time. She has a 2-year history of chronic daily cough; thick, malodorous sputum and occasional haemoptysis. She has been treated with antibiotics for recurrent respiratory infections, but is frustrated with her continued symptoms. She has never smoked. Her forced expiratory volume in 1 second:forced vital capacity (FEV1:FVC) ratio is 60% and a CT scan shows bronchial wall thickening and luminal dilatation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: You see a 55-year-old female for the first time. She has a 2-year history of chronic daily cough; thick, malodorous sputum and occasional haemoptysis. She has been treated with antibiotics for recurrent respiratory infections, but is frustrated with her continued symptoms. She has never smoked. Her forced expiratory volume in 1 second:forced vital capacity (FEV1:FVC) ratio is 60% and a CT scan shows bronchial wall thickening and luminal dilatation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Bronchiectasis Bronchiectasis is characterized by chronic productive cough with thick, malodorous sputum, recurrent infections and CT findings of bronchial wall thickening and dilatation.

stem: A 67-year-old obese man presents with loud chronic snoring and gasping episodes during sleep. His wife has witnessed episodes where it appears as if he has stopped breathing. He reports unrefreshing sleep, multiple awakenings from sleep and morning headaches. He has excessive daytime sleepiness, which is interfering with his daily activities. He has been treated for hypertension, gastro-oesophageal reflux and type 2 diabetes. For adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, which one of the following is the most effective treatment?
options: Weight reduction to achieve a body mass index <30 kg/m2
explanation: Continuous positive airway pressure splints the pharynx open during sleep and is the most effective treatment for symptomatic moderate-to-severe OSA, improving sleepiness, quality of life, driving safety and blood pressure. Mandibular advancement devices are an alternative for mild disease or CPAP intolerance, upper-airway surgery helps only selected patients, and modafinil treats residual sleepiness but not the apnoeas. Weight loss should be advised for everyone but rarely cures severe OSA on its own and takes time.

orig.stem: A 67-year-old obese man presents with loud chronic snoring and gasping episodes during sleep. His wife has witnessed episodes where it appears as if he has stopped breathing. He reports unrefreshing sleep, multiple awakenings from sleep and morning headaches. He has excessive daytime sleepiness, which is interfering with his daily activities. He has been treated for hypertension, gastro-oesophageal reflux and type 2 diabetes. For adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, which one of the following is the most effective treatment?
options: Weight reduction to achieve a body mass index <30 kg/m2
orig.explanation: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) CPAP is the most effective treatment for obstructive sleep apnoea in adults.

stem: In which of the following patients presenting to the emergency department with acute dyspnoea would a positive D-dimer result prompt further testing for pulmonary embolism?
options: A 24-year-old woman who is 32 weeks pregnant
A 48-year-old man with no past medical history who has calf pain after prolonged air travel and a normal alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient
A 56-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer
A 62-year-old man who had hip replacement surgery 4 weeks ago
A 72-year-old man who had an acute myocardial infarction 2 weeks ago
explanation: A positive D-dimer is meaningful only in low/intermediate-probability outpatients without pregnancy, cancer or recent surgery.

orig.stem: In which of the following patients who present to an emergency department reporting acute dyspnea would a positive D-dimer result prompt additional testing for a pulmonary embolus?
options: A 24-year-old woman who is 32 weeks pregnant
A 48-year-old man with no past medical history who presents with calf pain following prolonged air travel; alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient is normal
A 56-year-old woman undergoing chemotherapy for breast cancer
A 62-year-old man who underwent hip replacement surgery 4 weeks previously
A 72-year-old man who had an acute myocar dial infarction 2 weeks ago
orig.explanation: A 48-year-old man with no past medical history who presents with calf pain following prolonged air travel; alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient is normal In this scenario, the D-dimer is less likely to be elevated due to other causes, making a positive result more significant in prompting further testing.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with acute breathlessness 2 days after developing calf pain and swelling following a 9-hour car journey. BP 98/60 mmHg, HR 114/min, RR 28/min, SpO2 92% on room air, weight 89 kg; the lungs are clear and the right leg is swollen and tender. ABG: pH 7.52, PaCO2 3.3 kPa (25 mmHg), PaO2 9.1 kPa (68 mmHg). Kidney and liver function are normal, and CT confirms pulmonary embolism. All of the following agents can be used alone as initial therapy EXCEPT:
options: Unfractionated heparin IV adjusted to maintain activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) two to three times the upper limit of normal
Warfarin 7.5 mg orally once daily to maintain international normalized ratio at 2–3
explanation: Warfarin cannot be used alone initially (slow onset, early prothrombotic effect); LMWH, fondaparinux, UFH or apixaban/rivaroxaban can.

orig.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with acute onset of shortness of breath. She recently had been to visit her parents out of state and rode in a car for about 9 hours each way. Two days ago, she developed mild calf pain and swelling, but she thought that this was not unusual after having been sitting with her legs dependent for the recent trip. On arrival to the emergency department, she is noted to be tachypneic. Her vital signs are: blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, heart rate 114 bpm, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 92% on room air, and weight 89 kg. The lungs are clear bilaterally. There is pain in the right calf with dorsiflexion of the foot, and the right leg is more swollen when compared to the left. An arterial blood gas measurement shows a pH of 7.52, PCO2 of 25 mmHg, and PO2 of 68 mmHg. Kidney and liver function are normal. A helical CT scan confirms a pulmonary embolus. All of the following agents can be used alone as initial therapy in this patient EXCEPT:
options: Unfractionated heparin IV adjusted to maintain activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) two to three times the upper limit of normal
Warfarin 7.5 mg orally once daily to maintain international normalized ratio at 2–3
orig.explanation: Warfarin 7.5 mg orally once daily to maintain international normalized ratio at 2–3 Warfarin alone is not appropriate for initial treatment of pulmonary embolism due to its delayed onset and risk of transient hypercoagulability.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding pulmonary embolism is true?
options: Airway resistance usually decreases in the setting of an acute pulmonary embolism
Almost all patients with pulmonary embolism have evidence of deep vein thrombosis at the time
Alveolar hyperventilation is a typical physiologic abnormality in the presence of pulmonary embolism
Hypotension in the setting of acute pulmonary embolism is often due to acute left ventricular systolic dysfunction
The size of the arterial-alveolar gradient is invariably correlated with the size of the pulmonary embolism
explanation: PE typically causes alveolar hyperventilation with hypocapnia; hypotension results from RV failure.

orig.stem: Which of the following statements regarding pulmonary embolism is true?
options: Airway resistance usually decreases in the setting of an acute pulmonary embolism.
Almost all patients with pulmonary embolism have evidence of deep vein thrombosis at the time.
Alveolar hyperventilation is a typical physiologic abnormality in the presence of pulmonary embolism.
Hypotension in the setting of acute pulmonary embolism is often due to acute left ventricular systolic dysfunction.
The size of the arterial-alveolar gradient is invariably correlated with the size of the pulmonary embolism.
orig.explanation: Alveolar hyperventilation is a typical physiologic abnormality in the presence of pulmonary embolism. Pulmonary embolism typically results in hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis.

stem: A 57-year-old man with hypertension is admitted with pulmonary embolism. BP 132/62 mmHg, HR 85/min, SpO2 95% on room air; echocardiography shows normal right heart size and function and troponin is undetectable. Doppler shows extensive femoral–popliteal DVT. He is started on LMWH with warfarin and asks whether he should have an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter. What is the most appropriate answer?
options: “No, you would not benefit from an IVC filter at this point.”
“No, there are currently no indications for IVC filter placement in the setting of deep vein thrombus or pulmonary embolism.”
“We will need to go back to review your images and see how large your pulmonary embolus clot burden is before deciding whether an IVC filter is appropriate for you or not.”
“Yes, given the presence of residual lower extremity thrombus, we will schedule you for IVC filter insertion.”
“Yes, given your age and gender, we will schedule you for an IVC filter insertion.”
explanation: An IVC filter is only for contraindication to or failure of anticoagulation; it does not improve survival.

orig.stem: A 57-year-old man with a history of hypertension is admitted to the hospital with pulmonary embolism after having sudden onset of chest discomfort. His blood pressure is 132/62 mmHg, heart rate is 85 bpm, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. Echocardiography reveals normal right heart size and function, and cardiac troponin I is undetectable. Lower extremity Doppler ultrasound reveals an extensive deep vein thrombus from the right femoral popliteal vein. The patient is started on low-molecular-weight heparin and concomitant warfarin. On rounds the following day, he asks if insertion of an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter would be appropriate. What is the most appropriate answer?
options: “No, you would not benefit from an IVC filter at this point.”
“No, there are currently no indications for IVC filter placement in the setting of deep vein thrombus or pulmonary embolism.”
“We will need to go back to review your images and see how large your pulmonary embolus clot burden is before deciding whether an IVC filter is appropriate for you or not.”
“Yes, given the presence of residual lower extremity thrombus, we will schedule you for IVC filter insertion.”
“Yes, given your age and gender, we will schedule you for an IVC filter insertion.”
orig.explanation: No, you would not benefit from an IVC filter at this point. IVC filters are reserved for patients with contraindications to anticoagulation or recurrent embolism despite therapy.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with morbid obesity (weight 140 kg), hypertension and diabetes is on day 4 after open gastric bypass surgery. She develops sudden breathlessness, tachycardia, hypoxia and a sense of impending doom. CT pulmonary angiography shows a saddle pulmonary embolism. Her blood pressure is 70/45 mmHg and urine output is poor. After intravenous 0.9% saline and dobutamine, her blood pressure improves only modestly. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Massive PE with shock 4 days after major surgery (thrombolysis contraindicated): surgical or catheter embolectomy.

orig.stem: Mrs. Tupulo is a 45-year-old woman with a history of morbid obesity (weight 140 kg), hypertension, and diabetes who has been in the hospital for 4 days after open surgical gastric bypass. On postoperative day 4, she experiences sudden breathlessness, tachycardia, hypoxia, and an overwhelming sense of impending doom. Urgent chest CT angiography reveals a saddle pulmonary embolism. Her blood pressure is 70/45 mmHg, and urine output is poor. After administration of IV normal saline and dobutamine, her blood pressure modestly improves. What is the next most appropriate step?
orig.explanation: Surgical pulmonary embolectomy In a massive PE with contraindications to thrombolysis post major surgery, surgical embolectomy is the next appropriate intervention. Respiratory Pharmacology

stem: A 30-year-old man with tetraplegia and a long-term indwelling urinary catheter presents with fever, breathlessness and cough. He has had recurrent urinary tract infections for years and takes long-term prophylactic therapy to suppress them. There is mild bilateral wheeze and a diffuse erythematous rash. Chest X-ray shows diffuse alveolar infiltrates. WBC 13.5 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 50%, lymphocytes 30%, eosinophils 20%). What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Sepsis with ARDS secondary to urinary tract infection
A drug reaction to one of his medications
explanation: Fever, wheeze, rash, infiltrates and 20% eosinophils on long-term UTI suppression is a drug (nitrofurantoin) reaction; stop it.

orig.stem: A 30-year-old quadriplegic male presents to the emergency room with fever, dyspnea, and a cough. He has a chronic indwelling Foley catheter. Recurrent urinary tract infections have been a problem for a number of years. He has been on therapy to suppress the urinary tract infections. On examination, mild wheezing is audible over both lungs. A diffuse erythematous rash is noted. The chest x-ray shows a diffuse alveolar infiltrate. The CBC reveals a WBC of 13,500, with 50% segmented cells, 30% lymphocytes, and 20% eosinophils. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Sepsis with ARDS secondary to urinary tract infection
A drug reaction to one of his medications
orig.explanation: A drug reaction to one of his medications Nitrofurantoin toxicity → acute eosinophilic pneumonitis → chronic fibrosis if unrecognized; stop drug, give steroids; eosinophilia and diffuse rash support.

stem: A 68-year-old woman with asthma attends for a routine review. She has occasional palpitations and tremor, but her breathlessness is well controlled. She was admitted with mild heart failure 2 months ago and has occasional postprandial acid reflux. Her medications are lisinopril, digoxin, furosemide, an as-required short-acting inhaled beta-agonist and theophylline, and she takes an over-the-counter tablet (name unknown) for reflux. Her heart rate is 112/min, heart sounds are normal and there is a mild tremor of the outstretched hands. What is the best next step?
options: Chest X-ray to exclude heart failure
Lorazepam 0.5 mg orally three times daily
Stop the beta-agonist and substitute inhaled ipratropium
explanation: Tachycardia and tremor on theophylline (narrow range 10–20 mg/L, raised by cimetidine) suggest toxicity: check the level.

orig.stem: A 68-year-old woman with a prior diagnosis of asthma presents to your clinic for a routine clinic visit. She complains of occasional palpitations and tremor. Her dyspnea is well controlled. Her past medical history is remarkable for hospitalization for mild congestive heart failure 2 months ago; she notes occasional postprandial acid reflux. Her medications include lisinopril, digoxin, furosemide, an intermittent short-acting inhaled beta agonist, and theophylline. She uses an over-the-counter pill (whose name she cannot remember) for the reflux symptoms. On examination her heart rate is 112 beats per minute. S1 and S2 are normal; she has a mild tremor of the outstretched hands. What is the best next step in her management?
options: Chest x-ray to rule out congestive heart failure.
Discontinue beta agonist and substitute inhaled ipratropium.
orig.explanation: Theophylline level. Theophylline toxicity precipitated by CYP inhibition (e.g., cimetidine, macrolides, ciprofloxacin) or CHF/infection/age → tremor, palpitations; stop drug and check level; β-agonists preferred bronchodilators.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with breathlessness, wheeze and rhinorrhoea. On examination there is bilateral expiratory wheeze. Blood results: Hb 120 g/L, platelets 228 × 10^9/L, WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L, eosinophils 2.2 × 10^9/L, Na+ 138 mmol/L, K+ 4.1 mmol/L, urea 5.8 mmol/L, creatinine 62 µmol/L, CRP 8 mg/L. p-ANCA is positive. Which of the following drugs should be avoided?
explanation: Late asthma with eosinophilia and positive p-ANCA suggests EGPA; montelukast may unmask it and is best avoided.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is started on varenicline to help her stop smoking. Which one of the following adverse effects is most likely to occur?
explanation: Nausea is the commonest varenicline adverse effect (~a third); vivid dreams and insomnia also occur.

orig.stem: A 23-year-old female is commenced on varenicline to help her stop smoking. Which one of the following adverse effects is most likely to occur?
orig.explanation: Nasal continuous positive airway pressure OSA with desaturations → CPAP first-line; grade by AHI; advise weight loss; surgery rarely first; oxygen alone inferior to CPAP.

stem: A 47-year-old man is reviewed in the smoking cessation clinic. Which one of the following conditions would contraindicate the prescription of bupropion?
explanation: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in epilepsy.

orig.stem: A 47-year-old man is reviewed in the smoking cessation clinic. Which one of the following conditions would contraindicate the prescription of bupropion?
orig.explanation: Epilepsy Bupropion lowers seizure threshold → contraindicated in epilepsy.

stem: An 18-year-old woman has an acute pulmonary embolism at 9 weeks of pregnancy. There are no obvious risk factors. What is the most appropriate treatment for the remainder of her pregnancy?
explanation: PE in pregnancy: weight-adjusted LMWH for the rest of pregnancy and ≥ 6 weeks postpartum; warfarin and DOACs are avoided.

orig.stem: An 18-year-old woman presents with an acute pulmonary embolism in the ninth week of pregnancy. No obvious factors contributed to the risk of pulmonary embolus. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient throughout her pregnancy?
orig.explanation: C Subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin Postpartum PE/DVT risk → treat with daily LMWH; screen later for thrombophilia given age and no other risks.

stem: A 51-year-old woman with asthma and severe rheumatoid arthritis presents with 3 days of cough, wheeze and fever following a cold. She has taken naproxen for several years without any respiratory symptoms. Chest X-ray is clear, peak flow is 380 L/min (predicted 510 L/min) and CRP is 49 mg/L. She has already received nebulised salbutamol in the clinic with only partial improvement. Which single treatment is most appropriate now?
explanation: Moderate viral-triggered asthma exacerbation with partial SABA response: oral prednisolone 40–50 mg for ≥ 5 days.

orig.stem: A 51-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis comes to the clinic with cough, wheeze and fever. Chest X-ray is clear and peak flow is reduced at 380 (510 expected). Labs show CRP 49 mg/l. Which single treatment is most appropriate now?
orig.explanation: Bronchiectasis Daily copious sputum → bronchiectasis; HRCT shows dilated bronchi with signet-ring; exclude TB, COPD bullae, abscess, cancer.

stem: A 26-year-old man presents with fever, headache and a non-productive cough. He has mildly raised liver enzymes, raised lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and anaemia and he is positive for cold agglutinins. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Mycoplasma (cold agglutinins, haemolysis) lacks a cell wall: use a macrolide (erythromycin) or doxycycline, not beta-lactams.

orig.stem: A 26-year-old man presents with fever, headache and a non-productive cough. He has mildly raised liver enzymes, raised lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and anaemia and he is positive for cold agglutinins. What is the most appropriate treatment?
orig.explanation: Obtain carboxyhemoglobin level. Firefighter with headache/dizziness → suspect CO poisoning; draw carboxyhemoglobin before O₂, then give high-flow or hyperbaric O₂; CXR may be normal.

stem: A 46-year-old woman is admitted with acute breathlessness. Arterial blood gas on air: PaO2 7.4 kPa, PaCO2 3.8 kPa, pH 7.45. Peak expiratory flow is 250 L/min (about 50% of predicted) and the chest X-ray is normal. What is the most appropriate initial management step?
explanation: Acute severe asthma with PaO2 < 8 kPa: oxygen to 94–98% and high-dose nebulised salbutamol first.

orig.stem: 46-A 46-year-old woman is admitted with acute dyspnoea. Investigation shows: Po₂ 7.4 kPa, Pco₂ 3.8 kPa, pH 7.45, peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) 250 L/min (~50% predicted), chest X-ray normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management step?
orig.explanation: E Nebulised salbutamol Severe acute asthma: give high-dose nebulized β₂-agonist first; severity markers include PEFR <50%, RR >25, incomplete sentences.

stem: A 40-year-old man with alcohol dependence develops cough and fever. His chest X-ray (shown) demonstrates a cavity with an air–fluid level in the superior segment of the right lower lobe. What is the most likely causative agent?
explanation: A cavity with air–fluid level in the superior segment of the right lower lobe in an alcoholic is an aspiration abscess from anaerobes.

orig.stem: A 40-year-old alcoholic develops cough and fever. Chest x-ray, shown below, shows an air-fluid level in the superior segment of the right lower lobe. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent?
orig.explanation: Anaerobes RLL abscess with air–fluid level after aspiration risk and poor dentition → anaerobic necrotizing infection (superior segment RLL typical).

stem: A 25-year-old man is referred for evaluation of infertility. He has had a productive cough and recurrent chest infections all his life, together with chronic abdominal pain, diarrhoea and difficulty gaining weight. He also has diabetes mellitus. His chest X-ray suggests bronchiectasis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Bronchiectasis with pancreatic insufficiency, diabetes and male infertility (absent vas) is cystic fibrosis; sweat test and genotyping.

orig.stem: A 25-year-old male presents to the clinic for evaluation of infertility. He has a life-long history of a productive cough and recurrent pulmonary infections. On his review of symptoms he has indicated chronic problems with abdominal pain, diarrhea, and difficulty gaining weight. He also has diabetes mellitus. His chest x-ray suggests bronchiectasis. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Cystic fibrosis Adult CF (≈7%) → bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, DM, male infertility; asthma/COPD less consistent at this age without A1AT deficiency.

stem: A previously well 40-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of fever and shaking chills, including a 15-minute rigor. He also has a non-productive cough, anorexia and right-sided pleuritic chest pain, and has been breathless for 12 hours. Chest X-ray shows right middle lobe consolidation, and the full blood count shows neutrophilia with many band forms. Which of the following statements about this patient's pneumonia is correct?
options: If the sputum Gram stain shows many squamous epithelial cells and culture grows mixed flora, the patient probably has a viral infection
If the Gram stain shows numerous Gram-positive diplococci, numerous white cells and few epithelial cells, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most likely pathogen
Although S. pneumoniae is the most likely cause, the diagnosis would be unlikely if blood cultures are negative
The absence of rigors would rule out pneumococcal pneumonia
A negative urinary pneumococcal antigen test excludes pneumococcal pneumonia
explanation: A good sputum sample with Gram-positive diplococci and many neutrophils strongly supports S. pneumoniae.

orig.stem: A 40-year-old man without a significant past medical history comes to the emergency room with a 3-day history of fever and shaking chills, and a 15-minute episode of rigor. He also reports a nonproductive cough, anorexia, and the development of right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Shortness of breath has been present for the past 12 hours. Chest x-ray reveals a consolidated right middle lobe infiltrate, and CBC shows an elevated neutrophil count with many band forms present. Which of the following statements regarding pneumonia in this patient is correct?
options: If the sputum Gram stain shows multiple squamous epithelial cells and the culture is reported as mixed flora, the patient probably has a viral infection.
If the Gram stain reveals numerous gram-positive diplococci, numerous white blood cells, and few epithelial cells, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most likely pathogen.
Although S pneumoniae is the agent most likely to be the cause of this patient’s pneumonia, this diagnosis would be unlikely if blood cultures prove negative.
The absence of rigors would rule out a diagnosis of pneumococcal pneumonia.
Penicillin is still the drug of choice in pneumococcal pneumonia.

orig.stem: A 60-year-old obese male complains of excessive daytime sleepiness. He has been in good health except for mild hypertension. He drinks alcohol in moderation. The patient’s wife states that he snores at night and awakens frequently. Examination of the oropharynx is normal. Which of the following studies is most appropriate?
options: Study of muscles of respiration during sleep
orig.explanation: Polysomnography Daytime somnolence + snoring → evaluate with polysomnography (distinguish obstructive vs central); oximetry alone can miss OSA.

stem: A 60-year-old man becomes short of breath 2 days after cholecystectomy. He has no fever, chills, sputum or pleuritic chest pain. Temperature 37.2 °C, pulse 75/min, respiratory rate 20/min, BP 120/70 mmHg. There are diminished breath sounds and dullness at the left base, and the trachea is shifted to the left. Chest X-ray shows a retrocardiac opacity obscuring the left hemidiaphragm. What is the most likely underlying problem?
options: Loss of volume of the left lower lobe (postoperative atelectasis)
explanation: Tracheal shift towards a retrocardiac opacity after upper abdominal surgery is left lower lobe collapse (atelectasis); physiotherapy.

orig.stem: A 60-year-old male complains of shortness of breath 2 days after a cholecystectomy. He denies fever, chills, sputum production, and pleuritic chest pain. On physical examination, temperature is 37.2C (99F); pulse is 75; respiratory rate is 20; and blood pressure is 120/70. There are diminished breath sounds and dullness over the left base. Trachea is shifted to the left side. A chest x-ray shows a retrocardiac opacity that silhouettes the left diaphragm. Which of the following is the most likely anatomical problem in this patient?
options: Diminished lung volume in the left lower lobe, postoperative atelectasis
orig.explanation: Diminished lung volume in the left lower lobe, postoperative atelectasis Post-op basilar atelectasis → tracheal shift toward side, elevated density, hemidiaphragm loss; distinguish from pneumonia by lack of consolidation without volume loss.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing chronic lung disease and recurrent episodes of acute bronchitis reports that her sputum, now produced daily and thick, has increased markedly over several months. There are flecks of blood in the sputum and she has lost 3.6 kg (8 lb). She has no fever or chills, and sputum cultures have not grown specific pathogens. Her chest X-ray and CT are shown. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation: Dilated thick-walled bronchi larger than their arteries (signet ring) with daily sputum is bronchiectasis; investigate the cause.

orig.stem: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing chronic lung disease and episodes of acute bronchitis complains of increasing sputum production, which is now on a daily basis. Sputum is thick, and daily sputum production has dramatically increased over several months. There are flecks of blood in the sputum. The patient has lost 8 lb. Fever and chills are absent, and sputum cultures have not revealed specific pathogens. Chest x-ray and CT are shown on page 78. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s symptoms?

stem: A 20-year-old firefighter attends the emergency department with headache and dizziness after helping to put out a garage fire. He is not breathless, and arterial blood gas shows a normal PaO2. What is the best first step in management?
options: Give high-flow 100% oxygen via a non-rebreather mask
Reassure him, as a normal PaO2 excludes significant poisoning
Obtain a CT scan of the head
explanation: CO poisoning after smoke exposure (normal PaO2): give 100% oxygen via non-rebreather immediately; measure COHb by co-oximetry.

orig.stem: A 20-year-old fireman comes to the emergency room complaining of headache and dizziness after helping to put out a garage fire. He does not complain of shortness of breath, and the arterial blood gas shows a normal partial pressure of oxygen. Which of the following is the best first step in the management of this patient?

stem: An 18-year-old man's family have noticed blue discoloration of his nose, ears and fingers over the past few weeks. Which of the following statements is true?
options: Total haemoglobin is important in determining whether a patient will have cyanosis
Central cyanosis with hypoxia suggests methaemoglobinaemia or sulfhaemoglobinaemia
The presence of clubbing in a cyanotic patient confirms an acute cause of the cyanosis
Large amounts of methaemoglobin are required to produce cyanosis
explanation: Cyanosis depends on total Hb (needs ~40–50 g/L deoxy-Hb): easy in polycythaemia, absent in severe anaemia.

orig.stem: An 18-year-old male presents to your office. His family has noted a blue discoloration of his nose, ears, and fingers. This finding has only been noticed for a few weeks. Which of the following is true?
options: Total hemoglobin is important in determining whether or not a patient will have cyanosis.
Central cyanosis with hypoxia suggests methemoglobinemia or sulfhemoglobinemia.
The presence of clubbing in a cyanotic patient confirms an acute cause of the cyanosis.
Large amounts of methemoglobin are required to produce cyanosis.
orig.explanation: Total hemoglobin is important in determining whether or not a patient will have cyanosis. Cyanosis workup: chronic vs new; peripheral vs central; central requires ≥4 g/dL deoxy-Hb—interpret with total Hb; check PaO₂/SaO₂; if normoxemic, test met-/sulf-Hb.

stem: A 77-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted with worsening breathlessness. His GP started amoxicillin 5 days ago. BP 88/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 36/min. Chest X-ray shows left lower lobe consolidation. Arterial blood gas on air: pH 7.37, PaCO2 5.5 kPa, PaO2 9.1 kPa. What is the most suitable antibiotic therapy?
explanation: CURB-65 ≥ 3 pneumonia failing amoxicillin: IV co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin.

orig.stem: A 77-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted to hospital with worsening shortness-of-breath. He started a course of amoxicillin given by his GP 5 days ago. On examination blood pressure is 88/60 mmHg with a respiratory rate of 36 / min. A chest x-ray reveals left lower lobe consolidation. Arterial blood gases on air are as follows: pH 7.37 | pCO2 5.5 kPa | pO2 9.1 kPa. What is the most suitable antibiotic therapy?
orig.explanation: Intravenous co-amoxiclav + clarithromycin CURB-65 = 3 → severe pneumonia → give IV combination antibiotics per BTS.

stem: A 22-year-old with cystic fibrosis is assessed for lung transplantation after multiple chest infections and a poor response to chest physiotherapy, nutritional supplementation and a trial of lumacaftor/ivacaftor. He meets the criteria and is placed on the transplant waiting list. Chronic infection with which organism would be a contraindication to transplantation?
explanation: Chronic Burkholderia cepacia (especially cenocepacia) infection worsens transplant survival and is usually a contraindication.

orig.stem: A 22-year-old with known cystic fibrosis is being worked up for a potential lung transplant have suffered multiple chest infections and receiving a minimal response to treatments including chest physio, supplementation and a trial of lumacaftor/ivacaftor. Following assessment, the patient is deemed to meet the criteria for transplant and is placed on the national transplant list to await a potential donor. In this patient, chronic infection with what organism would be a contraindication to this treatment?
orig.explanation: Burkholderia cepacia CF with chronic Burkholderia cepacia infection → contraindication to lung transplant due to poor outcomes; Aspergillus colonization alone is not a strict contraindication.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with asthma is referred with worsening breathlessness over the past few months. Her asthma was diagnosed in her teens; she uses an inhaled corticosteroid and rarely needs her salbutamol. She has no wheeze or nocturnal symptoms, her inhaler technique is excellent and she is adherent. She has no other medical problems and does not smoke. She is comfortable at rest, SpO2 is 96% on air, BMI is 30 kg/m² and the chest is clear. Chest X-ray shows a normal heart size and clear lung fields. Lung function: FEV1 3.30 L (96.1%), FVC 3.92 L (88.6%), FEV1/FVC 0.84, TLCO 77.4%, KCO 101.9%. What is the likely cause of her breathlessness?
explanation: No obstruction, clear CXR and a slightly low TLCO with normal KCO (small alveolar volume) point to obesity as the cause of breathlessness.

orig.stem: A 64-year-old woman with a background of asthma is referred to the respiratory clinic with worsening shortness of breath over the past few months. She was diagnosed with asthma when she was in her teens and currently takes an inhaled corticosteroid inhaler with an as required salbutamol inhaler which she rarely uses. She does not describe any wheeze or noctur nal symptoms and her inhaler technique in the clinic is excellent. She tells you that she is compliant with her medications. She has no other medical problems and is a non-smoker. On examination, the patient is sitting comfortably at rest and talking in full sentences. Her oxygen saturations are 96% on air and her body mass index is 30 kg/m^2. Chest examination is clear. As part of the work up the patient had a chest x-ray which shows a normal sized heart and clear lung fields. She has also had some lung function tests which show: FEV1 3.30L (96.1%); FVC 3.92L (88.6%); FEV1/FVC 0.84; TLCO 77.4%; KCO 101.9%. What is the likely cause of the patient’s shortness of breath?
orig.explanation: Obesity Normal CXR/spirometry, normal KCO with slightly low TLCO, controlled asthma → exertional dyspnea most likely from obesity after excluding other causes.

stem: A 76-year-old woman with alcohol dependence is in hospital receiving antibiotics for a urinary tract infection. Over the last few days she has developed a cough productive of thick, blood-stained, jelly-like sputum and feels very nauseous. Chest X-ray shows bilateral cavitating upper-lobe opacities. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation: Upper-lobe cavitating pneumonia in an alcohol-dependent inpatient is classically Klebsiella pneumoniae ('redcurrant jelly' sputum).

orig.stem: A 76-year-old woman is currently being treated with antibiotics in hospital for a urinary tract infection. Over the last few days, she has developed a cough with productive sputum and is feeling very nauseous. She is also a known alcoholic with difficult social circumstances. A chest X-ray is carried out which shows bilateral cavitating opacities in the upper lobe. What is the most likely causative organism of this clinical picture?

stem: A 55-year-old man attends his GP with 7 day history of general fever and malaise, and a 2 day history of non-productive cough. His eyes have also been sticky and sore for the last few days. He appears visibly unwell, with a fever of 38.2°C and a respiratory rate of 20 /min. There is also some mild splenomegaly. He has no history of recent foreign travel and denies any tuberculosis exposure or contact with anyone who has been ill. He is, however, the proud new owner of George, a red-crested Australian King Parrot, who he has had for a month. What is the most likely cause of this gentleman’s symptoms?

orig.stem: A 55-year-old man attends his GP with 7 day history of general fever and malaise, and a 2 day history of non-productive cough. His eyes have also been sticky and sore for the last few days. He appears visibly unwell, with a fever of 38.2°C and a respiratory rate of 20 /min. There is also some mild splenomegaly. He has no history of recent foreign travel and denies any tuberculosis exposure or contact with anyone who has been ill. He is, however, the proud new owner of George, a red-crested Australian King Parrot, who he has had for a month. What is the most likely cause of this gentleman’s symptoms?
orig.explanation: Chlamydia psittaci infection Bird exposure + atypical pneumonia → Chlamydia psittaci; severity ranges from mild to multisystem.

stem: A 54-year-old man who lives alone and works at a bird sanctuary is admitted with a 10-day history of worsening breathlessness, cough and fever. He is started on intravenous co-amoxiclav, but after 72 hours there is no clinical improvement. PCR of a respiratory sample is positive for Chlamydia psittaci. What is the most appropriate action?
explanation: C. psittaci is intracellular, so beta-lactams fail: switch to doxycycline 100 mg bd for 10–14 days (macrolide if pregnant).

orig.stem: A 54-year-old man is admitted following presentation with a 10-day history of worsening shortness of breath, cough and fever. He has no past medical history of note. He lives alone and works at a bird sanctuary. He is commenced on treatment with IV co-amoxiclav, however, after 72 hours of treatment, there has been no clinical improvement. Blood culture results taken on admission are obtained and are as follows: Gram stain Negative; Culture positive for Chlamydia psittaci. What action will you take based on these results?
orig.explanation: Switch to doxycycline Psittacosis (C. psittaci) → treat with tetracyclines.

stem: A 29-year-old man on an expedition on Mount Everest develops a headache at about 5000 m, followed by poor coordination and slurred speech. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Ataxia and slurred speech after ascent is high-altitude cerebral oedema: descend immediately and give dexamethasone (and oxygen).

orig.stem: A 29-year-old man is on a hiking expedition up Mount Everest. Upon reaching around 5000m, he starts to feel unwell, complaining to his team members of headache. He appears to have poor coordination and slurred speech. Given the likely occurrence, what is the most appropriate treatment?
orig.explanation: Descent and dexamethasone High-altitude cerebral edema → immediate descent + dexamethasone.

stem: A 34-year-old man climbing Mount Kilimanjaro has had nausea and headache for 2 days. At 4500 m he develops breathlessness and a cough with pink frothy sputum, and there are bibasal crackles. Other than descent, what is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Pink frothy sputum and crackles at altitude is HAPE: descent, oxygen and nifedipine to lower pulmonary artery pressure.

orig.stem: A 34-year-old man is climbing Mount Kilimanjaro. For the past two days he has complained of nausea and a headache. The climbing team is now at an altitude of 4,500m when he develops shortness of breath and a pink frothy cough. Examination reveals bibasal crackles. What is the most appropriate treatment, other than descent?

stem: A 28-year-old man develops nausea and a severe headache whilst trekking in Nepal. Within the next hour he becomes ataxic and confused. A diagnosis of high altitude cerebral oedema is suspected. Other than descent and oxygen, what is the most important treatment?

orig.stem: A 28-year-old man develops nausea and a severe headache whilst trekking in Nepal. Within the next hour he becomes ataxic and confused. A diagnosis of high altitude cerebral oedema is suspected. Other than descent and oxygen, what is the most important treatment?
orig.explanation: Dexamethasone Acetazolamide is mainly for prevention of altitude illness, not acute treatment.

stem: A 48-year-old male patient with a medical history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department with painful swelling in the left submandibular and submental areas. There was tenderness on palpation over the swelling with discharging pus. A facial and oral incision and drainage (R&D) was performed under general anaesthesia. Post-operatively 72-hours later the patient developed a new oxygen requirement with oxygen saturations dropping to 89%. He had a regular heart rate of 75 beats per minute and remained apyrexial. An urgent portable chest radiograph was requested. What is the most likely diagnosis?

orig.stem: A 48-year-old male patient with a medical history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department with painful swelling in the left submandibular and submental areas. There was tenderness on palpation over the swelling with discharging pus. A facial and oral incision and drainage (R&D) was performed under general anaesthesia. Post-operatively 72-hours later the patient developed a new oxygen requirement with oxygen saturations dropping to 89%. He had a regular heart rate of 75 beats per minute and remained apyrexial. An urgent portable chest radiograph was requested. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: Basal atelectasis Dyspnea and hypoxemia 72 h post-op without fever → suspect basal atelec tasis; CXR shows volume loss with mediastinal shift toward lesion; pneumonia or pneumothorax less likely here.

stem: A 59-year-old man is reviewed in clinic 3 months after coronary artery bypass grafting. He is breathless on exertion and particularly when lying flat in bed. The operation went well and he has no angina. His medications are ramipril 10 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg. He looks well; BP 123/72 mmHg, pulse 70/min and regular, BMI 31 kg/m², and the chest is clear. Hb 131 g/L, WCC 5.6 × 10^9/L, platelets 178 × 10^9/L, Na+ 138 mmol/L, K+ 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 110 µmol/L. Vital capacity is 88% of predicted sitting and falls to 55% of predicted lying down. What is the most likely cause of his breathlessness?
explanation: A fall in VC > 20–25% from upright to supine indicates diaphragm weakness — here phrenic palsy after cardiac surgery.

orig.stem: A 59-year-old man with a recent CABG some 3 months earlier presents to the clinic for review. His main complaint is shortness of breath on exercise, and particularly on lying flat in bed. His operation is thought to have gone well and he has no residual angina. Medication includes ramipril 10 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg. On examination he looks well, his BP is 123/72 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular; his BMI is 31. His chest is clear on auscultation. Investigations: Haemoglobin 131 g/l, WCC 5.6 × 10^9/l, Platelets 178 × 10^9/l, Sodium 138 mmol/l, Potassium 4.8 mmol/l, Creatinine 110 μmol/l, Vital capacity 88% of predicted, falls to 55% of predicted on lying down. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his shortness of breath?
orig.explanation: A Diaphragmatic palsy Marked fall in VC supine → diaphragmatic palsy post-surgery.

stem: An anxious 22-year-old woman has had mild exertional breathlessness and intermittent double vision over the last few weeks. Chest X-ray, lung function tests and ECG are all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Fluctuating diplopia with breathlessness in a young woman suggests myasthenia gravis; antibodies, EMG and CT for thymoma.

orig.stem: 24-An anxious 22-year-old woman presented with mild shortness of breath on exertion and intermittent diplopia over the last few weeks. Chest X-ray, lung function tests and electrocardiography were all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
orig.explanation: B Myasthenia gravis Fluctuating fatigable weakness with ocular signs → myasthenia gravis; baseline cardiopulmonary tests may be normal.

stem: A 37-year-old man with increasing breathlessness is found to have unilateral emphysema. Which of the following is most likely to have predisposed him to this?
explanation: Unilateral hyperlucent emphysematous lung is Swyer–James (MacLeod) syndrome after childhood obliterative bronchiolitis.

orig.stem: 30-A 37-year-old man presents with increasing breathlessness and is diagnosed with unilateral emphysema after investigation. Which of the following conditions is most likely to predispose to the development of emphysema?
orig.explanation: C Childhood bronchiolitis MacLeod syndrome = unilateral hyperlucent lung from childhood bronchiolitis.

stem: In which of the following respiratory diseases is finger clubbing NOT a feature?
explanation: Clubbing is not a feature of chronic bronchitis/COPD; it occurs in cancer, fibrosis, asbestosis and chronic suppurative lung disease.

orig.stem: 43-In which of the following respiratory diseases is clubbing not a feature?
orig.explanation: C Chronic bronchitis Clubbing with malignancy, fibrosing alveolitis, asbestosis; not with chronic bronchitis.

stem: Which one of the following features is seen least frequently in patients with obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome?
explanation: OSA is 2–3 times commoner in men, so female gender is the least frequent feature listed.

orig.stem: 50-Which one of the following features is encountered least frequently in patients with sleep apnoea syndrome?
orig.explanation: B Female gender Typical phenotype: male, middle-aged, obese.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who does not smoke is found to have normal lung volumes but a reduced transfer factor for carbon monoxide (TLCO) of 45% of predicted. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Isolated low TLCO with normal volumes suggests pulmonary vascular disease, e.g. arteriovenous malformation (HHT); bubble echo or CTPA.

orig.stem: 51-A 34-year-old woman, who is a non-smoker, is found to have normal lung volumes but a reduced Tico at 45% of predicted. The most likely cause for this picture is which one of the following?
orig.explanation: E Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation Normal volumes with isolated low TLCO → pulmonary vascular disease; TLCO rises in alveolar hemorrhage/polycythemia; emphysema shows hyperinflation.

items.stem: A 60-year-old smoker with diabetes has bilateral pitting leg oedema, a raised JVP, a pulsatile liver and a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge.
items.explanation: Raised JVP with giant v waves, pulsatile liver and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge (louder on inspiration) is tricuspid regurgitation.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman with well-controlled hypertension on regular treatment and no diabetes has bilateral pitting leg oedema; the JVP is normal and all investigations are normal.
items.explanation: Bilateral ankle oedema with normal JVP and investigations in a treated hypertensive is amlodipine oedema (arteriolar dilatation); it responds poorly to diuretics.

items.stem: A 65-year-old heavy smoker with a long history of cough, sputum and severe breathlessness has a raised JVP, bilateral pitting oedema and a flapping tremor; there is a prolonged expiratory phase with coarse crackles and scattered wheeze.
items.explanation: COPD with hypercapnia (flap), raised JVP and oedema is cor pulmonale: right heart failure from hypoxic pulmonary hypertension.

items.stem: A middle-aged woman has fatigue, abdominal distension and leg swelling. Pulse 112/min, regular, small volume with pulsus paradoxus; bilateral pitting oedema, raised JVP and an early third heart sound; hepatomegaly and ascites.
items.explanation: Raised JVP, pericardial knock (early S3), hepatomegaly and ascites out of proportion to oedema with a small pulse is constrictive pericarditis.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with rheumatic heart disease for 20 years has breathlessness, fatigue, oedema and ascites; there is a soft S1, a loud S3 and an apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla.
items.explanation: Rheumatic disease with an apical pansystolic murmur to the axilla, soft S1 and loud S3 is severe MR, with secondary right heart failure.

A 25-year-old man has sudden sharp right-sided chest pain worse on deep breathing and coughing, a short painful dry cough, fever, rigors, vomiting and malaise; there is dullness, bronchial breathing and fine crackles over the right lower zone.
items.explanation: Fever, rigors and pleuritic pain with dullness, bronchial breathing and crackles over one zone is lobar pneumonia; assess with CURB-65 and CXR.

items.stem: A 28-year-old tall smoker has sudden sharp right-sided chest pain and breathlessness; chest expansion is reduced on the right with a resonant percussion note and diminished breath sounds.
items.explanation: Sudden pleuritic pain in a tall young smoker with reduced expansion, hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax.

items.stem: A 54-year-old woman with diabetes has high fever, rigors, sweating, sharp left-sided chest pain, breathlessness and purulent sputum despite 10 days of amoxicillin; there is finger clubbing, reduced expansion, dullness and markedly diminished breath sounds over the left lower and middle zones.
items.explanation: Swinging fever despite antibiotics with dullness and absent breath sounds at the base is empyema; aspirate (pH < 7.2, pus) and insert a chest drain.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman has severe stabbing central chest pain radiating to the left jaw and shoulder, with fever and breathlessness; a friction rub is heard over the precordium.
items.explanation: Sharp central pain to the shoulder, fever and a friction rub is acute pericarditis (saddle ST elevation, PR depression); NSAID plus colchicine.

items.stem: An 18-year-old man has breathlessness, exertional chest pain and palpitations; there is a double apical impulse and an ejection systolic murmur.
items.explanation: Exertional pain in a young man with a double apical impulse and ejection systolic murmur is HOCM; louder with Valsalva, confirm by echo.

A 20-year-old student has headaches, weakness and leg cramps. BP is 165/95 mmHg in the arm and 120/75 mmHg in the leg; there is a systolic murmur and an ejection click in the aortic area.
items.explanation: Arm hypertension with lower leg pressures and an ejection click (bicuspid valve) in a young adult is coarctation; confirm by CT/MR angiography.

items.stem: A 26-year-old man has chest pain and breathlessness on exercise; there is a jerky pulse, a double apical impulse and a mid-systolic murmur at the base.
items.explanation: Exertional symptoms with a jerky pulse, double apical impulse and ejection murmur are HOCM; aortic stenosis gives a slow-rising pulse.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with lung cancer becomes breathless; pulse 112/min, regular and small-volume with pulsus paradoxus, BP 85/50 mmHg, a grossly raised JVP and soft heart sounds.
items.explanation: Hypotension, pulsus paradoxus, grossly raised JVP and soft heart sounds in lung cancer is malignant tamponade: urgent pericardiocentesis.

items.stem: An 18-year-old woman who had a flu-like illness a week ago develops acute heart failure; BP 70/40 mmHg, non-specific ECG changes and a markedly raised troponin.
items.explanation: Cardiogenic shock with a markedly raised troponin a week after a viral illness is fulminant myocarditis; support, and recovery is often good.

items.stem: A patient has fatigue, a rapid low-volume pulse with pulsus paradoxus, a raised JVP, a loud early third heart sound, hepatomegaly, ascites and peripheral oedema.
items.explanation: Raised JVP, pericardial knock, hepatomegaly, ascites and oedema is chronic constrictive pericarditis; tamponade is acute with soft heart sounds.

A 35-year-old woman has right leg swelling with mild pain. She has taken the oral contraceptive pill for 8 months and recently travelled a long distance.
items.explanation: Unilateral painful leg swelling on the pill after long-haul travel is DVT: Wells score, D-dimer/ultrasound, then a DOAC.

items.stem: A 65-year-old heavy smoker with a long history of cough, sputum and severe breathlessness has a raised JVP, bilateral pitting oedema and a flapping tremor; there is a prolonged expiratory phase with coarse crackles and scattered wheeze.
items.explanation: Long-standing COPD with a flap, raised JVP and oedema is cor pulmonale; LTOT improves survival in eligible patients.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes and ischaemic heart disease has a painful, swollen, red and tender left leg with pitting oedema; the white cell count is raised and Doppler ultrasound is normal.
items.explanation: Hot, red, tender swollen leg with raised WCC and normal Doppler is cellulitis; treat with flucloxacillin (doxycycline/clarithromycin if allergic).

items.stem: A middle-aged woman has fatigue, abdominal distension and leg swelling; pulse 112/min, regular and small-volume with pulsus paradoxus, a raised JVP, an early third heart sound, hepatomegaly and ascites.
items.explanation: Ascites and hepatomegaly out of proportion to oedema, raised JVP and pericardial knock indicate constrictive pericarditis; pericardiectomy is definitive.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease on irregular treatment has progressive breathlessness for 6 months with a dry cough; there is a raised JVP, leg oedema and bibasal fine inspiratory crackles.
items.explanation: Progressive breathlessness with raised JVP, oedema and bibasal crackles in poorly treated IHD is congestive heart failure; NT-proBNP and echo.

A 30-year-old woman with hypertension is found to have hypokalaemia and a mild metabolic alkalosis.
items.explanation: Hypertension with hypokalaemia and alkalosis in a young woman suggests Conn's syndrome; screen with the aldosterone:renin ratio.

items.stem: An anxious 26-year-old woman has episodes of chest pain and palpitations precipitated by stress and smoking. Her 24-hour urine shows raised catecholamines.
items.explanation: Paroxysmal palpitations and chest pain with raised urinary catecholamines is phaeochromocytoma; alpha-block before any beta-blocker.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has weight gain, muscle weakness and hirsutism; she is hypertensive with pedal oedema.
items.explanation: Weight gain, proximal weakness, hirsutism, oedema and hypertension suggest Cushing's syndrome; screen with overnight dexamethasone suppression.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with a severe headache; he has papilloedema and fundal haemorrhages, and BP 220/145 mmHg.
items.explanation: BP 220/145 with papilloedema and retinal haemorrhages is malignant hypertension; lower by ≤ 25% in the first hours with IV labetalol or nitroprusside.

items.stem: A 75-year-old heavy smoker with widespread peripheral vascular disease has hypertension.
items.explanation: New hypertension in an elderly smoker with widespread atherosclerosis suggests atheromatous renal artery stenosis; confirm with duplex or CT/MR angiography.

An anxious 26-year-old woman has episodes of chest pain and palpitations precipitated by stress and smoking. Her 24-hour urine shows raised catecholamines.
A 45-year-old woman has weight gain, muscle weakness and hirsutism; she is hypertensive with pedal oedema.
A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with a severe headache; he has papilloedema and fundal haemorrhages, and BP 220/145 mmHg.
A 75-year-old heavy smoker with widespread peripheral vascular disease has hypertension.
A 63-year-old man with high blood pressure presents with sudden-onset tearing chest pain radiating to the back.
items.explanation: Sudden tearing pain to the back in a hypertensive man is aortic dissection; confirm with CT angiography and never thrombolyse.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman develops sudden breathlessness at rest after hip replacement surgery; she is tachycardic and the ECG shows right axis deviation.
items.explanation: Sudden breathlessness and tachycardia after hip replacement with right axis deviation (RV strain) is PE; CTPA and anticoagulate.

items.stem: A 60-year-old businessman has central crushing chest pain radiating to both arms after running for a bus; it is relieved by rest and his ECG 1 hour later is normal.
items.explanation: Exertional crushing pain relieved by rest with a normal ECG afterwards is stable angina; CT coronary angiography is the first test.

items.stem: A 21-year-old high-jumper has acute breathlessness and right-sided pleuritic chest pain; there is increased resonance and reduced expansion on the right.
items.explanation: Pleuritic pain and breathlessness in a tall young athlete with hyper-resonance on one side is spontaneous pneumothorax.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman has localised left-sided chest pain that is worse on coughing and very tender to light pressure; it is relieved by aspirin and the ECG is normal.
items.explanation: Localised chest-wall pain reproduced by light pressure and relieved by NSAIDs, with a normal ECG, is costochondritis.

options: Digoxin plus warfarin for a month

items.stem: A 65-year-old man with heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction has had atrial fibrillation for more than 48 hours, with a ventricular rate of 120/min; he is haemodynamically stable. Choose his treatment before elective DC cardioversion.
items.explanation: Before elective cardioversion of AF > 48 h: ≥ 3 weeks of anticoagulation (DOAC now preferred) with rate control (digoxin in HFrEF), continued ≥ 4 weeks after.

items.stem: Initial therapy for a 60-year-old woman who is severely compromised by acute atrial fibrillation.
items.explanation: AF with haemodynamic compromise (shock, ischaemia, pulmonary oedema) needs immediate synchronised DC cardioversion. Start heparin as soon as possible without delaying the shock.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with an acute myocardial infarction has recurrent runs of ventricular tachycardia despite a beta-blocker and correction of potassium and magnesium; he needs prophylaxis against recurrence.
items.explanation: Recurrent VT in acute MI despite beta-blocker and electrolyte correction: IV amiodarone; lidocaine is a second-line IV alternative.

items.stem: A drug to aid diagnosis in a 50-year-old man with an unidentified regular narrow-complex tachycardia.
items.explanation: IV adenosine transiently blocks the AV node: it terminates AVNRT/AVRT and unmasks flutter, so it is diagnostic and therapeutic. Avoid in severe asthma.

items.stem: Prophylaxis of ventricular tachycardia with a varying QRS axis in a patient with a prolonged QT interval.
items.explanation: Torsades de pointes: IV magnesium 2 g, correct K⁺, stop QT drugs, and overdrive pacing or isoprenaline to prevent recurrence. Amiodarone is contraindicated.

items.explanation: A tapping apex with a low-pitched apical mid-diastolic rumble is mitral stenosis, almost always rheumatic.

items.stem: A patient with head nodding, a large-volume pulse, BP 130/50 mmHg and a diastolic murmur.
items.explanation: Head nodding (de Musset's sign), a large-volume collapsing pulse and a wide pulse pressure (130/50 mmHg) with an early diastolic murmur are chronic aortic regurgitation.

items.stem: A young patient with a pansystolic murmur at the left parasternal area.
items.explanation: A harsh pansystolic murmur at the left parasternal area (lower left sternal edge) in a young patient is a ventricular septal defect. Small defects are loudest and often close spontaneously.

items.stem: A young patient with fixed splitting of the second heart sound and a systolic murmur in the pulmonary area.
items.explanation: Fixed wide S2 splitting with a pulmonary flow murmur is ASD; the ECG shows RBBB.

items.stem: A patient with right upper abdominal discomfort, a distended JVP, a loud second heart sound and a pansystolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation.
items.explanation: Loud P2 with raised JVP, hepatic congestion and functional TR indicates pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure.

items.stem: A patient with a slow-rising, small-volume pulse, a heaving apex and an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the neck.
items.explanation: Slow-rising small-volume pulse, heaving apex and ejection murmur to the carotids is aortic stenosis; symptoms mean valve replacement.

items.stem: A patient with a mid-systolic murmur best heard over the back between the scapulae and a left-arm blood pressure of 170/110 mmHg.
items.explanation: Arm hypertension with a systolic murmur between the scapulae is coarctation; check radiofemoral delay and rib notching.

A barber has aching pain in both legs at the end of a day of standing, and has started to develop skin pigmentation around the ankles.
items.explanation: Aching legs after standing with haemosiderin pigmentation at the ankles is chronic venous insufficiency; compression once ABPI is normal.

items.stem: A 32-year-old teacher has severe left leg pain of 1 hour and an irregular pulse.
items.explanation: Sudden severe limb pain with an irregular pulse (AF) is embolic acute limb ischaemia: IV heparin and urgent embolectomy.

items.stem: A 40-year-old farmer with known rheumatic heart disease has breathlessness and an apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla.
items.explanation: An apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla with breathlessness in rheumatic heart disease is mitral regurgitation.

items.stem: A 2-year-old child has episodes of cyanosis when crying, squats after play, has SpO2 89% and a harsh ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge.
items.explanation: Cyanotic spells, squatting and an ejection systolic murmur in a toddler is tetralogy of Fallot.

items.stem: A 20-year-old has fixed splitting of the second heart sound and a systolic murmur.
items.explanation: Fixed S2 splitting with a pulmonary flow murmur in a young adult is ASD; echo confirms and significant defects are closed by device.
